Abelisauridae.description: Abelisauridae is a family of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaurs that were among the dominant large predators of the southern supercontinent Gondwana during the Cretaceous. Like most theropods they were carnivorous bipeds, but they are distinguished by short, tall skulls whose bones are heavily ornamented with grooves, pits, and protrusions, often bearing horns or brow ridges above the eyes, and by dramatically reduced, vestigial forelimbs set on stocky hind limbs. Most known members ranged from about 5 to 9 meters in length. Their fossils are found across Africa, South America, and western Europe, as well as the Indian subcontinent and Madagascar. A grade of more basal forms such as Rugops and Eoabelisaurus gives way to two derived branches: the Indo-Madagascan and European Majungasaurinae and the mostly South American Brachyrostra, the latter including well-known genera such as Carnotaurus and Aucasaurus.
Abelisauridae.authors: Bonaparte, J. F.; Novas, F. E.
diagnostic_features: Short, deep skull with heavy sculpturing of the frontal, nasal, and lacrimal bones
Extremely reduced forelimbs with short, stout metacarpals and vestigial manual digits
Thickened, co-ossified skull roof
Short, robust cervical vertebrae with prominent epipophyses

references.authors: Bonaparte, J. F.; Novas, F. E.
references.title: Abelisaurus comahuensis, n.g., n.sp., Carnosauria del Crétacico Tardio de Patagonia [Abelisaurus comahuensis, n.g., n.sp., Carnosauria from the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia]
references.notes: Named Abelisaurus and the family Abelisauridae. In Spanish.

Abelisauroidea.description: Abelisauroidea is a diverse superfamily of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaurs, divided into two families: the abelisaurids and the noasaurids. Though typically regarded as a Cretaceous group, its origins trace back to at least the Middle Jurassic, when abelisauroids had a nearly global distribution. By the Cretaceous they had disappeared from Asia and North America, possibly outcompeted by tyrannosauroids, and flourished instead across the southern continents of Gondwana, where the advanced abelisaurids persisted as dominant terrestrial predators until the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction 66 million years ago. The group spanned a wide range of forms, from small, nimble, lightly built noasaurids, some barely 5 feet (1.5 meters) long, to large, deep-skulled abelisaurids. Noasaurids retained comparatively long, usable arms, whereas the forelimbs of abelisaurids were reduced to tiny, diminished stubs.
diagnostic_features: Elongate cervical vertebrae with epipophyses and low neural spines
Anterior cervical ribs directed strongly anteroventrally
Femur with a proximally placed, medially oriented head and reduced trochanteric shelf

references.title: The Gondwanian theropod families Abelisauridae and Noasauridae
references.notes: United Abelisauridae and Noasauridae as closely related Gondwanan theropod families, the basis for the superfamily Abelisauroidea.

Aeolosaurini.description: Aeolosaurini is a clade of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs from the Cretaceous Period, best known from Argentina and Brazil. Its members include Aeolosaurus, Gondwanatitan, Maxakalisaurus, Panamericansaurus, and Rinconsaurus, and the group spans a wide range of body sizes, from relatively small forms such as Shingopana and Overosaurus to large animals like Aeolosaurus maximus. The clade is distinguished by a suite of features in the tail vertebrae, including angled centra, elongated prezygapophyses, and neural arches shifted forward relative to the centra. In life these traits may have given the tail a strong downward curve, which could have increased the pull of the caudofemoralis longus muscle used to draw back the hindlimb.
Aeolosaurini.authors: Franco-Rosas, A. C.; Salgado, L.; Rosas, C. F.; Carvalho, I. S.

Caudal prezygapophyses elongate, projecting beyond the anterior margin of the centrum
Strongly procoelous caudal centra with prominent distal condyles

Afrovenatorinae.description: Afrovenatorinae is one of the two subfamilies of Megalosauridae, a family of carnivorous theropod dinosaurs within the broader group Megalosauroidea. It is defined to include all megalosaurids more closely related to Afrovenator than to Megalosaurus, and it stands as the sister group to Megalosaurinae. Its members are the generally more gracile, largely Middle Jurassic megalosaurids and include such genera as Dubreuillosaurus, Magnosaurus, Leshansaurus and Piveteausaurus. The subfamily is set apart from other megalosaurids by details of the skull and pelvis.

Puboischiadic plate broadly open along the midline

Albertosaurinae.description: Albertosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of tyrannosaurid dinosaurs, the sister group to the Tyrannosaurinae. It comprises the two described genera Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus, both of which lived in the Late Cretaceous of western North America, in what is now the United States and Canada, though other undescribed species may belong to the group. Albertosaurines are large but relatively lightly built tyrannosaurids. Compared with the tyrannosaurines, they are more slender and gracile, with shorter, flatter skulls, shorter ilia, and proportionally longer, more running-adapted lower legs.
Albertosaurinae.authors: Currie, P. J.; Hurum, J. H.; Sabath, K.

Allosauria.description: Allosauria is a clade of allosauroid theropods comprising Allosauridae and Carcharodontosauria, recovered as the sister group of the metriacanthosaurids within Allosauroidea. The group unites the well-known Late Jurassic Allosaurus with the giant carcharodontosaurians that were among the largest terrestrial predators of the Cretaceous.
diagnostic_features: Maxilla with a prominent horizontal ridge (lingual bar) between the palatal process and the antorbital fenestra
Paradental plates of the dentary fused into a continuous medial lamina, with the tooth replacement groove absent
Retroarticular process wider mediolaterally than the posterior width of the dentary
Pneumatic pleurocoelous fossae on the sacral vertebral centra
Iliac pubic peduncle elongate, more than twice as long as wide
Ischial symphysis expanded into an apron

Allosauridae.description: Allosauridae is a family of medium to large, bipedal, carnivorous allosauroid theropod dinosaurs from the Late Jurassic, best known from Allosaurus. Their overall anatomy is fairly typical of other theropods, which has long made the family's precise membership difficult to define; Saurophaganax has been attributed to the group, though some later work reinterprets its remains as belonging to Allosaurus and a diplodocid sauropod. Allosaurid skulls carry prominent horns or hornlets on the lacrimal bones above the eyes that would have been sheathed in keratin, and show marked cranial kinesis, with flexible joints that cushioned the skull and let the animals gape their jaws very wide. Like most theropods they had short forelimbs relative to their hindlimbs, with three-fingered hands bearing long, strongly curved claws suited to raking and grasping prey. The pubis is greatly elongated and ends in a broad "foot" that likely helped support the body's weight when the animal rested in a crouch.
diagnostic_features: Prominent lacrimal horns or hornlets above the eyes
Strongly downturned paroccipital processes terminating well ventral to the basal tubera
Shortened quadrate relative to other allosauroids
Expanded distal end of the scapula

Allosauroidea.description: Allosauroidea is a superfamily of carnosaurian theropod dinosaurs comprising the metriacanthosaurids (sinraptorids), the allosaurids, and the carcharodontosaurians. Its members were among the first giant predators in theropod history, some weighing more than two tons, and together with the megalosauroids they served as apex predators from the Middle Jurassic to the early Late Cretaceous. Fossils have been recovered across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, though in North America and Asia allosauroids were eventually replaced by the tyrannosauroids during the Late Cretaceous. These medium- to gigantic-sized bipedal hunters are distinguished by large, narrow skulls roughly two and a half to three times longer than tall, frequently ornamented with crests or rugosities, and by long, laterally compressed, serrated teeth well suited to slicing flesh from prey.
diagnostic_features: Antorbital sinus invades the interior of the lacrimal, nasal, and jugal
Quadrate–quadratojugal fenestra present, with an associated pneumatic sinus
Pneumatic basisphenoid recess opening the braincase posteriorly between non-pedunculate basal tubera
Downturned paroccipital processes
Triangular, elongate scapular blade sharply set off from the acromial process and glenoid lip
Obturator fenestra of the ischium opening into a notch to form a distinct obturator process

Alvarezsauridae.description: Alvarezsauridae is a family of small, long-legged maniraptoran theropods known from the Late Cretaceous of South America, North America, and Asia, spanning roughly 86 to 66 million years ago. Though once interpreted as some of the earliest flightless birds, they are now regarded as an early-diverging branch of the theropod lineage. The family includes basal South American forms, the larger-bodied Patagonykinae, and the diverse, miniaturized Asian species of the subfamily Parvicursorinae (also called Mononykinae). Alvarezsaurids are highly specialized animals, with tiny but powerful forelimbs ending in compact hands dominated by a single greatly enlarged claw, and long, tube-shaped snouts filled with numerous tiny teeth. These traits have led most researchers to interpret them as insect-eaters that used their stout arms to dig into ant and termite nests, while their long legs suggest they were fast, agile runners.
diagnostic_features: Presacral vertebrae with ball-and-socket (opisthocoelous) intercentral joints
Humerus with a figure-of-eight cross-section
Hypertrophied olecranon process of the ulna
Symmetrical iliac blade
Fully procoelous caudal vertebrae

references.title: Los vertebrados fósiles de la Formación Rio Colorado, de la Ciudad de Neuquén y Cercanías, Cretácico Superior, Argentina [The vertebrate fossils of the Rio Colorado Formation, from the city of Neuquén and surrounding areas, Upper Cretaceous, Argentina]

Alvarezsauroidea.description: Alvarezsauroidea is a group of small maniraptoran theropod dinosaurs that split into two grades separated chiefly by their hand anatomy. The basal, non-alvarezsaurid alvarezsauroids include long-armed forms such as Haplocheirus from the Late Jurassic of Asia, which retained grasping hands, recurved serrated teeth, and a carnivorous diet interpreted as the ancestral condition for the clade. The derived family Alvarezsauridae, ranging through the Cretaceous, shows a greatly enlarged single functional finger flanked by two tiny vestigial digits, along with a long snout and simplified, closely spaced teeth; these features have been read as adaptations for digging and for feeding on insects such as ants and termites. Most derived members were small, roughly 0.5 to 2 meters in body length, and the clade appears to have undergone a rare trend toward miniaturization. Fossils are best known from Asia but also occur in North and South America and possibly Europe, and current evidence points to an Asian origin followed by repeated dispersal events.

Hypertrophied internal tuberosity of the humerus, separated from the humeral head by a distinct notch and lying level with or projecting above the head

Greatly enlarged ungual on manual digit I, much larger than the unguals of the other digits

Anchiornithidae.description: Anchiornithidae is a family of small, lightly built, feathered paravian theropod dinosaurs known mostly from the Late Jurassic of China, with the majority of fossils coming from the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning. Members include Anchiornis, Eosinopteryx, Serikornis, Caihong, Aurornis, Pedopenna, and Fujianvenator, alongside a few genera found beyond their Chinese heartland, such as Ostromia from Germany and the Early Cretaceous Yixianosaurus. These were long-legged, long-armed carnivores similar in build to Archaeopteryx and early troodontids, and most carried extensive pennaceous feathers down the legs as well as the arms, earning them the nickname "four-winged dinosaurs." Their arm feathers were slender, symmetrical, and unspecialized, likely useless for true flight. The group's exact place among paravians is unsettled, having been recovered at various times as the earliest-branching birds, as basal members of Troodontidae, or as part of Archaeopterygidae, and membership at the edges of the clade remains unstable.

Ankylopollexia.description: Ankylopollexia is a clade of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaurs that ranged from the Late Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous. Its members are united by a distinctive conical thumb spike, and the group encompasses everything from small, roughly five-meter bipedal forms such as Camptosaurus through the iguanodonts to the hadrosaurs, or duck-billed dinosaurs. Universally herbivorous, ankylopollexians varied enormously in size, with the largest hadrosaurs such as Shantungosaurus reaching around 15 meters in length and weighing up to 16 tonnes. First appearing about 156 million years ago, the clade became one of the most successful and widespread groups of the Cretaceous, spreading across the world before dying out at the close of the Maastrichtian.

Ankylosauria.description: Ankylosauria is a clade of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs that includes the great majority of the armored dinosaurs, whose bodies were sheathed in bony osteoderms much like a turtle's shell. Its members were bulky, low-slung quadrupeds carried on short, powerful limbs. The group first appeared in North Africa during the Middle Jurassic and persisted until the end of the Late Cretaceous. It is traditionally split into two main Northern Hemisphere families, the Nodosauridae and the Ankylosauridae, while the more basal Parankylosauria arose in southern Gondwana during the Cretaceous. Together with the plated and spiked stegosaurs, ankylosaurs make up the Thyreophora, the armored branch of ornithischians distinct from the ornithopods and marginocephalians.

Laterally projecting cervical or shoulder spines in many taxa
Secondary palate present

Ankylosauridae.description: Ankylosauridae is a family of armored dinosaurs within Ankylosauria, forming the sister group to the nodosaurids. Its members were mainly herbivorous, obligate quadrupeds with leaf-shaped teeth and robust, scute-covered bodies, distinguished by a short, deeply domed snout bearing wedge-shaped cranial osteoderms and, in more derived forms, a heavy bony tail club built from interlocking tail vertebrae and enlarged, bulbous armor. The family is known exclusively from the Northern Hemisphere, with fossils recovered across North America, Europe, and Asia. It ranges from the Early Cretaceous, roughly 122 million years ago, to the end-Cretaceous extinction 66 million years ago. Ankylosaurids are typically divided into the basal Shamosaurinae, a small Asian group, and the more diverse and derived Ankylosaurinae.

Ankylosaurinae.description: Ankylosaurinae is a subfamily of armored ankylosaurid dinosaurs that ranged from the Early Cretaceous, roughly 105 million years ago, to the very end of the Late Cretaceous around 66 million years ago. It encompasses the derived, tail-clubbed ankylosaurids and includes such genera as Ankylosaurus, Pinacosaurus, Euoplocephalus, and Saichania, most of them known from Asia and North America. The group is delimited as the largest clade containing Ankylosaurus but excluding Shamosaurus. Members are distinguished by details of the back of the skull, including a nuchal shelf that hides the occiput when the skull is viewed from above and a quadrate condyle partly concealed by a bony boss on the quadratojugal.

Anteriorly facing external nares in derived members

Apatosaurinae.description: Apatosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of diplodocid sauropods, the other being Diplodocinae, together forming the family Diplodocidae. It contains the large, robustly built genera Apatosaurus and Brontosaurus, with the dubious Amphicoelias and a species sometimes placed in Atlantosaurus proposed as further possible members. All of its members lived during the Late Jurassic and are known from the Morrison Formation of the western United States, roughly 157 to 147 million years ago. The clade is stem-based, encompassing all diplodocids closer to Apatosaurus than to Diplodocus. Compared with the more gracile diplodocines, apatosaurines were stockier animals with proportionally shorter necks built from short, boxy, heavily constructed cervical vertebrae, and their forelimbs and shoulder girdles were unusually massive. The exceptional robustness of the neck has prompted the suggestion that these sauropods used their necks in combat between individuals.
diagnostic_features: Cervical ribs massive and ventrally displaced well below the centrum
Cervical vertebrae short and stout relative to those of diplodocines
Robustly constructed forelimb and pectoral girdle

Arctometatarsalia.description: Arctometatarsalia is a largely abandoned clade of theropod dinosaurs originally proposed to unite all forms possessing an arctometatarsalian foot — a condition in which the upper bones of the foot are pinched tightly together, interpreted as an adaptation for fast running. As first conceived in the early 1990s, it grouped the troodontids, tyrannosauroids, and ornithomimosaurs under the assumption that this distinctive foot structure marked a single natural lineage. Later phylogenetic studies undermined that idea, showing that tyrannosaurids and troodontids were more closely related to other coelurosaurs than to the ostrich-like ornithomimosaurs. Because its strictest definition was anchored on Ornithomimus, the name became redundant with Ornithomimosauria and fell out of general use.

references.title: The phylogenetic position of the Tyrannosauridae: implications for theropod systematics
references.notes: Coined the clade Arctometatarsalia.

Averostra.description: Averostra, meaning "bird snouts," is a clade of theropod dinosaurs within Neotheropoda that encompasses most theropods, uniting the two great branches Ceratosauria and Tetanurae. It represents the only lineage of theropods to survive beyond the Early Jurassic, and so includes nearly every theropod from the Middle Jurassic onward, from the horned ceratosaurs and abelisaurs to the megalosaurs, allosaurs, and the feathered coelurosaurs that ultimately gave rise to birds. Its members are among the most derived theropods, distinguished by the complete loss of the fifth metacarpal, a hand bone that other saurischians retained in reduced form. They also share a promaxillary or maxillary fenestra, an extra opening near the front of the upper jaw, together with fewer teeth in the maxilla, a tooth row set further back along the jaw, and a lacrimal fenestra.

Avetheropoda.description: Avetheropoda is a clade of tetanuran theropod dinosaurs comprising Allosaurus, modern birds, and all descendants of their most recent common ancestor. In effect it unites the two great advanced theropod lineages, the allosauroid carnosaurs and the coelurosaurs, which diverge from one another at the base of the group; it is often treated as equivalent to Neotetanurae. Avetheropods account for the bulk of predatory dinosaur diversity of the Late Jurassic and Cretaceous, and they include the only theropods to survive to the present day, the living birds. They are set apart from more basal tetanurans such as the megalosauroids by skeletal details, including a femoral head oriented fully medially rather than anteromedially. The group's monophyly is well supported in many analyses, though some recent studies instead favor a model in which allosauroids and megalosauroids are each other's closest relatives.
diagnostic_features: Maxillary fenestra present and well-developed
Reduced or absent prefrontal bone
Enlarged orbit relative to skull length
Fused interdental plates
Opisthopubic or mesopubic pelvis in derived members

Avialae.description: Avialae is the bird-line clade of theropod dinosaurs, encompassing the only living dinosaurs, the birds, together with their closest extinct relatives. It is usually defined as all theropods more closely related to modern birds than to the deinonychosaurs, and in most recent analyses it forms the sister group of Deinonychosauria. Its members range from early forms such as Archaeopteryx and the anchiornithid-grade taxa of the late Jurassic, known from Germany and from the roughly 160-million-year-old deposits of China, through the pygostylian and ornithothoracine birds. Avialans diversified into a wide variety of forms during the Cretaceous, when many still retained primitive traits such as clawed wings and toothed jaws. Over the course of their evolution the long bony tail of their ancestors was progressively shortened, and the group as a whole shows a trend toward feathered wings used in flapping flight.
diagnostic_features: Forelimb modified into a feathered wing with asymmetric flight feathers
Forelimb longer than the hindlimb in most members
Caudal series shortened, trending toward a pygostyle in derived members
Reversed or partially reversed hallux in many members

Bagualosauria.description: Bagualosauria is a clade of sauropodomorph dinosaurs uniting Bagualosaurus with its more derived relatives, including the group Plateosauria and, nested within it, the sauropods. It is the sister lineage to Saturnaliidae, a group of smaller, more basal Carnian sauropodomorphs from South America such as Saturnalia and Chromogisaurus, and Bagualosauria excludes these earliest-diverging forms. Bagualosaurus itself, among the most basal known members of the clade, already shows skull and dental modifications linked to more efficient herbivory along with a moderate increase in body size compared to its saturnaliid relatives, hinting at trends that became far more pronounced later in the group's history. Because it excludes only that earliest-diverging grade, Bagualosauria encompasses most sauropodomorph diversity, ranging from moderate-sized Triassic and Early Jurassic forms to the giant long-necked sauropods of the later Mesozoic.

Baryonychinae.description: Baryonychinae is a subfamily of spinosaurid dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of Europe and West Africa, including Baryonyx, Suchomimus, and their relatives, along with the tribe Ceratosuchopsini (Ceratosuchops, Riparovenator, and Suchomimus) recognized by some authors. Its members were large, bipedal predators with elongated, crocodile-like skulls whose jaw tips fanned out into rosettes of conical teeth, and robust forelimbs bearing three-fingered hands with a greatly enlarged first-finger claw. Unlike the more derived spinosaurines, baryonychines had only low sails along the back or none at all, and they were on average somewhat smaller. Their small, recurved teeth show little to no serration and resemble those of crocodiles, an arrangement generally read as an adaptation for catching fish, though at least one well-preserved member also fed opportunistically on other prey. It is usually recovered as the sister group of Spinosaurinae, but its monophyly is contested, with some analyses interpreting it instead as a grade of successive outgroups united by plesiomorphic serrated teeth.

Brachiosauridae.description: Brachiosauridae is a family of large, quadrupedal, plant-eating sauropod dinosaurs and one of the main groups within Titanosauriformes, alongside the Euhelopodidae and the Titanosauria. Its members, which include Brachiosaurus, the African Giraffatitan, and the possible island dwarf Europasaurus, lived from the Late Jurassic into the Cretaceous across what are now North and South America, Africa, and Europe. Brachiosaurids are best known for their unusually long necks, which let them browse foliage from the tops of tall conifers beyond the reach of other sauropods. Their forelimbs are longer than or roughly equal to the hindlimbs, more so than in other macronarians, giving them an elevated, giraffe-like stance. They also bore broad, spoon-shaped teeth suited to biting through tough vegetation, along with distinctive traits of the back vertebrae and pelvis that set the group apart.
diagnostic_features: Forelimbs longer than or subequal in length to the hindlimbs
Humerus elongate, exceeding or approaching femoral length
Highly elevated, arched narial region on the skull
Spatulate teeth distributed along the full extent of the jaw margins
Coracoid with a quadrangular outline
Relatively short tail compared with other macronarians
Maxillary teeth twisted axially through an arc of 30 to 45 degrees
Middle and posterior dorsal vertebrae with elongate, rod-like transverse processes
Ischium with an abbreviated pubic peduncle

Brachyrostra.description: Brachyrostra, whose name means "short snouts," is a clade of abelisaurid theropod dinosaurs known mainly from the Cretaceous of South America. It is defined as all abelisaurids more closely related to Carnotaurus than to Majungasaurus, and it groups horned genera such as Carnotaurus and Aucasaurus with their close relatives; the more deeply nested Furileusauria and, within it, the tribe Carnotaurini fall inside the clade. Members are the most derived of the abelisaurids, relatively lightly built for large theropods and distinguished by very short, narrow skulls and extremely reduced forearms, even more so than in other members of the family. Many carried horns or roughened bosses on the frontal and nasal bones, interpreted as supports for cornified structures or dermal armor. They were also swift runners, with an enlarged tail-based locomotory musculature that made them among the fastest large theropods known. Long thought to be exclusively South American, the group is now recognized as far afield as France with the taxon Caletodraco.

Progressive enclosure of the orbit by the postorbital and lacrimal
Strongly ornamented cranial bones
Anteriorly expanded cnemial crest of the tibia in derived members

Caenagnathidae.description: Caenagnathidae is a family of beaked, feathered oviraptorosaurs known from the Cretaceous of North America and Asia. Its members range enormously in size, from the turkey-sized Caenagnathasia to the giant Beibeilong and Gigantoraptor, which reached roughly 8 meters in length. Like other oviraptorosaurs they had long necks and short tails, but they were more lightly built than their oviraptorid relatives, with slender arms and long, gracile legs. Their toothless lower jaws were relatively long and shallow, hollow and connected to the air-sac system, and lined internally with complex ridges, toothlike processes, and shelf-like structures. This variation in body size and beak shape suggests that caenagnathids adapted to a range of ecological niches, and the group persisted until the very end of the Cretaceous, vanishing with the other non-avian dinosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Fully fused, edentulous mandibular symphysis with paired lingual ridges
Deep dentary bearing a prominent lateral fossa and pneumatic foramen
Elongate, gracile, cursorial hindlimb with a fused tarsometatarsus in some genera
Preacetabular process of the ilium expanded ventrally

Caenagnathoidea.description: Caenagnathoidea is a superfamily of advanced oviraptorosaurs, the feathered, beaked maniraptoran dinosaurs of the Cretaceous Period. It groups the two principal families of that lineage, Caenagnathidae and Oviraptoridae, together with their most recent common ancestor. Its members lived across what are now Asia and North America and share the short, deep, parrot-like skulls typical of oviraptorosaurs, but in a more specialized form: the jaws are entirely toothless and sheathed in a horny beak, and the skull and palate are extensively hollowed by air spaces. The group unites the often crested oviraptorids, best known from Asia, with the toothless, frequently long-legged caenagnathids of both Asia and North America. It is a stable and widely used grouping, standing just apart from close relatives such as the similarly beakless Avimimus, which falls outside it.
diagnostic_features: Fully edentulous jaws sheathed in a keratinous rhamphotheca
Deep, foreshortened skull with a secondarily pneumatized palate
Dentary with an elongate symphysis bearing lingual occlusal ridges
Mandibular articular facet for the quadrate formed almost entirely by the articular

Camarasauridae.description: Camarasauridae is a family of small to medium-sized sauropod dinosaurs occupying a basal position within Macronaria, one of the two major branches of Neosauropoda. Camarasaurids are recognizable by their comparatively short necks and short skulls bearing large nostril openings and broad, spoon-shaped teeth packed along a thick jaw; the biomechanics of their neck vertebrae suggest they raised and lowered the neck vertically rather than sweeping it from side to side like most diplodocids. Camarasaurus is the only genus universally accepted as a member, though the Portuguese Lourinhasaurus is treated as a camarasaurid in most analyses, and forms such as Tehuelchesaurus, Bellusaurus, and Oplosaurus have been proposed with less certainty. The group is best known from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of North America and was largely restricted to the northern continents during the Late Jurassic.
diagnostic_features: Deep, dorsoventrally tall snout with a steeply inclined premaxillary margin
Stout, spoon-shaped teeth with broad crowns
Cervical vertebrae with deeply excavated, chambered pleurocoels
Anterior dorsal neural spines bifurcate
Relatively short cervical series compared with other macronarians

Camarasauromorpha.description: Camarasauromorpha is a node-based clade of macronarian sauropod dinosaurs comprising the most recent common ancestor of Camarasaurus and the titanosaurs, together with all of its descendants. It is the most basal group within the larger macronarian radiation, uniting the Late Jurassic Camarasauridae with Titanosauriformes (the brachiosaurids plus the somphospondylans), and it includes a handful of basal forms, such as Europasaurus, whose finer placement within Macronaria remains unresolved. Fragmentary limb bones from the Middle Jurassic of Kachchh, western India, are the oldest known record of the clade. Camarasauromorphs are distinguished from the narrower-toothed diplodocoid sauropods by their broad, spatulate teeth and a more robustly built body plan.

Carcharodontosauria.description: Carcharodontosauria is a clade of allosauroid theropods comprising Carcharodontosauridae and their closest relatives, encompassing many of the largest terrestrial predators of the Cretaceous across both Gondwana and Laurasia. Its basal members are medium-sized forms that grade into the giant carcharodontosaurids. The carcharodontosaurids underwent a worldwide dispersal during the Early Cretaceous before the family died out in the Turonian, roughly 90 million years ago, after which other large theropods took over the apex-predator role.

Carcharodontosauridae.description: Carcharodontosauridae is a family of giant carnivorous theropod dinosaurs forming a clade within Carnosauria. Its members include some of the largest land predators ever known, among them Acrocanthosaurus, Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, and Tyrannotitan, the biggest of which rivaled Tyrannosaurus and Spinosaurus in size, with the heaviest estimated at 8 to 10 metric tons. Together with the spinosaurids, carcharodontosaurids were the dominant large predators of the Early and mid-Cretaceous across Gondwana, and species also occur in North America, Europe, and possibly Asia. Their fossil record spans the Cretaceous from the Barremian to the Turonian, after which they were replaced by smaller abelisaurids in Gondwana and by tyrannosaurids in North America and Asia. An advanced South American subfamily, the Giganotosaurinae, groups the most closely related giant forms.

Prominent ornamentation on the lacrimal and postorbital bones

Carcharodontosaurinae.description: Carcharodontosaurinae is a subfamily of carcharodontosaurid theropods that contains Carcharodontosaurus together with a closely knit group of South American giants, Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus, Meraxes, Taurovenator, and Tyrannotitan, often grouped together as the tribe Giganotosaurini. It includes some of the largest members of the family, with some species rivaling Tyrannosaurus and Spinosaurus in size and ranking among the biggest land carnivores known. Carcharodontosaurus lived in North Africa while the Giganotosaurini radiated across South America, so together these animals spanned much of Gondwana during the Cretaceous.

Caudipterygidae.description: Caudipterygidae is a family of small, feathered oviraptorosaurian theropod dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of China, known from the Yixian and Jiufotang Formations roughly 125 to 120 million years ago. It groups Caudipteryx with close relatives such as Similicaudipteryx, forms that sit near the base of the oviraptorosaur radiation. A distinguishing trait of the group is a unique dagger-shaped pygostyle, the fused bone at the tip of the tail that in birds anchors a fan of feathers. For a time the family held only a single genus and was regarded as redundant, until further members were recognized. Its standing as a natural group remains debated, with some analyses recovering it as a clade and others treating its members as a paraphyletic grade of basal oviraptorosaurs.

Centrosaurinae.description: Centrosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of horned ceratopsid dinosaurs, encompassing large quadrupedal herbivores of the Late Cretaceous. Its fossils come primarily from the northern part of Laramidia, in present-day Alberta, Montana, and Alaska, with isolated members reaching as far south as Utah and Mexico and one debated occurrence in China. Centrosaurines are typically marked by a prominent nasal horn, short horns over the eyes, and an ornamented frill projecting from the back of the skull, and are relatively small for ceratopsids, roughly the size of a rhinoceros at body lengths of about 2.5 to 8 meters. The subfamily is divided into several tribes, including the early-diverging nasutoceratopsins and albertaceratopsins and the more derived centrosaurins and pachyrhinosaurins; the last group replaces the nasal horn with a thickened bony boss. Their classification is complicated by wide variation between individuals and growth stages, and some researchers argue the group may have evolved largely as a single changing lineage rather than through repeated branching.

Premaxilla with a pronounced ventral angle and a subcircular external narial region

Cerapoda.description: Cerapoda is the most diverse clade of neornithischian dinosaurs, uniting the two great herbivorous lineages Ornithopoda and Marginocephalia; its name is a blend of Ceratopsia and Ornithopoda. As that name suggests, it is split into two branches: the ornithopods, ranging from small bird-footed forms to the more derived iguanodontians and hadrosaurs, and the marginocephalians, which comprise the dome-skulled pachycephalosaurs and the frilled, horned ceratopsians. Cerapodans span an enormous range of body plans, from small bipeds to giant quadrupedal plant-eaters, and share refined tooth and jaw mechanics that let them process tough vegetation efficiently. The clade nests within Neornithischia, more derived than the small-bodied, early-diverging forms such as the thescelosaurids and jeholosaurids.

Reduction or loss of the premaxillary teeth

Ceratopsia.description: Ceratopsia is a group of beaked, herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs, popularly known as the horned dinosaurs, that lived from the Late Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous across what are now Asia, North America, and Europe. Every member carries a rostral bone, a toothless ossification capping the upper jaw that pairs with the predentary of the lower jaw to form a parrot-like beak found in no other dinosaurs. The skull is further marked by prominent jugal bones that flare outward beneath the eyes, giving it a triangular outline from above. The earliest forms, such as Psittacosaurus and the Chaoyangsauridae, were small bipedal animals, while later members grew into very large quadrupeds that developed elaborate facial horns and neck frills. The most derived members, the ceratopsids like Centrosaurus and Triceratops, were among the dominant herbivores of their environments, with the group as a whole spanning animals from about a meter long to over nine meters.
diagnostic_features: Rostral bone, a unique median ossification forming the tip of the upper beak
Tall, narrow skull that is triangular in anterior view
Laterally flared jugals giving the skull a broad cheek region
Vaulted palate

Ceratopsidae.description: Ceratopsidae is a family of large, quadrupedal, herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous, including well-known forms such as Triceratops, Centrosaurus, and Styracosaurus. Nearly all known species come from western North America, which formed the island continent of Laramidia at the time, ranging from Alaska to Mexico; the sole named exception is Sinoceratops, from China. Ceratopsids are recognized by their toothless beaks, rows of shearing teeth packed into batteries at the back of the jaw, elaborate nasal and brow horns, and a thin parietal-squamosal shelf that sweeps back and up into a bony frill. The family is split into two subgroups: the chasmosaurines, which typically bear long triangular frills and well-developed brow horns, and the centrosaurines, which have prominent nasal horns or bosses, shorter and more rectangular frills, and elaborate spines along the frill margin. These horns and frills vary enormously between species and were likely display structures used to signal to rivals and mates, though some may also have served in combat or defense. Many centrosaurines are found in dense bone beds, suggesting that these animals gathered in large herds.
diagnostic_features: Large parietosquamosal frill with marginal epiossifications (epoccipitals)
Prominent nasal horn and/or paired supraorbital horns
Very large skull, often exceeding 1.5 meters in length
Double-rooted, shearing cheek teeth arranged in dental batteries
Obligate quadrupedal stance with robust, graviportal limbs
Syncervical (fused anterior cervical vertebrae) supporting the massive skull

Ceratopsoidea.description: Ceratopsoidea is a clade of coronosaurian ceratopsian dinosaurs, defined as the group containing Ceratops and Triceratops but not Protoceratops. It brings together the family Ceratopsidae — the large, elaborately horned and frilled quadrupeds that dominated Late Cretaceous North America, such as Triceratops — with a handful of closely related but more basal animals like Zuniceratops that approach the ceratopsid condition without belonging to it. This grouping sits apart from the Asian protoceratopsids, the other major branch of Coronosauria. Ceratopsidae, the derived heart of the clade, is further divided into the short-frilled centrosaurines and the long-frilled chasmosaurines. Ceratopsoids and their immediate ancestors were long presumed endemic to western North America, though later finds such as Turanoceratops raised the possibility of an Asian origin.
diagnostic_features: Postorbital (brow) horncores
Trend toward double-rooted cheek teeth
Frontal excluded from the dorsal orbital margin
Large body size relative to other neoceratopsians

Ceratosauria.description: Ceratosauria is a clade of theropod dinosaurs that ranged from the Early Jurassic through the end of the Cretaceous, reaching its greatest diversity on the southern landmasses of Gondwana. It is composed of three major groups: the Ceratosauridae, the Noasauridae, and the Abelisauridae, the last of which thrived across the southern continents until the mass extinction 66 million years ago. Earlier definitions also placed the coelophysoids and dilophosaurids within the group, but most recent work excludes them, treating ceratosaurs as a more restricted assemblage. Members are generally moderately large predators, ranging from small, lightly built noasaurs to the bulky Carnotaurus. The clade is distinguished by a robust, often heavily ornamented or tall skull and by a marked shortening of the forelimbs, features that grow more pronounced in later forms such as the abelisaurids, while basal members remain closer in build to other early theropods.
diagnostic_features: Camellate internal pneumatic structure of the presacral vertebrae
Six sacral vertebrae, incorporating an additional dorsosacral
Strongly pneumatic sacral neural spines with paired lateral fossae and foramina
Very low deltopectoral crest on the humerus
Continuous ridge on the lateral ilium linking the supra-acetabular crest to the brevis shelf
Distal ischium expanded into a fused, anteroposteriorly elongate triangular foot
Enlarged iliofibularis tubercle on the fibula
Astragalar distal condyles rotated 10 to 30 degrees anteriorly
Fusion of the pelvic elements and of the astragalus and calcaneum in mature individuals

Ceratosauridae.description: Ceratosauridae is a family of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaurs known mainly from the Late Jurassic Ceratosaurus, with the fragmentary Genyodectes of Cretaceous Patagonia being the only other widely recognized member. It falls within the more exclusive clade Neoceratosauria as the sister group to Abelisauroidea, the branch of ceratosaurs that includes the abelisaurids and noasaurids. Because Genyodectes is known from such incomplete remains, it is difficult to separate features that characterize the whole family from those unique to Ceratosaurus, and the traits shown to unite the two genera come chiefly from their teeth. Its members were large-bodied predators, and the group's limits remain unsettled: animals such as Eoabelisaurus and Ostafrikasaurus are probable ceratosaurs whose membership in the family is uncertain.
diagnostic_features: Greatly elongate maxillary and dentary tooth crowns that extend below the ventral margin of the jaws when the mouth is closed
Nasal horn and paired lacrimal ridges (in Ceratosaurus)
Row of small median osteoderms along the dorsal midline (in Ceratosaurus)
Retention of a relatively deep, unornamented antorbital region compared to abelisaurids

Cetiosauridae.description: Cetiosauridae is a family of basal sauropod dinosaurs from the Jurassic. Traditionally it served as a wastebasket for various unrelated species, but some recent studies find that it may represent a genuine natural group. Alongside Cetiosaurus from the Middle Jurassic of Britain, taxa assigned to the family include Patagosaurus from the late Early to Middle Jurassic of Patagonia and Lapparentosaurus from the Middle Jurassic of Madagascar, which share distinctive features not seen in other eusauropods. At least one study has suggested that the mamenchisaurids form a subgroup within it. Its validity and contents remain debated, with several analyses instead recovering it as a paraphyletic grade of early sauropods rather than a true clade.
diagnostic_features: Loss of the spinodiapophyseal lamina on the dorsal vertebrae
Pyramid-shaped, non-bifid dorsal neural spines
Generalized non-neosauropod eusauropod axial and appendicular morphology

Chaoyangsauridae.description: Chaoyangsauridae is a family of small, early-diverging ceratopsian dinosaurs from Asia (and possibly Europe, if the German genus Stenopelix belongs here). They are among the earliest known marginocephalians, with the oldest remains dating to roughly 160 million years ago in the Late Jurassic and others extending into the Early Cretaceous. Its members bore sharp beaks for snipping off leaves and only a very small frill, retaining many primitive features while already showing the rostral bone that characterizes ceratopsians. The family is usually taken to comprise Chaoyangsaurus, Xuanhuaceratops, Yinlong, and Hualianceratops, and lies outside the more advanced Neoceratopsia.

Flat dorsal surface of the squamosal bearing a stalked quadrate process
Deep sulcus dividing the quadrate condyles

Reduced predentary
Rostrally converging dentary margins

Chasmosaurinae.description: Chasmosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of horned ceratopsid dinosaurs, comprising the long-frilled forms of the Late Cretaceous of western North America (Laramidia). Its members are distinguished by prominent, elongate brow horns, reduced nasal horns, and long frills that lack the long spines seen in their short-horned relatives the centrosaurines. Chasmosaurines first appeared in the early Campanian and persisted until the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction that ended the age of non-avian dinosaurs, and their remains are known from western Canada, the western United States, and northern Mexico. The group was highly diverse, ranging from earlier forms such as Chasmosaurus and Pentaceratops to the derived and often gigantic Triceratopsini, which includes Triceratops, Torosaurus, and their close relatives. The distinctive shape of the frill and the small hornlets along its margin allow many species to be recognized even from fragmentary remains, contributing to the group's high named diversity.
diagnostic_features: Elongate postorbital (brow) horncores, contrasting with the abbreviated horns of centrosaurines
Reduced nasal horncore or boss
Greatly elongate parietosquamosal frill with large parietal fenestrae and elongate squamosals
Only three epiparietal loci (P1-P3) per side along the parietal lateral ramus
Premaxilla longer than tall, with subequal dorsal and ventral rami of the rostral

Citipatiinae.description: Citipatiinae is a subfamily of oviraptorid dinosaurs, a group of small, bird-like, beaked maniraptoran theropods that lived during the Late Cretaceous of Asia. It contains Citipati and its close relatives, the larger, long-armed, crested oviraptorids that were traditionally lumped into the subfamily Oviraptorinae. The clade was recognized after phylogenetic analysis placed Oviraptor in a more basal position outside these crested forms, leaving the remaining genera to be grouped on their own. Its members are distinguished by tall midline cranial crests, comparable to those of a cassowary, together with relatively long hands that retain three functional fingers.
Citipatiinae.authors: Funston, G. F.; Chinzorig, T.; Tsogtbaatar, K.; Kobayashi, Y.; Sullivan, C.; Currie, P. J.
diagnostic_features: Tall, well-developed bony cranial crest
Relatively long manus retaining three functional digits
Nasal region incorporated into a raised, pneumatic crest

Coelophysidae.description: Coelophysidae is a family of early theropod dinosaurs within the superfamily Coelophysoidea, flourishing from the Late Triassic into the Early Jurassic. Its members were geographically widespread, with fossils recovered across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and the group includes such genera as Coelophysis, Procompsognathus, Camposaurus, Powellvenator, and Panguraptor. Coelophysids were slender, lightly built carnivores with narrow skulls and skeletons adapted for speed, making them fast and agile runners. As fairly basal theropods, they retained primitive characteristics such as hollow air sacs in the neck vertebrae and habitual bipedalism. Several members are known from sites preserving numerous individuals together, and some, notably Coelophysis, have been the subject of debated claims of cannibalism.
diagnostic_features: Long, low skull with a pronounced subnarial gap and a loosely attached premaxilla
Numerous slender, recurved and finely serrated teeth
Fused clavicles forming a furcula
Elongate, gracile limb bones with a strongly cursorial hindlimb

Coelophysoidea.description: Coelophysoidea is a clade of slender, carnivorous theropod dinosaurs that was widespread during the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic, with fossils known from most continents. It contains the family Coelophysidae along with a range of other early forms, including such genera as Coelophysis, Procompsognathus, and Liliensternus. Its members were lightly built bipeds ranging from about 1 to 6 meters in length, with long, narrow skulls opened by large fenestrae and light skeletons suited to fast, agile running; some species bore delicate cranial crests. Coelophysoids are regarded as basal neotheropods lying outside the more advanced Averostra, and many taxa once grouped here, including the larger crested forms, are now placed elsewhere along the early theropod stem.
diagnostic_features: Elongate, lightly built skull with a low, narrow, pointed snout
Subnarial gap between the premaxillary and maxillary tooth rows
Elongate cervical vertebrae with low neural spines, producing a long, flexible neck
Slender cursorial hindlimbs with a tightly appressed metatarsus

Coelurosauria.description: Coelurosauria is a large and diverse subgroup of theropod dinosaurs, defined as all theropods more closely related to birds than to carnosaurs. It encompasses compsognathids, tyrannosauroids, ornithomimosaurs, and the bird-line maniraptorans, along with megaraptorans, whose exact position remains uncertain. Coelurosaurs range from some of the largest carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Tyrannosaurus, to some of the smallest, and they diversified into omnivorous, insectivorous, herbivorous, and carnivorous forms. Most feathered dinosaurs found so far are coelurosaurs, and many lineages bore filamentous integument or true feathers, though some retained scales over parts of the body. The clade appears by the Middle Jurassic and includes birds, the only dinosaur lineage to survive the end-Cretaceous extinction and the only one alive today.
diagnostic_features: Elongate distal caudal vertebrae with reduced or absent transverse processes
Filamentous integument or feathers present in many lineages
Reduced or absent prefrontal bone
Semilunate carpal bone in the wrist of many derived taxa
Enlarged cerebrum relative to body size

Colossosauria.description: Colossosauria is a clade of titanosaur sauropod dinosaurs that lived in South America from the latest Early Cretaceous through the Late Cretaceous. Originally erected around Mendozasaurus, it is delimited in current usage as all titanosaurs closer to Patagotitan than to Saltasaurus, a framework that places it as the opposing branch to Saltasauroidea within the larger group Eutitanosauria. Its core subgroups are Lognkosauria, which includes some of the largest land animals ever known, and the smaller-bodied Rinconsauria, so the clade spans a wide range of body sizes. Depending on the phylogenetic analysis, it may also take in other similar titanosaurs and various unclassified forms on the stem toward either subgroup. Members are distinguished mainly by traits of the limb girdles and limbs, including a wide-gauge stance.

Compsognathidae.description: Compsognathidae is a family of small, conservatively built coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs known from the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous of Europe, Asia, and South America. Its members were lightly built carnivores that preyed on small vertebrates such as lizards, and several are among the smallest dinosaurs known, most no larger than about a meter long. For many years Compsognathus was the group's only member, but paleontologists have since added a number of presumably related genera, including Sinosauropteryx, Sinocalliopteryx, Huaxiagnathus, Aristosuchus, Mirischia, and Scipionyx, several of which preserve some of the earliest known primitive feathers. Assignment to the family has traditionally hinged on a distinctive short, stocky first metacarpal supporting an enlarged thumb, though the lack of features shared by all members has left both its monophyly and its exact membership contested.
diagnostic_features: Small body size with a proportionally long tail
Skull low and lightly built with numerous small teeth
Manus with a robust, enlarged first digit
Filamentous integument preserved in several members

Coronosauria.description: Coronosauria is a clade of neoceratopsian dinosaurs, defined as the smallest group containing both Protoceratops and Triceratops. Its members show the first development of the elaborate neck frill and the fusion of the first several neck vertebrae into a single unit, an adaptation that helped support their increasingly heavy heads. Two subgroups are generally recognized within it: the Protoceratopsidae, a set of small Asian forms including Protoceratops and its closest relatives, and the Ceratopsoidea, which contains the large horned Ceratopsidae along with related animals such as Zuniceratops. Coronosaurs lived during the Cretaceous of Asia and North America.

Dacentrurinae.description: Dacentrurinae is a subfamily of stegosaurid dinosaurs uniting the forms most closely related to Dacentrurus, including Miragaia, Adratiklit, and Thyreosaurus. Its members lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic of Europe and North Africa. Compared with their close relatives the Stegosaurinae, dacentrurines tend to carry narrower spines running along the back rather than broad plates concentrated toward the tail, and their forelimb bones show robust proportions suggesting powerful musculature. Dacentrurinae and Stegosaurinae are sister lineages grouped together within the more inclusive clade Neostegosauria, which also includes the African stegosaur Kentrosaurus as a close relative standing just outside either subfamily.

Deinocheiridae.description: Deinocheiridae is a family of ornithomimosaurian dinosaurs that lived across Asia and North America during the Cretaceous, roughly 115 to 69 million years ago. Alongside the more lightly built, cursorial ornithomimids, it represents one of the two main branches of the ornithomimosaurs, but its members tended to be large and robustly proportioned, retaining broader, less specialized feet rather than the tightly pinched running foot of their relatives. The group ranged from the comparatively primitive Beishanlong to the giant, deep-jawed Deinocheirus at its most derived, and also takes in the Mongolian Garudimimus and the Mexican Paraxenisaurus, with Harpymimus and Hexing sometimes assigned here as well. The once-separate family Garudimimidae is now treated as a junior synonym, since Deinocheiridae contains its type genus.

Deinonychosauria.description: Deinonychosauria is a clade of paravian theropod dinosaurs that lived from the Late Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous, with fossils recovered on nearly every continent, from North America and Europe to Asia, Africa, South America, and Antarctica. It traditionally unites the dromaeosaurids and the troodontids, two families whose members bore enlarged, sickle-shaped claws on the second toe. That claw was held clear of the ground in a hyperextended position, so that only the third and fourth toes carried the animal's weight while walking, an arrangement known as functional didactyly. Most deinonychosaurs were predators, though some of the smaller troodontids appear to have been at least omnivorous. The group has long been considered among the closest relatives of birds, but its exact makeup remains debated: some analyses place troodontids nearer to birds than to dromaeosaurids, which would leave the composition of the clade unstable beyond the dromaeosaurids themselves.
Deinonychosauria.authors: Colbert, E. H.; Russell, D. A.

Functionally didactyl foot with a raised second toe

Diamantinasauria.description: Diamantinasauria is a clade of somphospondylan titanosauriform sauropods with close affinities to Titanosauria, known from the early Late Cretaceous of South America and Australia. It groups the Australian Diamantinasaurus, Savannasaurus, and Australotitan from the Winton Formation of Queensland with the Patagonian Sarmientosaurus of the Bajo Barreal Formation, and may also include Wintonotitan. This shared membership across two continents points to a faunal connection between Australia and South America by way of Antarctica during the Cretaceous. Distinguishing traits are drawn from the sternal plate, braincase, and limb skeleton, and dental microwear suggests these animals were mid-height browsers that fed on vegetation roughly one to ten meters above the ground. While the group is consistently recovered as a coherent clade, its exact position relative to Titanosauria has shifted between analyses.

Dicraeosauridae.description: Dicraeosauridae is a family of flagellicaudatan sauropods that are the sister group to the whip-tailed diplodocids. The family includes genera such as Amargasaurus, Suuwassea, and Brachytrachelopan, and its members are best known from Africa, South America, and North America, spanning the Early or Middle Jurassic through the Early Cretaceous; several Asian taxa, including Lingwulong and Tharosaurus, have been proposed as dicraeosaurids, though this remains contested. The group stands apart from other advanced sauropods, which trend toward gigantism, in being relatively small at roughly 10 to 13 meters long and in bearing distinctively short necks built from comparatively few vertebrae. Their most striking feature is a series of extremely tall neural spines running along the neck and back, reaching bizarre proportions in forms such as Amargasaurus and Bajadasaurus. As obligate herbivores with short necks, they are thought to have browsed close to the ground or at mid height. Amargasaurus was the latest-surviving member, persisting into the Early Cretaceous.
diagnostic_features: Tall, dorsoventrally elongate neural spines on the cervical and dorsal vertebrae, bifurcated along much of the column
Relatively short neck with comparatively few, foreshortened cervical vertebrae
Postparietal fenestra present, with an expanded crista prootica on the braincase
Reduced or absent pneumaticity of the presacral vertebral centra

Dinosauria.description: Dinosauria is a clade of archosaurian reptiles that first appeared early in the Triassic period and went on to become the dominant terrestrial vertebrates for much of the Mesozoic era, through the Jurassic and Cretaceous. The group is extraordinarily diverse, with paleontologists having identified more than 900 genera and over 1,000 species of extinct non-avian dinosaurs alone, ranging from small bipeds to the largest land animals that ever lived, the biggest sauropods reaching nearly 40 meters in length. Dinosaurs share an erect, birdlike leg posture that set them apart from the sprawling stance of most other reptiles, and elaborate display structures such as horns and crests appear across the group, while some lineages evolved bony armor and spines. They were ancestrally bipedal, though many groups became quadrupedal, and the evidence indicates that all laid eggs, with nest-building widespread. Birds are the one dinosaur lineage to have survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction roughly 66 million years ago, so the clade is divided into the avian dinosaurs (birds) and the extinct non-avian dinosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Fully erect, parasagittal hindlimb posture
Perforated (fully open) acetabulum
Three or more sacral vertebrae
Elongate deltopectoral crest on the humerus
Asymmetrical fourth trochanter on the femur
Open hip socket allowing pillar-erect stance

Diplodocidae.description: Diplodocidae is a family of sauropod dinosaurs that includes some of the longest animals ever to walk the Earth, among them Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Barosaurus, and the enormous Supersaurus, which may have exceeded 30 meters in length. Even by sauropod standards these were large animals, with exceptionally long necks and tapering tails, small heads set with the bony nasal openings high on the skull, and slender teeth clustered at the front of the jaws that were likely used to strip foliage from branches. Not all members were giants; the South American Leinkupal, at roughly 9 meters, was one of the smallest. The family divides into two subfamilies, the robust apatosaurines and the more slender diplodocines, the latter grouping Diplodocus with close relatives such as Barosaurus. Diplodocids probably originated in North America, where most of their fossils are found, but they ranged across most continents, occurring also in South America, Europe, and Africa. They flourished during the Late Jurassic and persisted into the Early Cretaceous in Africa and South America.
diagnostic_features: Extremely elongate tail terminating in a whip-like series of rod-shaped distal caudals
Pencil-shaped (cylindrical) teeth restricted to the front of the jaws
Bifurcated neural spines on the cervical and anterior dorsal vertebrae
Tail chevrons with both anterior and posterior projections (double-beamed) in the middle of the tail

Diplodocimorpha.description: Diplodocimorpha is a clade of sauropod dinosaurs that encompasses most members of the broader diplodocoid group, the long-necked, whip-tailed giants that included some of the longest animals ever to live. It unites the rebbachisaurids with the flagellicaudatans, a lineage that combines the diplodocids and the short-necked dicraeosaurids, together with their most recent common ancestor. A few more basal diplodocoids, such as Haplocanthosaurus and possibly Amphicoelias, fall outside the clade. Because it is anchored on a shared common ancestor (a node-based definition) rather than on everything branching from a reference taxon, it captures a slightly narrower assemblage than Diplodocoidea as a whole, with which it was once treated as synonymous before the two were shown to differ in content.
diagnostic_features: Contains the narrow-toothed rebbachisaurids and the whip-tailed flagellicaudatans to the exclusion of basal diplodocoids
Further retraction and enlargement of the external nares relative to basal diplodocoids
Marked reduction of the hyposphene-hypantrum accessory articulations in the dorsal vertebrae of derived members

Diplodocinae.description: Diplodocinae is a subfamily of diplodocid sauropod dinosaurs that lived from the Late Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, roughly 161 to 136 million years ago, with fossils known from North America, Europe, Africa, and South America. Its members include Diplodocus, Barosaurus, Galeamopus, Tornieria, Supersaurus, Leinkupal, and Ardetosaurus. These are among the most gracile and elongate of the diplodocids, distinguished by especially long necks and tails built from extremely elongate cervical vertebrae and slender overall proportions.
diagnostic_features: Mid-cervical vertebrae extremely elongate, with elongation indices commonly exceeding four
Slender, gracile cervical and dorsal proportions relative to Apatosaurinae
Cervical ribs slender and not ventrally displaced

Diplodocoidea.description: Diplodocoidea is a superfamily of sauropod dinosaurs that includes some of the longest animals ever to have lived. It brings together the narrow-snouted rebbachisaurids, the short-necked, high-spined dicraeosaurids, and the extremely elongate diplodocids, along with basal forms such as Haplocanthosaurus. Most diplodocoids had very long necks and long, whip-like tails, and among their ranks are slender giants like Supersaurus, Diplodocus, and Apatosaurus. The dicraeosaurids are the only known sauropods to have re-evolved a short neck, presumably an adaptation for feeding close to the ground, a trend taken to the extreme in the highly specialized Brachytrachelopan. Diplodocoids are distinguished by slender, pencil-like teeth restricted to the front of the jaws and squared-off snouts, and they had the highest tooth replacement rates of any vertebrates, with some forms erupting new teeth roughly every month.
diagnostic_features: Tooth crowns slender and subcylindrical (pencil-like), restricted to the anterior part of the jaws
External nares retracted to a position dorsal to or behind the orbits
Elevated tooth replacement rates with multiple replacement teeth per alveolus
Squared-off (rather than rounded) anterior margin of the snout in dorsal view

Dromaeosauridae.description: Dromaeosauridae is a family of small to medium-sized feathered coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs, popularly known as "raptors" after Velociraptor. They were agile, bird-like carnivores that ranged from animals around 1.5 to 2 meters long, such as Velociraptor, up to giants approaching or exceeding 6 meters, such as Utahraptor and Achillobator. The group flourished mainly in the Cretaceous, with definitive fossils known from North America, Europe, and Asia, and survived until the mass extinction at the end of that period. Its members span several subgroups: the basal, possibly semiaquatic Halszkaraptorinae, the enigmatic and flight-adapted Unenlagiinae, the small, often tree-dwelling Microraptoria, and the derived, stocky Eudromaeosauria, which includes ambush hunters such as Deinonychus and Velociraptor. Dromaeosaurids are among the closest known relatives of birds, and abundant fossils show they were extensively feathered, some even bearing well-developed wings on the forelimbs and, in a few forms, the hind limbs.
diagnostic_features: Enlarged, hyperextensible, sickle-shaped ungual on pedal digit II
Stiffened tail with elongate prezygapophyses and chevrons
Pennaceous feathers on the forelimbs and tail
Semilunate carpal bone enabling a folding motion of the manus
Lateral teeth with denticles larger on the distal than the mesial carina

Dromaeosaurinae.description: Dromaeosaurinae is a subfamily of eudromaeosaurian dromaeosaurids, one of the three main branches of these "true dromaeosaurs" alongside Velociraptorinae and Saurornitholestinae. It is defined as the group containing Dromaeosaurus and all dromaeosaurs more closely related to it than to Velociraptor, and it includes some of the largest members of the family, such as Utahraptor and Achillobator, which reached roughly 6 to 7 meters in length. Dromaeosaurines tend to be medium- to giant-sized predators with deep, broadly box-shaped skulls, in contrast to the narrower snouts of the other subfamilies. Their teeth are also distinctive, bearing serrations of roughly equal size along both the front and back cutting edges, rather than the enlarged rear serrations typical of velociraptorines. Members are known almost entirely from the Northern Hemisphere, appearing in the Early and middle Cretaceous before any unambiguous velociraptorines or saurornitholestines and persisting through the Late Cretaceous.
diagnostic_features: Deep, robust, and heavily constructed skull
Large, coarse denticles on both carinae of the lateral teeth
Robust, D-shaped premaxillary teeth

Dryomorpha.description: Dryomorpha is a clade of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaurs that brings together the small, gracile dryosaurids and the more robust, thumb-spiked ankylopollexians, along with basal forms such as Hesperonyx that fall outside those two groups. It is defined as the smallest clade containing Dryosaurus and Iguanodon, and so unites the last common ancestor of those animals with all of its descendants. The clade captures a key stage in ornithopod evolution, spanning the transition from lightly built browsers toward the large, quadrupedal bulk feeders that culminated in the hadrosaurs, or duck-billed dinosaurs, of the Cretaceous.
diagnostic_features: Antorbital fenestra closed or greatly reduced
Brevis shelf of the ilium broadly exposed in lateral view
Loss of the first distal tarsal
Reduced manual and pedal digit counts relative to basal iguanodontians

Dryosauridae.description: Dryosauridae is a family of small, gracile, bipedal ornithopod dinosaurs known from Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous rocks of Africa, Europe, and North America. Its members include Dryosaurus, Dysalotosaurus, Valdosaurus, Elrhazosaurus, and Callovosaurus, several of which were once dismissed as dubious or as species of Dryosaurus before later studies re-established them as valid. These were lightly built, long-legged herbivores adapted for running, and were originally set apart from the hypsilophodonts because they more closely resembled the larger iguanodontians and hadrosaurs. They lacked the specialized thumb spike of their more advanced relatives and sit as an early branch just outside the ankylopollexian ornithopods.

Elaphrosaurinae.description: Elaphrosaurinae is a subfamily of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaurs, usually classified within the family Noasauridae. Its members were lightly built animals with small skulls, long necks, and long legs, and the group ranges from the Middle Jurassic through the Late Cretaceous. Most of the best-known forms, including Elaphrosaurus and Limusaurus, lived during the Jurassic, while Huinculsaurus extends the group into the Cretaceous. Adults were completely toothless, their jaws instead edged with a horny beak, and evidence from Limusaurus — including preserved gastroliths and chemical signatures — suggests they were largely herbivorous, though juveniles retained teeth and may have been omnivorous or carnivorous. The subfamily is distinguished by cervical vertebrae with strongly concave articular faces and cervical ribs fused to the vertebral bodies, along with unusually small hips set against long legs, the thigh bone measuring more than 1.3 times the length of the ilium.

Elongate, low cervical vertebrae producing a long neck
Reduction or complete loss of the dentition (edentulism in Limusaurus)
Gracile, cursorial hindlimb proportions

Elasmaria.description: Elasmaria is a clade of small to medium-sized ornithopod dinosaurs known from Cretaceous deposits across the former supercontinent of Gondwana, including South America, Antarctica, Australia, and possibly Africa. It groups together many lightly built, bipedal ornithopods that were once loosely lumped as "hypsilophodonts." Originally erected to unite just Macrogryphosaurus and Talenkauen, the clade was later found to be far more inclusive, drawing in a variety of Southern Hemisphere forms such as the Antarctic Morrosaurus and Trinisaura, as well as Anabisetia. Its members are distinguished chiefly by thin, mineralized plates arranged along the ribs, together with gracile, cursorial hindlimbs suited to running. Elasmaria represents a major southern radiation of ornithopods that persisted through much of the Cretaceous.

Euceratopsia.description: Euceratopsia is a clade of neoceratopsian dinosaurs that groups the more derived horned forms while excluding the most basal members of that lineage. Defined as the smallest group containing Leptoceratops, Protoceratops, and Triceratops, it brings together the Leptoceratopsidae — a mostly North American assemblage of small-bodied, quadrupedal ceratopsians — with Coronosauria and all more advanced ceratopsians. The coronosaurs within it show the first development of the neck frill and the fusion of the first several neck vertebrae to support an increasingly heavy head, a trend that reaches its extreme in the large, horned ceratopsids of the Late Cretaceous.

Eudromaeosauria.description: Eudromaeosauria is the group of "true" dromaeosaurids, the ground-living theropod predators that flourished across the Cretaceous. It is a node-based clade anchored on Dromaeosaurus, Velociraptor, Deinonychus, and Saurornitholestes, and it excludes the small, often piscivorous or flight-capable branches of the family such as the microraptorines and the Gondwanan unenlagiines. Its fossils are known almost exclusively from the Northern Hemisphere, a distribution taken to mean the group arose after Pangaea split into Laurasia and Gondwana, leaving it unable to colonize the southern continents. Eudromaeosaurs are conventionally divided into three subfamilies, Dromaeosaurinae, Velociraptorinae, and Saurornitholestinae, though the boundaries between them and the placement of individual genera remain contested. Compared with their smaller relatives, they were generally larger-bodied hypercarnivores that hunted prey of comparable or greater size, and they are set apart by distinctive features of the foot, including a shortened metatarsus and an enlarged, blade-like sickle claw held clear of the ground.

Euhelopodidae.description: Euhelopodidae is a family of long-necked sauropod dinosaurs of disputed membership and affinities, most of whose proposed members are known from the Early Cretaceous of East Asia. It is generally recovered as an early-diverging branch of Somphospondyli, the sauropod lineage that also includes the titanosaurs, and its members are marked by distinctive neck vertebrae, including forked neural spines toward the base of the neck and elongate, strongly air-filled centra. Its content remains uncertain because the relationships of Euhelopus itself are unstable: some analyses instead place that genus well outside this group, close to Mamenchisaurus, which would render the family equivalent to Mamenchisauridae. A core of taxa including Erketu, Qiaowanlong, Gobititan, Phuwiangosaurus, and Tangvayosaurus is reasonably stable, while the placement of several fragmentary Chinese forms shifts between this clade and the base of Titanosauria.

Elongate cervical centra with strongly developed pneumatic excavations

Eumaniraptora.description: Eumaniraptora, the "true maniraptorans," is a node-based clade of bird-line theropod dinosaurs that unites the avialans, which include Archaeopteryx and the more than 11,000 living species of birds, with the deinonychosaurs, the grouping of dromaeosaurids and troodontids. It is often treated as synonymous with Paraves, though some analyses recover a few feathered theropods, such as scansoriopterygids, as paravians that fall outside Eumaniraptora. Its members are marked by long, winged forelimbs carrying large asymmetric feathers and an increasingly flexible, folding wrist, adaptations that set the stage for flapping flight in this lineage. Many forms also bore an enlarged, sickle-shaped claw on the second toe that was held retracted off the ground while walking. From small-bodied ancestors, dromaeosaurids and troodontids repeatedly evolved into larger animals through the Cretaceous, while body size continued to shrink in many of the avialans that led to modern birds.
Eumaniraptora.authors: Padian, K.; Hutchinson, J. R.; Holtz, T. R.

Large asymmetric pennaceous feathers on the forelimb forming an aerofoil

Eusauropoda.description: Eusauropoda ("true lizard foot") is a derived clade of sauropod dinosaurs that encompasses the great majority of sauropod diversity. Defined as a node-based group beginning with basal forms such as Shunosaurus, and possibly Barapasaurus and Amygdalodon, it excludes the more primitive vulcanodontids. Its members were strictly herbivorous, long-necked quadrupeds that grew to enormous size, and their remains have been found on every major continent, ranging in time from the Early Jurassic to the latest Cretaceous. The group includes the largely Asian family Mamenchisauridae, the clades Turiasauria and Cetiosauridae, and Neosauropoda, which in turn contains the widespread diplodocoids and titanosaurs. Eusauropods are set apart by skeletal specializations for bulk browsing, including broad, U-shaped jaws and lateral plates along the tooth rows, together with retracted nostrils, a further-elongated neck built from additional cervical vertebrae, and a semi-digitigrade, weight-bearing foot posture.

Eutitanosauria.description: Eutitanosauria is a clade of titanosaurs that gathers together the more derived members of the group. Under its current node-based definition it spans the smallest grouping that contains both Patagotitan and Saltasaurus, making it the immediate parent of two major branches: Colossosauria, which includes the enormous lognkosaurs and the comparatively small-bodied rinconsaurs, and Saltasauroidea, which includes the smaller, heavily armored saltasaurids. Members are distinguished by the loss of the hyposphene-hypantrum articulation between the vertebrae, and many bore bony osteoderms embedded in the skin. Because the definition has shifted repeatedly and often overlaps with the broader Lithostrotia, the label is frequently left unused or unlabeled on phylogenetic trees.
Eutitanosauria.authors: Sanz, J. L.; Powell, J. E.; Le Loeuff, J.; Martínez, R.; Pereda-Suberbiola, X.

Reduced fourth trochanter of the femur

Eutyrannosauria.description: Eutyrannosauria is a clade of large-bodied tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaurs of the Northern Hemisphere, encompassing the family Tyrannosauridae together with its closest non-tyrannosaurid relatives, such as the eastern North American genera Dryptosaurus and Appalachiosaurus and the southwestern North American Bistahieversor. It was defined to set these advanced, often gigantic northern forms apart from the more basal, globally distributed tyrannosauroids. Members are distinguished by their great size and by prominent cranial ornamentation, including roughened, ridge-bearing nasal bones. Some analyses further recover a distinct family, Dryptosauridae, of non-tyrannosaurid eutyrannosaurs that persisted along the Late Cretaceous Atlantic coastline of eastern North America.

Pneumatic recess on the anterior surface of the quadrate condyles
Medial margins of the distal condyle and diaphysis of metatarsal III aligned (not offset)

Flagellicaudata.description: Flagellicaudata is a node-based clade of diplodocoid sauropod dinosaurs, comprising the families Dicraeosauridae and Diplodocidae along with their most recent common ancestor and all of its descendants. The name refers to the long, whip-like tails characteristic of its members, from the Latin flagellum, meaning "whip," and cauda, meaning "tail." Its two constituent families span a broad range of body forms: dicraeosaurids are unusual among sauropods for having re-evolved short necks, an apparent adaptation for browsing close to the ground, whereas diplodocids include some of the longest and most slender animals ever known, with greatly elongated necks. Together they represent a more derived grouping within Diplodocoidea, nested above the rebbachisaurids.
diagnostic_features: Distal caudal vertebrae elongate and rod-like, forming a whip-like tail
Bifurcated (forked) neural spines on the cervical and anterior dorsal vertebrae
Anterior caudal vertebrae with the neural arch positioned on the anterior half of the centrum

Furileusauria.description: Furileusauria (meaning "stiff back lizards") is a clade of derived abelisaurid theropod dinosaurs nested within Brachyrostra, the short-snouted, largely South American branch of the abelisaurids. It is a stem-based group defined by the inclusion of Carnotaurus but the exclusion of Ilokelesia, Skorpiovenator, and Majungasaurus, and it encompasses most of the latest Cretaceous abelisaurids of South America, among them Carnotaurus, Aucasaurus, Viavenator, and Llukalkan. Its members were among the larger brachyrostrans, averaging roughly 7 meters (23 feet) in length. A more restrictive tribe within the group, Carnotaurini, unites Carnotaurus and Aucasaurus. The clade is distinguished by a suite of features in the skull, cervical vertebrae, tail, and hindlimb, and the recently described French taxon Caletodraco extends its range beyond South America into Europe.
