Genasauria.description: Genasauria is a clade that encompasses the great majority of ornithischian dinosaurs, excluding only the earliest-diverging forms such as Lesothosaurus. It unites two major branches: Thyreophora, the armored dinosaurs including ankylosaurs, stegosaurs, and more primitive relatives like Scelidosaurus; and Cerapoda, which gathers the ornithopods, ceratopsians, pachycephalosaurs, and various small early forms. Members were primarily herbivores that typically held their heads about a meter off the ground, suggesting they fed mainly on ground-level plants such as ferns, cycads, and other low-growing gymnosperms. A hallmark of the group is the presence of fleshy cheeks bounding inset tooth rows, an adaptation for more efficient processing of plant material in the mouth.
diagnostic_features: Buccal emargination of the tooth rows, with maxillary and dentary teeth inset from the lateral jaw margin (implying muscular cheeks)
Spout-shaped, edentulous anterior margin of the predentary and premaxilla
Reduced number of premaxillary teeth
Cheek-tooth crowns bearing a prominent primary ridge

Gravisauria.description: Gravisauria is a clade of sauropod dinosaurs that unites the vulcanodontid grade, including Vulcanodon and Tazoudasaurus, with the more derived Eusauropoda, along with several basal forms such as Antetonitrus, Gongxianosaurus, and Isanosaurus that fall outside Vulcanodontidae. It corresponds to the group that some workers instead treat as Sauropoda under a narrower definition, and it encompasses essentially the full radiation of the massive, fully graviportal sauropods. Members share dorsal vertebrae that are broader from side to side than front to back and asymmetrical condyles at the lower end of the femur. The clade is thought to have originated in the Early Jurassic, around the Pliensbachian and Toarcian roughly 183 million years ago, as part of a broader faunal turnover that saw the decline of the prosauropods, coelophysoids, and basal thyreophorans.
diagnostic_features: Dorsal neural spines broader transversely than anteroposteriorly
Asymmetry of the femoral distal condyles, with a transversely broader tibial condyle
Fully columnar, graviportal forelimbs and hindlimbs
Four or more sacral vertebrae

Hadrosauridae.description: Hadrosauridae is a family of ornithopod dinosaurs commonly known as duck-billed dinosaurs, after the flattened, broadened snouts that give their skulls a duck-bill appearance. Descended from iguanodontian ancestors, they were among the most dominant and diverse large herbivores of the Late Cretaceous, especially in Asia and North America, and near the close of the period several lineages dispersed into Europe, Africa, and South America. Their success is often attributed to their grinding teeth, which were stacked into complex batteries that provided an efficient chewing surface for processing tough vegetation. The family divides into two principal subfamilies: the Lambeosaurinae, distinguished by hollow cranial crests and tubes, and the Saurolophinae, which bore solid crests or none at all. A grade of early-diverging taxa such as Eotrachodon, Aquilarhinus, and Yamatosaurus falls outside both subfamilies. Hadrosaurids were facultative bipeds, with juveniles of some species walking mostly on two legs and adults shifting toward walking on all four.

Broad, spatulate, edentulous premaxillary bill
Complete loss of the manual first digit and its ungual
Extensive ossified epaxial tendons forming a lattice along the vertebral column
Hoof-like unguals on the weight-bearing pedal digits

Hadrosauriformes.description: Hadrosauriformes is a clade of styracosternan ornithopods defined as the most recent common ancestor of Iguanodon and Hadrosaurus and all its descendants, uniting iguanodontid-grade forms with the hadrosauroids and the duck-billed Hadrosauridae. Across the clade, dental batteries grew increasingly complex, and the snout trended from the narrower beak of early iguanodontian-grade members toward the broad, edentulous bill of the most derived hadrosaurids. Its members were large-bodied herbivores known from Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas, making Hadrosauriformes one of the most geographically widespread and successful ornithischian radiations of the Cretaceous.
diagnostic_features: Dental battery with multiple stacked replacement teeth per tooth position
Broad, flattened, edentulous premaxillary bill

Elongate, dorsoventrally low rostrum

Hadrosauroidea.description: Hadrosauroidea is a superfamily of ornithischian dinosaurs that includes the duck-billed hadrosaurids and all dinosaurs more closely related to them than to Iguanodon. Alongside the advanced duck-bills, it takes in a long series of more primitive relatives such as Probactrosaurus, Altirhinus, Eolambia, Bactrosaurus, and Telmatosaurus, many of which were once lumped into a now-abandoned catch-all "Iguanodontidae." These early forms document the gradual assembly of the hadrosaurid body plan, including the specialized grinding dental battery and the broad, toothless bill. Their remains have been recovered across Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas, charting the Cretaceous spread of duck-billed dinosaurs, with the closest kin of the true hadrosaurids grouped together as Hadrosauromorpha.
diagnostic_features: Dental battery with strongly reduced or absent cingula on the crowns
Loss of the manual pollex (thumb spike)
Broad, transversely expanded edentulous premaxillary bill

Hadrosauromorpha.description: Hadrosauromorpha is a clade of iguanodontian ornithopods that divides the broader hadrosauroids into the basal forms, which retain compressed hand bones and a spike-like thumb, and the more derived forms that have lost them. It comprises the duck-billed hadrosaurids together with the stem taxa immediately ancestral to them, a group that has variously been taken to include Tethyshadros, Bactrosaurus, Gilmoreosaurus, Telmatosaurus, and Levnesovia, though membership shifts from one analysis to another and their internal relationships remain poorly resolved. Members are distinguished by a suite of skull and skeletal traits approaching the hadrosaurid condition: the loss of the thumb spike and reduced, less mobile wrist and hand, more slender lower forelimb bones, shoulder blades bearing an overhanging projection rather than a J-shaped curve, a straight thigh bone, and shortened foot bones. These animals lived across Eurasia and North America during the Cretaceous, forming the evolutionary grade leading up to the true duck-billed dinosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Loss of the surangular foramen
Shallow embayment of the jugal wing of the quadrate
Reduction of the antorbital fenestra
Further elaboration of the dental battery toward the hadrosaurid condition

Halszkaraptorinae.description: Halszkaraptorinae is a clade of small, early-diverging predatory dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, and includes the enigmatic genera Halszkaraptor, Natovenator, Mahakala, and Hulsanpes. Its members were roughly the size of modern ducks and are distinguished by their unusually long necks, along with a suite of features in the tail vertebrae, forelimbs, hips, and hindlimbs. On the basis of their forelimb and body proportions, some researchers have interpreted these animals as semiaquatic swimmers that used their long necks to forage in water while remaining bipedal on land, though this lifestyle has been questioned. The clade is usually recovered at or near the base of Dromaeosauridae, but its exact placement is contested, with some analyses instead allying it with Unenlagiidae or drawing it toward the bird lineage.

Herrerasauria.description: Herrerasauria is a clade of carnivorous dinosaurs from the Late Triassic, among the oldest dinosaurs known, first appearing roughly 233 million years ago during the Carnian stage. Its best-known members come from South America, including Herrerasaurus and Staurikosaurus of Argentina and Brazil, though possible relatives have also been recovered in North America, Africa, and perhaps other continents. Most were small to mid-sized predators, typically no more than about 4 meters long. Their anatomy blends primitive and derived features: they only superficially resemble later theropods and are not thought to be ancestral to any later dinosaur group. Distinctive traits include a hip socket that is only partly open, just two sacral vertebrae (the fewest of any dinosaur), and a hinged lower jaw. Their exact position on the dinosaur family tree remains debated, with analyses variously placing them as basal saurischians that diverged before the split between theropods and sauropodomorphs, or as early theropods.

Herrerasauridae.description: Herrerasauridae is a family of early carnivorous dinosaurs from the Late Triassic (Carnian to Norian) of South America, with more fragmentary possible members reported from North America, Africa, and Europe. They are among the oldest known dinosaurs, appearing in the fossil record around 233 million years ago. The best-known members — Herrerasaurus and Sanjuansaurus from Argentina and Staurikosaurus and Gnathovorax from Brazil — were bipedal predators; most were relatively small, generally no more than about four meters long, though the largest reached roughly six meters. Herrerasaurid anatomy is unusual and specialized, mixing very primitive and derived traits, and the group is not thought to be ancestral to any later dinosaur lineage. They only superficially resemble the theropods, sharing three-fingered grasping hands with curved claws and a hinged lower jaw while retaining a number of more primitive features.

Heterodontosauridae.description: Heterodontosauridae is a family of small, early-diverging ornithischian dinosaurs, most of them fox-sized and less than two meters long including a long tail. Their fossils are relatively rare, but the group achieved a near-worldwide distribution, turning up on every continent except Australia and Antarctica and ranging from the Early Jurassic into the Early Cretaceous. The family is best known for its strongly heterodont dentition: enlarged, canine-like tusks in both the upper and lower jaws, set off by a gap called a diastema, together with chisel-shaped cheek teeth whose overlapping crowns formed a continuous grinding surface convergent with the dental batteries of later hadrosaurs and ceratopsians. Its members include the South African Abrictosaurus, Lycorhinus, and Heterodontosaurus, along with later and more far-flung forms such as Echinodon, Fruitadens, and the filament-bearing Tianyulong, with the more derived, largely southern-hemisphere genera grouped in the subfamily Heterodontosaurinae. Their diet was herbivorous or possibly omnivorous, and their long, slender hindlimbs suggest they were fast, primarily bipedal runners.

Heterodontosaurinae.description: Heterodontosaurinae is the derived, largely Gondwanan subfamily of the heterodontosaurids, a group of small, early ornithischian dinosaurs. It gathers the heterodontosaurids more closely related to Heterodontosaurus than to Tianyulong, Fruitadens, or Echinodon, and includes such genera as Heterodontosaurus, Lycorhinus, Abrictosaurus, Manidens, and Pegomastax. Its members display the most specialized heterodontosaurid jaw and tooth anatomy: whereas basal relatives kept widely spaced, low-crowned cheek teeth, these derived forms bore chisel-shaped teeth with much taller crowns that lost the ridge separating crown from root and overlapped to form a continuous surface for grinding tough plant food. This chewing apparatus, unusual among early ornithischians, foreshadowed the analogous dental batteries later evolved by hadrosaurs and ceratopsians.

Heyuanninae.description: Heyuanninae is a subfamily of oviraptorid dinosaurs, small bird-like theropods known from the Late Cretaceous of Asia, especially the Gobi Desert and southern China. Within Oviraptoridae it is traditionally set apart as the short-armed, mainly crestless branch, in contrast to the larger, long-armed, crested oviraptorines. Its members were small-handed and weakly clawed, with the hand progressively reduced across the group, and include such genera as Heyuannia, Conchoraptor, and Khaan. Like other oviraptorids they bore toothless, parrot-like beaks and are generally thought to have been primarily herbivorous or omnivorous, feeding on the tough, low-growing plants of the arid habitats where their fossils are most abundant. Some phylogenetic studies have questioned the clean split between crestless and crested oviraptorids, suggesting that this traditional division may be partly artificial.
diagnostic_features: Small body size with a low, usually uncrested or weakly crested skull
Progressive reduction and shortening of the manus, digit III reduced or lost

Hypsilophodontidae.description: Hypsilophodontidae is a traditionally used family of small-bodied, bipedal ornithopod dinosaurs. Historically it functioned as a wastebasket for a wide range of lightly built ornithischians from around the world, spanning the Middle Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous, but this broad grouping is now generally regarded as an unnatural assemblage. Modern phylogenetic analyses have drastically restricted the family, moving most former members into groups such as Thescelosauridae and Elasmaria, so that only Hypsilophodon itself and a handful of close relatives are retained. It is typically recovered as the earliest-diverging clade within Ornithopoda and the sister group to Iguanodontia. Its restricted membership remains unsettled, with proposed members drawn from the Barremian of Europe, including Hypsilophodon from the Isle of Wight along with such genera as Vectidromeus and Gideonmantellia, though the affinities of these smaller relatives are disputed.

Iguanodontia.description: Iguanodontia is a major clade of derived ornithopod dinosaurs that includes the lineage leading up to the duck-billed hadrosaurs. While the most primitive ornithopods were small bipeds, advanced iguanodontians became quadrupedal and grew to large body size, so the group spans everything from modest cursorial forms to some of the largest plant eaters of their era. Members were traditionally lumped into a superfamily and family of "iguanodontids," but phylogenetic studies have shown that assemblage to be a paraphyletic grade rather than a natural cluster of close relatives. Larger, more derived iguanodontians were bulk feeders, able to subsist on tough, low-nutrition vegetation thanks to a long gut passage time and an increasingly sophisticated chewing apparatus. They were among the most successful and widespread herbivores of the Cretaceous.

Jeholosauridae.description: Jeholosauridae is a family of small, herbivorous neornithischian dinosaurs that lived across East Asia during the Cretaceous Period, roughly from the Aptian to the Cenomanian. It is named for the genus Jeholosaurus, a lightly built early ornithischian. The group's exact makeup is unsettled: as first proposed it was defined to include the Chinese Changchunsaurus, the Mongolian Haya, and Yueosaurus alongside Jeholosaurus, but later analyses have rearranged these taxa. Some studies keep Changchunsaurus and Haya within the family while shifting Yueosaurus to the related Thescelosauridae, whereas other comprehensive analyses recover Changchunsaurus and Haya within Thescelosaurinae and restrict Jeholosauridae to Jeholosaurus and Yueosaurus. In these later trees the clade sits as an early-diverging lineage near the base of Neornithischia, stemward of Thescelosauridae and Cerapoda.

Jinfengopteryginae.description: Jinfengopteryginae is a subfamily of small, bird-like troodontid dinosaurs known from the Cretaceous of Eurasia. The group contains relatively few genera, among them Jinfengopteryx, the European Tamarro, and Liaoningvenator, with some analyses also referring Philovenator and several unnamed specimens to it. Its members were small-bodied, ranging from roughly 0.5 to 2 meters long, and, like other troodontids, bore a raised sickle claw on each foot. They were feathered, with plumage around the body and neck and especially long, vaned feathers along the tail, and are thought to have been about as capable in the air as gliding forms such as Microraptor. Distinguishing features cited for the group include large antorbital openings in the skull and a forked jugal bone. Unlike most troodontids, which were primarily carnivorous, some specimens preserve possible plant material in the gut, hinting at omnivory. The monophyly of the group is contested (see dispute).

Khebbashia.description: Khebbashia is a node-based clade of rebbachisaurid sauropods that unites the two most derived subfamilies, Limaysaurinae and Rebbachisaurinae, to the exclusion of the more basal rebbachisaurid forms. It is defined as the least inclusive clade containing Limaysaurus tessonei, Nigersaurus taqueti, and Rebbachisaurus garasbae, and the node-based framing keeps it distinct from the stem-based family Rebbachisauridae. Its members were medium-sized sauropods that lived during the Early Cretaceous of South America, Africa, and Europe. These were among the most specialized rebbachisaurids, notable for highly modified feeding apparatus, with broad batteries of closely packed teeth and slender limb proportions.

Lambeosaurinae.description: Lambeosaurinae is a group of crested hadrosaurid dinosaurs that includes Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, Hypacrosaurus, Parasaurolophus, Tsintaosaurus, Olorotitan, and the European and North African genera Arenysaurus and Ajnabia. Its members are set apart by elaborate hollow cranial crests that enclose looping extensions of the nasal passages, inferred to have functioned in vocalization and visual display. The group originated in Laurasia during the Late Cretaceous and was initially found across Europe and Asia. Around the Campanian, one lineage colonized western North America via Beringia and spread south to Mexico, radiating into a diverse array of body plans, while other members reached the Late Cretaceous islands of Europe and later crossed into northern Africa. Its internal classification into tribes such as Aralosaurini, Tsintaosaurini, Parasaurolophini, Lambeosaurini, and the sometimes-recognized Arenysaurini remains unsettled.

Leptoceratopsidae.description: Leptoceratopsidae is a family of neoceratopsian dinosaurs known from Asia, western North America, and possibly Europe. Its members closely resembled the horned dinosaurs' other relatives, such as the protoceratopsids and ceratopsids, but were more primitive and generally smaller. Definitive leptoceratopsids lived during the Late Cretaceous, roughly 83 to 66 million years ago, with the group ranging in age from the late Santonian Gryphoceratops — the oldest and probably smallest known member — to Leptoceratops at the very end of the period. Fragmentary material from North Carolina and Sweden may extend the family's range into eastern North America and Europe, suggesting complex patterns of dispersal across the isolated landmasses of the time.

Lessemsauridae.description: Lessemsauridae is a clade of early sauropodiform dinosaurs that lived from the Late Triassic into the Early Jurassic of Gondwana, with fossils known from Argentina, South Africa, and possibly Lesotho. It unites Lessemsaurus, Antetonitrus, and Ingentia, with Ledumahadi added shortly afterward and the genera Kholumolumo and Meroktenos later assigned to the group as well. Its members were quadrupeds among the first dinosaurs to reach truly large size, with Lessemsaurus estimated near 7 tonnes and Ledumahadi near 12. Unlike the columnar-limbed sauropods that followed, lessemsaurids retained somewhat flexed forelimbs, and they are further marked by highly pneumatic neck and back vertebrae, short but tall and robust cervicals, and a broadly expanded shoulder blade. Sitting on the boundary between sauropodiforms and true sauropods, the group is recovered either as the most basal sauropods or as their immediate sister lineage depending on how Sauropoda is defined.

Limaysaurinae.description: Limaysaurinae is a subfamily of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaurs, one of the two subfamilies recognized within the rebbachisaurid clade Khebbashia. It is a stem-based group that gathers those rebbachisaurids more closely related to Limaysaurus than to Nigersaurus, and in current usage is typically restricted to the South American genera Limaysaurus and Cathartesaura. Its members were medium-sized, long-necked sauropods that lived in Patagonia during the mid- to Late Cretaceous. Like other rebbachisaurids, they were among the last surviving diplodocoids, persisting alongside the titanosaurs until fairly late in the Cretaceous.

Lirainosaurinae.description: Lirainosaurinae is a subfamily of lithostrotian titanosaur sauropods known from the Late Cretaceous of Europe, spanning roughly the late Campanian to the early Maastrichtian. It groups a set of European titanosaurs—among them Lirainosaurus, Ampelosaurus, Atsinganosaurus, Lohuecotitan, and Paludititan—along with their common ancestor and all of its descendants. Its members are generally small- to medium-sized and gracile forms recovered from France, Spain, and Romania, distinguished by details of their teeth, vertebrae, and osteoderms. The subfamily's broader position among titanosaurs remains unsettled, having been recovered as intermediate between the Saltasauridae and clades such as Aeolosaurini and Lognkosauria.

Lithostrotia.description: Lithostrotia is a clade of derived titanosaur sauropods that lived through the Early and Late Cretaceous, encompassing much of the group's diversity from Malawisaurus through the more derived saltasauroids and colossosaurians. Its name means "inlaid with stones," referring to the bony osteoderms preserved in many of its members, though those osteoderms are not actually diagnostic of the clade: they appear sporadically inside and outside it and may have evolved more than once. The trait that truly sets it apart is its tail, with caudal vertebrae whose front faces are strongly concave, so that they socketed together, except for the most distal ones. The clade excludes more basal titanosaurs such as Andesaurus, Argentinosaurus, and Phuwiangosaurus, which retain flatter or only weakly hollowed tail vertebrae. Its boundaries remain unsettled, because the anchoring genus Malawisaurus may be a mix of unrelated remains, and different analyses have recovered Lithostrotia as anything from a small group to one taking in nearly all titanosaurs.

Lognkosauria.description: Lognkosauria is a clade of giant, long-necked sauropod dinosaurs within Titanosauria, encompassing Futalognkosaurus, Mendozasaurus and their close relatives. It includes some of the largest and heaviest land animals ever known, among them Argentinosaurus, Patagotitan, Puertasaurus, Notocolossus, Drusilasaura and Traukutitan, with Malawisaurus possibly related as well. Its members lived mainly in the Cretaceous of South America, with occurrences reported from Africa and possibly Asia. Lognkosaurians are set apart from other titanosaurs by the wide, unusually thick rib loops on their neck vertebrae, a relatively narrow neural canal, and huge vaulted neural arches. Their trunk vertebrae are also very broad, bearing wing-like lateral processes roughly level with the neural canal, and their rib cages are exceptionally wide.

Macronaria.description: Macronaria is a clade of sauropod dinosaurs that takes its name from the enlarged nasal opening of the skull, which exceeds the size of the eye socket. Nested within Neosauropoda as the sister group to Diplodocoidea, it encompasses Camarasauridae and Titanosauriformes, and so includes such animals as Camarasaurus, Brachiosaurus, and the titanosaurs, with camarasauromorphs forming its most basal branch. Macronarians lived from the Middle Jurassic through the end of the Cretaceous and have been found across the globe, from Argentina and the United States to Portugal, China, and Tanzania. In addition to their large nostrils, they are distinguished by box-like skulls bearing broad, spoon-shaped teeth, unlike the elongate skulls and peg-like teeth of the diplodocoids. Their body sizes diverged dramatically: some titanosaurs such as Argentinosaurus rank among the largest land animals ever to have existed, while others, including Saltasaurus and Magyarosaurus, dwindled to just a few metric tons.

Majungasaurinae.description: Majungasaurinae is a subfamily of abelisaurid theropods, one of the two main branches of the family Abelisauridae, and is defined as all abelisaurids more closely related to Majungasaurus than to Carnotaurus. It represents a largely Indo-Madagascan radiation of the Late Cretaceous whose members include Majungasaurus, Rajasaurus, Indosaurus, and Rahiolisaurus, alongside European forms such as Arcovenator. These were mid-sized, bipedal predators with tall, deep skulls and powerful jaws but greatly reduced, immobile forearms; their stout legs suited striding rather than fast running, and they are thought to have preyed mainly on the large sauropods they lived among. The group is set apart from its sister branch, the carnotaurines, chiefly by features of the frontal bones and braincase. Its ancestors originated in Gondwana and became distinct from their South American relatives as the southern landmasses broke apart.

Mamenchisauridae.description: Mamenchisauridae is a family of eusauropod dinosaurs known from the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous of Asia and Africa, best known for their proportionately extremely long necks. The group was predominantly a Chinese radiation, including such genera as Mamenchisaurus, Omeisaurus, Chuanjiesaurus, Eomamenchisaurus, and Tonganosaurus, but its range extended to the Tanzanian outlier Wamweracaudia and, based on fragmentary remains, into Siberia. Some members reached gigantic sizes, ranking among the largest of all sauropods. The family has historically been confused with the somphospondylan Euhelopus and its relatives, and some phylogenetic analyses have again recovered those Cretaceous forms as close relatives of the mamenchisaurids.

Maniraptora.description: Maniraptora is a clade of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs that includes birds along with the non-avian dinosaurs more closely related to birds than to the ornithomimosaurs. Its major subgroups are the dromaeosaurids, troodontids, oviraptorosaurs, therizinosaurs, and avialans (the bird lineage), with alvarezsauroids and Ornitholestes often included as well; together with its sister group Ornithomimosauria it forms the larger clade Maniraptoriformes. Maniraptorans first appear in the fossil record during the Jurassic and survive today as living birds. They are distinguished by long arms and three-fingered grasping hands, a half-moon-shaped wrist bone that allowed the hand to fold, and, in many lineages, a backward-pointing pubis unlike the forward-pointing hip of most other saurischians. Some form of feathers or downy covering appears to have been present across the group, and Maniraptora is the only dinosaur clade known to include flying members. Once assumed to be strictly meat-eaters, maniraptorans are now thought to have been ancestrally omnivorous, giving rise to several plant-eating groups while only the dromaeosaurids reverted to pure carnivory.
diagnostic_features: Elongated forelimbs relative to body size
Semilunate (half-moon shaped) carpal bone allowing wrist folding
Pennaceous feathers present in many lineages
Elongate and mobile manus
Opisthopubic pelvis (posteriorly directed pubis) in many taxa
Reduced or absent postorbital bar

references.title: Saurischian monophyly and the origin of birds
references.journal: Memoirs of the California Academy of Sciences

Maniraptoriformes.description: Maniraptoriformes is a clade of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs encompassing the ornithomimosaurs and the maniraptorans, the latter group including birds, the only dinosaur lineage still alive today. It is one of the more exclusive subgroups within Coelurosauria, defined as all descendants of the most recent common ancestor of the ornithomimosaurs and birds. Its members may have been united by the presence of pennaceous feathers and wings, and one proposed distinguishing trait is feathers homologous to those of modern birds. The now-abandoned grouping Bullatosauria, once erected to unite ornithomimosaurs and troodontids, is today regarded as synonymous with this clade.

Marginocephalia.description: Marginocephalia is a clade of ornithischian dinosaurs characterized by a bony shelf or margin at the back of the skull, a fringe that was most likely used for display. It contains two major groups: the thick-skulled Pachycephalosauria and the horned Ceratopsia. Its members were primarily herbivores, ranging from small facultative bipeds and quadrupeds in the more primitive forms to large, obligately quadrupedal animals among the more derived ones. The group first appeared in the Jurassic and became more common through the Cretaceous. The earliest marginocephalians are known from Asia, and the group later spread into North America.
diagnostic_features: Parietosquamosal shelf or frill projecting from the posterior margin of the skull
Rostral bone at the tip of the upper jaw (in ceratopsians) or thickened skull roof (in pachycephalosaurs)
Short postorbital region of the skull
Reduction of the supratemporal fenestra
Herbivorous dentition with leaf-shaped or shearing teeth

Massopoda.description: Massopoda is a clade of sauropodomorph dinosaurs that lived from the Late Triassic through the Late Cretaceous. It is defined as all sauropodomorphs more closely related to Saltasaurus than to Plateosaurus, and its name is a contraction of Massospondylidae and Sauropoda, two very different groups that both fall within it. Nested inside is the more exclusive Sauropodiformes, the most inclusive group that contains Saltasaurus but excludes Massospondylus. Its members range from small, bipedal massospondylids to the gigantic, quadrupedal true sauropods, and together they encompass the great majority of sauropodomorph diversity.
diagnostic_features: Anterior end of the premaxilla deflected to form an enlarged narial region
Reduced or absent lateral lamina of the prefrontal
Distal end of the tibia with a transversely expanded, sub-rectangular outline
Trend toward enlarged body size and graviportal limb proportions

Massospondylidae.description: Massospondylidae is a family of early massopod sauropodomorph dinosaurs that lived from the Late Triassic to the Early Jurassic, with a near-global spread that reached Asia, Africa, North America, South America, and Antarctica. It is defined as a stem-based group encompassing all animals more closely related to Massospondylus carinatus than to Plateosaurus or Saltasaurus. Large cladistic analyses of early sauropodomorphs consistently recover a core membership that includes Adeopapposaurus, Coloradisaurus, Glacialisaurus, Leyesaurus, Lufengosaurus, and the relatively basal Indian form Pradhania, with genera such as Mussaurus and Xixiposaurus also sometimes placed here. Its members were small to medium-sized, long-necked, facultatively bipedal herbivores or omnivores that represent an early-branching lineage of sauropodomorphs rather than close relatives of the true sauropods.

Strongly ventrally curved symphyseal end of the dentary
Cervical vertebrae 4 or 5 more than four times longer than the anterior centrum height
Lacrimal with a web of bone spanning the junction of its anterior and ventral rami

Megalosauria.description: Megalosauria is a node-based clade of tetanuran theropod dinosaurs, comprising the most recent common ancestor of Megalosaurus and Spinosaurus together with all of its descendants. It sits within the broader superfamily Megalosauroidea and unites two major lineages: the megalosaurids, large-bodied terrestrial predators such as Megalosaurus and Torvosaurus, and the specialized spinosaurids such as Spinosaurus. The more basal piatnitzkysaurids fall outside the clade, while Streptospondylus, known mainly from fragmentary remains, is difficult to place with confidence and is treated as a wildcard taxon near its base. Its members lived from the Middle Jurassic through the Late Cretaceous.

Lateral lamina of the maxilla forming a large shelf that obscures the anteroventral corner of the antorbital fossa
Broad midline depression on the basioccipital about two-thirds the width of the occipital condyle
Enlarged, subcircular third dentary alveolus
Iliac pubic peduncle with a length-to-width ratio of about 1.55 to 1.75
Stout, bar-like medial distal crest on the femur

Megalosauridae.description: Megalosauridae is a family of large-bodied carnivorous theropod dinosaurs, among the first major radiation of big predatory dinosaurs, appearing in the Middle Jurassic and persisting into the Late Jurassic. These relatively primitive basal tetanurans comprise two subfamilies, Megalosaurinae and Afrovenatorinae, together with the more basal Eustreptospondylus, whose placement remains unresolved. Long recognized mainly from Europe on the strength of fossils from France and the United Kingdom, the group is now known from North America, Africa and South America, and possibly Asia. Megalosaurids were obligate bipeds that reached especially giant size, with some members weighing more than a tonne. They are distinguished by a long, low skull with roughly a 3:1 length-to-height ratio and a relatively unornamented skull roof, bearing only very small crests or none at all. Within the broader group Megalosauria, the family is closely allied to the spinosaurids.
diagnostic_features: Humeral deltopectoral crest extending at least 0.52 of the way down the humeral shaft
Absence of a fibular anterolateral tubercle
Absence of the quadrate foramen
Paroccipital processes directed dorsolaterally to laterally
Well-defined longitudinal groove for neurovascular foramina on the lateral surface of the dentary
Ischial shaft curving anteroventrally, with the antitrochanter absent and the symphysis expanded as an apron

Megalosaurinae.description: Megalosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of Megalosauridae, a group of large, robust carnivorous theropod dinosaurs that lived from the Middle to Late Jurassic. It is defined as all megalosaurids more closely related to Megalosaurus than to Afrovenator, making it the counterpart to the subfamily Afrovenatorinae. Its members include Megalosaurus, Torvosaurus, Duriavenator, and Wiehenvenator, which were among the largest predators of their time, with some exceeding a tonne in weight. Their fossils come chiefly from Europe and North America, and scattered teeth suggest the group may have ranged more widely across the Jurassic world.
diagnostic_features: Premaxilla with a greater height-to-length ratio below the external naris than in other megalosaurids, giving a taller snout tip

Megalosauroidea.description: Megalosauroidea is a superfamily of basal tetanuran theropod dinosaurs that lived from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous. It is defined as all theropods sharing a more recent common ancestor with Megalosaurus than with Allosaurus or modern birds, and it brings together the family Piatnitzkysauridae with the clade Megalosauria, which unites the megalosaurids and the spinosaurids. Its members range from large-bodied terrestrial predators such as Megalosaurus and Torvosaurus to the elongate-snouted, likely semiaquatic spinosaurids, including Spinosaurus. Some analyses recover the traditional megalosauroids as paraphyletic with respect to Allosauroidea rather than as a single natural group. The name Spinosauroidea is sometimes used for the same assemblage but is treated as a junior synonym in most modern work.
diagnostic_features: U-shaped ventral process of the postorbital
Chevrons whose proximal articular surface lacks distinct anterior and posterior facets
Iliac pubic peduncle with a length-to-width ratio of about 1.3 to 1.4
Anterior dorsal vertebrae with prominent ventral keels inset from the lateral surfaces
Step-like ridge within the infrapostzygapophyseal fossa of the dorsal vertebrae
Dorsal neural spines about 1.4 to 1.7 times the centrum height

Megaraptora.description: Megaraptora is a clade of medium-to-large carnivorous theropod dinosaurs from the Cretaceous. They were most diverse in the early Late Cretaceous of South America, particularly Patagonia, but ranged widely, with basal members also known from Thailand, Japan, and Australia. Megaraptorans are distinguished by their powerfully built forelimbs, which were tipped with enormous, strongly curved claws on the first two fingers rather than being reduced as in most other large theropods. Their skeletons were heavily pneumatized, riddled with air pockets, and their slender legs and long foot bones suggest they were fast-running hunters. The clade contains the derived family Megaraptoridae, united by specialized adaptations of the arm and claws, together with more basal forms such as Fukuiraptor and Phuwiangvenator. Their broader relationships have long been disputed: once classified among the allosauroids, megaraptorans are now most often recovered within Coelurosauria, close to the tyrannosauroids.

Megaraptoridae.description: Megaraptoridae is the derived family within Megaraptora, a group of carnivorous theropod dinosaurs noted for their powerfully built forelimbs and enormous hand claws. It encompasses the more advanced megaraptorans, including Megaraptor, Orkoraptor, Murusraptor, Aerosteon, and the Australian Australovenator, while excluding the basal-most members Fukuiraptor and Phuwiangvenator. Its members are set apart by a distinctive ulna that is T-shaped in cross section, formed by a thin, blade-like olecranon crest and a perpendicular ridge called the lateral tuberosity, and by thin, oval-sectioned claws bearing asymmetric grooves and a sharp lower edge. Most are known only from fragmentary remains, but collectively they were medium to large predators with slender, running-adapted limbs and heavily air-filled bones. They ranked among the apex predators of Late Cretaceous Gondwana, reaching their greatest diversity in Patagonia and also occurring in Australia.

Metriacanthosauridae.description: Metriacanthosauridae is a family of allosauroid theropod dinosaurs that lived in Europe and Asia from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous. The family is split into two subgroups: Metriacanthosaurinae, containing forms such as Metriacanthosaurus, and a group of close relatives of Yangchuanosaurus that includes Sinraptor. Its members span a wide range of body sizes, and their most distinctive feature is their tall neural spines. The group's fossil record is largely confined to Asia, with a few members known from Europe, and phylogenetic evidence points to a Southeast Asian origin. Metriacanthosauridae is the senior synonym of Sinraptoridae.

Metriacanthosaurinae.description: Metriacanthosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies within Metriacanthosauridae, a family of allosauroid theropod dinosaurs that lived across Europe and Asia from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous. It comprises the metriacanthosaurids more closely related to Metriacanthosaurus than to the other subgroup's namesake, Yangchuanosaurus. Its members are set apart from the family's more basal forms chiefly by details of the skull, vertebrae, and hindlimb, including a ridged front border to the antorbital opening, a keeled underside to the front back-vertebrae, and distinctive proportions of the pubis, ischium, and lower leg. Like other metriacanthosaurids, these were carnivores whose most notable feature was their tall neural spines, and they spanned a wide range of body sizes.

Microraptorinae.description: Microraptorinae (also called Microraptoria) is a clade of small, basal dromaeosaurid theropods, best known from the Early Cretaceous Jehol Biota of Liaoning, China, with a few fragmentary members reported later and farther afield, including putative Late Cretaceous forms from North America. Its members were slender, long-limbed carnivores that ranged from some of the smallest known non-bird dinosaurs, such as Microraptor and Zhongjianosaurus, to larger genera like Tianyuraptor and Changyuraptor. The exceptional preservation of the Jehol deposits has captured extensive feathering, and several genera bear long pennaceous feathers on both the arms and legs, earning them the popular label "four-winged dinosaurs." Some, including Microraptor, appear to have used these surfaces to glide or launch from the ground, and perhaps for limited powered flight. The group is most often recovered as basal dromaeosaurids, though some researchers have placed it outside Dromaeosauridae proper.

Nemegtosauridae.description: Nemegtosauridae is a family of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs known chiefly from their distinctive skulls. Its core members are Nemegtosaurus and Quaesitosaurus of the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia, with Tapuiasaurus and Rapetosaurus sometimes included; the group is generally defined as all titanosaurs more closely related to Nemegtosaurus than to Saltasaurus. Its members have long, low skulls bearing slender, peg-like teeth crowded at the front of the jaws, a build that superficially resembles the diplodocids and long obscured their true relationships. For decades these animals were classified among the diplodocoids, but cladistic work has since placed them firmly within Titanosauria. The family's monophyly remains contested, as several analyses instead scatter its members across the titanosaur tree, and the skull of Nemegtosaurus has even been proposed to belong to the otherwise-headless Opisthocoelicaudia.

Neoceratopsia.description: Neoceratopsia is a clade of ceratopsian dinosaurs that takes in every member of the group except the earliest forms, Psittacosaurus and the chaoyangsaurids, and so encompasses all of the more derived horned dinosaurs. It spans small, basal taxa through to the large horned and frilled ceratopsids such as Triceratops. Within it, Euceratopsia unites the mostly small-bodied, largely North American Leptoceratopsidae with the more advanced ceratopsians, while the nested subgroup Coronosauria marks the first appearance of the bony neck frill and the fusion of the leading neck vertebrae to brace an increasingly heavy head. Neoceratopsians are set apart by a progressively enlarging skull and the growth of a frill extending back from the skull roof. Although the group originated in Asia, neoceratopsian fossils appear in North America by the middle of the Cretaceous, showing that it had dispersed across the Bering land bridge.

Development of a parietosquamosal frill from the rear of the skull

Neornithischia.description: Neornithischia ("new ornithischians") is a clade of ornithischian dinosaurs and the sister group of the armored Thyreophora within the larger clade Genasauria. It brings together a variety of basal, small-bodied early-diverging forms historically lumped together as "hypsilophodonts" — including the thescelosaurids — with the more derived Cerapoda, which in turn splits into the bird-footed Ornithopoda and the Marginocephalia, the latter comprising the dome-headed pachycephalosaurs and the horned ceratopsians. Members are set apart by a thicker layer of asymmetrical enamel on the inner face of their lower teeth, which wore unevenly during chewing to develop sharp ridges that let them break down tougher plant food than other dinosaurs. The earliest neornithischians were small, gracile, cursorial bipeds, but the clade went on to encompass some of the most successful herbivore radiations of the Mesozoic, among them the duck-billed, dome-headed, and horned dinosaurs.

Neosauropoda.description: Neosauropoda is a clade of sauropod dinosaurs that contains the majority of sauropod genera and is divided into two major subgroups, Diplodocoidea and Macronaria. Its members include familiar long-necked giants such as Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, and Diplodocus, as well as some of the largest land animals ever to have lived, among them Argentinosaurus, Patagotitan, and Sauroposeidon. Neosauropods arose in the Early Jurassic, quickly becoming the dominant large herbivores, and persisted until the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction; diplodocids and brachiosaurids made up much of the group during the Jurassic before being widely replaced by titanosaurs through the Cretaceous. Like all sauropods they shared the basic body plan of great size, long necks, and columnar legs, but they are set apart by a suite of derived features of the skull, teeth, hand, and hindlimb, including the loss of tooth denticles and a hand reduced to two or fewer wrist bones.
diagnostic_features: Tooth crowns lacking marginal denticles
Carpus reduced to two or fewer ossifications
Reduction of the manual phalanges
External nares retracted and dorsally positioned

Neotheropoda.description: Neotheropoda, meaning "new theropods," is a clade that encompasses nearly all theropod dinosaurs, from the small, lightly built coelophysoids of the Late Triassic to the more advanced ceratosaurs and tetanurans, the latter of which ultimately gave rise to modern birds. Its members are distinguished by a reduction of several foot bones, which left the characteristic three-toed (tridactyl) footprints associated with theropods. It is the only group of theropods to survive the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event, after which it radiated into the dominant terrestrial predators of the Jurassic and Cretaceous. The more derived members form the clade Averostra, which unites the ceratosaurs and the tetanurans; by the Early Jurassic the non-averostran lineages had died out.

Noasauridae.description: Noasauridae is a family of small to medium-sized ceratosaurian theropods closely related to the short-armed abelisaurids, but built along more conventional lines: nimble, lightly constructed animals whose feet show running adaptations such as an elongated central foot bone. The family is usually divided into two subfamilies. The Noasaurinae are Late Cretaceous forms of the southern continents and islands, including South America, Madagascar, and India, best represented by Masiakasaurus with its downturned jaw and forward-splaying teeth; some, such as the sickle-clawed members, bore an enlarged hand claw. The Elaphrosaurinae, whose best-known members lived earlier in the Jurassic, developed long necks, small skulls, and toothless beaked jaws, and were largely herbivorous as adults. The group is highly disparate, spanning tiny predators under 1.5 meters long to much larger genera exceeding 6 meters, and its exact composition, including controversial members like Deltadromeus, remains debated.
Noasauridae.authors: Bonaparte, J. F.; Powell, J. E.
diagnostic_features: Small body size and lightly constructed, gracile skeleton
Elongate cervical vertebrae relative to abelisaurids
Strongly modified, enlarged manual or pedal ungual in some members
Slender, cursorial hindlimb proportions

Noasaurinae.description: Noasaurinae is a subfamily of small ceratosaurian theropod dinosaurs that formed a Late Cretaceous radiation across the southern landmasses, with members known from South America, Madagascar, and India (then an island near Madagascar), plus indeterminate remains later reported from Australia. Because many of its members are fragmentary, much of their appearance and biology is inferred from Masiakasaurus, the most complete noasaurine. These animals generally had bodies resembling more conventional theropods, but with unusual jaws: Masiakasaurus bore a downturned lower jaw whose long, spoon-shaped front teeth splayed forward and carried serrations along their outer edges. At least one member, Noasaurus, had a large, deeply curved sickle-shaped hand claw, while Velocisaurus took the group's foot-bone reductions to an extreme. Their diet is uncertain, with proposals ranging from fish to insects and other small prey.

diagnostic_features: Reduced proximal end of metatarsal II
Procumbent, forward-projecting anterior dentary teeth in several members
Strongly recurved, enlarged pedal or manual ungual
Cervical vertebrae with well-developed epipophyses

Nodosauridae.description: Nodosauridae is a family of armored, quadrupedal, herbivorous ankylosaurian dinosaurs known from the Late Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous of Asia, Europe, North America, and possibly South America. Like their close relatives the ankylosaurids, nodosaurids were heavily built and clad in rows of bony nodules and spines set into the skin and sheathed in keratin, but they lacked the mace-like bony tail club of the ankylosaurids and instead retained a more flexible tail. Many bore prominent spikes projecting outward from the neck and shoulders, and they carried a narrower, more elongate skull than the broad-headed ankylosaurids. The family is traditionally composed of the spiny, basal polacanthines, together with the panoplosaurine and struthiosaurine lineages of the more derived Nodosaurinae. One exceptionally preserved nodosaurid, the "mummy" of Borealopelta, retains its armor in life position along with keratin and skin traces that record a reddish, countershaded coloration.
diagnostic_features: Absence of a bony tail club
Narrow, anteroposteriorly elongate skull
Prominent laterally projecting cervical, shoulder, and flank spines in many taxa
Closed lateral temporal fenestra concealed by cranial armor

Opisthocoelicaudiinae.description: Opisthocoelicaudiinae is a subfamily of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous, with fossils known from Mongolia, Argentina, and the United States. Studies have grouped genera such as Alamosaurus and Opisthocoelicaudia within it, and its members are large, robustly built sauropods. They are distinguished above all by opisthocoelous front tail vertebrae — ball-and-socket joints that face the opposite way to the socket-and-ball (procoelous) arrangement seen in most other advanced titanosaurs — along with stout, columnar limbs. Their hands were highly reduced, lacking wrist bones and finger phalanges. The group's relationships remain debated: some analyses place it as a close relative of the saltasaurines, while others have instead linked Opisthocoelicaudia to other Asian sauropods such as Nemegtosaurus and Quaesitosaurus.
diagnostic_features: Opisthocoelous anterior caudal vertebrae
Robust, columnar limb bones
Strongly developed neural-spine bifurcation reduced or absent
Posteriorly positioned, dorsally directed neural spines on anterior caudals

Ornithischia.description: Ornithischia, meaning "bird-hipped," is one of the two great branches of dinosaurs, encompassing a mostly herbivorous radiation whose members are known from every continent and across an enormous range of sizes. The group takes its name from a pelvis superficially resembling that of birds, though this is a case of convergence, since birds are in fact theropods and only distantly related. Its major subgroups include the horn-faced ceratopsians, the thick-domed pachycephalosaurs, the armored thyreophorans such as stegosaurs and ankylosaurs, and the ornithopods, alongside a scattering of small, early-diverging forms near the base of the group. The earliest members were lightly built bipeds around one to two meters long with long counterbalancing tails, but later lineages grew far larger and many became quadrupedal. Most were browsers or grazers of ground-level plants, though a few were opportunistic omnivores. Several ornithischians are known to have lived in herds, sometimes with juveniles flocking apart from adults, and exceptionally preserved specimens reveal a range of skin coverings from mosaic scales to disputed filamentous, quill-like structures.
diagnostic_features: Opisthopubic pelvis with the pubis rotated posteriorly to parallel the ischium
Predentary bone capping the tip of the lower jaw
Leaf-shaped cheek-tooth crowns with denticulate margins
Palpebral (supraorbital) bone roofing the orbit
Ossified epaxial tendons along the vertebral column in many members

Ornithomimidae.description: Ornithomimidae is a family of theropod dinosaurs that bore a superficial resemblance to modern ostriches, earning them the nickname "ostrich mimics." They were fleet-footed, likely omnivorous or herbivorous animals known mainly from the Late Cretaceous of Laurasia, in what is now Asia and North America, with a few reports from the Early Cretaceous of Australia. Members had small skulls with large eyes set atop long, slender necks, and all bore toothless, keratinous beaks. Their forelimbs were long and slender with powerful claws, while their long, muscular hindlimbs and elongate feet made them among the fastest of all dinosaurs, and like many coelurosaurs their bodies were feathered rather than scaly. The family includes Ornithomimus, Struthiomimus, Gallimimus, and numerous related genera, though beyond a reliably basal Archaeornithomimus its internal relationships remain largely unresolved.

Edentulous skull bearing a keratinous beak
Elongate, gracile, cursorial hindlimbs
Long neck formed of elongate cervical vertebrae

Ornithomimosauria.description: Ornithomimosauria, the "ostrich dinosaurs," is a group of theropod dinosaurs that bore a superficial resemblance to modern ostriches. Its members lived during the Cretaceous of Laurasia, now Asia, Europe, and North America, with possible records from Africa, first appearing in the Early Cretaceous and persisting until the close of the period. The most primitive forms, such as Pelecanimimus and Shenzhousaurus, retained small teeth, while the more derived species of the family Ornithomimidae, including Gallimimus and Struthiomimus, had toothless beaks. Ornithomimosaurs were lightly built and long-limbed, with feathered bodies and long, powerful hind legs that likely made them among the fastest of all dinosaurs. Numerous specimens preserving gastroliths in the gut, together with their peculiar hook-like hands, suggest that most were herbivores or omnivores rather than the carnivores typical of theropods.
diagnostic_features: Elongate cervical vertebrae forming a long, gracile neck
Reduced or absent dentition, with a keratinous beak in derived members
Small, lightly built skull with large orbits
Long, slender, cursorial hindlimbs
Manus with subequal, elongate metacarpals and weakly curved unguals

Ornithopoda.description: Ornithopoda, meaning "bird feet," is a clade of ornithischian dinosaurs that includes the iguanodonts and hadrosaurs along with a range of smaller, more basal members. Known worldwide, ornithopods were among the most successful herbivorous dinosaurs of the Cretaceous, ranging from small, fast-running Jurassic bipeds to the large quadrupedal duck-billed hadrosaurs, some of which grew as heavy as medium-sized sauropods before dying out in the end-Cretaceous extinction. Their key evolutionary advantage was a progressively refined chewing apparatus, ultimately the most sophisticated of any non-avian dinosaur, that let them process tough plant material through a grinding, transverse jaw action. They are further distinguished by their characteristic birdlike feet, the lack of body armor, an elongated pubis, and the absence of an opening in the lower jaw. Early forms were mainly browsers or fruit-eaters, while larger, more derived members were bulk feeders capable of subsisting on coarse, low-nutrient vegetation.
diagnostic_features: Pleurokinetic skull permitting lateral rotation of the maxillae during chewing
Jugal positioned well above the level of the quadrate condyles
Lowered mandibular glenoid, offsetting the jaw joint below the tooth row
Dentary crowns lacking a primary labial swelling; dentary tooth roots curved
Elongate prepubic process of the pubis

Orodrominae.description: Orodrominae is one of the two subfamilies of Thescelosauridae, a group of small plant-eating neornithischian dinosaurs from the Cretaceous of North America. It gathers genera such as Orodromeus, Oryctodromeus, Zephyrosaurus, and Albertadromeus, and is defined as the thescelosaurids more closely related to Orodromeus than to Thescelosaurus. Like other thescelosaurids, its members were highly selective browsers that likely fed mainly on soft, pulpy plant material. Several orodromines show skeletal features associated with a burrowing lifestyle; Oryctodromeus in particular has been found preserved inside fossil burrows, its bones packed tightly together in a way rarely seen when a carcass is left exposed.

Oviraptoridae.description: Oviraptoridae is a family of bird-like, feathered maniraptoran theropods known only from the Late Cretaceous of Asia, with the finest specimens coming from the Gobi Desert of Mongolia and northwestern China. Most were fairly small animals, roughly one to two meters long, with toothless parrot-like beaks and, in many genera, an elaborate bony head crest resembling that of a cassowary. They were probably herbivorous or omnivorous rather than the egg predators once imagined, and are famous for fossils preserving adults brooding atop circular clutches of eggs, a posture seen today only among birds. The family is traditionally split into two subfamilies: the small, short-armed, mostly crestless Heyuanninae and the larger, long-armed, crested Citipatiinae, with several basal genera falling outside both groups.
diagnostic_features: Deep, foreshortened, box-like skull, frequently bearing a tall bony crest
Robust, edentulous, downturned beak with a shortened snout
Pair of tooth-like premaxillary processes projecting into the palate
Shortened neck and tail relative to basal oviraptorosaurs

Oviraptorosauria.description: Oviraptorosauria is a clade of feathered, bipedal maniraptoran theropods from the Cretaceous of what are now Asia and North America, and among the dinosaur groups closest to the ancestry of birds. Its members are distinguished by short, deep, parrot-like skulls, often bearing bony crests, with jaws that carry few or no teeth. The most primitive forms, such as Caudipteryx and Incisivosaurus, retain a few front teeth, in the latter enlarged into prominent bucktoothed incisors, while more derived members are toothless. The group spans a wide size range, from turkey-sized early-diverging species to the eight-meter Gigantoraptor, and its more advanced members are typically divided between the toothless caenagnathids and the crested oviraptorids. Several species are preserved with pennaceous feathers on the wings and tail, and oviraptorids are famously known from specimens frozen in a brooding posture over circular clutches of eggs. Their diet appears to have been generalized, ranging from herbivory to omnivory, with some evidence of small vertebrates and gastroliths.
diagnostic_features: Short, deep skull with a reduced dentition trending toward edentulism
Downturned, robust dentary with an extensive symphysis
Pneumatic, tall-spined cervical vertebrae with a long, mobile neck
Shortened tail, in derived members terminating in coossified distal caudals
Large, three-fingered grasping hand (reduced in derived oviraptorids)

Pachycephalosauria.description: Pachycephalosauria, meaning "thick-headed lizards," is a clade of ornithischian dinosaurs that together with the horned ceratopsians makes up the group Marginocephalia. Its members were bipedal herbivores and omnivores, mostly small animals in the range of 2 to 3 meters long, and lived exclusively in the Northern Hemisphere during the Cretaceous, with all known genera coming from North America and Asia. They are best known for their heavily ossified skulls, which may be domed, flat, or wedge-shaped depending on the species and are often ringed with bony nodes and spikes. Because most specimens consist only of these durable skull caps, the group is classified almost entirely on cranial features, and flat-headed forms may in some cases represent juveniles of dome-headed adults. The function of the thickened dome has been much debated, with intraspecific head-butting or flank-butting the leading hypotheses. Well-known members include Pachycephalosaurus and Stegoceras.
diagnostic_features: Dramatically thickened frontoparietal dome on the skull roof
Peripheral ornamentation of nodes and horns around the dome margin
Wide, shelf-like squamosal
Relatively large orbits
Bipedal stance with stiffened tail
Broad body with flared iliac blades

Pachycephalosauridae.description: Pachycephalosauridae is a family of dome-headed ornithischian dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of western North America and central Asia. Its members are small bipedal, herbivorous to omnivorous animals distinguished by heavily thickened skulls formed by the fusion of the frontal and parietal bones and the closing of the supratemporal fenestrae; the skull roof may be raised into a full dome or remain flat or wedge-shaped, and is typically ringed by blunt horns and nodes on the squamosals, jugals, and postorbitals. The family spans basal, Stegoceras-grade forms with incipient or flat skull roofs through the fully domed subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae, defined as sister to Stegoceras and encompassing the more derived genera such as Prenocephale, Tylocephale, and Pachycephalosaurus. Because most specimens consist only of the durable frontoparietal dome, classification within the group relies almost entirely on cranial features, and several genera once assigned here have since been reidentified as other kinds of animals. The domes are widely interpreted as structures used in head- or flank-butting contests, an idea supported by the high frequency of healed cranial injuries found on them.
diagnostic_features: Thickened frontoparietal ranging from flat to fully domed
Squamosal developed into a deep plate on the occiput with enlarged upper-outer corners
Variably developed nodes, in rows or clusters, on the squamosal
Broad squamosal exposure on the occiput
Supratemporal fenestrae ranging from open to closed

Pachycephalosaurinae.description: Pachycephalosaurinae is the derived subfamily of pachycephalosaurid dinosaurs, encompassing the dome-headed members of the group that are more closely related to Pachycephalosaurus than to the earlier-branching Stegoceras. Its members were small, bipedal, plant-eating ornithischians known from the Cretaceous of North America and Asia, distinguished by a thickened skull roof formed from the fused and greatly enlarged frontal and parietal bones. Alongside the classic high-domed forms, the subfamily also takes in several flatter-skulled taxa that fall on the Pachycephalosaurus side of the family tree, some of which may represent juveniles or females of domed species. The heavily ossified skulls are typically ornamented with blunt horns and nodes around their margins, and the domes themselves have often been interpreted as weapons used in intraspecific head- or flank-butting.
diagnostic_features: Fully domed frontoparietal (sensu Sereno, 1998)
Supratemporal fenestrae closed in adults
Parietosquamosal contact positioned caudodorsal to the occiput
Epaxial muscle scars restricted to a position dorsolateral to the foramen magnum

Parankylosauria.description: Parankylosauria is an early-diverging clade of armored dinosaurs that lived across the former southern supercontinent of Gondwana — in what are now South America, Antarctica, and Australia — during the Cretaceous. It is recovered as the first lineage to branch off from the rest of the ankylosaurs, making it the sister group to Euankylosauria, the ankylosaurids and nodosaurids that dominate the Northern Hemisphere. Its members, including Stegouros, Antarctopelta, and Kunbarrasaurus, were relatively small, roughly 1.5 to 4 meters long, and retained a number of primitive traits shared with early armored dinosaurs and stegosaurs but lost in other ankylosaurs, such as longer, more slender limbs and simple, narrow hips. Their skulls bear elongate snouts with distinctive narrow nasal bones and lack the elaborate horns and bosses seen in other ankylosaurs. Rather than a knob-like tail club, several parankylosaurs carried a frond-like tail weapon known as a macuahuitl, formed from flattened osteoderms arranged along both sides of the tail.

Paraves.description: Paraves is a widespread group of bird-like theropod dinosaurs that originated in the Middle Jurassic. It includes the dromaeosaurids, troodontids, and anchiornithids, possibly the scansoriopterygids, and the avialans, the last of which encompass Archaeopteryx and the more than 11,000 species of living birds. Its members are small, gracile, feathered animals, and many bear long winged forelimbs, though these became reduced in flightless forms and in lineages that branched off before the origin of flight. The best-known paravian trait is an enlarged, strongly curved sickle-shaped claw on the second toe, held clear of the ground when walking; in many basal forms only the third and fourth toes bore the animal's weight. Most of the earliest members were carnivorous, though some smaller troodontids and early avialans were omnivorous. The precise relationships among paravian groups remain an active subject of research.
diagnostic_features: Elongate penultimate manual and pedal phalanges
Forelimbs elongate relative to body size, bearing pennaceous feathers
Reduced number of maxillary and dentary teeth in many members
Distally placed obturator process on the ischium

Parvicursorinae.description: Parvicursorinae is the derived subfamily of alvarezsaurids that dominated the Late Cretaceous of Asia, with a few members in North America. It contains the smallest, most specialized alvarezsaurs, in which the forelimb is reduced to a stout, single-clawed digging or probing tool and the hindlimb is elongate and extensively fused. Defined as the most inclusive clade containing Parvicursor but not Patagonykus, it is the senior name for the derived Mongolian radiation and is used in preference to the synonymous Mononykinae; its internal relationships are poorly resolved and largely form a polytomy.
Parvicursorinae.authors: Karhu, A. A.; Rautian, A. S.

Absent or reduced, laterally facing fibular facet of the astragalus
Broad ascending process of the astragalus covering most of the anterior surface of the distal tibia
Notch on the medial edge of the ascending process of the astragalus
Metatarsal III not reaching the proximal end of the metatarsus
Penultimate manual phalanges with a straight shaft

Patagonykinae.description: Patagonykinae is a subfamily of large-bodied, plesiomorphic South American alvarezsaurids comprising Patagonykus and Bonapartenykus from the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia. It groups the biggest known alvarezsaurs, which retain comparatively robust proportions relative to the miniaturized Asian parvicursorines.

Piatnitzkysauridae.description: Piatnitzkysauridae is a family of comparatively small, basal megalosauroid theropods that lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic. It comprises only three to four genera: Piatnitzkysaurus and Condorraptor from the Cañadón Asfalto Formation of Argentina, Marshosaurus from the Morrison Formation of the United States, and possibly the Chinese Xuanhanosaurus, whose fragmentary remains leave its placement uncertain. These were among the first large theropods known from South America and are seen as evidence for a radiation of basal tetanurans in the Middle Jurassic. The group is usually recovered as the basalmost branch of Megalosauroidea and the sister group of Megalosauria, though it also shares some features with allosaurs, including a sigmoidal (S-shaped) humerus, and a few analyses instead place it within Allosauroidea. Piatnitzkysaurids can be distinguished by details of the maxilla, paradental plates, axis vertebra, dorsal neural spines, and the forward-canted condyles of the humerus.
Piatnitzkysauridae.authors: Carrano, M. T.; Benson, R. B. J.; Sampson, S. D.
diagnostic_features: Two parallel rows of nutrient foramina on the lateral surface of the maxilla
Vertically striated (ridged) paradental plates
Reduced atlas-axis parapophyses
Anteriorly inclined posterior dorsal neural spines
Canted distal humeral condyles

Plateosauria.description: Plateosauria is a large, node-based clade within Sauropodomorpha, conventionally defined as the last common ancestor of Plateosaurus and Massospondylus (or, in some analyses, Jingshanosaurus) together with all of that ancestor's descendants. So defined, it unites the Plateosauridae with the more inclusive Massopoda and takes in Late Triassic and Early Jurassic sauropodomorphs such as Coloradisaurus, Euskelosaurus, Jingshanosaurus, Massospondylus, Mussaurus, Sellosaurus, and Yunnanosaurus, while its descendant lineages also encompass the giant, long-necked true sauropods. It groups the more derived, generally herbivorous members of the lineage, spanning the transition from largely bipedal early forms toward larger-bodied, increasingly quadrupedal ones. In all, it accounts for the bulk of sauropodomorph diversity above the earliest, most basal grade.
diagnostic_features: Leaf-shaped cheek teeth with coarse marginal denticles set at an angle to the crown margin
Robust, weight-bearing limb proportions
Enlarged, broad-bladed manual pollex
Anteroposteriorly elongate, low ilium

Plateosauridae.description: Plateosauridae is a family of plateosaurian sauropodomorph dinosaurs known from the Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic of Europe, Greenland, Africa, and Asia, built around the well-known Plateosaurus. Although many early dinosaurs have been referred to the family over the years, its membership is now restricted, anchored by Plateosaurus and its close relative Issi, with several historically included taxa such as Yimenosaurus and Euskelosaurus regarded as uncertain or disputed; some analyses also recover forms like Macrocollum and Unaysaurus within the group. Its members are medium- to large-bodied, long-necked, facultatively bipedal herbivores. Some workers treat the older concept Prosauropoda as effectively a synonym of Plateosauridae, since both come to contain the same set of taxa. Within the broader clade Plateosauria, the family is typically placed as the sister group to the more sauropod-like Massopoda.
diagnostic_features: Large external naris
Transversely broad, leaf-shaped cheek teeth with coarse marginal denticles
Robust, elongate cervical vertebrae
Large, recurved manual pollex ungual

Proceratosauridae.description: Proceratosauridae is a family of tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaurs that lived from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, representing some of the earliest and most basal members of the tyrannosaur lineage. It is defined as all theropods more closely related to Proceratosaurus than to Tyrannosaurus, Allosaurus, Compsognathus, Coelurus, Ornithomimus, or Deinonychus. Unlike the giant, short-armed tyrannosaurids that came later, proceratosaurids were generally small and retained fairly long, three-fingered arms capable of grasping prey, though possible members such as Yutyrannus and Sinotyrannus grew much larger. The group is distinguished above all by an elaborate midline crest along the nasals and by greatly elongated external nares. Genera commonly assigned to the family include Proceratosaurus, Guanlong, Kileskus, and Sinotyrannus, with taxa such as Stokesosaurus, Juratyrant, and Dilong recovered here in some analyses.
Proceratosauridae.authors: Rauhut, O. W. M.; Milner, A. C.; Moore-Fay, S.
diagnostic_features: Strongly enlarged external nares
Slight anterior offset of the maxillary ascending ramus from the anterior margin of the maxillary body
Midline cranial crest or horn on the nasals

Protoceratopsidae.description: Protoceratopsidae is a family of small, primitive horned dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of Asia, with most specimens recovered from China and Mongolia and dating to roughly 75 to 71 million years ago. Its members were modest in size, around 1 to 2.5 meters long, and included Protoceratops, Bagaceratops, and Breviceratops. Like all ceratopsians they were herbivores equipped with a hooked beak and slicing tooth batteries, but their bony frill and horns were far smaller than those of the later, larger ceratopsids. Distinctive features include a wedge-shaped snout carrying tall, narrow nostrils set high on the skull, an unusually small antorbital fenestra, and a maxillary sinus not seen in other ceratopsians. Along the backbone, the tail bore very long neural spines that made it tall and flattened from side to side. The concept has narrowed over time, with genera such as Leptoceratops and Montanoceratops now assigned instead to the mostly North American Leptoceratopsidae.
diagnostic_features: Solid (unfenestrated or minimally fenestrated) parietosquamosal frill
Deep, narrow snout with a prominent nasal horn or boss in some members
Reduced or absent premaxillary dentition
Tall neural spines over the sacrum and tail

Rebbachisauridae.description: Rebbachisauridae is a family of diplodocoid sauropods known from fragmentary remains from the Cretaceous of Gondwana and beyond, with records in South America, Africa, Europe, and possibly North America and Central Asia. They include such genera as Nigersaurus and Limaysaurus, and are grouped into subfamilies, chiefly the Limaysaurinae and the Rebbachisaurinae, both nested within the clade Khebbashia. Though firmly placed within the superfamily Diplodocoidea, rebbachisaurids lack the divided (bifid) cervical neural spines of the diplodocids and dicraeosaurids and are regarded as more primitive than those groups. They are set apart from other sauropods by their distinctive teeth, which show low-angle internal wear facets and asymmetrical enamel, and some members such as Nigersaurus evolved dental batteries comparable to those of hadrosaurs and ceratopsians. Restricted to the early and middle part of the Late Cretaceous, they were the last surviving diplodocoids and lived alongside the titanosaurs until fairly late in the period.
diagnostic_features: Loss of the hyposphene-hypantrum accessory articulations in the anterior caudal vertebrae (retained in the basalmost members)
Spinodiapophyseal lamina present and often festooned on the dorsal neural spines
Middle caudal centra nearly cylindrical with a flattened ventral margin
Scapular acromion expanded, with a racquet-shaped distal scapular blade in many taxa

Rebbachisaurinae.description: Rebbachisaurinae is a subfamily of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaurs, one of the two branches of the clade Khebbashia alongside Limaysaurinae. It groups forms more closely related to Rebbachisaurus than to Limaysaurus, a largely Euro-African assemblage that includes Nigersaurus, Demandasaurus, and Tataouinea and ranged across South America, Africa, and Europe during the Cretaceous. Like other rebbachisaurids, these sauropods lacked the divided cervical neural spines of their diplodocid and dicraeosaurid relatives, and they bore distinctive teeth with asymmetrical enamel and low-angle internal wear facets. Some members, most notably Nigersaurus, developed dental batteries reminiscent of those in hadrosaurs and ceratopsians, an unusual feeding adaptation for a sauropod. As rebbachisaurids, they were among the last surviving diplodocoids, persisting alongside the titanosaurs until relatively late in the Cretaceous.
diagnostic_features: Deep centroprezygapophyseal fossa on the middle and posterior dorsal vertebrae
Divided centropostzygapophyseal lamina on the middle and posterior dorsal neural arches
Anterior caudal vertebrae with a triangular lateral expansion of the neural spine

Rhabdodontidae.description: Rhabdodontidae is a family of herbivorous iguanodontian ornithopods, ranging in adult body length from about 1.6 to 6 meters, that are best known from the Late Cretaceous of the European archipelago. Its members include Rhabdodon, Zalmoxes, Mochlodon, Matheronodon, and Transylvanosaurus, though the earliest stem forms appeared as far back as the Early Cretaceous. These were stocky, deep-skulled animals resembling robust iguanodonts, with a simple dentition of spade- or leaf-shaped teeth bearing a distinctive ridge pattern that worked as a powerful scissors-like shear against tough, fibrous island plants. They are also set apart by uniquely shaped femur, humerus, and ulna bones. Isolated on islands within the western Tethyan archipelago, rhabdodontids formed a characteristic element of insular European faunas, with the smaller eastern genera contrasting against the giant western Rhabdodon, before hadrosaurs replaced them as the dominant browsing herbivores near the close of the Cretaceous.
Rhabdodontidae.authors: Weishampel, D. B.; Jianu, C.; Csiki, Z.; Norman, D. B.

Strongly reduced number of tooth positions

Rhabdodontomorpha.description: Rhabdodontomorpha is a clade of early-diverging iguanodontian ornithopods, small to large plant-eaters thought to have split from other iguanodont lineages as far back as the Middle Jurassic. It brings together the family Rhabdodontidae, whose short-snouted members such as Zalmoxes and Mochlodon are known largely from Europe, and the family Tenontosauridae, a North American radiation built around Tenontosaurus and its relatives that has been tentatively recovered as a basal branch of the group. Iani, from North America, is interpreted as a transitional form linking the tenontosaurids to the rhabdodontids. Other members reach into Gondwana, including the Australian Fostoria. Together these animals span much of the Cretaceous and retain a number of plesiomorphic ornithopod features.

Rinconsauria.description: Rinconsauria is a clade of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of South America. Its members are all relatively small for titanosaurs, generally less than about 11 meters long. The group is anchored on Rinconsaurus and Muyelensaurus, the two genera used to define it, but its wider membership is highly unstable: various phylogenetic analyses have placed more than twenty other titanosaur genera within it, and few of those assignments are consistent from one study to the next. Several analyses recover it as the sister group of Lognkosauria within the larger clade Colossosauria, while others tie it closely to the Aeolosaurini, at times finding that tribe nested inside Rinconsauria.

diagnostic_features: Suboval tooth crowns with labial and lingual faces differentiated by crests
Bony processes supporting the postzygapophyseal facets in the middle caudal vertebrae

Riojasauridae.description: Riojasauridae is a small family of sauropodomorph dinosaurs that lived during the Late Triassic, from the late Carnian into the Norian. It contains only two genera, Riojasaurus and Eucnemesaurus, whose fossils come from the Los Colorados Formation of La Rioja Province, Argentina, and the Lower Elliot Formation of South Africa, respectively. As sauropodomorphs rather than true sauropods, these were heavily built, medium- to large-bodied plant-eaters that were much smaller than the giant sauropods of later periods and may not have been fully committed to walking on all fours. The group is defined as a stem lineage within Massopoda, an early radiation of long-necked herbivores. Its precise placement remains unsettled, shifting in successive analyses between an early-branching position near Massospondylidae and a more crownward one closer to the sauropod line.
diagnostic_features: Tall crest-like lesser (anterior) trochanter of the femur, higher than wide
Large posterior proximal tubercle on the femur
Rounded, convex profile of the fourth trochanter of the femur
Heavily built, weight-bearing postcranium
