Saltasauridae.description: Saltasauridae is a family of armored, herbivorous titanosaurian sauropods from the Late Cretaceous, known from fossils across South America, North America, Africa, Asia, and Europe. It splits into two subfamilies: the Saltasaurinae, which includes the often small and armored Saltasaurus, Neuquensaurus, and Rocasaurus, and the Opisthocoelicaudiinae, which includes larger forms such as Opisthocoelicaudia and the giant Alamosaurus. As sauropods they were quadrupeds with small heads, peg-like teeth, long necks, and counterbalancing tails, and were among the last of their kind, persisting until the very end of the Cretaceous. They are recognized by convexities in certain tail vertebrae and by distinctive markings on the coracoid bones of the shoulder. Many members bore bony scutes, or osteoderms, embedded in the skin of their backs, though such armor has not been found in every genus and its distribution across the group remains uncertain.
diagnostic_features: Six co-ossified sacral vertebrae
Strongly procoelous caudal vertebrae with prominent distal condyles
Osteoderms present, including large and small morphotypes
Posterior dorsal vertebrae with reduced neural spines

Saltasaurinae.description: Saltasaurinae is a subfamily of titanosaurian sauropods from the Late Cretaceous, ranging from the early Campanian to the Maastrichtian, roughly 80 to 66 million years ago. Its members are among the smallest of the sauropods, retaining the group's characteristic small head, long neck, four columnar limbs, and long tail while spanning from forms only about 5.7 meters long to the larger Neuquensaurus at around 15 meters. The core South American genera include Neuquensaurus, Saltasaurus, Rocasaurus, and Bonatitan, with additional members such as Ibirania and outliers like Jainosaurus of India and Abditosaurus of Europe extending the group beyond its South American heartland. Saltasaurines are the only sauropods in which nearly every species is known to bear body armor, a dense covering of large keeled osteoderms set among numerous small bony ossicles that likely evolved as defense against predatory theropods such as Abelisaurus and Carnotaurus. They also share strongly procoelous tail vertebrae and reduced dorsal neural spines, and they include the tribe Saltasaurini, which groups the type genus with its closest relatives.
diagnostic_features: Dermal armor of large keeled osteoderms set among numerous small ossicles
Strongly procoelous caudal vertebrae with anteriorly displaced neural arches
Posterior dorsal vertebrae with reduced, posteriorly inclined neural spines
Small body size

Saltasauroidea.description: Saltasauroidea is a superfamily of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs, defined as all taxa closer to Saltasaurus than to Patagotitan. This definition splits the derived titanosaur group Eutitanosauria roughly in half, making Saltasauroidea the sister branch to the inversely defined Colossosauria. As originally proposed the clade united the aeolosaurins and the heavily armored, often dwarfed saltasaurids, along with intermediate genera such as Baurutitan, Diamantinasaurus, and Isisaurus. Later analyses placed the long-skulled Nemegtosauridae alongside Saltasauridae within the group while excluding the aeolosaurins. Its members account for much of the terminal-Cretaceous titanosaur diversity across both Gondwana and Laurasia.
diagnostic_features: Strongly procoelous caudal vertebrae throughout the tail
Osteoderms present in many members
Posterior dorsal vertebrae with well-developed lateral pneumatic foramina
Reduced and block-like carpus and manus

Saturnaliidae.description: Saturnaliidae is a family of small, basal sauropodomorph dinosaurs from the Late Triassic, with fossils known from Brazil, Argentina, and possibly Zimbabwe. Its best-supported members are Saturnalia and Chromogisaurus, with Pampadromaeus and Panphagia added as close relatives when the group was elevated from subfamily to family rank; Eoraptor, Buriolestes, Bagualosaurus, and Nhandumirim have also been recovered as possible members in more recent phylogenetic analyses. The group is typically defined as the most inclusive sauropodomorph clade that contains Saturnalia but not Plateosaurus. Although saturnaliids were once treated as a subgroup within Guaibasauridae, most recent studies instead place them as an independent lineage at the very base of the sauropodomorph family tree. These were lightly built, cursorial animals that retained slender proportions and partly serrated teeth suited to a mixed, still partly meat-eating diet.
diagnostic_features: Small body size with slender, cursorial hindlimb proportions
Lanceolate, partly serrated teeth retaining a faunivorous component
Elongate, lightly built cervical vertebrae
Gracile, plesiomorphic manus and pes

Saurischia.description: Saurischia, meaning "lizard-hipped," is one of the two major divisions of dinosaurs, distinguished from the ornithischians by hip structure. Its members retain the ancestral, three-pronged pelvic arrangement in which the pubis points forward, the same configuration seen in modern lizards and other reptiles, rather than the backward-rotated pubis of ornithischians. The group encompasses the mostly carnivorous, typically bipedal theropods together with the long-necked, herbivorous sauropodomorphs, and because birds are a lineage of maniraptoran theropods, they too fall within Saurischia. It is traditionally defined as all dinosaurs more closely related to birds than to Triceratops. All saurischians except birds died out in the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event at the end of the Cretaceous, while birds survive as the clade's only living descendants.
diagnostic_features: Forward-pointing (anteroventrally directed) pubis in basal members
Elongate, mobile neck with cervical vertebrae bearing well-developed pleurocoels
Asymmetrical hand with digit II longest
Subnarial foramen present between premaxilla and maxilla

Saurolophinae.description: Saurolophinae is one of the two major subfamilies of hadrosaurid dinosaurs, alongside the hollow-crested Lambeosaurinae. It gathers the solid-crested and crestless duck-bills long grouped as the "hadrosaurines," including such genera as Saurolophus, Edmontosaurus, Gryposaurus, Kritosaurus, Brachylophosaurus, and Maiasaura, and is further divided into tribes such as Brachylophosaurini and Kritosaurini. The older name Hadrosaurinae was largely set aside once its namesake genus, Hadrosaurus, was found to fall outside the traditional grouping, and the clade was recircumscribed to exclude it. Where its members bear cranial ornamentation at all, it takes the form of a solid crest built mainly from the nasal bones rather than the inflated, hollow nasal passages seen in lambeosaurines. Saurolophines were a diverse radiation of the Late Cretaceous, ranging across North America and Asia and reaching South America, where an endemic group of southern kritosaurs is thought to have arrived by island-hopping and rafting around 85 million years ago.
diagnostic_features: Cranial ornamentation, when present, a solid crest formed mainly by the nasals and premaxillae rather than a hollow narial chamber
Reflected, often arched dorsal margin of the premaxilla bordering the external naris
Caudally extended circumnarial fossa
Reduced or absent supraorbital contribution to the dorsal orbital margin

Sauropoda.description: Sauropoda is a clade of saurischian, or lizard-hipped, dinosaurs, whose members are known as sauropods. They are the largest animals ever to have lived on land, with very long necks, long tails, small heads relative to the body, and four thick, pillar-like legs supporting massive bodies. Air-filled, hollow bones are a characteristic feature of the group, lightening the enormous skeleton and aiding a bird-like system of air sacs. Well-known members include Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Camarasaurus, and the giant titanosaurs such as Argentinosaurus. The oldest unequivocal sauropods appear in the Early Jurassic; by the Late Jurassic groups like the diplodocids and brachiosaurids had become widespread, and by the Late Cretaceous the titanosaurs had replaced all other sauropods and achieved a near-global distribution. Their fossils have been found on every continent, including Antarctica.
diagnostic_features: Gigantic body size with columnar, graviportal limbs
Extremely elongated neck with 12 or more opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae
Extensive postcranial skeletal pneumaticity
Spatulate or peg-like teeth
Obligate quadrupedal posture
Reduced or absent manual phalanges on lateral digits

Sauropodiformes.description: Sauropodiformes is a clade of sauropodomorph dinosaurs that gathers the true sauropods together with their closest non-sauropod relatives. As a stem-based group, it embraces every taxon on the sauropod side of the split from Massospondylus, running from the "near-sauropod" grade of animals such as Anchisaurus, Melanorosaurus, Aardonyx, and Mussaurus, through the lessemsaurids, and on to the sauropods themselves. Its members chart one of the defining transitions in dinosaur evolution: the shift from the ancestral part-time two-legged posture to obligate four-legged walking, accompanied by the march toward enormous body size on the line leading to Sauropoda.
diagnostic_features: Trend toward obligate quadrupedality with a shortened, weight-bearing manus
Robust, columnar limb bones with reduced shaft torsion
Broadened, weight-bearing pes with a reduced pollex
Massive scapular blade in derived members

Sauropodomorpha.description: Sauropodomorpha is a clade of saurischian dinosaurs that includes the long-necked, herbivorous sauropods together with their earlier relatives, the basal forms traditionally grouped as "prosauropods." The clade first appeared among the earliest dinosaurs in the Late Triassic, around 230 million years ago, and persisted until the end-Cretaceous extinction. Its earliest members were small bipeds that were omnivorous or even carnivorous, but over time the group shifted toward plant-eating, larger body size, and, in the true sauropods, quadrupedal locomotion. The sauropods became the dominant terrestrial herbivores through much of the Mesozoic and include the largest animals ever to walk on land. Their remains have been found on every continent, including Antarctica.
diagnostic_features: Elongated neck with ten or more cervical vertebrae
Small skull relative to body size
Leaf-shaped or spatulate teeth adapted for herbivory
Enlarged external nares
Large pollex (thumb) claw on manus digit I
Evolutionary trend toward increasing body size

Saurornitholestinae.description: Saurornitholestinae is a subfamily of eudromaeosaurian dromaeosaurid dinosaurs known only from the Late Cretaceous of western North America. Its members are medium-sized predators generally distinguished by their comparatively short snouts, and the group is typically taken to include Atrociraptor, Bambiraptor, and Saurornitholestes. It is most often recovered as the sister group to a clade uniting the dromaeosaurines and velociraptorines. Its exact position is contested, however: some analyses instead find its proposed members to be the earliest-diverging branch of the eudromaeosaurs rather than a clade of their own.

Scansoriopterygidae.description: Scansoriopterygidae is a family of small, unusual maniraptoran theropod dinosaurs from the Middle to Late Jurassic of China, known from a handful of well-preserved fossils recovered from the Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning and Hebei. The group includes Scansoriopteryx, Epidexipteryx, Ambopteryx, and Yi, and counts among the smallest non-avian dinosaurs known. Its members are set apart by an extremely long third finger, longer than the first and second digits, the reverse of the usual theropod hand in which the second finger is longest. In at least Yi and Ambopteryx, this elongated finger paired with a long styliform bone at the wrist to support a bat-like membranous wing used for gliding, making scansoriopterygids the only known dinosaurs to develop true membranous wings. They also share short, deep skulls with down-turned jaws and large front teeth, long arms, and a body covering of simple feathers. Their placement among coelurosaurs remains contentious, in part because much of the material is fragmentary or juvenile.
diagnostic_features: Greatly elongate third manual digit, longer than the first two
Membranous wing supported by an ossified styliform wrist element in some members

Small body size with a proportionally large head

Shamosaurinae.description: Shamosaurinae is a basal subfamily of ankylosaurid dinosaurs, the heavily armored, quadrupedal herbivores of the Cretaceous. It is defined as the group containing Gobisaurus and Shamosaurus but excluding the more derived Ankylosaurus, and is recognized only when those two Asian genera form a clade to the exclusion of the ankylosaurines. As early-diverging members near the base of the family, its genera retain a comparatively long, lightly ornamented skull and lack the fully developed tail club that distinguishes their later ankylosaurid relatives.

Sinovenatorinae.description: Sinovenatorinae is a subfamily of small, basal troodontids from the Early Cretaceous Jehol Biota of China, grouping Sinovenator with Mei, Sinusonasus, and Daliansaurus, and in some analyses Jianianhualong. Its members are among the smallest and most basal of the troodontids, the bird-like, gracile theropods known for their large braincases and long, slender legs built for fast running. Members of the group share a distinctively wide, flattened fourth metatarsal. The clade's exact composition and internal relationships remain debated, with some analyses instead recovering these Chinese taxa as a graded succession of lineages rather than a single well-defined clade.

Somphospondyli.description: Somphospondyli is a clade of titanosauriform sauropod dinosaurs that lived from the Late Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous, with remains found on every continent. It embraces all titanosauriforms more closely related to the giant, largely Cretaceous titanosaurs than to the brachiosaurids, and so unites the diverse Titanosauria with the East Asian euhelopodids and an assortment of more basal, non-titanosaurian forms. Members are distinguished by details of their vertebrae, including a long neck and internal bone tissue riddled with a sponge-like network of air-filled chambers. It is this spongy, camellate texture pervading the backbone that gives the group its name.
Somphospondyli.authors: Wilson, J. A.; Sereno, P. C.

Spinosauridae.description: Spinosauridae is a family of large, bipedal tetanuran theropod dinosaurs known from the Cretaceous of Africa, Europe, Asia, and South America. It is traditionally divided into two subfamilies: the Baryonychinae, which include smaller-bodied forms such as Baryonyx, Suchomimus, Ceratosuchops, and Riparovenator with slightly recurved, faintly serrated teeth; and the Spinosaurinae, which include Irritator, Ichthyovenator, Sigilmassasaurus, and the giant Spinosaurus, with straight, unserrated teeth and nostrils set even further back on the skull. Members are marked by long, low, narrow crocodile-like snouts whose tips fan out into a spoon-shaped rosette of enlarged teeth, retracted nostrils, and robust forelimbs ending in three-fingered hands with an enlarged first-finger claw. In many species the tall neural spines of the back vertebrae supported a skin- or fat-covered sail, most extreme in Spinosaurus. Direct fossil evidence and anatomical adaptations point to at least partially fish-eating, often semiaquatic habits, though spinosaurids also preyed on other dinosaurs and pterosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Elongate, laterally compressed (crocodile-like) rostrum
Subconical teeth with reduced or absent serrations
Dorsal neural spines 1.9 or more times the centrum height, forming a sail in derived taxa

Spinosaurinae.description: Spinosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of spinosaurids, the large, crocodile-snouted theropod dinosaurs, and forms the sister group to Baryonychinae. Its members—including Spinosaurus, Irritator, Ichthyovenator, Oxalaia, and Sigilmassasaurus, along with Iberian forms such as Vallibonavenatrix—are marked by straight, conical, unserrated teeth and by nostrils set even further back on the skull than in baryonychines. Spinosaurines include the largest and most specialized spinosaurids, and appear to have evolved across the southern landmasses of Gondwana, in Africa and South America, during the Cretaceous. In several members the tall, reclined neural spines and elongated chevrons of the tail formed a deep, paddle-like structure—most pronounced in Spinosaurus—that has been linked to a semiaquatic lifestyle. Their jaws and teeth were well suited to processing the meat of relatively large vertebrate prey, not just fish.
diagnostic_features: Straight, conical tooth crowns lacking recurvature and serrations
Widely spaced dentary tooth crowns
Strongly reduced first premaxillary tooth
External nares retracted farther posteriorly than in baryonychines

Stegosauria.description: Stegosauria is a clade of herbivorous, armored ornithischian dinosaurs belonging to the Thyreophora, best known for the arrays of bony plates and spikes that run along the back, hips, and tail. Stegosaurs lived from the Middle Jurassic into the Early Cretaceous, with fossils recovered mostly across the Northern Hemisphere as well as Africa and South America. They were quadrupedal plant-eaters with small, narrow heads and hindlimbs much longer than the forelimbs, and a broad pelvis that held the tail out almost horizontally behind the animal. The tail ended in paired spikes, informally called a thagomizer, which at least in older adults served as a defensive weapon. The clade contains two families: the small, early-diverging Huayangosauridae and the larger, more diverse Stegosauridae, which account for the great majority of known genera and reached their peak diversity in the Late Jurassic before declining through the Cretaceous.

Tail spines (thagomizer) used for defense
Hindlimbs substantially longer than forelimbs
Small skull with simple, leaf-shaped teeth and weak jaw musculature
Low, arched body profile
Relatively small brain (low encephalization quotient)

Stegosauridae.description: Stegosauridae is a family of plated, quadrupedal stegosaurian dinosaurs that accounts for the vast majority of known stegosaurian diversity. Its members lived from the later part of the Jurassic into the Early Cretaceous and ranged widely, with fossils found across the Northern Hemisphere as well as Africa and South America. Stegosaurids are set apart from more basal stegosaurians by the loss of the premaxillary teeth and of the lateral rows of bony scutes along the trunk, together with long, narrow skulls and hindlimbs markedly longer than the forelimbs. The most derived forms carry very large, thin dorsal plates arranged in two staggered parasagittal rows, along with paired spikes at the end of the tail. The family is conventionally divided into two subfamilies, the long-spined Dacentrurinae and the plate-bearing Stegosaurinae, which together make up the clade Neostegosauria; several basal and fragmentary members fall outside this split.

Stegosaurinae.description: Stegosaurinae is a subfamily of stegosaurid dinosaurs comprising Stegosaurus and its closest relatives, defined as the stegosaurs more closely related to Stegosaurus than to Dacentrurus. Its plate-backed members range in age from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, with fossils known from North America, Europe, and Asia. Stegosaurinae is among the most derived stegosaurian lineages, and some of its members, including Stegosaurus itself, bear large, broad dorsal plates arranged in two staggered, alternating rows along the back. Alongside the more spike-bearing Dacentrurinae, it makes up one of the two principal branches of the most advanced stegosaurids.

Styracosterna.description: Styracosterna is a clade of ankylopollexian ornithopod dinosaurs defined to include Iguanodon and all its relatives that are closer to it than to Camptosaurus. It encompasses the classic "iguanodont-grade" forms as well as the more derived Hadrosauriformes, which in turn contains the duck-billed hadrosaurids. Body size within the clade ranges widely, from small, lightly built, likely fast-running species known from the latest Cretaceous to some of the largest ornithopod dinosaurs that ever lived. The oldest known styracosternans date to the Late Jurassic of Europe, and by the Cretaceous the clade had spread worldwide, with hadrosaurids becoming among the dominant large plant-eaters of Late Cretaceous ecosystems across Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Americas.

Tetanurae.description: Tetanurae, meaning "stiff tails," is a large clade of theropod dinosaurs that includes most predatory dinosaur diversity, encompassing the megalosauroids, the allosauroids, and the coelurosaurs, the last of which contains tyrannosauroids, ornithomimosaurs, compsognathids, and the maniraptorans, including living birds. The group is defined as all theropods more closely related to modern birds than to Ceratosaurus, its sister lineage, from which it likely diverged in the late Triassic. Tetanurans appear in the fossil record by the Early Jurassic and had become globally distributed by the Middle Jurassic. Their evolution was marked by the parallel diversification of several lineages that repeatedly attained large body size and similar locomotor forms; basal members were the first theropods to reach truly giant sizes, with some megalosauroids and allosauroids exceeding a ton. Distinctive features of the group include stiffened tails, the loss of the fourth finger to leave a three-fingered hand, maxillary teeth restricted to the front of the snout, and, in more advanced forms, an air-sac-ventilated lung system resembling that of modern birds. Birds are the only living survivors of the clade.
diagnostic_features: Stiffened distal tail with interlocking zygapophyses
Reduction of the hand to three functional digits (loss of digit IV)
Maxillary tooth row restricted to anterior portion of skull, not extending posterior to antorbital fenestra
Large, well-developed maxillary fenestra
Tibia longer than or equal to femur

Therizinosauria.description: Therizinosauria is a clade of secondarily herbivorous maniraptoran theropods, once known as segnosaurs, whose fossils come mainly from Cretaceous rocks of Asia and North America, with fragmentary remains hinting at a history reaching back into the Jurassic of Asia and Europe. Its members range from small, lightly built early-diverging forms such as Falcarius and Beipiaosaurus to the giant Therizinosaurus, which grew around 10 meters long and ranks among the largest known theropods. They combined a puzzling mix of traits: long necks, wide barrel-shaped torsos, and four-toed walking feet reminiscent of basal sauropodomorphs, together with backward-pointing, partly fused hip bones that once suggested a link to the bird-hipped ornithischians. Their most striking feature is the enormous claws on their hands, reaching roughly a meter in Therizinosaurus, which they likely used to grasp and shear leafy branches much as later mammals like ground sloths and giant pandas did. Skin impressions show that at least some members bore a coat of down-like feathers along with longer, quill-like structures that may have served in display.

Small lanceolate crowns with coarse denticles and a constricted base
Enlarged, mediolaterally compressed manual unguals
Opisthopubic pelvis with a broadly everted preacetabular process of the ilium
Reduced, robust pes trending toward a functionally weight-bearing first digit

Therizinosauridae.description: Therizinosauridae is a family of large, derived therizinosaur dinosaurs known mainly from the Late Cretaceous of Asia and North America, though footprints and isolated remains suggest the group ranged across much of the Laurasian supercontinent, reaching Europe and Africa. As of 2025 it comprises roughly nine well-supported genera, among them Segnosaurus, Erlikosaurus, Nothronychus, and the giant Therizinosaurus, whose elongated hand claws reached about a meter long, the largest of any known land animal. Despite their theropod ancestry these were herbivores that converged on a body plan resembling that of ground sloths: a wide, rounded belly carried on a broad pelvis, stout four-toed feet with a weight-bearing first digit, a long neck, and a small skull tipped with a keratinous beak and leaf-shaped teeth unlike those of other theropods. Their pelvis was unusually opisthopubic, with the pubis directed backward as in birds and ornithischians, and a nearly avian inner ear gave them acute hearing and balance. They nested in colonies, laying clutches of eggs, and are widely regarded as the theropods most specialized for plant eating.

Wide, barrel-shaped torso accommodating an enlarged herbivorous gut
Small skull with an edentulous premaxilla and leaf-shaped cheek teeth
Opisthopubic (posteriorly directed) pubis
Broad, functionally tetradactyl pes with a weight-bearing first digit

Therizinosauroidea.description: Therizinosauroidea is a superfamily of large, herbivorous maniraptoran theropod dinosaurs known mainly from the Cretaceous of Asia, with a possible Jurassic tooth from England representing its oldest record. As restricted here, it comprises the more derived therizinosaurs, including genera such as Beipiaosaurus, Enigmosaurus, Erliansaurus, Neimongosaurus, and Suzhousaurus together with the families Alxasauridae and Therizinosauridae, and excludes the most primitive members of the broader group Therizinosauria, such as Falcarius. Its members share the distinctive therizinosaur mix of features: long necks, wide torsos, and four-toed weight-bearing feet reminiscent of early plant-eating dinosaurs, backward-pointing and partially fused hip bones once thought to recall those of ornithischians, and greatly enlarged, strongly curved hand claws. The name has largely replaced the older term Segnosauria in phylogenetic work, though some studies instead apply it to the entire therizinosaur lineage rather than to this more nested grouping.

Coossification of the sacral neural spines into a supraneural plate

Progressively enlarged, transversely broadened preacetabular ala of the ilium

Theropoda.description: Theropoda is one of the three major clades of dinosaurs, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha, and is generally grouped among the saurischians as a nearer relative of the sauropodomorphs. Theropods were ancestrally carnivorous and included the majority of large terrestrial predators from the Early Jurassic until the end of the Cretaceous, among them the largest meat-eating land animals ever to exist, such as Tyrannosaurus and Giganotosaurus. First appearing in the Late Triassic, the group spans an enormous range of body sizes and lifestyles, with several lineages independently shifting to herbivory or omnivory. Its major subgroups include the early coelophysoids and the often horned ceratosaurs, together with the sprawling tetanuran radiation, which encompasses the semiaquatic spinosaurids, the allosauroids, and the feathered coelurosaurs, the last including tyrannosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, dromaeosaurids, and therizinosaurs. From small, specialized coelurosaurs, birds arose during the Jurassic and endure today as roughly 11,000 living species, making theropods the only dinosaur lineage still present on Earth.

Obligate bipedal stance

Thescelosauridae.description: Thescelosauridae is a clade of small to medium-sized neornithischian dinosaurs from the Cretaceous of North America and East Asia, lying outside the more derived Cerapoda. It is divided into two subgroups: Orodrominae, which includes Orodromeus, Oryctodromeus, Zephyrosaurus, and Albertadromeus, and Thescelosaurinae, which unites Parksosaurus, Thescelosaurus, and several long-snouted Asian forms once placed with the jeholosaurids. Its members were stocky, ground-dwelling herbivores that browsed selectively on soft, pulpy plant matter. Some of the orodromines appear to have been burrowers, a habit demonstrated by Oryctodromeus, whose remains have been found preserved within a burrow. The name Parksosauridae has been applied to the same group of animals, but Thescelosauridae holds nomenclatural precedence and is the name in prevailing use.

Fossa on the pterygoid wing of the quadrate

Thescelosaurinae.description: Thescelosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of Thescelosauridae, a group of small, plant-eating neornithischian dinosaurs from the Cretaceous of North America and East Asia. It unites Thescelosaurus and Parksosaurus with several long-snouted Asian forms that had previously been classified under Jeholosauridae, and it is recognized as the counterpart to the smaller, burrow-associated Orodrominae. Thescelosaurus, the largest known thescelosaurid, is notably robust and large-bodied, though several other thescelosaurine genera, including Haya, Changchunsaurus, and Doolysaurus, were much smaller. Like other thescelosaurids, they are thought to have been highly selective browsers that fed mainly on soft, pulpy plant material.

Thyreophora.description: Thyreophora, meaning "shield bearers," is a clade of armored ornithischian dinosaurs. It contains two major subgroups, the plated stegosaurs and the heavily armored ankylosaurs, together with a grade of early-diverging forms such as Scutellosaurus, Emausaurus, and Scelidosaurus. Its members are defined by body armor arranged in longitudinal rows along the back and flanks: primitive forms bore simple low keeled scutes, while more derived members developed elaborate spikes and plates. Thyreophorans first appeared in the Early Jurassic and persisted until the end of the Cretaceous. The earliest species were small and at least partly bipedal, but the group trended toward a robust, low-slung body plan, with the large stegosaurs and ankylosaurs becoming obligate quadrupeds whose forelimbs were much shorter than their hindlimbs.

Titanosauria.description: Titanosauria is a diverse clade of sauropod dinosaurs known from every continent, including Antarctica, and the last group of long-necked sauropods to survive up to the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous. It spans the widest range of body size of any sauropod group, encompassing some of the largest land animals ever to have lived, such as Patagotitan, Argentinosaurus, and Puertasaurus, alongside dwarf forms like the island-dwelling Magyarosaurus. Titanosaurs had small, wide heads and whip-like tails, and the skin of many was studded with a mosaic of small bead-like scales. Together with the brachiosaurids and their relatives, they make up the larger clade Titanosauriformes, and most members apart from a few basal genera fall within a subgroup called Lithostrotia. Their fossil record is the least complete of any major sauropod group, and the relationships among the species remain poorly resolved.

Titanosauriformes.description: Titanosauriformes is a clade of macronarian sauropods defined as the least inclusive group containing Brachiosaurus and Saltasaurus, comprising the two sister lineages Brachiosauridae and Somphospondyli. The clade is known from the fossil record beginning in the Late Jurassic and persisted to the end of the Cretaceous, achieving a global distribution across most continents. Titanosauriforms include some of the largest known terrestrial animals, among them the giant titanosaurs of the Late Cretaceous.

Troodontidae.description: Troodontidae is a family of small, slender, bird-like maniraptoran theropod dinosaurs that lived from the Late Jurassic through the Late Cretaceous, radiating across North America, Asia, and Europe and possibly reaching the southern continents. Its members include the primitive Sinovenatorinae, the Jinfengopteryginae, and the more advanced Troodontinae, and the group is among the closest known relatives of birds. Troodontids had some of the largest brains relative to body size of any non-avian dinosaurs, along with large forward-facing eyes that gave them good binocular vision and enlarged, sometimes asymmetrical ear cavities that suggest acute hearing. They walked on unusually long legs and bore a curved, retractable claw on the second toe, though this "sickle-claw" was smaller and less strongly recurved than that of the dromaeosaurids. Their jaws held many closely spaced teeth, and while most were probably predators of small prey, the tooth form of some species points toward omnivory.
diagnostic_features: Numerous, closely packed teeth with large denticles on the distal carina
Large, forward-facing orbits with well-developed binocular vision
Enlarged braincase with a high encephalization quotient
Slender, subarctometatarsalian metatarsus with an asymmetric metatarsal IV trochlea
Retractable pedal ungual II smaller than in dromaeosaurids

Troodontinae.description: Troodontinae is a subfamily of troodontid dinosaurs, comprising the more derived members of the family that lived across North America and Asia during the Cretaceous. It is defined as the least inclusive clade containing Saurornithoides mongoliensis and Troodon formosus, and unites genera such as Troodon, Saurornithoides, Zanabazar, Gobivenator, Stenonychosaurus, Latenivenatrix, Linhevenator, and Philovenator. Like other troodontids, these were small, bird-like maniraptorans with a retractable, sickle-clawed second toe and some of the largest brains known among dinosaurs, but troodontines include the biggest and most heavily encephalized members of the group. Their lower jaws are distinctively deep and deflected inward toward the midline, setting them apart from more primitive troodontids. The exact membership of the subfamily varies between phylogenetic analyses.

Turiasauria.description: Turiasauria is a clade of eusauropod dinosaurs known from the Middle Jurassic to Early Cretaceous of Europe, Africa, Asia, and North America. Its members sit within the broader eusauropod radiation but fall outside Neosauropoda, the advanced group that includes the diplodocids and titanosaurs. The clade was first recognized for a group of large Iberian sauropods such as Turiasaurus, Losillasaurus, and Zby, but later finds extended its range to include North American forms like Mierasaurus and Moabosaurus as well as African and Asian material. Turiasaurs are readily distinguished by their heart-shaped tooth crowns, a hallmark trait of the group, along with distinctive features of the neck vertebrae and forelimb bones. The very large body size reached by some turiasaurs shows that gigantism evolved independently in this comparatively basal lineage, not just among the neosauropods.

Tyrannosauridae.description: Tyrannosauridae is a family of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs that lived near the end of the Cretaceous period, with fossils known only from North America and Asia. It is divided into two subfamilies: the more lightly built Albertosaurinae, comprising the North American genera Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus, and the Tyrannosaurinae, which includes Daspletosaurus, Tarbosaurus, Teratophoneus, Zhuchengtyrannus, and Tyrannosaurus itself, among others. Estimates of how many genera the family contains range from as few as three to around fifteen. Though descended from smaller ancestors, tyrannosaurids were almost always the largest predators in their ecosystems, standing at the apex of the food chain. They were bipedal carnivores with massive, deep skulls packed with large teeth, proportionally long and cursorial hindlimbs for their size, and greatly reduced forelimbs bearing only two functional fingers.

Tyrannosaurinae.description: Tyrannosaurinae is one of the two subfamilies of tyrannosaurid theropods, known from Late Cretaceous deposits of western North America and east Asia. Compared with their albertosaurine relatives, tyrannosaurines were generally more robust, larger, and more heavily built, with deep, powerful skulls; the exceptions were the long-snouted, more gracile alioramins. The group includes some of the oldest tyrannosaurids, such as Lythronax, alongside its youngest and most famous member, Tyrannosaurus rex. Its genera are usually sorted into several lineages: the basal Alioramini, the American southwestern Teratophoneini, and a group uniting the Daspletosaurini and the Tyrannosaurini, which contains Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus. Studies of Tyrannosaurus growth suggest these animals changed markedly with age, shifting from slender, semi-long-snouted juveniles into robust, heavy-headed adults that likely occupied different ecological niches as they matured.

Tyrannosauroidea.description: Tyrannosauroidea is a superfamily of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs that unites the family Tyrannosauridae with a range of smaller, more basal relatives such as the proceratosaurids. The group arose on the northern supercontinent Laurasia in the Jurassic and persisted until the end of the Cretaceous, when tyrannosauroids became the dominant large predators of the Northern Hemisphere, culminating in the giant Tyrannosaurus; their fossils are known from what are now North America, Europe, and Asia. All members were bipedal carnivores distinguished by a suite of skull and pelvic features, including a tall premaxilla that blunted the front of the snout, fused and often roughly textured nasal bones, and small, D-shaped premaxillary teeth. Early forms were small animals with long, three-fingered forelimbs, whereas the later giants reached enormous size yet had proportionately tiny, two-fingered arms; the derived forms also developed a pinched third metatarsal, the arctometatarsus, tied to running efficiency. Primitive filamentous feathers are preserved in several species, and many tyrannosauroids bore bony crests of varied shape on the skull that likely served for display.

Unaysauridae.description: Unaysauridae is a clade of early-branching sauropodomorph dinosaurs from the Late Triassic of Brazil and India, comprising Unaysaurus, Macrocollum, and Jaklapallisaurus. These were small to medium-sized, long-necked bipeds recovered as the sister group to the more derived plateosaurs. Members are united chiefly by a strongly expanded front portion of the inner ankle bone and, where the skull is known, by an extra opening in the upper jaw. The grouping's validity has been questioned, since several of its defining traits cannot be confirmed across all its members owing to their incomplete and fragmentary remains, and some analyses instead place Unaysaurus and Macrocollum among the plateosaurids.

Unenlagiinae.description: Unenlagiinae is a clade of long-snouted, paravian theropod dinosaurs known mainly from the Late Cretaceous of South America, with most members discovered in Argentina and additional forms reported from Antarctica and possibly Australia. The group includes Unenlagia, Buitreraptor, Austroraptor, Neuquenraptor, and Rahonavis among others, ranging from turkey-sized, long-armed predators to Austroraptor, which reached roughly 5 to 6 meters and ranks among the largest dromaeosaurids. Members are distinguished by very elongated, lightly built snouts bearing numerous small teeth, a tail stiffened by long chevrons and vertebral processes, a reduced second toe claw, a backward-oriented pubis, and slender hindlimbs with a subarctometatarsalian foot. These slender feet and less rigid joints likely gave them greater running speed than their Laurasian relatives, suiting them to catching smaller, faster prey. Their distinctive anatomy is thought to reflect the geographic isolation of Gondwana following the breakup of Pangaea. Their placement relative to Dromaeosauridae and Avialae remains contested (see dispute).

Velociraptorinae.description: Velociraptorinae is a subfamily of eudromaeosaurian dromaeosaurid dinosaurs, traditionally comprising the more slender, narrow-snouted species and centered on Velociraptor and its close relatives. Its members are found primarily in Asia and include such genera as Tsaagan, Kuru, and Adasaurus, though several North American forms like Acheroraptor, Dineobellator, and possibly Deinonychus have also been assigned to it. Velociraptorine teeth are often distinguished by having larger serrations along the rear edge than the front, or by lacking front serrations altogether. It is one of three major eudromaeosaurian subgroups, and while widely used, its exact composition is contentious: analyses vary greatly over which species truly belong, with some placing traditional members closer to Dromaeosaurus instead. Velociraptorines appear in the Late Cretaceous, and the bulk of their diversity, including the famous Velociraptor itself, is known from Asia.

Abdarainurus.etymology: Named after Abdrant Nuru, the holotype locality in Mongolia, combined with Latin 'urus' meaning 'tail'
Abdarainurus.description: Abdarainurus is a genus of titanosaur dinosaur from the Alagteeg Formation in Mongolia. The type and only species is A. barsboldi. Currently seen as an indeterminate titanosaur, it may represent a previously unknown lineage of Asian macronarians. Abdarainurus is not known from many remains; it is only known from eight front tail vertebrae and a middle tail vertebra and several chevrons.

dispute.summary: Placed at Somphospondyli incertae sedis. Abdarainurus is known only from highly unusual caudal vertebrae, including opisthocoelous anterior and middle caudals otherwise seen in Opisthocoelicaudia, and was erected as Titanosauria incertae sedis (Averianov and Lopatin, 2020). Their preferred (implied weighting) analysis recovers a basal titanosaur, as does the most recent dedicated analysis (Han et al., 2024, which recovers it as sister to Gandititan), but the equal-weighting strict consensus of the erecting paper allows a non-titanosaurian somphospondylan position. Somphospondyli is the least-inclusive clade all these hypotheses accept.

history.note: Placed at Titanosauria incertae sedis per Averianov and Lopatin (2020); a non-titanosaurian somphospondylan position is noted as possible.

Abditosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'abditus' meaning 'forgotten' or 'hidden' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'forgotten lizard'
Abditosaurus.description: Abditosaurus is an extinct genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) Conques Formation (Tremp Group) of Catalonia, Spain. The genus contains a single species, Abditosaurus kuehnei, known from a partial specimen representing the most complete titanosaur skeleton found in Europe. Phylogenetic analyses recover it within a clade of South American and African saltasaurines, distinct from other insular dwarf sauropods from the European archipelago. Abditosaurus inhabited the Ibero-Armorican Island, a prehistoric island made up of what is now Spain, Portugal, and southern France, and would have been the largest titanosaur species in its environment.

dispute.summary: Placed within Saltasauridae as incertae sedis. The describing analysis (Vila et al., 2022) recovered Abditosaurus more precisely as a saltasaurine, within a clade of South American and African saltasaurines (sister to Paralititan) distinct from the lirainosaurine titanosaurs of the European archipelago. Because that saltasaurine topology rests on a single analysis whose recovered neighbors (Paralititan, Maxakalisaurus) are atypical relative to most studies, it is placed conservatively at Saltasauridae rather than within Saltasaurinae.

history.note: Placed at Saltasauridae incertae sedis; Vila et al. (2022) recover it within Saltasaurinae, but the supporting topology is not yet corroborated.

Abrosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'abros' meaning 'delicate' or 'dainty' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to the delicate skull structure.
Abrosaurus.description: Abrosaurus is a genus of macronarian sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic Period of what is now Asia. It is one of many dinosaurs found at the Dashanpu Quarry in the Sichuan Province of China. Like most sauropods, Abrosaurus was a quadrupedal herbivore. It was rather small for a sauropod, measuring no more than 9.1 meters (30 ft) long. Its head was boxy and topped with a tall, bony arch containing the nostrils. The generic name refers to the nature of the skull, with large openings separated by thin, bony struts. The only named species is A. dongpoi, named after eleventh-century Chinese poet Su Shi, also known as Su Dongpo, who was born in Sichuan.

Spine-like dermal plates wholly asymmetrical, with convex anterior edge, concave posterior edge, and a deep notch interrupting the posterior ridge near the base that likely received the anterior edge of the adjacent spine.
Teeth lance-head shaped with acute point, sharp serrated edges bearing eight serrations on each side of the apex, and a crown that expands suddenly and asymmetrically into a swollen base.
Crown surface ornamented with vertical dark chocolate-colored bands alternating with pale brown bands running from the serrated edges to the swollen base, a feature not reported in allied genera.

Occipital condyle more elongated transversely and more excavated above than in Crocodile, with exoccipitals entering more largely into its composition; Eustachian tubes not in Crocodilian disposition; carotids running up the side of the basisphenoid in Lacertilian fashion.

Achelousaurus.etymology: Named after Achelous, the Greek deity of rivers, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Achelous lizard'
Achelousaurus.description: Achelousaurus is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period of what is now North America, about 77 to 74.8 million years ago. The first fossils of Achelousaurus were collected in Montana in 1987, by a team led by Jack Horner, with more finds made in 1989. In 1994, Achelousaurus horneri was described and named by Scott D. Sampson; the generic name means "Achelous lizard", in reference to the Greek deity Achelous, and the specific name refers to Horner. The genus is known from a few specimens consisting mainly of skull material from individuals, ranging from juveniles to adults.

Parietal with single pair of curved spikes projecting posterolaterally from the rear margin.

Acheroraptor.etymology: From Greek 'Acheron' (the underworld river) and Latin 'raptor' meaning 'thief' or 'plunderer'; meaning 'underworld thief'
Acheroraptor.description: Acheroraptor is an extinct genus of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in present-day Montana in the United States during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous period. It was described by Canadian paleontologists David Evans, Derek Larson, and Philip J. Currie in 2013. The genus contains a single species, A. temertyorum, named on an isolated maxilla with teeth. An incomplete dentary found nearby was also assigned to the species. These fossils were initially discovered by fossil poachers, though they were later sold to the Royal Ontario Museum, in layers belonging to the Hell Creek Formation. This indicates that these fossils date to the upper Maastrichtian stage, 67.2-66 million years ago.

The genus is currently monotypic, only including the type species A. giganticus. The first remains were found in 1989 during a Mongolian-Russian field expedition and later described in 1999. Acristavus.etymology: From Latin 'a-' meaning 'without', 'crista' meaning 'crest', and 'avus' meaning 'grandfather' or 'ancestor'; meaning 'non-crested grandfather'
Acristavus.description: Acristavus is a genus of saurolophine dinosaur. Fossils have been found from the Campanian Two Medicine Formation in Montana and Wahweap Formation in Utah, United States. The type species A. gagslarsoni was named in 2011. Unlike nearly all hadrosaurids except Edmontosaurus, Acristavus lacked ornamentation on its skull. The discovery of Acristavus is paleontologically significant because it supports the position that the ancestor of all hadrosaurids did not possess cranial ornamentation, and that ornamentation was an adaptation that later arose interdependently in the subfamilies Saurolophinae and Lambeosaurinae. It is closely related to Brachylophosaurus and Maiasaura, and was assigned to a new clade called Brachylophosaurini.
diagnostic_features: Enlarged posterodorsal brow of postorbital and basioccipital extending posteriorly well beyond the dorsal border of the foramen magnum to a greater extent than in other hadrosaurine species.
Deep laterally squared frontonasal suture, with posterolateral corners at nearly 90-degree angles, not seen in other hadrosaurids.
Swelling of the interdigitate suture between the prefrontal and frontal, not seen in other hadrosaurids.
Deep depression on the lateral surface of the postorbital jugal process, absent in all other known hadrosaurids.
Dentary with nearly flat (straight) ventral margin, differing from the downturned anterior dentary of all other hadrosaurids.

Acrocanthosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'akros' meaning 'high', 'akantha' meaning 'spine', and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to its high-spined vertebrae.
Acrocanthosaurus.description: Acrocanthosaurus is a genus of carcharodontosaurid dinosaurs that existed in what is now North America during the Barremian and early Cenomanian stages of the Early Cretaceous and Late Cretaceous, from 125 to 99.6 million years ago. Like most dinosaur genera, Acrocanthosaurus contains only a single species, A. atokensis. It had a continent-wide range, with fossil remains known from the U.S. states of Oklahoma, Texas, and Wyoming in the west and Maryland in the east. However, most of these remains are assigned to the species based on the assumption that Acrocanthosaurus is the only large carcharodontosaurid from North America during this time, and the possibility exists that some referred specimens could represent distinct taxa.

Acrotholus.etymology: From Greek 'akros' meaning 'highest' and 'tholos' meaning 'dome', referring to its prominent domed skull.
Acrotholus.description: Acrotholus is an extinct genus of pachycephalosaurian dinosaur that lived during the Santonian of the late Cretaceous, in the Milk River Formation of Canada. The type species, A. audeti, was named after Roy Audet allowing access to his ranch leading to the discovery of the species. The discovery of this specimen lead to several new revelations in the fossil records questioning the preservation of small-bodied organisms along with the evolution of early pachycephalosaurs. The iconic cranial dome found on Acrotholus makes it one of the earliest indisputable known members of the pachycephalosaur family. Like others of its clade, Acrotholus was a bipedal herbivore characterized by a dome-shaped head. The dome had often been associated with intra-species combat, although the exact methods of contact have been debated.

Adelolophus.etymology: From Greek 'adelos' meaning 'unknown' or 'obscure' and 'lophos' meaning 'crest'; meaning 'unknown crest'
Adelolophus.description: Adelolophus is a genus of lambeosaurine dinosaur (a crested "duck-bill") from Upper Cretaceous rocks in the U.S. state of Utah. The type and only known species is A. hutchisoni; the type specimen consists only of a broken maxilla. It constitutes the oldest known lambeosaur remains from North America, as well as the only known lambeosaur species from the Wahweap Formation, of which it pertains to the Upper Member. Among its relatives, it seems to be particularly similar to Parasaurolophus, rather than animals like Lambeosaurus; phylogenetic analysis confirms this, finding it in Parasaurolophini (tube-headed lambeosaurs). It would have lived in a wet environment, bordering on the sea but with a more arid season during some times of the year. This environment would have been shared with a diverse variety of fish and turtles, as well as other dinosaurs like ceratopsids and tyrannosaurids.

Strongly rugose depression bordered by a protuberance with a series of foramina in a sub-vertical row on the lateral surface of the anterior end of the dentary.
Eleven anteroposteriorly elongated cervical vertebrae.
Thirteen dorsal vertebrae with neural arches taller than their respective centra.

Adratiklit.description: Adratiklit is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaur that lived on the supercontinent Gondwana during the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian age). The genus contains a single species, Adratiklit boulahfa. Its remains were found in the El Mers III Formation, near Boulemane in north Morocco.

Adynomosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'adynamos' meaning 'weak' or 'powerless' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to its underdeveloped shoulder musculature.
Adynomosaurus.description: Adynomosaurus is a genus of lambeosaurine dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Catalonia, Spain. First discovered in 2012, it was named in 2019 with the type and only species being Adynomosaurus arcanus. It is only known from scant material, but is distinguished from other hadrosaurs by its weakly developed shoulder blade which would have had underdeveloped musculature, which lends it its scientific name, partially from the Greek word for "weak". Its exact relationships with other hadrosaurs remain unresolved, with it not consistently being recovered as a relative of any other specific genera, though some studies have allied it with Tsintaosaurini or even found it outside of Hadrosauridae. It would have lived as part of a diverse coastal estuary ecosystem, made up of meandering rivers and mud flats. The discovery of Adynomosaurus adds to the very incomplete fossil record of hadrosaurid dinosaurs in the Late Cretaceous of Europe, and it fits into a picture of major ecological turnover that was occurring during the Maastrichtian stage in the region.
diagnostic_features: Scapula with shallow blade: maximum depth of distal scapular blade is less than 75% of the depth of the proximal end (measured from dorsal margin of acromion process to ventral apex of glenoid).

Aegyptosaurus.etymology: From 'Aegyptus' (Latin for Egypt) and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', meaning 'Egypt's lizard', reflecting its discovery in Egypt.
Aegyptosaurus.description: Aegyptosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur discovered in Egypt, that lived in what is now Africa, around 95 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous Period (Cenomanian faunal stage).

Aeolosaurus.etymology: Named after Aeolus, the Greek god of winds, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Aeolus' lizard'
Aeolosaurus.description: Aeolosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Period of what is now South America. Like most sauropods, it would have been a quadrupedal herbivore with a long neck and tail. Aeolosaurus is well known for a titanosaur, as it is represented by the remains of several individuals belonging to at least two species. However, like most titanosaurs, no remains of the skull are known.

Aepisaurus.etymology: From Greek 'aipeinos' meaning 'lofty' or 'high' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', meaning 'lofty lizard'.
Aepisaurus.description: Aepisaurus was a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Albian-age Lower Cretaceous Grès vert of Département du Vaucluse, France, around 100.5 million years ago. It is an obscure genus from an unknown family, represented by a single humerus, now partly lost. Despite its lack of popularity, or perhaps because of it, it has been misspelled several ways in the scientific literature, with multiple dates given to the year of description as well.
diagnostic_features: Humerus approaching the size of an elephant humerus in a reptile, with total length 0.090 m, width at tuberosities 0.33 m, width at middle 0.15 m, width at condyles 0.25 m.
Humerus form and structure indicating a gigantic reptile with analogy to Monitors and Iguanas, but distinct from Wealden saurians described by Mantell.
Humerus shape closer to Iguanas and Monitors than to any other known group, but with some differences from both.

species.etymology: From Latin 'elephantinus' meaning 'elephant-like', likely referring to the large size of the humerus on which the genus is based.

Aepyornithomimus.description: Aepyornithomimus is a genus of ornithomimid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Djadochta Formation of Mongolia. It lived in the Campanian, around 75 million years ago, when the area is thought to have been a desert. The type and only species is A. tugrikinensis.

Aerosteon.etymology: From Greek 'aer' meaning 'air' and 'osteon' meaning 'bone', referring to its air-filled bones.
Aerosteon.description: Aerosteon is a genus of megaraptoran dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period of Argentina. Its remains were discovered in 1996 in the Anacleto Formation, which is from the late Campanian. The type and only known species is A. riocoloradensis. Its generic name can be translated as "air bone" and derives from Greek ἀήρ (aer, "air") and ὀστέον (osteon, "bone"), whereas its specific name indicates that its remains were found 1 km (0.6 miles) north of the Río Colorado, in Mendoza Province, Argentina. The genus shows evidence of a bird-like respiratory system.

Enlarged quadrate foramen located entirely within the quadrate shaft, not shared with the quadratojugal.
Large tympanic diverticulum (pneumatocoel) extending deep into the quadrate shaft above the articular condyle.
Furcula with a median pneumatocoel opening as a slit-shaped pneumatopore on the posterior surface.
Medial gastral elements coossified with anterior and posterior flanges in the midline.
Posteriormost dorsal vertebra with a pneumatic canal running within the transverse process and an anterodorsally inclined neural spine.

dispute.summary: Originally described as a basal ornithomimosaur (Sereno, 2017), but subsequent analyses reject that placement and recover Afromimus among ceratosaurs. Cerroni et al. (2019) place it within Abelisauroidea, and possibly Noasauridae, reinterpreting its proposed ornithomimosaur characters as ceratosaurian; Hendrickx et al. (2024) recover it in Berthasauridae, the sister group of Abelisauroidea. Its fragmentary material precludes confident assignment to any abelisauroid subclade, so it is placed conservatively at Ceratosauria.

It contains a single species, A. tenerensis, named in 2017 by Paul Sereno from parts of the right leg, vertebrae, and ribs found in the Ténéré Desert. It was originally described as a genus of ornithomimosaurian, but subsequent arguments have placed it as a taxon within or close to the superfamily Abelisauroidea.

Afrovenator.etymology: From Latin 'Afro' referring to Africa and 'venator' meaning 'hunter', meaning 'African hunter'.
Afrovenator.description: Afrovenator is an extinct genus of megalosaurid theropod dinosaur from the Middle or Late Jurassic Tiourarén Formation and maybe the Irhazer II Formation of the Sahara region of Niger in western Africa. Afrovenator represents the only named definitive Gondwanan megalosaur, with proposed material of the group present in the Tacuarembó Formation of Uruguay and the Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania, both dated to the Late Jurassic.

Agathaumas.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'αγαν' (agan, 'much') and 'θαυμα' (thauma, 'wonder'); meaning 'much wonder', given by Cope in reference to the large size of the type material.
Agathaumas.description: Agathaumas is a dubious genus of a large ceratopsid dinosaur that lived in Wyoming during the Late Cretaceous (late Maastrichtian stage, 66 million years ago). It was seen as the largest land animal known at the time of its discovery.

dispute.summary: Agathaumas is a nomen dubium based on postcranial material that lacks diagnostic ceratopsid characters and is widely regarded as indeterminate, possibly referable to Triceratops. It cannot be assigned to either subfamily and is retained at Ceratopsidae incertae sedis.

Agilisaurus.etymology: From Latin 'agilis' meaning 'agile' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', meaning 'agile lizard'.
Agilisaurus.description: Agilisaurus is a genus of ornithischian dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic Period of what is now eastern Asia. The only named species is A. louderbacki, recovered from the Lower Shaximiao Formation of Sichuan, China. It was about 1.2-1.7 m (3.9-5.6 ft) in length, 60 cm (2.0 ft) in hip height, and 40 kg (88 lb) in weight. It has leaf-shaped teeth that were well-adapted to its abrasive, plant-based diet. Most surprisingly, the wavy enamel of the teeth of this genus (and all other ornithopods), presumed to make them more resistant to wear, was previously thought to be exclusive to hadrosaurs. This is also the case for Changchunsaurus from the Cretaceous Period.

Agrosaurus.etymology: From Greek agros ('field') and sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'field lizard'
Agrosaurus.description: Agrosaurus is a potentially dubious genus of thecodontosaurid sauropodomorph probably originating from the Magnesian Conglomerate of England that was originally believed to be a Triassic prosauropod from Australia. Agrosaurus would thus be the oldest dinosaur from that country. However, this appears to have been an error, and the material actually appears to come from Thecodontosaurus or a Thecodontosaurus-like animal from Bristol, England (Avon Fissure Fill). The type species is Agrosaurus macgillivrayi.

dispute.summary: Agrosaurus macgillivrayi is a nomen dubium; its material is most likely referable to Thecodontosaurus from the Late Triassic of England rather than Australia.

history.note: Reparented from the deprecated Prosauropoda to Sauropodomorpha incertae sedis; nomen dubium, possibly Thecodontosaurus.

Agujaceratops.etymology: Named after the Aguja Formation where it was found, combined with Greek 'keras' meaning 'horn' and 'ops' meaning 'face'; meaning 'horned face from Aguja'
Agujaceratops.description: Agujaceratops is a genus of chasmosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) of western Texas. Two species are known: A. mariscalensis and A. mavericus, both recovered from the Aguja Formation.

Maxilla lacks a lateral horizontal shelf and premaxilla lacks a posterodorsal extension.
Supraorbital horncores relatively long and curved posteriorly (not anteriorly).
Posterior border of parietal flattened and plate-like rather than square and bar-like, with a marked but shallower embayment of the posterior median parietal.
Nasal horncore not centered above the external naris; premaxilla bears a septal flange along the entire anterior edge of the naris.

dispute.summary: The affinities of Agustinia are contested. Dedicated rebbachisaurid analyses recover it within Rebbachisauridae but disagree on where: Bellardini et al. (2022) found it a basal rebbachisaurid, while Lerzo et al. (2024b) recovered it as a derived rebbachisaurid within Nigersaurinae under implied weighting. It is an unstable operational taxonomic unit that is pruned from the consensus in several analyses (Lerzo et al., 2024a, 2024b). Earlier assessments differ more broadly: D'Emic et al. (2009) found no diagnostic features placing it in Diplodocoidea or Titanosauria and regarded it as a neosauropod of uncertain affinity, while Mannion et al. (2013), reinterpreting its purported osteoderms as displaced ribs and ischia, tentatively regarded it as an indeterminate somphospondylan.

history.note: Retained at Rebbachisauridae following the prevailing recent view (Bellardini et al., 2022; Jones, 2026); the alternative somphospondylan and neosauropod incertae sedis interpretations are noted, and its position within Rebbachisauridae is unresolved.

Replaced the reference-work citation (Jones, 2026) with the primary analysis of Lerzo et al. (2024b), which recovers Agustinia as a derived rebbachisaurid within Nigersaurinae under implied weighting and prunes it as unstable under equal weighting; the genus is retained as a rebbachisaurid of unresolved position, not incertae sedis.

The genus contains a single species, A. ligabuei, known from a single specimen that was recovered from the Lohan Cura Formation of Neuquén Province in Argentina. It lived about 116-108 million years ago, in the Aptian-Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous Period.

Ahshislepelta.etymology: Named after Ah-shi-sle-pah Wash, the locality where the fossil was found, combined with Greek 'pelta' meaning 'shield'; meaning 'Ah-shi-sle-pah Wash shield'
Ahshislepelta.description: Ahshislepelta is a monospecific genus of ankylosaur dinosaur from New Mexico that lived during the Late Cretaceous (late Campanian stage, 74.5 Ma) in what is now the Hunter Wash Member of the Kirtland Formation. The type and only species, Ahshislepelta minor, is known only from an incomplete postcranial skeleton of a small subadult or adult individual. It was named in 2011 by Michael Burns and Robert M. Sullivan. Based on the size of the humerus, Ahshislepelta is larger than Pinacosaurus mephistocephalus but smaller than Talarurus and Pinacosaurus grangeri.

dispute.summary: The family placement of Ahshislepelta is contested, recovered as a basal ankylosaurid by Arbour and Currie (2015) but as a nodosaurine by Jones and Viola (2026). It is retained at Ankylosauria incertae sedis pending resolution.

history.note: Placed at Ankylosauria incertae sedis, family placement contested between Ankylosauridae and Nodosauridae.

Osteodermal surface texture characterized by uniformly distributed pitted rugosity.
Sparse reticular pattern of neurovascular grooves on osteoderm surface.
Neurovascular foramina extending perpendicularly to obliquely into the osteoderm bone.

Ahshislesaurus.etymology: Named for the Ah-shi-sle-pah Wilderness in New Mexico, a phonetic transliteration of the Navajo áshįįh łibá meaning 'salt, it is gray', combined with Ancient Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'. The species name honors Swedish paleontologist Carl Wiman.
Ahshislesaurus.description: Ahshislesaurus is an extinct genus of saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous of what is now New Mexico, United States. It is known from a partial skull and three neck vertebrae discovered in 1916 and first described in 1935. Prior to its scientific naming, researchers debated whether the specimen belonged to Kritosaurus navajovius, a related species from the same layers of rocks, or a distinct animal. The genus contains a single species, Ahshislesaurus wimani, named in 2025. A partial skeleton and isolated limb and girdle bones found in the same rock layers may also belong to Ahshislesaurus.

Dentary with dorsoventrally deep anterior end, whereas in most other hadrosaurids the anterior end is dorsoventrally narrow

Ajkaceratops.etymology: Named for Ajka, the town in Hungary near where it was discovered, combined with Greek 'keratops' meaning 'horned face'.
Ajkaceratops.description: Ajkaceratops is a genus of ceratopsian dinosaur described in 2010. It lived during the Late Cretaceous in the western Tethyan archipelago, in what is now Europe. The type species, A. kozmai, was originally described as a ceratopsian most closely related to forms in east Asia, from where its ancestors may have migrated by island-hopping. Later research, however, questioned this assignment and treated Ajkaceratops as an ornithischian of unresolved affinity. In 2026, more complete cranial remains referable to the species were described, supporting its placement as a ceratopsian.

dispute.summary: Ajkaceratops kozmai is a bizarre European ornithischian of contested affinity. Its redescribers (Czepiński and Madzia, 2024) classify it only as ?Ceratopsia, noting that a ceratopsian position depends on interpreting its anterior snout element as a rostral and that it may not be a ceratopsian at all; Bertozzo and others (2025) recovered it as a non-ceratopsian basal ornithopod, sister to Changmiania, only under an alternate scoring of the snout element — their main analysis retained it within Ceratopsia. Maidment and others (2026), working from a much more complete referred skull, again recover it as a ceratopsian near the Ceratopsoidea.

history.note: Placed at Ceratopsia incertae sedis following Czepiński and Madzia (2024); the finer ceratopsoid placement of Maidment and others (2026) and the possibility of a non-ceratopsian identity both reflected, not adopted.

Re-evaluated; Ceratopsia incertae sedis retained. The non-ceratopsian result of Bertozzo and others (2025), recovered only under an alternate snout scoring, is outweighed by the more complete referred skull of Maidment and others (2026); Czepiński and Madzia (2024) mostly recovered it within or close to Ceratopsia. The finer near-Ceratopsoidea (sister to Zuniceratops) position of Maidment and others holds only in their implied-weights parsimony analysis and is not adopted.

Ajnabia.etymology: From Arabic 'ajnabia' meaning 'stranger' or 'foreigner', reflecting the unexpected presence of hadrosaurs in Africa
Ajnabia.description: Ajnabia is a genus of lambeosaurine hadrosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) of Morocco. It is the first definitive hadrosaur from Africa and is thought to be related to European hadrosaurs like Adynomosaurus and Pararhabdodon. The discovery of Ajnabia came as a surprise to the paleontologists who found it because Africa was isolated by water from the rest of the world during the Cretaceous, such that hadrosaurs were assumed to have been unable to reach the continent.

Akainacephalus.etymology: From Greek 'akaina' meaning 'thorn' or 'spike' and 'kephale' meaning 'head'; meaning 'thorn head'
Akainacephalus.description: Akainacephalus is a monospecific genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur from southern Utah that lived during the Late Cretaceous (late Campanian, 76.26 Ma) in what is now the Horse Mountain Gryposaur Quarry of the Kaiparowits Formation. The type and only species, Akainacephalus johnsoni, is known from the most complete ankylosaur specimen ever discovered from southern Laramidia, including a complete skull, tail club, a number of osteoderms, limb elements and part of its pelvis, among other remains. It was described in 2018 by Jelle P. Wiersma and Randall B. Irmis. It is closely related and shares similar cranial anatomy to Nodocephalosaurus.

Alamosaurus.etymology: Named after the Ojo Alamo rock formation combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Ojo Alamo lizard'
Alamosaurus.description: Alamosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs containing a single known species, Alamosaurus sanjuanensis, from the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now southwestern North America. It is one of the few known titanosaurs to have inhabited North America after the nearly 30-million-year absence of sauropods from the North American fossil record ("sauropod hiatus") and probably represents an immigrant from South America.

dispute.summary: Placed within Saltasauridae as incertae sedis. Alamosaurus has long resisted precise placement: an early assessment (Lehman, 2002) found it a mosaic of titanosaur features and could not resolve it beyond an indeterminate derived titanosaur. More recent work disagrees over its affinities: Navarro et al. (2022) recovered it within Saltasaurinae as the sister taxon of Baurutitan, and it has been grouped among Laurasian titanosaurs close to Saltasaurinae (Santucci and Filippi, 2022), whereas Cerda et al. (2021) instead recovered a South American affinity close to Pellegrinisaurus. These placements fall within Saltasauridae under some definitions. It is placed at Saltasauridae pending resolution.

history.note: Placed at Saltasauridae incertae sedis; Laurasian (near Saltasaurinae) and South American (near Pellegrinisaurus) affinities remain unresolved.

No superior fossa on upper side of scapular ridge, unlike many sauropod scapulae
Ischium extremely short, lacking the long slender posterior extension characteristic of all other known sauropod ischia
Ischium with unusually great dorsoventral diameter at proximal end and pubic articular surface extending distalward more than half the total bone length

Alaskacephale.etymology: Named for Alaska, where it was discovered, combined with Greek 'kephale' meaning 'head', referring to its pachycephalosaurid dome-headed nature.
Alaskacephale.description: Alaskacephale is an extinct genus of pachycephalosaurid, a group of dome-headed, herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs, that lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now northern Alaska. The genus is one of the few known Arctic dinosaurs and was found in the Prince Creek Formation, which preserves a menagerie of fossils. The only known specimen, a squamosal bone, was found in 1999 and later described in 2005. However, Alaskacephale was not formally named until the next year.
diagnostic_features: Two divergent rows of nodes on the squamosal, converging toward the midline of the skull
Nodes with well-defined polygonal bases and prominent apices

Albalophosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'albus' meaning 'white' and Greek 'lophos' meaning 'crest' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to the snow-covered crest of Mount Hakusan near where it was found.
Albalophosaurus.description: Albalophosaurus is a genus of marginocephalian ornithischian dinosaur that lived in Japan during the Early Cretaceous. The type species is Albalophosaurus yamaguchiorum.

dispute.summary: Albalophosaurus yamaguchiorum is a fragmentary taxon of uncertain affinity, recovered as a basal ceratopsian (Han and others, 2012; Jones, 2026) but, by Fonseca and others (2024), variously as a basal pachycephalosaur, the sister to Marginocephalia, or a basal ceratopsian.

history.note: Placed at Marginocephalia incertae sedis given conflicting basal-ceratopsian and basal-pachycephalosaurian results; not assigned within Ceratopsia pending resolution.

diagnostic_features: Lateral surface of the maxilla lacks a buccal emargination (buccal ridge and buccal emargination absent), in contrast to the majority of other ornithischians.
Exceptionally deep, well-defined cheek recess (buccal emargination) present on the lateral surface of the dentary, bounded laterally by a thick, prominent ridge.
Labial surfaces of the maxillary tooth crowns ornamented with 10-12 fine apicobasally extending striations not present in other basal ornithischians.
Maxillary tooth crowns bear a strong primary ridge offset distally and prominent secondary ridges along mesial and distal margins, with areas between ridges gently concave.

Dentary tooth crowns bear a primary ridge situated near the center that splits into several branches apically, each supporting a marginal denticle; numerous secondary ridges cover the remaining crown surface.

Albertaceratops.etymology: Named after Alberta, Canada, combined with Greek 'keras' meaning 'horn' and 'ops' meaning 'face'; meaning 'Alberta horned face'
Albertaceratops.description: Albertaceratops is a genus of centrosaurine horned dinosaur from the middle Campanian-age Upper Cretaceous Oldman Formation of Alberta, Canada.

Unmodified adult-sized postorbital horncores wide-based, elongated, massive, and oriented rostrolaterally
Parietal with pair of wide-based, large, pachyostotic, dorsoventrally depressed, rostrally curved processes originating from the caudolateral margin of the parietals (P3 processes)

Albertadromeus.etymology: Named after Alberta, Canada, combined with Greek 'dromeus' meaning 'runner'; meaning 'runner from Alberta'
Albertadromeus.description: Albertadromeus is an extinct genus of orodromine thescelosaurid dinosaur known from the upper part of the Late Cretaceous Oldman Formation (middle Campanian stage) of Alberta, Canada. It contains a single species, Albertadromeus syntarsus.
diagnostic_features: Distal fibula reduced to a thin sheet of bone fused to the anterior surface of the tibia for the distal one-third of its length
Prominent cnemial crest that projects dorsally (in addition to anterolaterally), resulting in a posteriorly sloped dorsal extremity of the proximal tibia
Lateral condyle of proximal tibia strongly bilobed and prominent
Tibia and femur characterized by dense cortical bone with reduced cancellous bone, giving a hollow cross-section similar to theropods

species.etymology: From Greek words 'syn' meaning 'together' and 'tarsus' meaning 'ankle', a reference to the condition where the distal fibula is fused to the distal tibia.

Albertavenator.etymology: Named after Alberta, Canada, combined with Latin 'venator' meaning 'hunter'; meaning 'Alberta hunter'
Albertavenator.description: Albertavenator is a genus of small-bodied troodontid theropod dinosaur that lived during the early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 71 million years ago. It is known from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, Canada, and is currently represented by a single species, Albertavenator curriei. The species name honors Canadian paleontologist Philip J. Currie for his extensive contributions to theropod research. The animal is known from parts of the skull.
diagnostic_features: Primary supraciliary foramen truncated anteriorly by the lacrimal contact, unlike all other troodontids where it is completely enclosed by the frontal
Superficial (ectocranial) surface of the frontal proportionally shorter than all known troodontids, with a length to width ratio less than 1.3
Frontoparietal contact bearing an enlarged lappet of the frontal extending medially to extensively overlap the lateral region of the interfrontal (anterior) process of the parietal

Albertonykus.etymology: Named after Alberta, Canada, combined with Greek 'onyx' (genitive 'onykos') meaning 'claw'; meaning 'Alberta claw'
Albertonykus.description: Albertonykus is an extinct genus of alvarezsaurid dinosaur from the Maastrichtian-age (Upper Cretaceous) rocks of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, Canada. It is known from forelimb and hindlimb remains from multiple individuals. All but two of the specimens come from a bonebed dominated by Albertosaurus, located at the top of Unit 4 of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation, dating to ~68.5 million years ago.

Distinct tubercle on medial margin of ulna, absent or only weakly developed as a small ridge in other alvarezsaurs
Manual ungual I with Y-shaped lateral grooves, absent in both Asian and South American alvarezsaurs
Ventral groove of manual ungual I extends proximally to the level of the ventral foramina, further than in Mononykus
Metatarsal III shaft with sharp longitudinal ventral keel and flat, unexpanded dorsal surface, contrasting with rounded ventral and expanded dorsal surfaces of Asian taxa
