Cedarpelta.etymology: Named for the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'pelta' meaning 'shield', referring to its ankylosaurid armor.
Cedarpelta.description: Cedarpelta is an extinct genus of basal ankylosaurid dinosaur from Utah that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in what is now the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation. The type and only species, Cedarpelta bilbeyhallorum, is known from multiple specimens including partial skulls and postcranial material. It was named in 2001 by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Don Burge, and John Bird. Cedarpelta has an estimated length of 7 meters (23 feet) and weight of 5 tonnes (11,023 lbs). The skull of Cedarpelta lacks extensive cranial ornamentation and is one of the only known ankylosaurs with individual skull bones that are not completely fused together.

Centrosaurus.description: Centrosaurus is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur from the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous of Canada. Its remains have been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation, dating from 76.5 to 75.5 million years ago. The type and only species seen as valid today is Centrosaurus apertus.

Cerasinops.etymology: From Greek kerasos meaning 'cherry' and Greek ops meaning 'face'. Full meaning: 'cherry face', likely referring to the shape or color of its facial features.
Cerasinops.description: Cerasinops was a small ceratopsian dinosaur. It lived during the Campanian of the late Cretaceous Period. Its fossils have been found in Two Medicine Formation, in Montana. The type species of the genus Cerasinops is C. hodgskissi.
diagnostic_features: Prootic extends further caudodorsally on the paroccipital process than in either Protoceratops or Montanoceratops.
Horizontal jugal crest oriented at ninety degrees from the main dorsoventral jugal crest, unique among basal neoceratopsians.
Extremely robust surangular with a thick buttress of bone at the contact with the coronoid process of the dentary.
Pronounced medial bend of the distal ulna, more extreme than in other North American basal neoceratopsians.
Forelimb to hindlimb ratio of 0.60, lower than in any other basal neoceratopsian.
Forelimb bones have longitudinal vascular canal structure in cortical bone, contrasting with the circumferential pattern in the hindlimb elements of the same individual.

Ceratocaudia.etymology: Cerato- (Greek, horn) + caud- (Greek, tail), for the horn-like crest on the anterior caudal neural spines; gender feminine.
Ceratocaudia.description: Ceratocaudia is a genus of macronarian sauropod dinosaur from the Jurassic Kaladongar Formation of Gujarat, India. The genus contains a single species, the type species Ceratocaudia antiqua, known from a partial skeleton.
diagnostic_features: Small notch on the apex of the postzygapophyseal articular facet of the anterior cervical vertebra, positioned just below the epipophysis.
Anterior caudal vertebrae with tall neural spines bearing a flat dorsal edge and an anteriorly directed, curved horn-like crest on the posterodorsal corner.
Caudal centra amphicoelous to platycoelous through the anterior and middle series, with a gradual transition to procoelous articular facets in the posterior caudal vertebrae.
Anterior and middle chevrons with split (bifurcate) articular facets on their rami.
Distal tibia with a deeply concave, proximodistally oriented notch on its anterior surface.
Fibula with a well-developed anterior crest on the proximal diaphysis and a subtriangular distal epiphysis.

Ceratonykus.etymology: From Greek keras/keratos ('horn') + onyx/nykos ('claw'), meaning 'horned claw'.
Ceratonykus.description: Ceratonykus is a monospecific genus of alvarezsaurid dinosaur from Mongolia that lived during the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) in what is now the Barun Goyot Formation. The type and only species, Ceratonykus oculatus, is known from a fragmentary skeleton, including an incomplete skull, of an adult individual. It was named and described in 2009 by Vladimir Alifanov and Rinchen Barsbold. Its describers questioned the traditional placement of alvarezsaurs in Theropoda, instead suggesting they were ornithischians, but this has not been accepted since. Ceratonykus has an estimated length of 75 centimeters (2.46 feet) and weight of 760 grams (1.68 pounds). It has been considered as a possible junior synonym of Parvicursor.
diagnostic_features: Femora strongly curved and nearly half as long as tibiotarsus (shorter than in all other parvicursorids)

Carpometacarpus bears spikelike bones (interpreted as possible ungual phalanges of additional digits)
Natural endocast lacks vertical flexure at brain floor; optic lobes displaced ventrally; acoustic tubercles unusually wide
Deep proximodorsal notch between second and fourth metatarsals; dorsal and palmar surfaces of these bones ridgelike with deep grooves between them
Frontals each nearly four times as long as wide; narrowing rostrally into a narrow wedge; prefrontals adjoining each other medially

Ceratops.etymology: From Greek keras (horn) and ops (face); meaning "horn face".
Ceratops.description: Ceratops is a dubious genus of herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaur which lived during the Late Cretaceous. Its fossils have been found in the Judith River Formation in Montana. Although poorly known, Ceratops is important in the history of dinosaurs, since it is the type genus for which both the Ceratopsia and the Ceratopsidae have been named.

dispute.summary: Ceratops is a nomen dubium known only from a pair of postorbital horncores and an occipital condyle that lack diagnostic features, despite being the type genus by which both Ceratopsia and Ceratopsidae were named. It cannot be placed below family level and is retained at Ceratopsidae incertae sedis.

Ceratosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'keras/keratos' (horn) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'horn lizard', referring to the distinctive median nasal horn core.
Ceratosaurus.description: Ceratosaurus is the type genus of Ceratosauridae and one of the most iconic Late Jurassic theropods of the Morrison Formation. The type species, Ceratosaurus nasicornis, was erected by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1884 on a near-complete skeleton (USNM 4735) collected by M. P. Felch from Quarry No. 1, Garden Park, near Cañon City, Fremont County, Colorado. Originally housed at the Yale Peabody Museum, the holotype was transferred to the USNM in 1898-1899 and prepared by C. W. Gilmore over 1911-1918. Gilmore (1920) produced the canonical redescription as USNM Bulletin 110, correcting Marsh's restoration errors and supporting Ceratosauridae as distinct from Megalosauridae against Cope's 1892 referral. Madsen and Welles (2000) revised the osteology and named two additional Morrison species (C. dentisulcatus from Cleveland-Lloyd, C. magnicornis from the Fruita Paleontological Area), each based on more complete material from upper or lower Brushy Basin Member horizons. Ceratosaurus is most readily diagnosed by an unpaired nasal horn core, smaller paired protuberances above each orbit, an unusually low premaxillary tooth count, a tightly coossified pelvis, coossified metatarsals II-IV, and a row of small dermal ossicles running along the dorsal midline.
diagnostic_features: Unpaired median horn core formed from the nasals, transversely compressed and positioned above the external nares.
Paired horn-like protuberances on the lacrimal/prefrontal bones above the antorbital fenestra, partially overhanging each orbit.
Cervical vertebral centra plano-concave (flat anteriorly, deeply cupped posteriorly), with strongly shortened posterior cervicals.
Zygosphene-zygapophysis accessory articulation present in cervical and dorsal vertebrae.
Premaxilla bears only three teeth, an unusually low count among contemporaneous Jurassic theropods.
Pelvis tightly coossified — ilium, pubis, and ischium fused — with a closed obturator foramen on a slender pubis.
Metatarsals II-IV coossified to one another.
Row of small osseous dermal ossicles preserved along the dorsal midline from the base of the skull through the proximal tail.

synonyms.name: Megalosaurus nasicornis
synonyms.reason: Cope (1892) referred Ceratosaurus nasicornis to Megalosaurus; Gilmore (1920) rejected the referral and reaffirmed Ceratosaurus as a valid genus distinct from Megalosaurus.

dispute.summary: Ceratosuchops inferodios is a baryonychine spinosaurid from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight (Barker et al., 2021), recovered as a baryonychine by later analyses (Rauhut et al., 2025; Cau, 2025). Its own validity is not in doubt, but its relationship to the co-occurring Riparovenator milnerae is unsettled: Sereno et al. (2022) tentatively treated the two as a single taxon, Ceratosuchops, attributing their differences to individual variation, and Santos-Cubedo et al. (2023) followed that synonymy, whereas Barker et al. (2021) and Rauhut et al. (2025) kept them distinct and Cau (2025) left the question open. Because Ceratosuchops is the senior name, it is retained as valid regardless.

history.note: Placed at Baryonychinae following Barker et al. (2021) and Rauhut et al. (2025) (P2/P4; the tribe Ceratosuchopsini is not retained); the proposed synonymy with Riparovenator is unresolved.

Dispute resourced to the primary literature and Jones (2026) dropped from it — the Ceratosuchops–Riparovenator single-taxon proposal rests on individual (not ontogenetic) variation; Ceratosuchops kept valid as the senior name.

Ceratosuchops.etymology: From Greek keras/keratos ('horn') + Latin suchus ('crocodile', from Greek) + ops ('face'), meaning 'horned crocodile face', in reference to the bony boss on the postorbital bone.
Ceratosuchops.description: Ceratosuchops is a genus of spinosaurid from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) Wessex Formation of Britain. The type species is C. inferodios, known from skull fragments (a snout tip and a partial braincase) recovered between 2013-2017 from Chilton Chine on the Isle of Wight, and housed at the Dinosaur Isle Museum in Sandown. It was named in 2021 by a team consisting of Chris Tijani Barker, Darren Naish, David W. E. Hone, and colleagues, alongside Riparovenator milnerae.

dispute.summary: Long allied with diplodocoids, Cetiosauriscus is no longer regarded as a member of Diplodocoidea. Tschopp et al. (2015) recovered it outside Neosauropoda as a non-neosauropod eusauropod (near Omeisaurus) under implied weighting, though within Diplodocimorpha under equal weighting; the non-neosauropod eusauropod reading follows Moore et al. (2020) and is continued by later work (Jones, 2026). Its precise position among eusauropods is unresolved.

history.note: Removed from Diplodocoidea (formerly placed at Flagellicaudata) and reparented to Eusauropoda incertae sedis as a non-neosauropod eusauropod (Tschopp et al., 2015; Jones, 2026); finer placement among eusauropods remains unresolved.
Confirmed placement at Eusauropoda incertae sedis; recovered as a non-neosauropod eusauropod, with the historical diplodocid interpretation superseded and its finer position unresolved.

Cetiosauriscus.etymology: From Greek 'ketos' meaning 'sea monster' or 'whale', 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', and '-iskos' meaning 'resembling', meaning 'resembling Cetiosaurus' (the whale lizard).
Cetiosauriscus.description: Cetiosauriscus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived between 166 and 164 million years ago during the Callovian (Middle Jurassic Period) in what is now England. A herbivore, Cetiosauriscus had - by sauropod standards - a moderately long tail, and longer forelimbs, making them as long as its hindlimbs. It has been estimated as about 15 m (49 ft) long and between 4 and 10 t (3.9 and 9.8 long tons; 4.4 and 11.0 short tons) in weight.

Low, elongate ilium, lower than in Cetiosaurus, with a slender femur
Short humerus (about 0.69 of femoral length) with a proportionally long forearm, the radius lacking the proximal "Cetiosaurus beak"

Cetiosaurus.etymology: From Greek keteios/ketos ('sea monster', later 'whale') + sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'whale lizard'. Named by Richard Owen who initially believed it was a large marine creature.
Cetiosaurus.description: Cetiosaurus is a genus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic Period, living about 171 to 165 million years ago during the Bajocian and Bathonian ages in what is now Britain and probably France.
diagnostic_features: Posterior cervical and anterior dorsal neural spines symmetrically pyramid-shaped, with laminae nearly equal about both the sagittal and transverse planes
Spinodiapophyseal lamina lost (or completely fused with the spinopostzygapophyseal lamina) on all dorsal neural spines
Distal caudal centra with tongue-like projections at the dorsal margin of the articular faces, extending the floor of the neural canal anteroposteriorly
Distal shafts of the anterior chevrons anteroposteriorly compressed, not tapering to a transversely flattened distal end
A triangular hollow, bounded dorsally by a horizontal ridge, on the lateral surface of the base of the pubic process of the ilium

synonyms.name: Cardiodon
synonyms.reason: Possible junior subjective synonym of Cetiosaurus; identification is tentative. Per Olshevsky's Dinosaur Genera List.

species.etymology: Named for Oxford (Latin 'Oxonia'), the county where the type specimens were discovered by Professor John Phillips in 1868-1870.

type_specimen.institution: Oxford University Museum of Natural History

species.authors: Phillips, J.

notable_specimens.significance: Referred C. oxoniensis skeleton, about 40 percent complete and the most complete sauropod fossil found in the United Kingdom. It preserves a nearly complete cervical series (2-14), greatly extending known anatomy, especially the neck, absent in the type material. On display since 1985.

Chadititan.etymology: From Spanish chadi ('salt' or referring to the salt flats of the Salitral Moreno region) + Greek Titan (a giant from mythology), meaning 'titan of the salt'.
Chadititan.description: Chadititan is an extinct genus of titanosaurian dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) Anacleto Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, C. calvoi, known from several fragmentary skeletons. Chadititan is characterized by its small size compared to related taxa and its particularly gracile limbs.
diagnostic_features: Gracile humerus with very deep anterior excavation having well-defined dorsal and lateral margins
Homogeneously procoelous caudal vertebrae throughout the caudal series
Anterior caudals with neural arch continuous with the anterior margin of the vertebral centrum (not separated by a notch)
Caudal vertebrae elongate and transversely compressed with width/length index of 0.4-0.5 in anterior caudals
Femoral head dorsomedially projected, far from the level of the greater trochanter

species.name: Chadititan calvoi
species.etymology: Named for Argentine paleontologist Jorge O. Calvo, who coined the taxonomic group Rinconsauria, to which this taxon belongs.

Chakisaurus.etymology: From Mapudungun chaki ('elder guanaco') + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'elder guanaco lizard'.
Chakisaurus.description: Chakisaurus is an extinct genus of elasmarian ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Huincul Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, C. nekul, known from multiple partial skeletons belonging to individuals of different ages. Chakisaurus represents the first ornithischian species to be named from the Huincul Formation.
diagnostic_features: Anterior proximal caudal vertebrae with parallelogram-shaped centra in lateral view
Anterior caudals of the distal tail with rod-like, posterodorsally oriented transverse processes
Proximal end of the fibula with a deep, proximodistally extended fossa (possible autapomorphy, unknown in other elasmarians)
Transversely compressed calcaneus, its transverse width about one-third of its anteroposterior length (proportionally narrower than in other elasmarians)
Nearly flat tibial articular surface of the calcaneus
Posterior dorsal vertebrae with a hyposphene articulation bearing a deeply excavated lateral surface

species.name: Chakisaurus nekul
species.etymology: From Mapudungun 'nekul' meaning 'swift', in reference to the cursorial habits inferred for this ornithopod.

type_specimen.material: Incomplete postcranial skeleton: posterior dorsal neural arch and centrum, a partial sacrum, several caudal vertebrae, partial left femur, right tibia and left fibula, calcaneus, and pedal phalanges.

Changchunsaurus.etymology: Named after Changchun, the city near where it was discovered in Jilin Province, China, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Changchun lizard'.
Changchunsaurus.description: Changchunsaurus is an extinct genus of small herbivorous neornithischian dinosaur from Early or Late Cretaceous deposits of Gongzhuling, Jilin, China. It is the first named dinosaur genus from that region.
diagnostic_features: Jugal boss projects laterally near ventral margin of orbit with nubble (scaly) surface texture, not seen in any other known ornithopod
Predentary ventral process distinctly longer than lateral process, with bilobate end of ventral process
Longitudinal concave (median groove) present along midline suture of nasal
Quadratojugal triangular (equilateral) with no quadrate foramen
Five premaxillary teeth with only a very short edentulous anterior portion of premaxilla
Enamel on cheek tooth crowns distributed symmetrically on both buccal and lingual faces

species.etymology: From Latin 'parvus' meaning 'petite' or 'small', named for the small size of the animal.

Changmiania.etymology: From Chinese changmian (长眠, 'eternal sleep'), referring to the life-like buried positions of the specimens, which suggest they were buried alive while sleeping.
Changmiania.description: Changmiania is a genus of basal ornithopod dinosaur that lived in what is now China during the Early Cretaceous. It contains a single species, Changmiania liaoningensis.
diagnostic_features: Rostrocaudally elongated frontals with maximum length to width ratio >4, distinctly narrower than in all other basal ornithopods
Only six cervical vertebrae, reduced from the nine typical of basal ornithischians and ornithopods
Neural spines of sacral vertebrae completely fused together, forming a craniocaudally-elongated continuous bar
Fused scapulocoracoid with scapular blade asymmetrically expanded both ventrally and dorsally
Paired ilia symmetrically inclined dorsomedially, partially covering the sacrum in dorsal view
Proximal half of fibula as robust as the corresponding portion of the tibia

species.name: Changmiania liaoningensis
species.etymology: Named for the provenance of the fossils from Liaoning Province, China.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete articulated skeleton.

Changyuraptor.etymology: From Chinese 'chang' meaning 'long', 'yu' meaning 'feather', and Latin 'raptor' meaning 'thief' or 'seizer', referring to its long feathers.
Changyuraptor.description: Changyuraptor is a genus of "four-winged", predatory dinosaurs. It is known from a single fossil specimen representing the species Changyuraptor yangi, which was discovered from Early Cretaceous (125 million year old) deposits in Liaoning Province, China. C. yangi belongs to the group of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaurs called the Microraptoria.
diagnostic_features: Forelimb proportionally much longer relative to hindlimb than in other microraptorines (forelimb 96% of hindlimb length including digits)
Humerus much longer (420%) than ulna, as opposed to Microraptor zhaoianus in which these bones are more comparable in length
Well-developed semi-lunate carpal covering all of proximal ends of metacarpals I and II, as opposed to the small semi-lunate carpal covering about half the base in most other microraptorines
Fewer caudal vertebrae (estimated 22) than Microraptor zhaoianus (25-26) and Tianyuraptor ostromi (28)
Rectrices significantly longer than in other microraptorines; constitute the longest feathers recorded in any non-avian theropod
Midshaft of metatarsal IV significantly broader than that of metatarsal III or metatarsal II

species.name: Changyuraptor yangi
species.etymology: Named for researcher Professor Yang Yandong.

dispute.summary: Changzhousaurus was described from a specimen with a mosaic of troodontid, dromaeosaurid, anchiornithid, and avialan features; no quantitative analysis was run, and its describers preferred an early-diverging deinonychosaurian interpretation while conceding anchiornithine or avialan status is not impossible (Xu et al., 2026). It is placed at Deinonychosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Deinonychosauria incertae sedis (least-inclusive uncontested clade); mosaic morphology, no phylogenetic analysis, family-level placement unresolved.

Changzhousaurus.etymology: Named after Changzhou city (Jiangsu Province, China), honoring the Changzhou Municipal Government, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Changzhou lizard'.
Changzhousaurus.description: Changzhousaurus is an extinct genus of paravian theropod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian age) Jiufotang Formation of China. The genus contains a single species, Changzhousaurus sinensis, known from a nearly complete, articulated skeleton with extensive associated feather traces, preserved as a part and counterpart.
diagnostic_features: Premaxilla with a nearly vertical nasal process, a very small prenarial portion, and a large, sub-square subnarial portion
Anterior caudal vertebrae with a wide ventral intervertebral space occupied by a knob-like chevron lacking a distal process
Ossified intervertebral discs between the middle and posterior caudal vertebrae
Furcula with constant width throughout its length
Scapula with a rod-like acromion process, a dorsally curved and very thick blade, and a mushroom-like expanded distal end
About sixteen highly elongated tail feathers, around four times femoral length, near the end of the bony tail

species.name: Changzhousaurus sinensis
species.etymology: From Latin 'sinensis' meaning 'from China', for the country where the holotype was found.

type_specimen.material: A nearly complete, articulated skeleton with associated plumage across the body, preserved as part and counterpart.

species.authors: Xu, X.

Chaoyangsaurus.etymology: Named after Chaoyang, the region in Liaoning Province, China where fossils were found, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Chaoyang lizard'.
Chaoyangsaurus.description: Chaoyangsaurus is a genus of marginocephalian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic (about between 150.8 and 145.5 million years ago) of China. Chaoyangsaurus belonged to the Ceratopsia (Greek for "horned faces"). Chaoyangsaurus, like all ceratopsians, was primarily a herbivore.
diagnostic_features: Quadratojugal overlaps the posterior (caudal) surface of the quadrate shaft rather than its lateral surface.
Quadrate shaft lacks a broad lateral surface; lateral margin is very thin anteroposteriorly with no anterior ramus.
Posteroventral margin of the quadrate shaft is convex mediolaterally, not concave or planar as in other ornithischians.
Dorsal margin of the lower jaw extends nearly horizontally from the coronoid process to the jaw articulation, with ventral margin curving posterodorsally along the angular region.
A distinct ridge separates the planar lateral and ventral surfaces of the angular, which meet at approximately a right angle.

species.name: Chaoyangsaurus youngi
species.etymology: Named for the Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian (known as 'C. C. Young'), regarded as the founder of Chinese vertebrate paleontology.

type_specimen.institution: Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences
type_specimen.material: Dorsal part of a skull, nearly complete mandible, complete axis, an isolated cervical vertebra and five articulated cervicals, a fragmentary humerus and scapula.

Charonosaurus.etymology: Named after Charon, the ferryman of the dead in Greek mythology who ferried souls across the river (the Amur River, near where the fossils were found, divides China and Russia), combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'. Full meaning: 'Charon's lizard'.
Charonosaurus.description: Charonosaurus is a genus of lambeosaurine hadrosaurid dinosaur similar to Parasaurolophus that lived in the latest Cretaceous Yuliangze Formation of China. Its fossils were described by Godefroit, Zan, and Jin in 2000, on the south bank of the Amur River, dividing China from Russia. It is monotypic, consisting of the species, C. jiayinensis.
diagnostic_features: Dorsal surface of parietal regularly rounded, without sagittal crest
Lateral side of squamosal nearly completely covered by caudal ramus of postorbital
Paroccipital and postcotyloid processes very low, extending only at mid-height of foramen magnum
Alar process of basisphenoid prominent and symmetrical
Tricipital crest developed on the humerus
Forearm elongated and slender: ulna total length/proximal width ratio >6.3, radius >6.6; preacetabular process of ilium elongated, ilium length/preacetabular length >2.1

species.name: Charonosaurus jiayinensis
species.etymology: Named for the type locality of Jiayin, in Heilongjiang Province, China, where the fossils were discovered.

type_specimen.material: A partial skull

Chasmosaurus.etymology: From Greek chasma meaning 'opening/hollow/gulf' and Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'. Full meaning: 'opening lizard', referring to the large fenestrae (openings) in its frill.
Chasmosaurus.description: Chasmosaurus is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Period in North America. Its given name means 'opening lizard', referring to the large openings (fenestrae) in its frill (Greek chasma, meaning 'opening', 'hollow', or 'gulf'; and sauros, meaning 'lizard'). With a length of 4.3-4.8 meters (14.1-15.7 ft) and a weight of 1.5-2 tonnes (1.7-2.2 short tons)-or anywhere from 2,200 to nearly 5,000 lbs-Chasmosaurus was of a slightly smaller to "average" size, especially when compared to larger ceratopsids (such as Triceratops, which were about the size of an African bush elephant).
diagnostic_features: Skull broadly triangular in superior aspect with a narrow, abbreviated facial portion and a broad, greatly extended posterior crest ending squarely behind
Coalesced parietals forming a slender framework enclosing large sub-triangular fontanelles so large as to reduce posterior two-thirds of parietals to a mere slender framework
Squamosals very long and narrow with a scalloped free border bearing low sub-conical epoccipitals
Postfrontal fontanelle present, long and narrow, extending between the supraorbital horn-cores
Supraorbital horn-cores small and upright, broadly oval in cross section near the base with greater diameter fore and aft
Parietal crest remarkably flat, extending backward and laterally in almost a horizontal plane, with length to breadth ratio approximately 7 to 8

synonyms.name: Eoceratops
synonyms.reason: Originally described as Monoclonius canadensis and later re-erected as Eoceratops; the material is now treated as morphological variation within Chasmosaurus.

species.etymology: Named for collector Walter Bell, from whose discovery area the holotype parietal bone was recovered.

synonyms.name: Protorosaurus belli
synonyms.reason: Originally described as Protorosaurus belli; the genus name was preoccupied, and the species was reassigned to Chasmosaurus.

Rostral straight along the lower edge, not hooked downward at the tip.
Nasal horncore massive; skull broad between the orbits, without brow horncores.
Well-developed epijugal.
Parietals deeply indented posteriorly; epoccipitals small, giving a nearly smooth squamosal border.
Mandible massive, more robust than in C. belli.

Chebsaurus.etymology: From colloquial Arabic 'cheb' (شاب) meaning 'young man', referring to the juvenile nature of the fossils found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Chebsaurus.description: Chebsaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur, specifically a eusauropod. It lived in present-day Algeria, in the Callovian aged Aïssa Formation. The type species, C. algeriensis, was named in 2005 by Mahammed et al. and is the most complete Algerian sauropod known. It was around 8 to 9 meters (26 to 30 ft) long.

Tuberculated surface on both the crowns and roots of teeth
Short and robust basioccipital tubercles diverging in a V-shape (~60°), facets inclined ~70° to the horizontal in caudal view, with elliptical surface oriented along a craniodorsal long axis
Base of the postzygodiapophysial lamina of the transverse process included within the cranial part of the postzygapophysis in lateral view
Small elliptical fossa positioned caudodorsally to the lateral excavations (pseudopleurocoels) on a middle dorsal vertebra centrum

Chenanisaurus.etymology: Named after Sidi Chennane, the locality in Morocco (Khouribga phosphate mines) where the fossil was found, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Sidi Chennane lizard'.
Chenanisaurus.description: Chenanisaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Morocco. The genus belongs to the family Abelisauridae. It is known from a partial dentary (lower jawbone) and several teeth that were found in the phosphate mines of Khouribga, in rocks of the Maastrichtian-aged Ouled Abdoun Basin. Chenanisaurus was described in 2017 by British paleontologist Nicholas Longrich and colleagues. The genus contains a single species, Chenanisaurus barbaricus.
diagnostic_features: Lateral groove and associated neurovascular foramina located high (dorsally) on dentary, contrasting with the ventrally positioned groove in other derived abelisaurids
Anterodorsal margin of dentary downturned in lateral view
Massive symphysis with anterior margin nearly vertical in lateral view
Tip of jaws broad, with dentaries meeting at an obtuse angle

Chialingosaurus.etymology: Named after the Chialing River (now Jialing River) in Sichuan Province, China, where fossils were discovered, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Chialing lizard'.
Chialingosaurus.description: Chialingosaurus is a genus of herbivorous stegosaurian dinosaur similar to Kentrosaurus from the Upper Shaximiao Formation, Late Jurassic beds in Sichuan Province in China. Its age makes it one of the oldest species of stegosaurs, living about 160 million years ago. Since it was an herbivore, scientists think that Chialingosaurus probably ate ferns and cycads, which were plentiful during the period when Chialingosaurus was alive.

Chiayusaurus.etymology: From Chia-yü-kuan (Jiayuguan, in western Gansu/Kansu Province) and Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "Jiayuguan lizard". Originally erected as Chiayüsaurus and subsequently rendered Chiayusaurus to comply with ICZN orthography.
Chiayusaurus.description: Chiayusaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur known from teeth found in China and possibly also South Korea. Two species have been named for this obscure genus, though only the type, C. lacustris, is still seen as valid. It was originally named as Chiayüsaurus, but the ICZN does not permit special characters, so the name was corrected to Chiayusaurus. The obsolete name can still be seen in older sources, though. As a sauropod, Chiayusaurus would have been a large, quadrupedal herbivore.

Chilantaisaurus.etymology: Named after Jilantai (also romanized as Chilantai) Salt Lake in Inner Mongolia, China, where the fossils were found, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Jilantai Salt Lake lizard'.
Chilantaisaurus.description: Chilantaisaurus is an extinct genus of large theropod dinosaur that lived in present-day China during the Late Cretaceous period. It was described by Chinese paleontologist Hu Show-Yung in 1964. The genus contains a single valid species, C. tashuikouensis, though several other species have been assigned to the genus. C. tashuikouensis is known from a single, incomplete postcranial skeleton, the holotype specimen. This specimen was found by a joint Sino-Soviet expedition to Inner Mongolia in rock layers coming from the Ulansuhai Formation. This indicates these fossils date to the Santonian or Campanian stages of the Cretaceous period, around 85.7 to 72.2 million years ago. However, the age of the Ulansuhai Formation is debated.

Metatarsals short and stout relative to femur, not closely appressed, with unreduced metatarsal III shaft

Chilesaurus.etymology: Named after Chile, the country in South America where it was discovered, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'. Full meaning: 'Chile lizard'.
Chilesaurus.description: Chilesaurus is an extinct genus of herbivorous dinosaur. While its exact classification is uncertain, many researchers believe it is a theropod, with a minority of academics suggesting that it may be an ornithischian. The type and only known species so far is Chilesaurus diegosuarezi. Chilesaurus lived between 148-147 million years ago (Mya) in the Late Jurassic period of Chile. Showing a combination of traits from theropods, ornithischians, and sauropodomorphs, this genus has far-reaching implications for the evolution of dinosaurs, such as whether the traditional saurischian-ornithischian split is superior or inferior to the proposed group Ornithoscelida. This however, has been contested by several other authors, who believe that the weight of evidence supports its membership within Theropoda, and possibly as a member of Tetanurae.

dispute.summary: Chilesaurus diegosuarezi is an enigmatic herbivorous dinosaur of highly contested affinities, combining theropod, ornithischian, and sauropodomorph features. It was originally described as a basal tetanuran theropod (Novas and others, 2015), but later analyses have recovered it as an early-diverging ornithischian within Ornithoscelida (Baron and Barrett, 2017, 2018). Because the credible hypotheses span Theropoda and Ornithischia, it is placed conservatively at Dinosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed provisionally at Ornithischia; the placement straddles the Saurischia-Ornithischia boundary.
Moved from Ornithischia to Dinosauria incertae sedis; the theropod, ornithischian, and sauropodomorph hypotheses remain unresolved.

Dispute corrected — the "basal sauropodomorph" hypothesis attributed to Müller and others (2018) is unfounded, as that paper does not treat Chilesaurus (the sauropodomorph result traced to a since-corrected dataset). Retained at Dinosauria incertae sedis on the theropod-versus-ornithischian split.

Chindesaurus.etymology: Named for the Chinde Point area of Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Chindesaurus.description: Chindesaurus is an extinct genus of basal saurischian dinosaur from the Late Triassic (213-210 million years ago) of the southwestern United States. It is known from a single species, C. bryansmalli, based on a partial skeleton recovered from Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona. The original specimen was nicknamed "Gertie", and generated much publicity for the park upon its discovery in 1984 and airlift out of the park in 1985. Other fragmentary referred specimens have been found in Late Triassic sediments throughout Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas, but these may not belong to the genus. Chindesaurus was a bipedal carnivore, approximately as large as a wolf.
diagnostic_features: Diagnosed by a unique combination of character states rather than discrete autapomorphies; the 'glutealiform' astragalus formerly used to diagnose the genus is now referred to the Chindesaurus + Tawa hallae clade.

Dorsolateral ('greater') trochanter of the femur forming a rounded ridge.
Dorsal centra anteroposteriorly short, with centrum length less than 1.33 times the height of the anterior articular surface.
Prezygapophyses of the distal caudal vertebrae reduced, not extending farther anteriorly than 24% of centrum length.

Chinshakiangosaurus.etymology: Named after the Chinshakiang (now Jinsha River) in China, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Chinshakiang lizard'.

Choconsaurus.etymology: Named after Villa El Chocón, the locality in Neuquén Province, Argentina where the holotype was found, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'El Chocón lizard'.
Choconsaurus.description: Choconsaurus is an extinct genus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaur belonging to the group Titanosauriformes, which lived in the area of present-day Argentina at the end of the Cretaceous.

dispute.summary: Placed at Somphospondyli incertae sedis. The describing analysis (Simón et al., 2018) recovered Choconsaurus as a non-eutitanosaurian (basal) titanosaur in its most parsimonious trees, but reported that titanosaur membership is very weakly supported — a position outside Titanosauria (as a non-titanosaurian somphospondylan) is only one step less parsimonious. Somphospondyli is the least-inclusive clade both positions accept.

history.note: Placed at Titanosauria incertae sedis; the describing analysis found near-equal support for a non-titanosaurian somphospondylan position.

Broadened to Somphospondyli incertae sedis: the describing analysis found titanosaur membership very weakly supported, with a non-titanosaurian somphospondylan position only one step less parsimonious, so the conservative shared node is adopted.

Chondrosteosaurus.etymology: From Greek chondros ('cartilage') + osteon ('bone') + sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'cartilage and bone lizard', referring to the mix of cartilaginous and bony structures in its vertebrae.
Chondrosteosaurus.description: Chondrosteosaurus is a dubious genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation of England. Two species have been named: C. gigas and C. magnus, both of which are now considered invalid.
diagnostic_features: Flat under surface of vertebral centrum with predominant transverse over vertical diameter
Hemispherical convexity of anterior articular surface, concave posterior surface
Presence of bifid rib articulation indicated by both parapophysis and diapophysis on each side of centrum
Deep oblong lateral depressions on sides of centrum between para- and diapophyses
Neural canal at middle of vertebra approximately 1 inch 3 lines diameter, expanding to 2 inches at hinder outlet
Large cancellate structure within centrum, filled with unossified cartilage (chondrine) rather than air cells

species.name: Chondrosteosaurus gigas
species.etymology: From Latin 'gigas' meaning 'giant', referring to the large size of the sauropod vertebrae on which the species was based.

Choyrodon.etymology: Named for the city of Choyr in Mongolia, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'odon' meaning 'tooth'.
Choyrodon.description: Choyrodon is a genus of hadrosauroid dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Albian) Khuren Dukh Formation of Mongolia. The type and only species is Choyrodon barsboldi. The generic name is derived from the city of Choyr, and -odon, from Latin for tooth; the specific name barsboldi honors paleontologist Rinchen Barsbold. The material consists of a holotype partial skull and cervical ribs, with two other partial skulls both with associated postcranial material. It was found to be the sister taxon of Eolambia.

dispute.summary: Choyrodon barsboldi is an early-diverging hadrosauroid whose position within the group is poorly resolved. Gates et al. (2018), describing the genus, recovered it as the sister taxon of the North American Eolambia under the Norman (2015) matrix, but under the Wenhao and Godefroit (2012) matrix it fell into a large unresolved polytomy with other basal hadrosauroids.

history.note: Placed at Hadrosauroidea (basal) following the prevailing view.

diagnostic_features: Anterodorsal process of maxilla dorsoventrally broad with length-to-height ratio of 1, dorsal margin reaching and extending along ventral bony naris
Nasal possessing a low rise on dorsal surface positioned at posterior extent of nasal fenestra, with dorsoventrally thickened bone on posterior surface below the dorsal rise
Elongate, hypertrophied external narial fenestra with nasals comprising only a small portion of posteroventral margin
Lacrimal bearing rounded anterior margin and lobate shape in lateral view
Predentary with series of paired foramina below oral margin throughout lateral length of element, and flattened articulation surface across entire ventral margin
Surangular displays two deep osteological folds on lateral surface ventral to second foramen

Chromogisaurus.etymology: From Greek chroma meaning 'color' and Greek ge meaning 'earth', combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'. Full meaning: 'colored earth lizard', a reference to the Valle Pintado ('Painted Valley') where it was found.
Chromogisaurus.description: Chromogisaurus is an extinct genus of saturnaliid sauropodomorph which existed in Argentina during the Late Triassic (Carnian) period. It is from the Cancha de Bochas, Valle Pintado member of the Ischigualasto Formation. It was a small, bipedal herbivore, about 2 meters (6 ft 7 in) in length.
diagnostic_features: Proximal caudals without median notch separating the postzygapophyses
Femoral lateral surface with deep and large fossa immediately below the trochanteric shelf (autapomorphy)
Metatarsal II with strongly dorsoventrally asymmetric distal condyles (autapomorphy)
Ilium with strongly posteriorly developed postacetabular process
Incipiently perforated acetabulum

Chuanjiesaurus.etymology: Named for the village of Chuanjie in Yunnan Province, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Chuanjiesaurus.description: Chuanjiesaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaurs from the middle Jurassic Period. They lived in what is now China. The type species, Chuanjiesaurus anaensis, was first described by Fang, Pang, Lü, Zhang, Pan, Wang, Li and Cheng in 2000. Fossils of the species were found in the village of Chuanjie, Lufeng County, Yunnan Province, (in Chuanjie Formation deposits) and are named after the location where the fossils were discovered. Holtz gave a length of 25 meters (82 ft).
diagnostic_features: Cervical vertebrae relatively long and opisthocoelous, with well-developed but shallow pleurocoels and low neural spines.
Anterior caudals procoelous; posteriorly the posterior condyle weakens and centra become gently amphicoelous.
Caudal neural spines alter in morphology from baton-shaped to plate-shaped; haemal spines bifid.
Proximal scapula conspicuously broadened; proximal coracoid oval.
Ilium relatively large and nearly semicircular, with well-developed pubic peduncle located anterior to the midline and a weak iliac peduncle.
Forelimb/hind limb index 0.83/1; ulna/humerus index 0.65/1; tibia/femur index 0.65/1.

Chuanqilong.etymology: From Chinese chuanqi (传奇, 'legendary') + long (龙, 'dragon'), meaning 'legendary dragon'.
Chuanqilong.description: Chuanqilong is a monospecific genus of basal ankylosaurid dinosaur from the Liaoning Province, China that lived during the Early Cretaceous (late Barremian to Aptian stage, 122.0 to 118.9 Ma) in what is now the Jiufotang Formation. The type and only species, Chuanqilong chaoyangensis, is known from a nearly complete skeleton with a skull of a juvenile individual. It was described in 2014 by Fenglu Han, Wenjie Zheng, Dongyu Hu, Xing Xu, and Paul M. Barrett. Chuanqilong shows many similarities with Liaoningosaurus and may represent a later ontogenetic stage of the taxon.
diagnostic_features: Glenoid fossa for quadrate situated at same level as the dentary tooth row (unlike all other ankylosaurians in which it lies ventral to the tooth row).
Distally tapering ischium with constriction at midshaft length (unique among ankylosaurians).
Slender, wedge-like lacrimal forming rostral margin of orbit.
Long, slender retroarticular process.
Ratio of humerus to femur length = 0.88, notably higher than most known ankylosaurians.
Width of proximal humerus is half the length of the humeral shaft (ratio ~0.50, distinct from Liaoningosaurus at 0.38).

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete skeleton missing only the distal portion of the caudal series; two-dimensionally preserved in ventral view; skull, mandible, vertebral column, fore- and hind limbs, and armor all preserved.

Chubutisaurus.etymology: Named after Chubut Province in Patagonia, Argentina, where the fossils were discovered, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Chubut lizard'.
Chubutisaurus.description: Chubutisaurus is a genus of somphospondylan sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian to Albian) Cerro Barcino Formation of Argentina. The type species, Chubutisaurus insignis, was described by del Corro in 1975. Chubutisaurus had a more robust radius than Venenosaurus. In 2010 Gregory S. Paul gave a length of 18 meters (59 ft) and a weight of 12 tonnes (13 short tons). Thomas Holtz estimated its length at 23 meters (75 ft) in 2012.

Pleurocoels on the caudosacral vertebrae
Complete, unforked prespinal lamina on the posterior dorsal vertebrae

Chucarosaurus.etymology: From Mapudungun or Quechua chucaro ('indomitable' or 'wild, untamed') + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'indomitable reptile'.
Chucarosaurus.description: Chucarosaurus is an extinct genus of titanosaurian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (middle Cenomanian-lower Turonian) Huincul Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, C. diripienda, known from various limb and pelvic bones.

Humerus with proximally convex humeral head separated from major tubercle by a well-defined concavity
Femur with epicondyle extremely developed laterally, close to the lateral condyle
Femur with fourth trochanter located in the proximal third of the femur
Tibia with cnemial crest prominent and medially curved but dorsoventrally short

Chungkingosaurus.etymology: Named after Chongqing (formerly romanized as Chungking), the city in Sichuan Province, China where fossils were found, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Chongqing lizard'.
Chungkingosaurus.description: Chungkingosaurus is a genus of stegosaurian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Upper Shaximiao Formation in what is now China. The type species is Chungkingosaurus jiangbeiensis.

dispute.summary: Chungkingosaurus has been recovered within Stegosauridae (Maidment et al., 2008), in a basal clade with Huayangosaurus (Raven and Maidment, 2017), and as the earliest-diverging stegosaurid (Sánchez-Fenollosa and Cobos, 2025). With its family placement unresolved and Huayangosauridae not retained, it is placed at Stegosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Stegosauria incertae sedis, family placement bounces between basal Stegosauridae and the Huayangosaurus group.

Armor thick and large, consisting of both spinous plates and pear-shaped dorsal plates with constricted acute apex and expanded transverse base
Femoral shaft tubular, straight, and lacks a fourth trochanter; femur-tibia ratio approximately 1.26 (proportionally long tibia)
Astragalus and calcaneum completely fused to distal tibia and fibula
Dentition small and slender in tight alignment but not superimposed; crowns asymmetrical and crescentic with weak enamel and inconspicuous denticles

Cienciargentina.etymology: From Spanish 'ciencia' meaning 'science' and 'Argentina', combining a tribute to Argentine science with the country of discovery.
Cienciargentina.description: Cienciargentina is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod from the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian-Turonian) Huincul Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, Cienciargentina sanchezi, known from three partial skeletons of different sizes. Cienciargentina is the fourth definitive rebbachisaurid to be named from the Huincul Formation.

Dorsal centra amphicoelous to slightly opisthocoelous anteriorly and slightly opisthocoelous posteriorly; mid and posterior dorsals with an intrapostzygapophyseal lamina supporting the postzygapophyses, an accessory spinodiapophyseal lamina, and a spinoparapophyseal lamina on the posterior neural arches

Anterior caudal vertebrae with the spinoprezygapophyseal lamina more robust than the spinopostzygapophyseal lamina, and transverse processes bearing a full suite of diapophyseal laminae (anterior and posterior centrodiapophyseal, prezygodiapophyseal, and postzygodiapophyseal)
Posterior caudal vertebrae with the neural spine strongly displaced posteriorly and a length-to-height ratio of 5 or greater
Forked chevrons lacking anterior and posterior projections
Ischium with a constriction (neck) in the iliac peduncle and an ischial tuberosity; femoral head dorsally directed, rising well above the level of the greater trochanter

Cionodon.etymology: From Greek kion meaning 'column/pillar' and Greek odon meaning 'tooth'. Full meaning: 'column tooth', referring to the pillar-like shape of its teeth.
Cionodon.description: Cionodon is a dubious genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous. The type species, C. arctatus, was found in the Denver Formation of Lodge Pole Creek, Colorado and was formally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1874 based on the holotype AMNH 3951, collected in 1873. It is a nomen dubium because it is based on very fragmentary remains. A second species, Cionodon kysylkumensis (Riabinin, 1931), based on the holotype CCMGE 1/3760 (a set of vertebrae) from Uzbekistan, is known only from fragmentary remains and has since been reclassified as Bactrosaurus kysylkumensis.

dispute.summary: Cionodon is a nomen dubium based on fragmentary jaw and postcranial material lacking diagnostic features.

history.note: Placed at Hadrosauridae incertae sedis; nomen dubium.

diagnostic_features: Successional tooth crowns develop on the outer/posterior face of the shank (not the front, as in Hadrosaurus), so up to three teeth occupy each transverse row at once
Tooth with a keeled enamel plate over the flattened inner face and a dense outer layer roughened by numerous short, serrate longitudinal ridges
Femora, tibiae, and other long bones filled with solid cancellous bone, lacking a medullary cavity (unlike Hadrosaurus, Hypsibema, and other genera)
Distal femoral condyles forming a single trochlear surface, lacking the deep posterior fossae seen in Hadrosaurus

Citipati.etymology: From Sanskrit/Tibetan Buddhist mythology, citipati refers to the 'lords of the cemetery' or 'funeral pyre lords', two monks who became the guardians of the dead. The name alludes to individuals found atop nests, interpreted as brooding over eggs.
Citipati.description: Citipati is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period, about 75 million to 71 million years ago. It is mainly known from the Ukhaa Tolgod locality at the Djadochta Formation, where the first remains were collected during the 1990s. The genus and type species Citipati osmolskae were named and described in 2001. A second species from the adjacent Zamyn Khondt locality may also exist. Citipati is one of the best-known oviraptorids thanks to a number of well-preserved specimens, including individuals found in brooding positions atop nests of eggs, though most of them were initially referred to the related Oviraptor. These nesting specimens have helped to solidify the link between non-avian dinosaurs and birds.
diagnostic_features: Anterodorsally sloping occiput and quadrate (if braincase positioned horizontally)
Parietal much longer along the midline than the frontal, reaching nearly to the level of the anterior end of the orbit
Ascending process of the jugal perpendicular to the horizontal ramus rather than extending posterodorsally
Ascending process of the premaxilla vertical rather than sloping posterodorsally
Cervical vertebrae more elongate (approximately twice as long as they are wide)
Ischia form a symphysis distally

species.name: Citipati osmolskae
species.etymology: Named for the noted Polish paleontologist Halszka Osmólska, whose work dealt extensively with Mongolian theropods.

type_specimen.institution: Paleontological Center, Mongolian Academy of Sciences

notable_specimens.institution: Paleontological Center, Mongolian Academy of Sciences
notable_specimens.significance: Adult preserved in a bird-like brooding pose atop a nest of elongatoolithid eggs, forelimbs covering the nest perimeter; landmark evidence linking oviraptorids to avian brooding. Also shows a badly broken but healed right ulna with a prominent callus.

notable_specimens.institution: Paleontological Center, Mongolian Academy of Sciences
notable_specimens.significance: Second nesting oviraptorid specimen, slightly more complete than Big Mama; preserves the entire cervical series except atlas and axis, dorsal vertebrae with thoracic ribs, partial limbs and some sacral vertebrae. About 11% larger than IGM 100/979.

Claosaurus.etymology: From Greek klao (κλάω) meaning 'broken' and Greek sauros (σαῦρος) meaning 'lizard'. Full meaning: 'broken lizard', referring to the unusual position of the fossils when discovered.
Claosaurus.description: Claosaurus is a genus of hadrosauroid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period (Santonian-Campanian) of what is now North America. The type and only known valid species is Claosaurus agilis. Traditionally classified as an early member of the family Hadrosauridae, a 2008 analysis found Claosaurus to be outside of the clade containing Hadrosaurus and other hadrosaurids, making it the closest non-hadrosaurid relative of true hadrosaurids within the clade Hadrosauromorpha.

Clasmodosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'klasma' (fragment) and 'odon' (tooth) plus 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'fragment-tooth lizard', alluding to the fragmentary tooth material on which the genus was based.
Clasmodosaurus.description: Clasmodosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Mata Amarilla Formation and the Cerro Fortaleza Formation. It lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Argentina. It is known from five fossilized and assorted teeth, but is diagnosed by a unique combination of characters.
diagnostic_features: Tooth crown straight and sub-oval in cross-section in the lower portion, becoming laterally compressed and obliquely sharpened in the upper portion with lingual curvature.
Enamel smooth and shiny, bearing flat longitudinal folds — two on the labial surface and four on the lingual surface — each well separated from the others.
Longitudinal folds traverse the tooth crown in straight lines and pass without alteration into the root.
Posterior edge of the crown rectilinear, vertical and sharpened; anterior edge forming a convex arc, wider and more rounded, not sharpened.
Very small pulp lumen visible at apical fracture surfaces.

Coahuilaceratops.description: Coahuilaceratops is a genus of chasmosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur that lived during the early Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous epoch, about 71.5 to 70.5 million years ago in what is now northern Mexico. It contains a single species, Coahuilaceratops magnacuerna.

Coahuilasaurus.description: Coahuilasaurus is an extinct genus of kritosaurin ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) Cerro del Pueblo Formation of Coahuila, Mexico. The genus contains a single species, C. lipani, known from the associated tips of the upper and lower jaw and other fragmentary skull bones. Coelophysis.etymology: From Greek 'koilos' (hollow) and 'physis' (form, nature), referring to the hollow vertebrae.
Coelophysis.description: Coelophysis is the type genus of Coelophysidae and one of the best-known Triassic dinosaurs. The type and only valid species, Coelophysis bauri, was erected by Edward Drinker Cope in 1889 on fragmentary syntypes collected by David Baldwin from Arroyo Seco, Rio Arriba County, New Mexico. Cope's original syntypes were diagnostically inadequate, and the taxon's modern hypodigm overwhelmingly comes from the Whitaker Quarry at Ghost Ranch — a Late Triassic mass-mortality bonebed first opened in 1947 that has yielded hundreds of articulated skeletons across a complete ontogenetic series. Following decades of dispute about whether the Ghost Ranch material truly belonged to Cope's nominal taxon, the ICZN issued Opinion 1842 in 1996, designating the articulated Whitaker Quarry skeleton AMNH 7224 as the neotype of C. bauri and rejecting the rival genus Rioarribasaurus colberti (Hunt and Lucas, 1991) as a junior objective synonym. Rinehart et al. (2009) reanalysed the entire hypodigm and showed that Coelophysis was sexually dimorphic (gracile and robust morphs distinguished by skull/neck length and sacrum fusion), preserved the oldest known furcula in any non-avian dinosaur, had hawk-like vision (sclerotic-ring geometry), and engaged in genuine cannibalism (juvenile bones in adult coprolites and regurgitalites — separate from Colbert's earlier in-ribcage 'cannibalism' claim, which Nesbitt et al. 2006 showed was actually a small crurotarsan).
diagnostic_features: Skull long and narrow with an elongate preorbital region bearing a prominent preorbital groove anterior to the orbit, promoting binocular overlap of the visual fields.
Ten cervical vertebrae with elongate, rod-like cervical ribs that overlap up to five consecutive vertebrae posteriorly.
Thirteen dorsal vertebrae; cervical centra amphicoelous with elliptical pleurocoels on the lateral surfaces; pleurocoels absent in dorsals.
Sacrum of five vertebrae; variable fusion of s4-s5 centra constitutes a sexually dimorphic character (gracile-morph specimens unfused; robust- morph fused).
Pubis bears two foramina — an elliptical obturator foramen and a larger accessory 'ceratosaur foramen' medial to it.
V-shaped furcula present, with epicleidial facets near the distal rami tips — the oldest known furcula in any non-avian dinosaur.
Femur midshaft diameter shows an allometric growth constant of ~1.5 indicating cursorial adaptation; tibiotarsus longer than femur.

ICZN Opinion 1842 (1996) simultaneously designated AMNH 7224 as the neotype of Coelophysis bauri (under plenary powers, setting aside Cope's diagnostically inadequate syntypes), making Rioarribasaurus a junior objective synonym of Coelophysis and colberti a junior objective synonym of bauri. Both were placed on the Official Index of Rejected and Invalid Names.

dispute.summary: Coeluroides largus is based on a few vertebrae from the Lameta Formation and is widely regarded as a nomen dubium (Olshevsky, 1991; Tykoski and Rowe, 2004). Carrano and Sampson (2008) found the material too fragmentary for specific diagnosis and argued that the Lameta theropod assemblage is likely over-split, with Coeluroides and several other named taxa probably representing only one or two abelisaurids. Novas and colleagues (2004) left its validity open, noting only that it may represent a valid indeterminate abelisauroid — a weak and isolated case. It is retained as a nomen dubium.

Coeluroides.etymology: From Coelurus (a related theropod genus, itself from Greek 'koilos' (hollow) and 'oura' (tail)) and Greek '-oides' (resembling); meaning 'Coelurus-like'.
Coeluroides.description: Coeluroides is an extinct genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period in what is now India. It is based solely on the holotype caudal vertebrae GSI K27/562, K27/574 and K27/595, discovered in a layer of the Lameta Formation. The type species, C. largus, was described by Friedrich von Huene and Charles Alfred Matley in 1933.

Coelurus.etymology: From Greek 'koilos' (hollow) and 'oura' (tail); meaning 'hollow tail', referring to the extensively excavated, thin-walled vertebrae described in the holotype.
Coelurus.description: Coelurus is a genus of small coelurosaurian theropod from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Wyoming, United States. The single valid species, Coelurus fragilis, was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879 and is known from a partial skeleton with characteristically hollow, thin-walled vertebrae. It was a lightly built bipedal carnivore with elongate hind limbs.

Metatarsus very long and gracile, almost as long as the tibia or femur

Colepiocephale.etymology: From Greek kolepion ('knuckle') + kephale ('head'), meaning 'knucklehead', referring to the distinctive domed skull.
Colepiocephale.description: Colepiocephale is a genus of pachycephalosaurid dinosaur from Late Cretaceous (middle Campanian stage) deposits of Alberta, Canada. It was collected from the Foremost Formation. The type species, C. lambei, was originally described by Sternberg in 1945 as Stegoceras lambei, and later renamed by Sullivan in 2003. C. lambei is a small domed pachycephalosaur known only from incomplete frontoparietal domes. A 2009 redescription by Schott and colleagues showed that the posteromedial extension of the parietal is broken off in every specimen and that the supratemporal fenestrae remained open, refuting earlier interpretations of a reduced occiput and ontogenetically lost squamosals; the genus is now diagnosed chiefly by features of the dome, including prominent, columnar supraorbital lobes and a narrow, high frontonasal boss.

Diastema accompanied by a distinct indentation in the lateral wall of the dome.
Frontonasal boss narrow and high, flanked at its posterior end by the supraorbital lobes.
Supraorbital lobes highly distinct and columnar (pillar-like in larger specimens).

Compsognathus.description: Compsognathus is a genus of small, bipedal, carnivorous theropod dinosaur. Members of its single species Compsognathus longipes could grow to around the size of a chicken. They lived about 150 million years ago, during the Tithonian age of the late Jurassic period, in what is now Europe. Paleontologists have found two well-preserved fossils, one in Germany in the 1850s and the second in France more than a century later. Today, C. longipes is the only recognized species, although the French specimen was once thought to belong to a separate species named C. corallestris.

Very long and robust hind feet with five digits

Condorraptor.etymology: From Cerro Condor (a nearby village in Argentina) + Latin raptor, 'robber/thief'; means 'robber from Cerro Condor'
Condorraptor.description: Condorraptor is an extinct genus of megalosauroid theropod dinosaur. Its genus name means 'robber from Cerro Condor', referencing a nearby village, while its species name, currumili, is named after Hipolito Currumil, the landowner and discoverer of the locality. It was among the earliest large South American theropods, having been found in Lower Jurassic strata of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation in the Cañadón Asfalto Basin of Argentina. The type species, described in 2005, is Condorraptor currumili. It is based on a tibia, with an associated partial skeleton that may belong to the same individual. Initially described as a basal tetanuran, Benson (2010) found it to be a piatnitzkysaurid megalosauroid and the sister taxon of Piatnitzkysaurus, a finding supported by later studies.

Coronosaurus.description: Coronosaurus is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsian dinosaurs which lived in the Late Cretaceous, in the middle Campanian stage. Its remains, two bone beds, were discovered by Phillip J. Currie in the Oldman Formation of Alberta, Canada, and its type and only species, Coronosaurus brinkmani, was first described in 2005, as a new species within the genus Centrosaurus. Later studies questioned the presence of a direct relationship, and in 2012 it was named as a separate genus. Coronosaurus means "crowned lizard", coming from "corona", Latin for crown, and "sauros", Greek for lizard; this name refers to the unique, crown-like shape of the horns on the top of its frill.

Corythoraptor.etymology: From Greek korythos, 'helmet', + Latin raptor, 'thief'; means 'helmeted thief', referring to its tall cassowary-like head crest
Corythoraptor.description: Corythoraptor is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur from the late Maastrichtian Nanxiong Formation of South China. It contains one species, C. jacobsi, known from a single well-preserved skeleton, and named after paleontologist Louis L. Jacobs. It bears a tall crest similar to that of the modern cassowary, and possibly had a similar functionality of display and resonance to detect lower-frequency sounds.

dispute.summary: Corythoraptor is generally treated as a valid crested oviraptorid, recovered as the sister taxon of Huanansaurus within Citipatiinae (Lü et al., 2017; Funston et al., 2020). Its validity has been questioned: Cau (2024) argued that it is a junior synonym of Banji, treating the differences between them as ontogenetic, but this synonymy rests on a single analysis and has not been adopted by subsequent workers or reference works (e.g. Jones, 2026).

history.note: Retained as a valid genus within Citipatiinae; the proposed synonymy with Banji (Cau, 2024) is noted but not adopted pending broader corroboration.

diagnostic_features: Distinct cassowary-like helmet on the skull, highly pneumatic and very thin, with highest point of the crest projecting above the orbit.
No pleurocoels on the centra of the second through fourth cervical vertebrae (pleurocoels present from fifth through twelfth cervical vertebrae).
Neck length twice as long as the dorsal vertebral column, and slightly longer than the entire forelimb including the manus.
Supranarial process of the premaxilla bears two processes: a short posterodorsally extending process and a long process forming most of the anterodorsal process of the premaxilla.
Infratemporal fenestra dorsoventrally elongate and narrow anteroposteriorly; narial opening much longer than wide, long axis parallel to dorsal margin of antorbital fenestra.
Lesser trochanter (cranial trochanter) completely fused with the greater trochanter; distal ends of shafts of metatarsal II straight and metatarsal IV laterally deflected.

Corythosaurus.etymology: From Greek korys (κόρυς), 'helmet', + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'helmeted lizard', referring to its helmet-like head crest
Corythosaurus.description: Corythosaurus is a genus of hadrosaurid "duck-billed" dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period, about 77-75.7 million years ago, in what is now western North America. Its name is derived from the Greek word κόρυς, meaning "helmet", named and described in 1914 by Barnum Brown. Corythosaurus is now thought to be a lambeosaurine, thus related to Lambeosaurus, Nipponosaurus, Velafrons, Hypacrosaurus, and Olorotitan. Corythosaurus has an estimated length of 7.7-9 meters (25-30 ft) and has a skull, including the crest, that is 70.8 centimeters (27.9 in; 2.32 ft) tall.
diagnostic_features: Skull short with a high anterior helmet-like crest formed by nasals, prefrontals, and frontals
Nasals not separated in front by premaxillaries (unique among known hadrosaur genera at time of description)
Narial opening small; mouth narrow with elongate expanded portion of premaxillary in front of nares
Integument composed of low polygonal non-imbricating tuberculate scales on sides, back, and tail, with rows of conical limpet-like scales on belly
Prefrontal roughly triangular and less extensive than in Stephanosaurus; apparently forms no part of the orbital border

species.name: Corythosaurus casuarius
species.etymology: Named for the cassowary (Casuarius), a modern bird with a similarly prominent skull crest.

species.name: Corythosaurus intermedius
species.etymology: From Latin 'intermedius' ('intermediate'), for the crest form, intermediate between those of Lambeosaurus lambei and Corythosaurus casuarius.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete skull (specimen "A"): crested premaxillae and nasals, maxillae, jugals, squamosals, quadrates, palatines, pterygoids, braincase elements, and right dentary; no postcranial material.

diagnostic_features: Crest ascending more gradually from the snout and extending farther back, rather than rising abruptly.
Postero-inferior angle of the crest drawn out into a short, stout process.

Craspedodon.etymology: From Greek 'kraspedon' (edge, fringe, border) and 'odon' (tooth); meaning 'edge tooth', in reference to the ridges and denticles ornamenting the tooth crowns.
Craspedodon.description: Craspedodon is an extinct genus of ornithischian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Lonzée Member of Belgium. Only a single species, C. lonzeensis, is known.

dispute.summary: Craspedodon lonzeensis is based on fragmentary teeth from Belgium reinterpreted as neoceratopsian by Godefroit and Lambert (2007); Maidment and others (2026) caution that such teeth are difficult to distinguish from those of ornithopods. Treated as a nomen dubium.

history.note: Placed at Ceratopsia incertae sedis; nomen dubium.

diagnostic_features: Enamelled side of the crown bearing deep indentations and a prominent basal cingulum.
Non-enamelled side of the crown very convex vertically and bulbous in mesial/distal view.
Labiolingual diameter at the base of the crown largely exceeding the mesiodistal diameter.
Secondary ridges starting from the apical edge of the crown but not reaching the base.
Cingulum well developed on dentary teeth, with the primary ridge set back from the cingulum, forming a continuous ridge at the base of the lingual side of the crown.
Asymmetrical denticulation on crown edges; lateral edges forming everted lips limited by a prominent rough vertical ridge on the enamelled side.

species.name: Craspedodon lonzeensis
species.etymology: After Lonzée, near Gembloux (Namur Province, Belgium), the locality where the type material was discovered.

Craterosaurus.etymology: From Greek krater, 'bowl' or 'mixing vessel', + Greek sauros, 'lizard/reptile'; means 'bowl reptile' or 'krater reptile'
Craterosaurus.description: Craterosaurus is a dubious genus of stegosaurian dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous (possibly Aptian stage) of the Woburn Sands Formation of England. Estimated to measure around 4 m (13 ft) in length and weighing approximately 560 kg (1,230 lb), Craterosaurus may actually be a junior synonym of Regnosaurus, but only one fossil, a partial vertebra, was recovered.

dispute.summary: Craterosaurus is a nomen dubium based on a single partial vertebra whose features are now known to be widespread in Stegosauria (Maidment et al., 2008). It is retained at Stegosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Stegosauria incertae sedis, nomen dubium based on an undiagnostic vertebra.

diagnostic_features: Basioccipital condyle compressed laterally, V-shaped, tapering below, approximately 1⅛ inch wide and deep, projecting 2 inches backward from the posterior vertical surface of the bone.
Posterior vertical surface of basioccipital divided for two-thirds of its depth by a strong, sharp, elevated median ridge prolonged downward from the middle of the back of the condyloid process.
Basisphenoid bears a large ovate cerebral cup (2¼ inches long, >1 inch wide) interpreted as the base and anterior portion of the braincase, with Rhynchocephalian rather than avian character.
Two large, slightly diverging hypapophyses at the inferior end of the basisphenoid, separated by a deep anterior notch, presumed to articulate with the posterior angles of the pterygoid bones.
Lateral surfaces of the basisphenoid each perforated by an oval foramen (~1¼ inch long, ½ inch wide) near the upper posterior angle, with a slight bony elevation below.

species.name: Craterosaurus pottonensis
species.etymology: Named for Potton, the locality in Bedfordshire, England, near which the fossil was discovered.

type_specimen.material: Ankylosed basioccipital and basisphenoid bones.

Crichtonpelta.etymology: Named after author Michael Crichton (of Jurassic Park fame) + Greek pelta, 'small shield'; means 'Crichton's shield', referring to its ankylosaur armor
Crichtonpelta.description: Crichtonpelta is a genus of extinct herbivorous ankylosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian) of China.
diagnostic_features: Apex of quadratojugal horn directed dorsally (autapomorphy unique among ankylosaurids).
Quadratojugal horn apex posteriorly offset (not centrally located as in Gobisaurus and Shamosaurus).
Nuchal crest bears two distinct transversely elongate prominences.
Squamosal horns larger and more pointed than in Gobisaurus or Shamosaurus, though smaller than in Pinacosaurus mephistocephalus.
Rugose, amorphous frontonasal ornamentation not subdivided into discrete caputegulae.
Jugal dorsoventrally deeper than in Pinacosaurus grangeri or P. mephistocephalus.

Crichtonsaurus.etymology: From the surname Crichton (Michael Crichton, author of 'Jurassic Park') and Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning "Crichton's lizard".
Crichtonsaurus.description: Crichtonsaurus is a dubious genus of herbivorous ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now China. It was named after Michael Crichton, the author of the dinosaur novel Jurassic Park. A sister taxon was discovered, C. benxiensis, which is now identified as a separate genus.

dispute.summary: Crichtonsaurus is a nomen dubium; the holotype of C. bohlini lacks diagnostic characters (Arbour and Currie, 2015). It is retained at Ankylosauria incertae sedis (the valid related taxon is Crichtonpelta).

history.note: Placed at Ankylosauria incertae sedis, undiagnostic holotype.

diagnostic_features: Mandible thin and lacking osseous armor or sculpting marks on the lateral surface
Teeth small with symmetrical crown bearing vertical ridges, undeveloped central ridge, 4–5 marginal denticles per side, and incompletely developed cingulum
Scapula and coracoid not fused into a scapulocoracoid
Posterior caudal vertebrae fused into a rod-like structure with symmetrically arranged membranous osseous plates on both sides
Cervical armor plates fused into a semicircular ring

Cristatusaurus.etymology: From Latin 'cristatus' meaning 'crested' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to the crested skull of this spinosaurid dinosaur.
Cristatusaurus.description: Cristatusaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period of what is now Niger, 112 million years ago. It was a baryonychine member of the Spinosauridae, a group of large bipedal carnivores with well-built forelimbs and elongated, crocodile-like skulls. The type species Cristatusaurus lapparenti was named in 1998 by scientists Philippe Taquet and Dale Russell, on the basis of jaw bones and some vertebrae. Two claw fossils were also later assigned to Cristatusaurus. The animal's generic name, which means "crested reptile", alludes to a sagittal crest on top of its snout; while the specific name is in honor of the French paleontologist Albert-Félix de Lapparent. Cristatusaurus is known from the Albian to Aptian Elrhaz Formation, where it would have coexisted with sauropod and iguanodontian dinosaurs, other theropods, and various crocodylomorphs.
diagnostic_features: Premaxilla short and strongly hooked in lateral profile, increasing in height posteriorly with dorsal surface narrowing into a crest posteriorly.
Anteriormost premaxillary alveolus relatively large; lateral alveoli uniformly closely spaced.
Maxillary and dentary teeth laterally compressed in cross-section; maxillary teeth vertically oriented posteriorly.
Dentary only slightly constricted vertically in mid-section with alveoli closely spaced.
Maxillary and dentary teeth with finely serrated carinae (unlike Spinosaurus maroccanus).

Crittendenceratops.etymology: Named after the Fort Crittenden Formation in Arizona where the fossils were found, + Greek ceratops ('horned face'), meaning 'horned face from the Fort Crittenden Formation'.
Crittendenceratops.description: Crittendenceratops is a genus of horned centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur from the late Campanian Fort Crittenden Formation of Arizona. It contains a single species, C. krzyzanowskii, and represents the first dinosaur taxon from that formation to receive a formal scientific name.

Extensive epiparietals located along the lateroposterior margin of the parietal ramus.
Parietal ramus dorsoventrally thick with deep elongate fossa on dorsal surface.
Posteroventrolateral concavity pronounced and extensively rugose.
Squamosal dorsal ridge short, pronounced, and located in close proximity to dorsolateral margin of the bone.

Cruxicheiros.etymology: From Latin crux ('cross') + Greek cheir ('hand'), meaning 'cross hand', in reference to the Cross Hands Quarry in Warwickshire, England where the fossils were discovered.
Cruxicheiros.description: Cruxicheiros is a genus of theropod dinosaur which lived in the Middle Jurassic of England. The type species is C. newmanorum, described by Roger Benson and Jonathan Radley in 2010.
diagnostic_features: Proximomedially inclined ridge within the trochanteric fossa of the femur, running nearly parallel to the posterior flange of the femoral caput; absent in all other known basal theropods.
Prominent posterior flange of the femoral caput extending further posteriorly than the posterior surface of the femoral head.
Dorsal neural spines with relatively low dorsoventral height (approximately equal in length to transverse processes) combined with prominent rugose ridges and transversely expanded dorsal ends.
Vertebrae with more numerous, smaller internal pneumatic chambers (not the two large chambers divided by a midline septum typical of megalosauroids).
Fused and swollen scapulocoracoid suture.

species.etymology: Named for the Newman family, who own the Cross Hands Quarry in Warwickshire where the holotype was discovered.

It is placed conservatively at Neotheropoda incertae sedis.

Cryolophosaurus.etymology: From Greek kryos, 'cold/icy/frozen', + Greek lophos, 'crest', + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'frozen-crested lizard', referring to its discovery in Antarctica and its distinctive head crest
Cryolophosaurus.description: Cryolophosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur known from only a single species, Cryolophosaurus ellioti, from the Early Jurassic of Antarctica. It was one of the largest theropods of the Early Jurassic, with the subadult, being estimated to have reached 6-7 meters (20-23 ft) long and weighed 350-465 kilograms (772-1,025 lb).

Jugal crosses the lower lateral temporal opening and sutures with the squamosal, splitting the opening into two parts
Pneumatic lacrimal present but lacks the large lacrimal opening typical of larger carnosaurian tetanurans

Cryptarcus.etymology: From Latin 'crypticus' (hidden) and 'arcus' (arch); refers both to the morphology of the transverse parietal bar and to the type species long being hidden within the genus Chasmosaurus.
Cryptarcus.description: Cryptarcus is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, dating to the middle Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous. The holotype skull measures approximately 94 centimeters in length.
diagnostic_features: Posteroventral process of premaxilla terminates with a spatulate, non-tapering distal end.
Episquamosal bases become progressively longer posteriorly until the second-to-last episquamosal; the most posterior episquamosal then reverses the trend by being distinctly smaller.
Epiparietals 1 and 2 both have low dome-shaped profiles with lenticular loci.
Epiparietals 1 and 2 are fused with a visible suture and located entirely on the dorsal surface of the posterior parietal bar within the midline embayment.
Medial-most epiparietal (ep1) located at the base of the deep median parietal embayment with its locus nearly touching its bilateral counterpart at the midline.
Lateral portion of epiparietal 2 turns onto the posterior edge of the transverse parietal bar while its anteromedial end occupies the dorsal bar surface.
