Cryptosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'kryptos' (hidden) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'hidden lizard', in reference to the rarity of the find.
Cryptosaurus.description: Cryptosaurus is a dubious genus of dinosaur known from a partial femur from the Late Jurassic of England. The sole species is Cryptosaurus eumerus.

diagnostic_features: Femoral shaft triangular in cross-section at both proximal and distal ends, with flat outer side and compressed inner side proximally.
Proximal articular surface in two portions — an inner subspherical head and a continuous outer subquadrate facet obliquely concave from within outward.

It lived in what is now China (Sichuan Province), and was similar to Bellusaurus. Daanosaurus is known only from a partial skeleton of a juvenile, and it has been debated whether the specimen may be a juvenile mamenchisaurid.

Dacentrurus.etymology: From Greek dakno ('to bite' or 'pointed') + oura ('tail'), meaning 'tail full of points', referring to the spikes on the animal's tail.
Dacentrurus.description: Dacentrurus is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic and perhaps Early Cretaceous (154-140 million years ago) of Europe. Its type species, D. armatus, was named in 1875 as Omosaurus armatus, based on a skeleton found in a clay pit in the Kimmeridge Clay in Swindon, England. In 1902 the genus was renamed Dacentrurus because the name Omosaurus had already been used for a phytosaur in 1856. After 1875, half a dozen other species would be named but perhaps only Dacentrurus armatus is valid.
diagnostic_features: Humerus remarkably broad relative to length, especially at proximal half, with an unusually prominent anconal tuberosity and ridge (tricipital crest) absent or rudimentary in all other dinosaurs described by Owen.
Deep anconal depression at distal expansion of humerus, exceeding that of any other known Dinosaurian, Crocodilian, or Lacertian humerus.

Osseous dermal spine obliquely truncate at base with coarse marginal notching and paired vascular channels; elliptical in cross-section with central medullary canal; provision for attachment stronger than in Hylaeosaurus.
Ilium with distinctive superacetabular plate and ridge continuing onto outer surface of antacetabular prolongation, imparting a triedral form to that part of the bone.
Ischium extremely slender (styliform) relative to its length, with no process crossing the obturator interspace between ischium and pubis.
Pubis contributing no discernible share to the acetabular cavity; proximal end articulating only with the ischium, not with the ilium (Crocodilian character).

Daemonosaurus.etymology: From Greek daemon (δαίμων), 'spirit' or 'demon', + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'demon lizard' or 'spirit lizard', likely referring to its fearsome fang-like teeth
Daemonosaurus.description: Daemonosaurus is an extinct genus of possible theropod dinosaur from the Late Triassic of New Mexico. The only known fossil is a skull and neck fragments from deposits of the latest Triassic Chinle Formation at Ghost Ranch. Daemonosaurus was an unusual dinosaur with a short skull and large, fang-like teeth. It lived alongside early neotheropods such as Coelophysis, which would have been among the most common dinosaurs by the end of the Triassic. However, Daemonosaurus retains several plesiomorphic ("primitive") traits of the snout, and it likely lies outside the clade Neotheropoda. It may be considered a late-surviving basal theropod or non-theropod basal saurischian, possibly allied to other early predatory dinosaurs such as herrerasaurids or Tawa.

Dakotadon.etymology: Named after Dakota (the Lakota Formation of South Dakota, USA where the fossils were found) + Greek odon ('tooth'), meaning 'Dakota tooth'.
Dakotadon.description: Dakotadon is a genus of iguanodont dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Valanginian to Barremian) Lakota Formation of South Dakota, USA, known from a partial skull. It was first described in 1989 as Iguanodon lakotaensis, by David B. Weishampel and Philip R. Bjork. Its assignment has been controversial. Some researchers suggested that "I." lakotaensis was more basal than I. bernissartensis, and related to Theiophytalia, but David Norman has suggested that it was a synonym of I. bernissartensis. Gregory S. Paul, working on a revision of iguanodont species, gave "I." lakotaensis its own genus, Dakotadon, in 2008. He measured its length at 6 meters (20 ft) and body mass at 1 metric ton (1.1 short tons).

Dakotaraptor.etymology: Named after the Dakotas (the Hell Creek Formation of the western USA, spanning the Dakotas, Montana and Wyoming) + Latin raptor ('thief' or 'plunderer'), meaning 'thief from Dakota'.
Dakotaraptor.description: Dakotaraptor is a possible chimaeric genus of maniraptoriform theropod dinosaur that lived in western North America during the Late Cretaceous period. The remains have been found in the Maastrichtian-aged Hell Creek Formation, dated to the very end of the Mesozoic era, making Dakotaraptor potentially one of the last surviving dromaeosaurids, though other researchers have disputed its classification. One of the largest dromaeosaurids, measuring 4.35-6 m (14.3-19.7 ft) and weighing 220-350 kg (490-770 lb), the remains of D. steini were discovered in a multi-species bonebed. Elements of the holotype and referred specimens were later found to belong to trionychid turtles, and it is unclear whether further analysis of potential non-dromaeosaurid affinities of the holotype and referred material can be properly conducted, because currently the type specimen is housed in a private collection. Phylogenetic analyses of D. steini place it in a variety of positions within Dromaeosauridae.

Daliansaurus.etymology: Named after Dalian, a city in Liaoning Province, China, + Greek sauros ('lizard' or 'reptile'), meaning 'Dalian reptile'.
Daliansaurus.description: Daliansaurus is a genus of small troodontid theropod dinosaur, measuring approximately 1 meter (3 ft 3 in) long, from the Early Cretaceous of China. It contains a single species, D. liaoningensis, named in 2017 by Shen and colleagues from a nearly complete skeleton preserved in three dimensions. Daliansaurus is unusual in possessing an enlarged claw on the fourth digit of the foot, in addition to the "sickle claw" found on the second digit of the feet of most paravians. It also has long metatarsal bones, and apparently possesses bird-like uncinate processes (a first among troodontids). In the Lujiatun Beds of the Yixian Formation, a volcanically-influenced region with a cold climate, Daliansaurus lived alongside its closest relatives - Sinovenator, Sinusonasus, and Mei, with which it forms the group Sinovenatorinae.
diagnostic_features: Ungual of pedal digit IV is robust, dorsoventrally deep, and approximately the same size as the sickle-shaped ungual of pedal digit II (unique among troodontids).
Uncinate processes present on the dorsal ribs (not previously reported in troodontids).
Metatarsal IV lacks a prominent longitudinal lateroventral flange (unlike Sinovenator and Sinusonasus).
Ventral surface of the postacetabular process of the ilium is strongly concave in lateral view (not nearly straight as in Sinovenator and Mei).
Metatarsal II so short it terminates before the trochlea of metatarsal IV begins (unlike Sinovenator and Sinusonasus).

Dashanpusaurus.description: Dashanpusaurus is an extinct genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived during the middle of the Jurassic period. The dinosaur was described in 2005 by Peng Guangzhao, Ye Yong, Gao Yuhui, Shu Chunkang, and Jiang Shan. Its type and only species is Dashanpusaurus dongi, named in honor of the paleontologist Dong Zhiming.

Middle and posterior dorsal neural spines heightened into thick transverse plates with enlarged, nearly square apices wider at the top than the base
Ilium low and long with a prominent anterior process angled distinctly less than 90° to the pubic peduncle

Dasosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'dasos' (forest, copse) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'forest lizard', referring to the densely-vegetated dig site within Brazil's Legal Amazonia.
Dasosaurus.description: Dasosaurus is an extinct genus of somphospondylan sauropod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian) Itapecuru Formation of Maranhão, Brazil. The single species, Dasosaurus tocantinensis, is recovered as sister to the Spanish Barremian taxon Garumbatitan within a non-titanosaur Somphospondyli clade, and is among the largest known Brazilian sauropods at an estimated 18–22 m in length.
diagnostic_features: Anterior caudal neural spines expanded dorsolaterally ('stake-like' shaped), creating a quadrangular dorsal platform.
Anterior surface of the femur lacks a linea intermuscularis cranialis.
Pedal ungual phalanges I–II bear a distinct dorsolateral extensor tubercle extending ventrally along the lateroventral surface of the bone.

Dorsal-most of the three neural arch pedicel ridges on middle-posterior caudal vertebrae positioned at the level of the dorsal margin of the prezygapophysis, dorsally bounding a shallower, ellipsoid costovertebral concavity.
Femoral shaft more slender and more medially curved, with a lateral bulge corresponding to approximately 40% of the transverse minimal shaft width.

Daspletosaurus.etymology: From Greek daspletos ('frightful') + sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'frightful lizard'.
Daspletosaurus.description: Daspletosaurus is a genus of tyrannosaurid dinosaur that lived in Laramidia between about 77 and 74.4 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous Period. The genus Daspletosaurus contains three named species. Fossils of the earlier type species, D. torosus, have been found in Alberta, while fossils of a later species, D. horneri, have been found in Montana and Alberta. D. wilsoni has been suggested as an intermediate species between D. torosus and D. horneri that evolved through anagenesis, though further research may be required to definitively support the theory.
diagnostic_features: Premaxilla does not contact nasal below external naris.
Lacrimal 'horn' triangular in lateral aspect, with apex centered above antorbital ramus of bone; exceeds postorbital 'horn' in development.
Neural spine of fourth cervical vertebra much larger than that of fifth; spine of fifth distally pointed.
In adults humerus length estimated equal to 38 per cent of femur length; forelimb powerfully developed.
Anterodistal condyle of metacarpal I reduced, causing first digit to diverge distally from second.
In adults circumference of femur equals 38 to 41 per cent of femur length.

synonyms.name: Suciasaurus

diagnostic_features: Skull taller than in D. torosus, with a shorter rostral ramus of the lacrimal relative to the ventral ramus (rostral ramus longer in D. torosus).
Antorbital fossa of the lacrimal confluent with the ventral ramus of the bone (separated by a deep concavity in D. torosus).
Coronoid region of the surangular facing more laterally than dorsally (facing equally dorsally and laterally in D. torosus).
Primary lacrimal cornual process lower and less prominent, about 53% the height of the rostral ramus (about 69% in D. torosus).
Pneumatic foramen penetrating the lateral surface of the quadratojugal.
Humerus about 34% the length of the femur.

diagnostic_features: Mylohyoid foramen of the splenial elongate and dorsoventrally shallow (much deeper in D. torosus and D. horneri).
Cornual process of the lacrimal short (5.2 cm), intermediate in height between the tall process of D. torosus and the low one of D. horneri.
Prefrontal oriented rostrocaudally (rostromedially to mediolaterally in D. horneri).
Cornual process of the postorbital subdivided into a supraorbital shelf and a caudodorsal tuberosity (undivided in D. horneri).
Dorsal quadrate contact of the quadratojugal broadly visible in lateral view (concealed in D. torosus).
Premaxillary tooth row oriented entirely mediolaterally, concealing all but the distalmost tooth in lateral view (rostromedial, several teeth visible in D. torosus).

dispute.summary: Datanglong guangxiensis is a fragmentary theropod of uncertain position. It was described as a basal carcharodontosaurian (Mo et al., 2014) and is treated as an indeterminate carcharodontosaurid by Kellermann et al. (2025) and Jones and Viola (2026), but has also been recovered as a coelurosaur (Cau, 2014) and, in one of three analyses, as a basal megaraptoran (Samathi et al., 2024). Because these hypotheses span Allosauroidea and Coelurosauria, it is placed conservatively at Avetheropoda incertae sedis.

It shared the local Middle Jurassic landscape with other sauropods such as Shunosaurus, Omeisaurus, and Protognathosaurus, the neornithischian Xiaosaurus, and the early stegosaur Huayangosaurus as well as the carnivorous Gasosaurus.

It is known from a single partial skeleton consisting of most of the neck and back vertebrae, two tail vertebrae, a shoulder blade, and a thigh bone. At the time of its discovery in 2008, Daxiatitan was regarded as potentially the largest known dinosaur from China.

Deinocheirus.etymology: From Greek deinos, 'terrible/horrible', + Greek cheir, 'hand'; means 'horrible hand', named for the enormous arms and hands first discovered
Deinocheirus.description: Deinocheirus is a genus of large ornithomimosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous around 70 million years ago. In 1965, a pair of large arms, shoulder girdles, and a few other bones of a new dinosaur were first discovered in the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia. In 1970, this specimen became the holotype of the only species within the genus, Deinocheirus mirificus; the genus name is Greek for "horrible hand". No further remains were discovered for almost fifty years, and its nature remained a mystery. Two more complete specimens were described in 2014, which shed light on many aspects of the animal. Parts of these new specimens had been looted from Mongolia some years before, but were repatriated in 2014.

dispute.summary: The subfamily placement of Deinonychus is genuinely unresolved. It has been recovered as a velociraptorine (Turner et al., 2012; Napoli et al., 2021; Powers et al., 2020), as a dromaeosaurine (DePalma et al., 2015; the placement Jones et al., 2026 adopt), and in a distinct clade with Utahraptor and Achillobator outside both subfamilies (Hartman et al., 2019; Jasinski et al., 2020). It is placed at Eudromaeosauria incertae sedis pending resolution.

history.note: Placed at Eudromaeosauria incertae sedis (least-inclusive uncontested clade); velociraptorine, dromaeosaurine, and own-clade hypotheses all current.

Deinonychus.etymology: From Ancient Greek deinos (δεινός, 'terrible') + onyx/onuchos (ὄνυξ/ὄνυχος, 'claw'), meaning 'terrible claw', referring to the enlarged sickle-shaped claw on the second toe.
Deinonychus.description: Deinonychus is a genus of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaur with one described species, Deinonychus antirrhopus. This species could grow up to 3.4 meters (11 ft) long and lived during the Early and Late Cretaceous Period, about 115-93.9 million years ago. Fossils have been recovered from the U.S. states of Montana, Utah, Wyoming, and Oklahoma, in rocks of the Cloverly Formation and Antlers Formation.

dispute.summary: The affinities of Deltadromeus are deeply contested, spanning both major averostran lineages. On the ceratosaur side, Carrano and Sampson (2008) recovered it as a basal ceratosaur (explicitly rejecting the earlier noasaurid interpretation). On the tetanuran side, the describing paper (Sereno and others, 1996) recovered a basal coelurosaur, Apesteguía and others (2016) a neovenatorid allosauroid (sister to Gualicho), Motta and others (2016) a megaraptoran, and Delcourt and others (2025) an ornithomimosaur. A synonymy with Bahariasaurus has also been proposed but is not adopted. Averostra is the least-inclusive clade all these hypotheses accept.

history.note: Placed at Noasauridae following the prevailing interpretation (P2, P3); the non-ceratosaur alternatives are recorded.

Broadened from Noasauridae to Averostra incertae sedis: the credible hypotheses span Ceratosauria (basal ceratosaur — Carrano and Sampson (2008) reject a noasaurid position) and Tetanurae (coelurosaur, allosauroid, megaraptoran, ornithomimosaur), so the conservative shared node is adopted.

Deltadromeus.etymology: From Greek delta ('river delta' or 'change') + dromos ('runner'), meaning 'river delta runner' or 'change runner', possibly referring to the Nile River delta region where related material was found.
Deltadromeus.description: Deltadromeus is an extinct genus of controversial theropod dinosaur that lived in present-day Morocco during the mid-Cretaceous period. It was described by American paleontologist Paul Sereno and colleagues in 1996. The genus contains a single species, D. agilis, named based on an incomplete postcranial skeleton, the holotype specimen. However, some fossils from the Bahariya Formation of Egypt that were formerly referred to the theropod Bahariasaurus have been suggested to belong to Deltadromeus. The holotype specimen of Deltadromeus was unearthed by a joint expedition by the University of Chicago and the Service Géologique du Maroc in Errachidia Province, eastern Morocco in rock layers coming from the Gara Sbaa Formation of the Kem Kem Beds. This indicates that these fossils date to the Cenomanian stage of the Cretaceous period, 100-95 million years ago.

Demandasaurus.etymology: Named after the Sierra de la Demanda mountain range in Burgos Province, Spain, where the fossils were collected, + Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'Demanda lizard'.
Demandasaurus.description: Demandasaurus is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur from early Cretaceous (late Barremian - early Aptian stage) deposits of Spain. Demandasaurus is known from an incomplete but associated skeleton that includes cranial and postcranial remains. It was collected from the Castrillo de la Reina Formation in Burgos Province. It was first named by Fidel Torcida Fernández-Baldor, José Ignacio Canudo, Pedro Huerta, Diego Montero, Xabier Pereda Suberbiola, and Leonardo Salgado in 2011, and the type species is Demandasaurus darwini.

Centroprezygapophyseal laminae are divided (forked) in both cervical and dorsal vertebrae
Mid-dorsal vertebrae bear two large neural arch pneumatic foramina passing entirely through the neural arch anteroposteriorly, not previously described in sauropods
Anterior caudal transverse processes have two large deep pneumatic cavities divided by accessory laminae, combined with a broad laminar complex associated with the diapophysis

Diabloceratops.etymology: From Spanish diablo ('devil') + Greek ceratops ('horned face'), meaning 'devil-horned face', referring to the large, horn-like projections on the frill.
Diabloceratops.description: Diabloceratops is an extinct genus of centrosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur that lived approximately 81.4-81 million years ago during the latter part of the Cretaceous Period in what is now Utah, in the United States. Diabloceratops was a medium-sized, moderately built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore, that could grow up to an estimated 4.5 meters (15 ft) in length and 1.3 metric tons (1.4 short tons) in body mass. At the time of its discovery, it was the oldest-known ceratopsid, and first centrosaurine known from latitudes south of the U.S. state of Montana. The generic name Diabloceratops means "devil-horned face", coming from Diablo, Spanish for "devil", and ceratops, Latinized Greek for "horned face". The specific name honors Jeffrey Eaton, a paleontologist at Weber State University and long time friend of the lead author Jim Kirkland. Eaton had a big role in establishing the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument where the specimen was found. The type species, Diabloceratops eatoni, was named and described in 2010 by James Ian Kirkland and Donald DeBlieux.

Parietal fenestrae are triangular and caudorostrally elongate; lateral parietal epoccipitals decrease in size caudally

Diamantinasaurus.etymology: From Diamantina River (near the discovery site in Queensland, Australia) + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'Diamantina lizard'
Diamantinasaurus.description: Diamantinasaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod from Australia that lived during the early Late Cretaceous, about 94 million years ago. The type species of the genus is D. matildae, first described and named in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues based on fossil finds in the Winton Formation. Meaning "Diamantina lizard", the name is derived from the location of the nearby Diamantina River and the Greek word sauros, "lizard". The specific epithet is from the Australian song Waltzing Matilda, also the locality of the holotype and paratype. The known skeleton includes most of the forelimb, shoulder girdle, pelvis, hindlimb and ribs of the holotype, and one shoulder bone, a radius and some vertebrae of the paratype.

Diclonius.etymology: From Greek diklos ('double') + klonos ('sprout' or 'shoot'), meaning 'double sprout', referring to the tooth-replacement method in which newly erupting teeth could be in use simultaneously with older worn teeth.
Diclonius.description: Diclonius is a genus of dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous. It was a hadrosaur based solely on teeth. Its fossils were found in the Judith River Formation of Montana, northern US. The name is in reference to the method of tooth replacement, in which newly erupting replacement teeth could be in functional use at the same time as older, more worn teeth.

The genus was named for the neural spines on the back of its neck. The first fossil was described by paleontologist Werner Janensch in 1914.

Dilong.description: Dilong is a genus of small basal tyrannosauroid dinosaurs. The only species in the genus is Dilong paradoxus, known from the Lower Cretaceous Yixian Formation of East Asia (in what is now China). The discovery of Dilong was significant as it provided the first evidence of feathers in tyrannosaurs, something which had previously been suspected for the group.

Dilophosaurus.etymology: From Greek di- (two) + lophos (crest) + sauros (lizard): 'two-crested lizard', referring to the pair of bony crests on its skull.
Dilophosaurus.description: Dilophosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now North America during the Early Jurassic, about 186 million years ago. Three skeletons were discovered in northern Arizona in 1940, and the two best preserved were collected in 1942. The most complete specimen became the holotype of a new species in the genus Megalosaurus, named M. wetherilli by Samuel P. Welles in 1954. Welles found a larger skeleton in the same region belonging to the same species in 1964. Realizing it bore crests on its skull, he assigned the species to the new genus Dilophosaurus in 1970, as Dilophosaurus wetherilli. The genus name means "two-crested lizard", and the species name honors John Wetherill, an explorer and amateur archeologist. Further specimens have since been found, including an infant. Fossil footprints have also been attributed to the animal, including resting traces. Another species, Dilophosaurus sinensis from China, was named in 1993, but was later found to belong to the genus Sinosaurus.
diagnostic_features: Pair of parasagittal nasolacrimal crests, each formed by a ridge on the dorsolateral margin of the nasal process of the premaxilla, dorsolateral expansions of the nasal and lacrimal, and a posteriorly projecting process of the lacrimal behind the orbit.
Pyramidal process on the lateral surface of the surangular, anterior to the articulation with the quadrate.
Mandibular fenestra reduced in anteroposterior length.

Neural spines of the post-axial cervical vertebrae with a dorsal margin stepped in lateral view — anterior and posterior 'shoulders' flanking a taller central 'cap' that is cruciform in dorsal view, most pronounced in the posterior cervicals.
Serial variation (bifurcation and recombination) in the posterior centrodiapophyseal laminae of the cervical vertebrae.
Accessory laminae emanating from the anterior and posterior centrodiapophyseal laminae of the middle trunk vertebrae.
First primordial sacral rib articulating with the preacetabular process of the ilium.
Additional 'horizontal buttress' on the posteroventral part of the coracoid, next to the biceps tuber.

The only species is Dinheirosaurus lourinhanensis, first described by José Bonaparte and Octávio Mateus in 1999 for vertebrae and some other material from the Lourinhã Formation. Diplodocus.etymology: From Greek 'diplos' (double) and 'dokos' (beam), referring to the double-beamed chevrons of the tail (with both anterior and posterior rami) that distinguished the genus when Marsh erected it in 1878.
Diplodocus.description: Diplodocus is the type genus of Diplodocidae and one of the most iconic and best-known sauropod dinosaurs of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of western North America. Othniel Charles Marsh erected the genus in 1878 on a partial tail and posterior limb (YPM 1920) collected near Cañon City, Colorado, by S. W. Williston, designating Diplodocus longus as the type species. John Bell Hatcher (1901) produced the first comprehensive osteological monograph of the genus based on the near-complete Carnegie Museum specimens CM 84 and CM 94 from Sheep Creek in Albany County, Wyoming, and named those Carnegie skeletons as a new species, Diplodocus carnegii — the basis of the famous "Dippy" cast that Andrew Carnegie distributed to museums worldwide. Tschopp, Mateus and Benson (2015) reassessed all diplodocid material at the specimen level, argued that the fragmentary D. longus holotype was a nomen dubium, and applied to the ICZN to switch the type species to D. carnegii. The Commission ultimately ruled against the proposal in Opinion 2425 (2018), voting 16-4 to maintain D. longus as the type species. The same Tschopp et al. analysis recombined Seismosaurus hallorum (Gillette, 1991) as Diplodocus hallorum and reassigned D. hayi (Holland, 1924) to the new genus Galeamopus, leaving D. longus, D. carnegii, and D. hallorum as the three currently valid Diplodocus species.
diagnostic_features: Anteriorly inclined base of the posterior dorsal neural spines (unique within Diplodocinae).

Pneumatopores of anterior caudal centra persist through caudal vertebra 16 or more posteriorly (unique among Diplodocoidea).
Mid-caudal centra with trapezoidal articular surfaces (unique among Flagellicaudata).
Last caudal ribs occur on caudal vertebra 18 or more posteriorly.
Iliac blade height above the pubic peduncle ≥ 0.40 of its anteroposterior length (unique within Diplodocinae).
Anteromedially directed crest on the proximal fibula extending into a notch behind the cnemial crest of the tibia (unique within Diplodocinae).
Chevrons of the tail double-beamed (with both anterior and posterior rami) — Marsh's original diagnostic character and the source of the generic name.

Dolichosuchus.etymology: From Greek dolichos (long) + soukhos (crocodile): 'long crocodile', a name reflecting its originally uncertain archosaur affinities.
Dolichosuchus.description: Dolichosuchus is the name given to a genus of dinosaur from the Triassic. It was originally classified in the disused family Hallopodidae, but has since been reclassified as a coelophysoid. A single fossil (consisting of a single lower leg bone, or tibia) was found in Germany (specimen NHMUK PV OR 38058). Since only one bone was discovered, the genus is considered a nomen dubium. Some scientists have noted that the tibia closely resembles those of Liliensternus and Dilophosaurus.

Dongbeititan.etymology: From Chinese 'Dongbei' meaning 'Northeast' (referring to northeastern China, i.e. Manchuria/Liaoning), combined with Greek 'titan' meaning 'giant'.
Dongbeititan.description: Dongbeititan is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation of Beipiao, Liaoning, China. It is based on holotype DNHM D2867, a partial postcranial skeleton including bones from the limbs, shoulder and pelvic girdles, and vertebrae, which was described in 2007. Its describers suggested it was as a basal titanosauriform, not as derived as Gobititan or Jiutaisaurus, but more derived than Euhelopus, Fusuisaurus, and Huanghetitan. The type species is D. dongi, and it is the first named sauropod from the Yixian Formation, which is part of the well-known Jehol Group. The genus name refers to the region Dongbei and to Greek titan, "giant". The specific name honors the Chinese paleontologist Dong Zhiming. Like other sauropods, Dongbeititan would have been a large quadrupedal herbivore.

Dongyangopelta.etymology: From Dongyang (the city in Zhejiang Province, China, where it was found) + Greek pelte (shield): 'Dongyang shield', referring to its nodosaurid armor and discovery locality.
Dongyangopelta.description: Dongyangopelta is an monospecific genus of nodosaurid dinosaur that lived in China during the Early to Late Cretaceous period (Albian to Cenomanian stages, 105-96 Ma) in what is now the Chaochuan Formation. The type and only known species, Dongyangopelta yangyanensis, is known from a partial postcranial skeleton preserving osteoderms and ossified tendons. It was named in 2013 by Rongjun Chen, Wenjie Zheng, Yoichi Azuma, Masateru Shibata, Tianling Lou, Qiang Jin and Xinsheng Jin. Dongyangopelta represents one of the only nodosaurids known from Asia, along with Taohelong and Sauroplites.

Dongyangosaurus.etymology: Named for Dongyang in Zhejiang Province, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Dongyangosaurus.description: Dongyangosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous. The only species is Dongyangosaurus sinensis, from which only a single fragmentary skeleton is known, coming from the Zhejiang province of eastern China. It was described and named by Lü Junchang and colleagues. Like other sauropods, Dongyangosaurus would have been a large quadrupedal herbivore.

dispute.summary: Placed at Somphospondyli incertae sedis. The describing paper (Lü et al., 2008) referred Dongyangosaurus to Titanosauria as a basal titanosaur by comparison, though its formal systematics stopped at Titanosauriformes; the most recent dedicated analysis (Han et al., 2024) recovers it within Titanosauria in an eastern-Asian clade with Andesaurus, Huabeisaurus, Baotianmansaurus and others; but D'Emic (2012) considered these Chinese taxa to bear euhelopodid (non-titanosaurian somphospondylan) features. Somphospondyli is the least-inclusive clade all these hypotheses accept.

history.note: Retained in Titanosauria per Lü et al. (2008) and Han et al. (2024); a non-titanosaurian somphospondylan position recovered by other analyses is noted.

Broadened to Somphospondyli incertae sedis on re-evaluation: the within-Titanosauria placement is not universally accepted — D'Emic (2012) indicates euhelopodid affinities and the describing paper's formal systematics stopped at Titanosauriformes — so the conservative shared node is adopted.

Pubis shorter than ischium, with elongated and nearly closed obturator foramen

Doolysaurus.etymology: Combines a reference to 'Dooly the Little Dinosaur', a Korean cartoon character, with Ancient Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; the specific name huhmini honors paleontologist Min Huh, founder of the Korean Dinosaur Research Center.
Doolysaurus.description: Doolysaurus is an extinct genus of thescelosaurid ornithischian dinosaur known from the Cretaceous (Albian-lower Cenomanian) Ilseongsan Formation of South Korea. The genus contains a single species, Doolysaurus huhmini, known from the partial skeleton of a small juvenile individual. It is the first named South Korean dinosaur with diagnostic cranial material, providing important insight into the early evolution of thescelosaurid ornithischians in East Asia, and the second named basal neornithischian from South Korea after Koreanosaurus.

dispute.summary: Doolysaurus is recovered within Thescelosaurinae, as sister to a clade of Parksosaurus, Fona, and Thescelosaurus, in the primary (Bayesian and majority-rule) analyses of Jung and others (2026). A sensitivity analysis using the Avrahami and others (2024) matrix instead recovered it as a basal orodromine.

history.note: Placed at Thescelosaurinae following the primary result of Jung and others (2026); the Orodrominae alternative from their sensitivity analysis is recorded.

Dornraptor.etymology: From Anglo-Saxon 'Dornwaraceasetr' (the area roughly equivalent to modern Dorset, England) and Latin 'raptor' (one who seizes); meaning 'Dorset robber'.
Dornraptor.description: Dornraptor is an extinct genus of averostran theropod dinosaur from the Hettangian–Sinemurian of Charmouth, Dorset, England, alongside other Blue Lias theropods such as Sarcosaurus and Dracoraptor. The single species, Dornraptor normani, is known from a fragmentary right knee joint (distal femur and proximal tibia) originally described by Richard Owen as the armored ornithischian Scelidosaurus and subsequently reclassified by Baron (2024) as an indeterminate averostran theropod.
diagnostic_features: Large proximodistally oriented scar extending along the medial side of the anterior face of the distal end of the femur.

Sharp proximodistally oriented crest on lateral margin of proximal tibia running parallel to the fibular crest but not joining it distally to form a forked crest.
Antero-posteriorly elongate cnemial crest that reaches further proximally than either the medial or lateral condyles.
Lateral condyle of the proximal tibia with a posterolateral margin forming an acute angle in medial view (potential autapomorphy).

Dracoraptor.etymology: From Latin draco (dragon, here referencing the Welsh dragon) + raptor (robber/thief): 'dragon thief' or 'dragon robber', honoring Wales where it was found.
Dracoraptor.description: Dracoraptor is a genus of coelophysoid dinosaur that lived during the Hettangian stage of the Early Jurassic Period of what is now Wales dated at about 201 million years ago. The fossil was first discovered in 2014 by Rob and Nick Hanigan and Sam Davies at the Blue Lias Formation on the South Wales coast. The genus name Dracoraptor is from Draco, referring to the Welsh dragon, and raptor, meaning robber, a commonly employed suffix for theropod dinosaurs, with the type species being Dracoraptor hanigani. It is one of the oldest known Jurassic dinosaurs and is the first dinosaur skeleton from the Jurassic of Wales.

Dracovenator.description: Dracovenator is a genus of neotheropod dinosaur that lived approximately 201 to 199 million years ago during the early part of the Jurassic period in what is now South Africa. Dracovenator was a medium-sized, moderately built, ground-dwelling, bipedal carnivore, that could grow up to an estimated 5.5-6.5 meters (18-21 ft) in length and 250 kilograms (550 lb) in body mass. Its type specimen was based on only a partial skull that was recovered.

Dreadnoughtus.etymology: Named after the dreadnought class of battleships, from Old English meaning 'fears nothing', in reference to the animal's immense size which would have made it largely invulnerable to predators.
Dreadnoughtus.description: Dreadnoughtus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur containing a single species, Dreadnoughtus schrani. It is known from two partial skeletons discovered in Upper Cretaceous (Campanian to Maastrichtian, approximately 76-70 million years ago) rocks of the Cerro Fortaleza Formation in Santa Cruz Province, Argentina. It is one of the largest terrestrial vertebrates known from reasonably complete remains, with the immature type specimen measuring 26 meters (85 ft) in total body length and weighing up to 48-49 metric tons (53-54 short tons).

Anterior haemal arches with paddle-shaped distal expansion.

dispute.summary: Dromaeosauroides bornholmensis is based on isolated tooth crowns, and its diagnosability has been debated. Weishampel et al. (2004) and Lindgren et al. (2008) regarded the holotype as indeterminate, but Bonde (2012) rebutted this — arguing that the teeth differ from those of other Early Cretaceous dromaeosaurids and of Dromaeosaurus, and that the earlier critiques rested on incorrect stratigraphic information — and retained the taxon as valid. Longrich et al. (2022) treated it as a possible early eudromaeosaur. It is retained as a valid, if tooth-based, dromaeosaurid.

Dromaeosauroides.etymology: From Dromaeosaurus + Greek -oides, 'resembling'; means 'resembling Dromaeosaurus', indicating its morphological similarity to that genus
Dromaeosauroides.description: Dromaeosauroides is a genus of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of what is now Denmark and possibly also England. It was discovered in the Jydegaard Formation in the Robbedale valley, on the island of Bornholm in the Baltic Sea. This formation ranges from the Berriasian to the Valanginian ages. This is the only likely place for dinosaur remains to be discovered on Danish territory, since the Mesozoic deposits exposed in the rest of the country are marine. Dromaeosauroides is the first known dinosaur from Denmark, and the only one which has been scientifically named. It is one of the oldest known dromaeosaurs in the world, and the first known uncontested dromaeosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Europe.

Dromaeosaurus.etymology: From Greek dromaios, 'running/swift', + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'running lizard', referring to its presumed speed and agility
Dromaeosaurus.description: Dromaeosaurus is a genus of dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period (middle to late Campanian and Maastrichtian), sometime between 80 and 69 million years ago, in the Canadian province of Alberta and the western United States. The type species is Dromaeosaurus albertensis, which was described by William Diller Matthew and Barnum Brown in 1922. Its fossils were unearthed in the Hell Creek Formation, Horseshoe Canyon Formation and Dinosaur Park Formation. Teeth attributed to this genus have been found in the Prince Creek Formation. Dromaeosaurus is the type genus of both Dromaeosauridae and Dromaeosaurinae, which include many genera with similar characteristics to Dromaeosaurus such as possibly its closest relative Dakotaraptor. Dromaeosaurus was heavily built, more so than other dromaeosaurids that are similar in size, like Velociraptor.

Dromiceiomimus.description: Dromiceiomimus is a genus of ornithomimid theropod from the Late Cretaceous (early Maastrichtian) of Alberta, Canada. The type species, D. brevitertius, is considered a synonym of Ornithomimus edmontonicus by some authors, while others consider it a distinct and valid taxon. It was a small ornithomimid that weighed about 135 kilograms (298 lb).

Dryosaurus.etymology: From Greek drys (δρῦς), 'tree' or 'oak', + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'tree lizard', reflecting the forested habitat rather than the shape of its teeth
Dryosaurus.description: Dryosaurus meaning 'tree, oak' and σαυρος (sauros) meaning 'lizard' (the name reflects the forested habitat, not a vague oak-leaf shape of its cheek teeth as is sometimes assumed)) is an extinct genus of herbivorous ornithopod dinosaur that lived in the Late Jurassic period. It was an iguanodont (formerly classified as a hypsilophodont). Fossils have been found in the western United States and were first discovered in the late 19th century. Valdosaurus canaliculatus and Dysalotosaurus lettowvorbecki were both formerly considered to represent species of Dryosaurus.

Dryptosauroides.etymology: From Dryptosaurus (Marsh's North American genus) and Greek -oides (resembling); meaning "Dryptosaurus-like", in reference to the perceived similarity in vertebral shape.
Dryptosauroides.description: Dryptosauroides is a problematic large theropod from the Maastrichtian Lameta Group of central India, erected by Huene and Matley (1933) on a syntype series of six large vertebrae (GSI K20/334, K20/609, K27/549, K27/601, K27/602, K27/626) from the Carnosaur bed at Bara Simla, Jabalpur. Huene originally interpreted the type vertebrae as dorsals; the formal re-evaluation by Novas, Agnolín and Bandyopadhyay (2004) reinterprets them as anterior caudals, refers all the Carnosaur-bed theropod material to Abelisauroidea, and treats Dryptosauroides as a nomen dubium because the type material lacks unambiguous autapomorphies.

Cervical centrum 12 cm long with strong downward-directed parapophyses fully at the base; anterior margin projects ventrally and parapophyses pass into it; prezygapophyses very strong and broadly expanded laterally

Dryptosaurus.etymology: From Greek drypto (to tear) + sauros (lizard): 'tearing lizard'.
Dryptosaurus.description: Dryptosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived in the present-day East Coast of the United States during the Late Cretaceous period. The type, and only, species, D. aquilunguis was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1866 as Laelaps aquilunguis, however the genus name was preoccupied by a mite. As a result, Cope's rival in the Bone Wars, Othniel Marsh, replaced the genus name with Dryptosaurus. Dryptosaurus is known from a single, fragmentary skeleton including parts of the mandible (lower jaw), limbs, and vertebrae. These fossils were unearthed by fertilizer miners in New Jersey in rock layers of the New Egypt Formation. This formation dates to the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, around 67 to 66 million years ago. Several other fragmentary remains have been assigned to Dryptosaurus, however their referral is uncertain.

Third trochanter on femur small and positioned lower than in any known Dinosaur, less than one-third femur length from inner distal condyle
Tibia with cuneiform distal articular surface (not lozenge-shaped); anterior ridge very strong and much incurved; shaft much compressed antero-posteriorly
Ungueal phalanges remarkably large and strongly compressed, with eagle-like form; large flexor-tendon insertion process separated by groove extending to tip
Humeri relatively short (less than half femur length), proximally much dilated with strong postero-external ala and shorter antero-internal dilatation

Dubreuillosaurus.etymology: Named for French fossil collector and preparator Pascal Dubreuil, who found the specimen, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Dubreuillosaurus.description: Dubreuillosaurus is a genus of carnivorous megalosaurid theropod dinosaur from the middle Jurassic Period. Its fossils were found in France. The only named species, Dubreuillosaurus valesdunensis, was originally described as a species of Poekilopleuron, Poekilopleuron? valesdunensis, which is still formally the type species of the genus. It was later renamed Dubreuillosaurus valesdunensis when, in 2005, Allain came to the conclusion that it was not part of the genus Poekilopleuron. Its type specimen, MNHN 1998-13, is only rivalled in the number of preserved elements in this group by that of Eustreptospondylus. Dubreuillosaurus is considered to be a sister taxon of Magnosaurus. It did not show signs of insular dwarfism even though it was uncovered on an island.

Anterior caudal neural spines more strongly inclined posteriorly than in Poekilopleuron

Femoral head directed medioventrally at less than 90 degrees to shaft, unique among spinosauroids
No extensor groove on anterior surface of distal femur end; instead a convexity is present
Hypapophyses on anterior dorsal vertebrae simple and unbifurcated anteriorly, unlike Eustreptospondylus, Streptospondylus, and Lourinhanosaurus

Duonychus.etymology: From Greek duo (two) + onychos (claw): 'two claws', referring to the two-fingered hand bearing large curved claws.
Duonychus.description: Duonychus is an extinct genus of therizinosaurid theropod dinosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian to early Coniacian age) of what is now Mongolia. It is known from a partial skeleton, including several vertebrae, most of the forelimbs, and part of the pelvic girdle, found in outcrops of the Bayanshiree Formation. The remains were discovered in 2012 by the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and briefly mentioned in later conference abstracts. The genus contains a single species, Duonychus tsogtbaatari, which was formally described in 2025.
diagnostic_features: Didactyl manus with complete absence of digit III (digit formula 2-3-0) and a reduced metacarpal III forming a splint.
Fused distal carpals 1 and 2 semilunate-shaped with a mediodorsal process and a small angle (~15°) between articular surfaces of the radiale for the semilunate carpal and the radius.
Equally sized manual unguals I-2 and II-2, with absence or reduction of the flexor fossa in manual phalanges.
Dorsal vertebrae with long neural spines, a thick centrodiapophyseal lamina without additional laminae, and lacking pleurocoels; sacral vertebrae (2-4) with flat ventral surfaces.
Reduced dorsal process at the proximal end of manual phalanges and pneumatic dorsal ribs.
Entepicondyle reduced with a markedly narrow groove separating it from the ulnar condyle; deltopectoral crest positioned more proximally than in Erlikosaurus.

species.name: Duonychus tsogtbaatari
species.etymology: Named for Mongolian paleontologist Khishigjav Tsogtbaatar, a former director of the Institute of Paleontology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences.

Duriatitan.etymology: From Latin Duria, the Roman name for Dorset (England), + Greek Titan, a giant of mythology; means 'giant from Dorset'
Duriatitan.description: Duriatitan is a genus of titanosauriform sauropod dinosaur that lived in the Late Jurassic in what is now England. The holotype specimen of Duriatitan, BMNH 44635, is a partial left upper arm bone which was found by R.I. Smith near Sandsfoot, Weymouth in the lower Kimmeridge Clay from Dorset. The type species, D. humerocristatus, was described in 1874 by John Hulke as a species of Cetiosaurus and was noted as being similar to that of Gigantosaurus. The specific name refers to the deltopectoral crest, crista, on the upper arm bone, humerus. The specimen was assigned to its own genus by Paul M. Barrett, Roger B.J. Benson and Paul Upchurch in 2010. The generic name is derived from the Latin name for Dorset, Duria, and Greek Titan. Thomas Holtz estimated its length at 25 meters (82 ft).

species.etymology: From Latin 'humerus' (upper arm bone) and 'cristatus' (crested), referring to the distinctive deltopectoral crest on the humerus that is the basis of the holotype.

Duriavenator.etymology: From 'Duria', the Latinized name for Dorset (derived from the River Dour), combined with Latin 'venator' meaning 'hunter', meaning 'Dorset hunter'.
Duriavenator.description: Duriavenator is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now England during the Middle Jurassic, about 168 million years ago. In 1882, upper and lower jaw bones of a dinosaur were collected near Sherborne in Dorset, and Richard Owen considered the fossils to belong to the species Megalosaurus bucklandii, the first named non-bird dinosaur. By 1964, the specimen was recognized as belonging to a different species, and in 1974 it was described as a new species of Megalosaurus, M. hesperis; the specific name means 'the West' or 'western'. Later researchers questioned whether the species belonged to Megalosaurus, in which many fragmentary theropods from around the world had historically been placed. After examining the taxonomic issues surrounding Megalosaurus, Roger B. J. Benson moved M. hesperis to its own genus in 2008, Duriavenator; this name means "Dorset hunter".
diagnostic_features: Deep groove on dorsal surface of jugal process of maxilla containing numerous pneumatic foramina.
Array of small foramina (~11, ~2 mm diameter) in ventral part of articular surface of maxilla for premaxilla.
Enlarged, subcircular third dentary alveolus with subcylindrical, anteriorly inclined anterior dentary teeth.
Anterior Meckelian foramen located almost directly anterior to the posterior Meckelian foramen.
Prominent lip bounding the Meckelian groove ventrally, anterior to the Meckelian fossa.

species.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'hesperos' meaning 'the West' or 'western', reflecting that the specimen came from the western part of the area studied at the time.

Dynamoterror.etymology: From Greek dynamis (power) + Latin terror (terror): 'powerful terror'.
Dynamoterror.description: Dynamoterror is a monospecific genus of tyrannosaurid dinosaur from New Mexico that lived during the Late Cretaceous (lower Campanian age, 78 Ma) in what is now the upper Allison Member of the Menefee Formation. The type and only species, Dynamoterror dynastes, is known from a subadult or adult individual about 9 meters (30 feet) long with an incomplete associated skeleton. It was named in 2018 by Andrew T. McDonald, Douglas G. Wolfe and Alton C. Dooley, Jr. Dynamoterror was closely related to Teratophoneus and Lythronax.
diagnostic_features: Prefrontonasal and prefrontolacrimal processes in close proximity on the frontal, separated only by a shallow notch (unambiguous autapomorphy).
Caudal part of the postorbital suture subrectangular, concave, and laterally projecting, separated from the rostral part by a deep groove (provisional autapomorphy).

species.etymology: From Latin 'dynastes' meaning 'ruler', honoring the junior synonym 'Dynamosaurus imperiosus' which was a childhood favorite of one of the authors.

Dyoplosaurus.description: Dyoplosaurus is a monospecific genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur from Alberta that lived during the Late Cretaceous (middle Campanian, ~76.5-75 Ma) in what is now the Dinosaur Park Formation. Dyoplosaurus represents a close relative of Scolosaurus and Anodontosaurus, two ankylosaurids known from the Horseshoe Canyon and Dinosaur Park Formation.
diagnostic_features: Transverse processes of the third sacral vertebra projecting anterolaterally from the centrum and anteroventrally inclined (~25° from horizontal) — unique among ankylosaurids, giving a distinctive sacral-fenestra pattern.
Pedal unguals triangular in dorsal view, lacking the proximal constriction seen in Euoplocephalus.
Handle (tail-club) vertebrae with sharply pointed neural spines in dorsal view, unlike the broad, tongue-like spines of Ankylosaurus.

Free caudal centra subcircular in anterior and posterior view, with transverse processes directed anterolaterally and present on all free caudal vertebrae (unlike their loss on distal caudals in Pinacosaurus and Tarchia).
Transverse processes meeting the free caudal centrum at a sharp angle in anterior or posterior view, unlike the rounded, obtuse-angled condition in Nodocephalosaurus.

species.name: Dyoplosaurus acutosquameus
species.etymology: From Latin 'acutus' meaning 'sharp' and 'squama' meaning 'scale', referring to the sharp scale-like osteoderms of the holotype.

Dysalotosaurus.description: Dysalotosaurus is a genus of herbivorous iguanodontian dinosaur. It was a dryosaurid iguanodontian, and its fossils have been found in late Kimmeridgian-age rocks (Late Jurassic) of the Tendaguru Formation of Lindi Region in Tanzania. The type and only species of the genus is D. lettowvorbecki. This species was named by Hans Virchow in 1919 in honor of the Imperial German Army Officer, Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck. For much of the 20th century the species was referred to the related and approximately contemporary genus Dryosaurus, but newer studies reject this synonymy.

species.name: Dysalotosaurus lettowvorbecki
species.etymology: Named for Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, Imperial German Army officer, by Hans Virchow in 1919.

type_specimen.material: An axis (epistropheus) and an associated third cervical vertebra.
type_specimen.notes: No holotype was designated; the genus was established on the cervical vertebrae described by Virchow (1919).

notable_specimens.institution: Institut für Geowissenschaften, Universität Tübingen (English: Institute for Geosciences, Tübingen University) / Institut und Museum für Geologie und Paläontologie der Universität Tübingen
notable_specimens.significance: Semi-articulated juvenile (age 4–5 years) preserving ~40 associated elements, including cranial bones and a near-complete cervical series. Neurocentral sutures, closed in the cervicals but open in posterior dorsals, reveal a cervical fusion locus challenging the 'tail-to-head' model in Ornithopoda.

An isolated presacral centrum co-ossified with a hemivertebra, producing about 35 degrees of kyphosis and 15 degrees of scoliosis. Interpreted as forming early in embryogenesis via hemimetameric segmental shift, it is one of few hemivertebrae documented in fossil vertebrates.

A vertebral body showing macroscopic enlargement and, on micro-CT, the characteristic radiologic triad of Paget disease of bone in its mixed phase (trabecular coarsening, cortical thickening, and increased bone size). It is the oldest reported case of Paget disease in the fossil record.

Dysganus.etymology: From Greek dys- (bad/rough) + ganos (tooth enamel): 'rough enamel', referring to the texture of the fossil teeth.
Dysganus.description: Dysganus (meaning "rough enamel") is a dubious genus of ceratopsian dinosaur from the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous. The fossil teeth referred to Dysganus were first collected by Charles Sternberg from the Judith River Formation of Montana and later described by Edward Drinker Cope. All of the species are now seen as dubious ceratopsians, though referred material from tyrannosaurids and hadrosaurids were found in New Mexico.

dispute.summary: Dysganus is a tooth-based taxon whose material may be ceratopsid, hadrosaurid, or otherwise indeterminate; it is a nomen dubium.

dispute.summary: Dyslocosaurus is known only from fragmentary appendicular material, originally described as a diplodocid (McIntosh et al., 1992), and the association of that material has been questioned. Wilson and Sereno (1998) argued that two pedal phalanges and a small ungual are non-sauropod bones that do not belong with the specimen, while Tschopp et al. (2015) separately judged one pes phalanx to have been collected apart from the rest and excluded it. Both nonetheless retained the remainder as a valid taxon; Tschopp et al. (2015) found it diagnostic — uniting apatosaurine, diplodocine, and dicraeosaurid traits — and recovered it as the most basal dicraeosaurid.

Dyslocosaurus.description: Dyslocosaurus is an extinct genus of diplodocoid sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Wyoming, United States. The type and only species, Dyslocosaurus polyonychius, was described by McIntosh, Coombs, and Russell in 1992 from fragmentary remains including limb bones and a partial manus.
diagnostic_features: Proximodistal length of astragalus equal to about 50% of transverse breadth, a higher percentage than in other diplodocids.
Metatarsals with greater shaft circumference relative to length than in other diplodocids.

dispute.summary: Dystrophaeus is a poorly known taxon whose long-standing diplodocoid identification has been rejected. Tschopp et al. (2015) consistently recovered it within Dicraeosauridae under implied weighting but found it too unstable to place under equal weighting, with constrained searches supporting dicraeosaurid and camarasaurid positions nearly equally; Foster et al. (2016) rule out a diplodocoid identity but leave a macronarian versus outside-Neosauropoda position unresolved, and Jones (2026) favors basal Macronaria or a pre-Neosauropoda position. Its candidate positions span non-neosauropod Eusauropoda to several neosauropod clades.

Dystrophaeus.etymology: From Greek 'dys' meaning 'bad' and 'stropheus' meaning 'joint', giving 'coarse joint'; refers to the pitted joint surfaces that served as attachments for cartilage.
Dystrophaeus.description: Dystrophaeus is an extinct genus of sauropod dinosaur. Its type and only species is Dystrophaeus viaemalae, named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877. Its fossils were found in the Tidwell Member of the Morrison Formation of Utah. Due to the fragmentary condition of its only known specimen, the affinities of Dystrophaeus are uncertain, although excavations carried out at the discovery site since 1989 have uncovered more of the original specimen and hold the potential for an improved understanding of the taxon.

Dzharacursor.etymology: From Dzharakuduk (the type locality in Uzbekistan) and Latin 'cursor' (runner); meaning 'Dzharakuduk runner'.
Dzharacursor.description: Dzharacursor is an extinct genus of ornithomimid theropod dinosaur from the Turonian-age Bissekty Formation of the Kyzyl Kum Desert, Uzbekistan. The type and only species, Dzharacursor bissektensis, was originally named by Nessov (1995) as a tentative species of the North American genus Archaeornithomimus, then treated as a nomen dubium until Averianov and Sues (2024) erected the new genus on the basis of a juvenile femur holotype and a large hypodigm of referred postcranial and cranial material recovered from the Bissekty bonebed.

Dzharatitanis.etymology: From Dzharakuduk (the type locality in Uzbekistan) + Greek titan (giant): 'Dzharakuduk titan'.
Dzharatitanis.description: Dzharatitanis is an extinct genus of probable titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Turonian age) Bissekty Formation of Uzbekistan. The genus contains a single species, Dzharatitanis kingi, known from a single tail vertebra. Dzharatitanis was considered to be a member of the Rebbachisauridae when it was named in 2021, but subsequent research has considered it to be a titanosaur.

Echinodon.description: Echinodon is a genus of heterodontosaurid dinosaur that lived during the earliest Cretaceous of southern England and possibly western France in the Berriasian epoch. The first specimens were jaw bones named Echinodon becklesii by Sir Richard Owen in 1861, and since their original description only additional teeth have been discovered. The specific name honors collector Samuel Beckles who discovered the material of Echinodon and many other taxa from across England, while the genus name translates as "prickly tooth" in reference to the dental anatomy of the taxon.

Edmontosaurus.etymology: From Edmonton (city in Alberta, Canada, near the formation where it was found) + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'lizard from Edmonton'
Edmontosaurus.description: Edmontosaurus (meaning "lizard from Edmonton"), often colloquially and historically known as Anatosaurus or Anatotitan (meaning "duck lizard" and "giant duck"), is a genus of hadrosaurid (duck-billed) dinosaur. It contains two known species: Edmontosaurus regalis and Edmontosaurus annectens. Fossils of E. regalis have been found in rocks of western North America that date from the late Campanian age of the Cretaceous period 73 million years ago, while those of E. annectens were found in the same geographic region from rocks dated to the end of the Maastrichtian age, 66 million years ago. Edmontosaurus was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs ever to exist, and lived alongside dinosaurs like Triceratops, Tyrannosaurus, Ankylosaurus, and Pachycephalosaurus shortly before the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event.

Efraasia.etymology: Named after German paleontologist Eberhard Fraas, who collected the original specimens in the early twentieth century; the 'E.' prefix likely stands for Eberhard
Efraasia.description: Efraasia is a genus of basal sauropodomorph dinosaur. It was a herbivore which lived during the middle Norian stage of the Late Triassic, around 210 million years ago, in what is now Germany. It was named in 1973 after Eberhard Fraas, who during the early twentieth century collected what were the original type specimens. The specimens were at first assigned to three already existing genera and so became divided among three separate species: Teratosaurus minor, Sellosaurus fraasi and Paleosaurus diagnosticus. In 2003, these were combined into a single valid species: Efraasia minor. Efraasia was a lightly built, medium-sized sauropodomorph, about 6 to 7 meters (20 to 23 ft) long.

It was a large abelisaurid, measuring between 6.5 and 8 m (21 and 26 ft) in length and weighing 800 kg (1,800 lb).

Elaphrosaurus.etymology: From Greek elaphros (ελαφρός), 'light' or 'nimble', + Greek sauros, 'lizard'; means 'nimble lizard' or 'light-bodied lizard', referring to its lightly built frame
Elaphrosaurus.description: Elaphrosaurus is a genus of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived approximately 155 to 145 million years ago during the Late Jurassic Period in what is now Tanzania in Africa. Elaphrosaurus was a medium-sized but lightly built member of the group that could grow up to 6.2 m (20 ft) long. Morphologically, this dinosaur is significant in two ways. Firstly, it has a relatively long body but is very shallow-chested for a theropod of its size. Secondly, it has very short hindlimbs in comparison with its body. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that this genus is likely a ceratosaur. Earlier suggestions that it is a late surviving coelophysoid have been examined but generally dismissed. Elaphrosaurus is currently believed to be a very close relative of Limusaurus, an unusual beaked ceratosaurian which may have been either herbivorous or omnivorous.

dispute.summary: Elopteryx nopcsai is a small maniraptoran from the Maastrichtian of Romania, known from femora, and the debate around it concerns its affinities and the material referred to it rather than its validity. Its type femora were historically conflated with tibiotarsi that Harrison and Walker (1975) made the types of Heptasteornis andrewsi and Bradycneme draculae; Naish and Dyke (2004) separated these, placing the Elopteryx femora as a troodontid or a non-ornithuromorphan pygostylian (not an alvarezsaurid or dromaeosaurid), while regarding Heptasteornis as an alvarezsaurid nomen dubium and Bradycneme as Maniraptora indeterminate. Stoicescu et al. (2024) interpreted newer material as a secondarily flightless avialan and suggested Balaur bondoc may be its junior synonym. It is placed conservatively at Maniraptora incertae sedis.

history.note: Moved from Paraves to Maniraptora incertae sedis; the flightless-avialan interpretation and possible Balaur synonymy (Stoicescu et al., 2024) are noted, and the dubious status remains unresolved.

Dispute refocused on affinities and referred material and kept valid — no primary source treats Elopteryx nopcsai itself as dubious (Naish and Dyke, 2004, treat it as identifiable; the nomen-dubium call applies to Heptasteornis, a separate name), so the "dubious theropod" framing and the Jones (2026) citation for it were removed.

Elopteryx.etymology: From Greek 'helos' meaning 'marsh' or 'swamp' and Greek 'pteryx' meaning 'wing'; means 'marsh wing'.
Elopteryx.description: Elopteryx is a genus of paravian theropod dinosaur based on fragmentary fossils found in Late Cretaceous rocks of Romania. The single species, Elopteryx nopcsai, was known only from very incomplete material until new specimens were reported in the 21st century. Balaur bondoc might represent a junior synonym of this taxon.

Elrhazosaurus.description: Elrhazosaurus is a genus of basal iguanodontian dinosaur, known from isolated bones found in Early Cretaceous rocks of Niger. These bones were initially thought to belong to a species of the related dryosaurid Valdosaurus, but have since been reclassified.

Emausaurus is the only known Toarcian thyreophoran, as well as the only dinosaur from the zone of the same age with a formal name.

Embasaurus.etymology: From the Emba River (western Kazakhstan), the type locality, and Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "Emba lizard".
Embasaurus.description: Embasaurus is a dubious genus of tetanuran theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous period. It is known from two vertebrae found in the Neocomian Sands of Kazakhstan. As it is known only from fragmentary remains, Embasaurus is considered by some to be a possible nomen dubium. It was named after the Emba River, and it is believed to have lived during the Berriasian stage, around 140 million years ago. According to the Theropod Database, a personal website designed by Mickey Mortimer, further research may suggest that Embasaurus may be a basal tyrannosauroid. George Olshevsky, however, considered Embasaurus to be a megalosaurid, closely related to Magnosaurus, Megalosaurus, and Torvosaurus.

Emiliasaura.etymology: Named in honor of Emilia (likely a personal name) + Latin saura (lizard): 'Emilia's lizard'.
Emiliasaura.description: Emiliasaura is an extinct genus of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous (Valanginian) Mulichinco Formation of Neuquén Province, Argentina. The genus contains a single species, Emiliasaura alessandrii, known from three individual specimens. Emiliasaura was initially described as a rhabdodontomorph. If this identification is correct, it would represent the oldest member of this clade and the first named from South America. However, a later analysis of rhabdodontomorphs failed to recover Emiliasaura within this clade, instead placing it as a styracosternan.

dispute.summary: Emiliasaura alessandrii was described as an early-diverging rhabdodontomorph (Coria and others, 2025) — which would make it the oldest and first South American member of that clade — but the dedicated reanalysis of Czepiński and Madzia (2025) instead recovers it as an early-diverging styracosternan and considers a rhabdodontomorph identity unlikely. No analysis recovers it within Dryosauridae.

history.note: Placed at Dryosauridae following Czepiński and Madzia (2025) and Jones (2026); the rhabdodontomorph and styracosternan alternatives reflected, not adopted.

Re-evaluated and moved to Iguanodontia incertae sedis. Neither primary analysis supports Dryosauridae — the describing study (Coria and others 2025) recovers a rhabdodontomorph and Czepiński and Madzia (2025) recover a styracosternan — so Iguanodontia is the least-inclusive clade both accept. The earlier Dryosauridae placement, attributed to a within-Dryosauridae reading of Czepiński and Madzia (2025), is not supported by that paper.

Enigmosaurus.etymology: From Greek enigma (riddle/enigma) + sauros (lizard): 'enigma lizard' or 'enigmatic lizard', reflecting uncertainty about its affinities at the time of description.
Enigmosaurus.description: Enigmosaurus is a genus of therizinosauroid that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period. It was a medium-sized, ground-dwelling, bipedal herbivore that represents the third therizinosaur taxon from the Bayan Shireh Formation, although it is known from the lower part. The genus is monotypic, including only the type species E. mongoliensis, known from a well-preserved pelvis and other tentative body remains.

dispute.summary: Enigmosaurus is an intermediate-grade therizinosaur whose family-level assignment depends on how Therizinosauridae is defined. Zanno (2010) recovers it outside Therizinosauridae, as a successive outgroup to that family, a result followed by the Princeton Encyclopedia (Jones, 2026). Under the broader Therizinosaurus-anchored definition of Kobayashi et al. (2022, 2025) it is drawn into Therizinosauridae, recovered near the derived genera Erlikosaurus and Segnosaurus. It is placed conservatively in Therizinosauroidea. A proposed synonymy with Erlikosaurus has been rejected.

history.note: Placed at Therizinosauroidea (outside Therizinosauridae) following Zanno (2010) and Jones (2026); Kobayashi et al. (2022, 2025) include it in a more broadly defined Therizinosauridae.

Eoabelisaurus.etymology: From Greek 'eos' (ἠώς) meaning 'dawn' combined with the genus name Abelisaurus, indicating it is an early (dawn) relative of Abelisaurus.
Eoabelisaurus.description: Eoabelisaurus is a genus of abelisauroid theropod dinosaur from the Lower Jurassic Cañadón Asfalto Formation of the Cañadón Asfalto Basin in Argentina, South America. The generic name combines a Greek ἠώς, (eos), "dawn", with the name Abelisaurus, in reference to the fact it represents an early relative of the latter. Only one species is currently recognized, E. mefi; the specific name honors the MEF, the Museo Paleontológico "Egidio Feruglio", where discoverer Diego Pol is active. It is characterized by reduced forelimb proportions that show primitive characteristics of the Abelisauridae family.

It is placed conservatively at Carcharodontosauridae incertae sedis.

Eocarcharia.etymology: From Greek eos, 'dawn/early', + Greek karcharias, 'shark' (as in a sharp-toothed creature); means 'dawn shark', referring to its early geological age and shark-like serrated teeth
Eocarcharia.description: Eocarcharia is an extinct genus of theropod dinosaurs found in what is now the western Ténéré Desert of Niger. It is known from several skull bones collected in 2000 by an expedition to the Early Cretaceous (Aptian-Albian ages) Elrhaz Formation (Gadoufaoua locality) led by American paleontologist Paul Sereno. The fossil material was then described in 2008 by Sereno and Steve Brusatte. The genus contains a single species, Eocarcharia dinops. While Sereno and Brusatte identified all of the remains as belonging to a new carcharodontosaurid, later studies suggested that the species is chimaeric, comprising bones of at least two unrelated taxa. Some of the Eocarcharia material, including the holotype (name-bearing) specimen, likely belongs to a baryonychine spinosaurid. This would render Eocarcharia a member of this group, closely related to the coeval Suchomimus. Meanwhile, the definitively carcharodontosaurid bones, a maxilla and teeth, belong to a distinct unnamed taxon.

Eocursor.etymology: From Greek eos (dawn) + Latin cursor (runner): 'dawn runner', indicating it is one of the earliest known ornithischians.
Eocursor.description: Eocursor is genus of basal ornithischian dinosaur that lived in what is now South Africa during the Early Jurassic. Remains of this animal have been found in the Upper Elliot Formation and it is among the most completely known early ornithischians, shedding new light on the origin of the group.

Some analyses based on the Madzia, Boyd and Mazuch (2018) matrix instead place it within Heterodontosauridae (Boyd, 2015; Madzia and others, 2021).

Eodromaeus.etymology: From Greek eos (dawn) + dromeus (runner): 'dawn runner', reflecting its status as one of the earliest known theropods.
Eodromaeus.description: Eodromaeus is an extinct genus of probable basal theropod dinosaurs from the Late Triassic of Argentina. Like many other of the earliest-known dinosaurs, it hails from the Carnian-age (~230 Ma) Ischigualasto Formation, within the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión Basin of northwestern Argentina. Upon its discovery, it was argued to be one of the oldest true theropods, supplanting its contemporary Eoraptor, which was reinterpreted as a basal sauropodomorph.

Eolambia.etymology: From Greek eos (dawn) + Lambeosaurinae: 'dawn lambeosaurine', indicating it is an early relative of lambeosaurine hadrosaurs.
Eolambia.description: Eolambia is a genus of herbivorous hadrosauroid dinosaur from the early Late Cretaceous of the United States. It contains a single species, E. caroljonesa, named by paleontologist James Kirkland in 1998. The type specimen of Eolambia was discovered by Carole and Ramal Jones in 1993; the species name honors Carole. Since then, hundreds of bones have been discovered from both adults and juveniles, representing nearly every element of the skeleton. All of the specimens have thus far been found in Emery County, Utah, in a layer of rock known as the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.

dispute.summary: Eolambia caroljonesa was originally described as a lambeosaurine hadrosaurid (Kirkland, 1998), but Head (2001) reidentified it as a basal hadrosauroid, and it is now consistently recovered as a basal hadrosauromorph well outside Hadrosauridae (McDonald and others, 2017; Jones, 2026).

history.note: Placed at Hadrosauromorpha; the original lambeosaurine interpretation reflected, not adopted.

Lower jaw deepens rostrally with nearly no diastema; 30 tooth files with at least 3 teeth per file; teeth with single central carina
Ischium long and stout with large, flaring, blade-like distal end

Eomamenchisaurus.description: Eomamenchisaurus is a genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic Zhanghe Formation of Yuanmou, Yunnan, China. The type species is E. yuanmouensis, described by Lü Junchang and colleagues in 2008.

Eoneophron.description: Eoneophron is an extinct genus of caenagnathid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of South Dakota, US. The genus contains a single species, E. infernalis, known from a partial hindlimb.

Distal tarsal IV coossified with proximal end of metatarsal IV at maturity
Proximal ends of metatarsals III and IV project posteriorly to form a proximal protuberance

Eopinacosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'eos' meaning 'dawn' plus Pinacosaurus, referring to the apparent lower stratigraphic or systematic position of the species relative to Pinacosaurus grangeri.
Eopinacosaurus.description: Eopinacosaurus is an extinct genus of ankylosaurid armored dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) Bayan Mandahu Formation of Inner Mongolia, China, with a referred skull from the coeval Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia. The genus contains a single species, Eopinacosaurus mephistocephalus, originally assigned to the coeval genus Pinacosaurus.
diagnostic_features: Supranarial embayment absent.
Lacrimal incisure absent or rudimentary.
Nasoprefrontal pyramid absent.
Knife-shaped, caudolaterally directed squamosal horns.
Medial segments of first cervical half-ring (h.r.1) broadly oval, with scythe-shaped medial osteoderms.
Straight dorsal border of scapula; no sulcus between anterior and posterior supraorbitals.

Eoraptor.etymology: From Greek eos, 'dawn', + Latin raptor, 'seizer/thief'; means 'dawn thief' or 'dawn plunderer', reflecting its status as one of the earliest known dinosaurs
Eoraptor.description: Eoraptor is a genus of small, lightly built, basal sauropodomorph dinosaur. One of the earliest-known dinosaurs and one of the earliest sauropodomorphs, it lived approximately 231 to 228 million years ago, during the Late Triassic in Western Gondwana, in the region that is now northwestern Argentina. The type and only species, Eoraptor lunensis, was first described in 1993, and is known from an almost complete and well-preserved skeleton and several fragmentary ones. Eoraptor had multiple tooth shapes, which suggests that it was omnivorous.

dispute.summary: Eoraptor lunensis was originally described as a basal theropod (Sereno and others, 1993) and later argued to be a basal saurischian outside both Theropoda and Sauropodomorpha. Most analyses since its 2012 redescription (Sereno and others; Martínez and others, 2012) recover it as a basal sauropodomorph, the view followed by Jones (2026).

history.note: Placed at Sauropodomorpha incertae sedis (basal) following the prevailing post-2012 view and Jones (2026); the basal-theropod and basal-saurischian alternatives are recorded.

diagnostic_features: Premaxilla with a slender posterolateral process bearing a tongue-shaped distal expansion.
Nasal with a transversely broad, horizontal shelf with a convex lateral margin that overhangs the antorbital fossa.
Pterygoid process on the posterior palate margin that articulates laterally in a synovial socket in the ectopterygoid.
Narrow premaxilla-maxilla diastema, approximately one crown in width.
Maxillary crowns with a prominent lateral eminence.
Accessory articular process on the medial aspect of the midcervical prezygapophyses.
Extreme hollowing of the dorsal centra and neural arches.

Eotrachodon.etymology: From Greek eos (dawn) + Trachodon (an early hadrosaurid genus): 'dawn Trachodon', indicating it is a primitive relative of hadrosaurids.
Eotrachodon.description: Eotrachodon is a genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur that lived in the Late Cretaceous of eastern North America. The holotype was found in the Mooreville Chalk Formation (Upper Santonian) of Alabama in 2007 and includes a well-preserved skull and partial skeleton, making it a rare find among dinosaurs of Appalachia.

Caudodorsal region of circumnarial depression above bony naris excavating lateral nasal surface, deeply rostrally but gradually fading caudally.
Premaxillary lateral process abruptly deflected ventrally, forming a 165-degree angle with long axis of circumnarial depression.
Maxilla with subtriangular joint surface for jugal that is more laterally than dorsally facing and prominent dorsal jugal tubercle projected caudally.
Steeply down-warped sagittal crest of parietal substantially elevated above temporal bar.

Eotriceratops.description: Eotriceratops is a genus of herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaurs which lived in the area of North America during the late Cretaceous period. The only named species is Eotriceratops xerinsularis.

Oblique vascular trace on anterior surface of nasal horn core meeting a transverse vascular trace ventrally.
Sharply conical epijugal with pronounced proximoposterior process and separate fossa-like articular facets for jugal and quadratojugal on its proximal surfaces.

The remains (MIWG 1997.550), consisting of assorted skull, axial skeleton and appendicular skeleton elements, from a juvenile or subadult, found in a plant debris clay bed, were described by Stephen Hutt and colleagues in early 2001. The etymology of the generic name refers to the animal's classification as an early tyrannosaur or "tyrant lizard", while the specific name honors the discoverer of the fossil.

Non-shafted feathers with free distal barbs arising from the edge of a membranous structure, an arrangement not previously reported.

Erectopus.etymology: From Latin 'erectus' (upright) and Greek 'pous' (foot); meaning 'upright foot', a reference to the posture of the original syntype foot bones described by Sauvage (1882).
Erectopus.description: Erectopus is an extinct genus of basal allosauroid theropod from the Albian phosphate-bearing beds (La Penthièvre Formation) of Louppy-le- Château in the Argonne region of north-eastern France. The type and only species, Erectopus superbus, was originally named Megalosaurus superbus by Sauvage in 1882, transferred to the new genus Erectopus by von Huene in 1923, and subsequently split by Huene into a second species E. sauvagei in 1932. All of Sauvage's original syntypes were destroyed at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle during World War II; Allain (2005) recovered an associated maxilla in a Parisian fossil collection in the late 1990s, designated it the lectotype (MNHN 2001-4), and synonymised E. sauvagei into E. superbus.

Erketu.etymology: Named after Erketü Tengri, a deity in Mongolian mythology, honoring the region where the dinosaur was found.
Erketu.description: Erketu is a genus of somphospondylan dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, roughly between 96 million and 89 million years ago. It is known from the Bayanshiree Formation of Mongolia, and its fossils were found between 2002 and 2003 during field expeditions. Erketu was first described in 2006 and later on in 2010 due to some cervicals that were left behind in the expedition. This genus represents the first sauropod described from the Bayanshiree Formation. The elongated cervical vertebrae indicate that it probably had the longest neck relative to its body size of any sauropod.

Crescent-shaped (strongly concave lateral border) sternal plate.
Hypertrophied prezygodiapophyseal lamina in cervicals 4-5, extending far anterior of the articular facet as a thin plate perpendicular to the articular plane.
Cervical centra significantly taller than wide at the cotyle in postaxial vertebrae.
