Haplocanthosaurus.etymology: Simple spined lizard; from Greek haploos (simple), akantha (spine or thorn), and sauros (lizard)
Haplocanthosaurus.description: Haplocanthosaurus is a genus of diplodocoid sauropod dinosaur. Two species, H. delfsi and H. priscus, are known from incomplete fossil skeletons. They lived during the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian stage), 155 to 152 million years ago in North America. The type species is H. priscus, named in 1903 John Bell Hatcher , and the referred species H. delfsi was discovered by a young college student named Edwin Delfs in Colorado, United States and described by Jack McIntosh and Michael Williams in 1988. Haplocanthosaurus specimens have been found in the lowermost layer of the Morrison Formation, along with Hesperosaurus mjosi, Brontosaurus yahnahpin, and Allosaurus jimmadseni.
diagnostic_features: Cervical vertebrae of only moderate length with prominent but simple pleurocoels; neural spines of posterior cervicals and anterior dorsals undivided.
Dorsal centra relatively small with prominent pleurocoels; dorsal arches high with diapophyses directed upward at 45 degrees as well as outward; spines short and broad.

Sacrum of five vertebrae (dorso-sacral, three primary sacrals, caudo- sacral) with coossified centra and sacral ribs forming a yoke; spines with tendency toward coalescence particularly in sacrals one through three.

Caudal centra amphicoelous, short, without pleurocentral cavities; chevron facets very prominent giving the underside of each centrum a sculptured appearance; anterior caudal spines slender and curved backward.
Distal end of scapula thin and broadly splayed; proximal plate relatively small; sternal plates large and subquadrangular.
Ischium shaft straight with distal end slightly broadened but not thickened; femur with latero-medial shaft diameter significantly exceeding the antero-posterior diameter.

dispute.summary: Haplocheirus sollers is recovered as the basalmost alvarezsauroid by the dedicated alvarezsaur analyses (Choiniere et al., 2010, 2014; Xu et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2019; Meso et al., 2024), but its alvarezsauroid affinity is contested. The maniraptoromorph analysis of Hartman et al. (2019) recovered it as a compsognathid, and Agnolín et al. (2021) argued on cranial evidence that Haplocheirus and the other Jurassic Chinese "alvarezsauroids" resemble ornithomimosaurs and may fall outside Alvarezsauroidea.

history.note: Placed at Alvarezsauroidea following the prevailing dedicated analyses; the compsognathid and ornithomimosaur alternatives remain unresolved.

Haplocheirus.etymology: Simple hand; from Ancient Greek haplós (simple) and kheír (hand)

It is generally considered to be an alvarezsauroid, although some researchers have questioned this assignment. The genus contains a single species, H. sollers, which is known from a mostly complete skeleton including the skull.

Heterodont dentary tooth row with an enlarged tooth in the fourth alveolus
Alveolar margin at the anterior end of the dentary dorsally convex
Maxillary and dentary teeth with serrations on the distal carinae

Harenadraco.etymology: Sand dragon; from Latin harena (sand) and draco (dragon), referring to the sandy desert environment of the Baruungoyot Formation
Harenadraco.description: Harenadraco is an extinct genus of troodontid theropod dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous Baruungoyot Formation of Mongolia. The genus contains a single species, H. prima, known from a fragmentary skeleton. Harenadraco represents the first troodontid known from the Baruungoyot Formation. Since members of this family are also known from the Nemegt and Djadochta Formations, the discovery of Harendraco indicates that troodontids were important faunal components of every formation within the Nemegt Basin.

Greatly elongated flexor tubercle of pedal phalanx II-3 reaching preceding phalanx shaft in articulation (autapomorphy)
Distal articular surface of pedal phalanx III-3 not ginglymoid (autapomorphy)
Tarsometatarsus length to width ratio ~22:1, extremely slender among theropods

Unlike later, more derived ornithomimosaurs, Harpymimus still possessed teeth, although they appear to have been restricted to the dentary of the lower jaw.

Heishansaurus.etymology: Named after Heishan (Black Mountains) in Gansu Province, China, combined with Greek sauros (lizard); meaning 'Heishan lizard'
Heishansaurus.description: Heishansaurus, meaning "Heishan lizard" after the area in China where it was discovered, is the name given to a dubious genus of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaur, probably belonging to the Ankylosauridae.

dispute.summary: Heishansaurus is a nomen dubium; its holotype is lost and the material was undiagnostic (Arbour and Currie, 2015). It is retained at Ankylosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Ankylosauria incertae sedis, nomen dubium with lost holotype.

diagnostic_features: Skull roof of enormous thickness exceeding 8 cm, with well-developed parieto-squamosal shelf at a level considerably lower than the highest point of the skull roof and extraordinarily narrow upper temporal vacuities

Teeth with a small apical denticle, four or five equal-sized lateral denticles, a cingulum surrounding the crown base (thicker on inner side of upper teeth), and roots bearing an annular swelling near the tip with marked longitudinal ridges below the crown

Well-developed dermal armor including flat circular/tetragonal plates (up to ~1 dm diameter), innumerable very small bony nodules, true dermal spines with small basal surfaces, and a uniquely boat-like elongate keeled plate deeply concave on the internal side

Vertebral centra more or less amphicoelous; dorsal centra with a pronounced keel below and marked antler-burr-like exostoses anteriorly and posteriorly; anterior caudal vertebrae with very long transverse processes
Skull surface bones strongly rugose on all external surfaces; skull base very broad and thick with basioccipital and basisphenoid apparently completely fused

Helioceratops.etymology: From Greek helios (sun), keras (horn), and ops (face); meaning 'sun horned face', referencing the animal's Eastern (sunrise) origin and its relationship to other ceratopsians
Helioceratops.description: Helioceratops is a genus of herbivorous neoceratopsian dinosaur from the Middle Cretaceous of China.

dispute.summary: Helioceratops brachygnathus is persistently unstable in neoceratopsian phylogenies, a consequence of its fragmentary material. Jin et al. (2009), describing the genus, treated it as a non-coronosaurian neoceratopsian alongside Auroraceratops and Yamaceratops, mapping characters onto an existing cladogram rather than running an analysis. Morschhauser et al. (2018) recovered it within Leptoceratopsidae as sister to all other members, a composition adopted in the formal definition of that clade by Madzia et al. (2021). Other analyses leave it unresolved: Arbour and Evans (2019) place it in a polytomy outside Coronosauria in their strict consensus, though it is the leptoceratopsid outgroup in 63% of individual trees; Ryan et al. (2023) and Tanaka et al. (2024) both leave it unresolved among the leptoceratopsids and their relatives; and Son et al. (2022) treat it as an unstable wildcard whose removal resolves the basal neoceratopsian polytomy.

history.note: Placed at Neoceratopsia (basal) following the prevailing view (Jones, 2026); leptoceratopsid alternative reflected.
Retained at Neoceratopsia (basal) following Jin et al. (2009); the leptoceratopsid placement of Morschhauser et al. (2018) is recorded as the competing hypothesis.

Flagged incertae sedis within Neoceratopsia. Only Morschhauser et al. (2018) resolve the genus; Arbour and Evans (2019), Ryan et al. (2023) and Tanaka et al. (2024) leave it unresolved and Son et al. (2022) treat it as a wildcard, so it cannot be assigned to a subclade.

diagnostic_features: Dentary ramus deep with length/height ratio of 1.6
Ventral predentary facet more vertical than other basal neoceratopsians, forming ~130° angle with ventral dentary border
Denticles and secondary ridges asymmetrically distributed on dentary teeth: 9-10 on mesial side, 4-5 on distal side of primary ridge

Heptasteornis.etymology: From Greek 'hepta' meaning 'seven', 'asty' meaning 'city', and 'ornis' meaning 'bird', referencing the Latin 'septum urbium' / German 'Siebenbürgen' ('seven cities/castles') - historical names for the Transylvanian region.
Heptasteornis.description: Heptasteornis is a dubious genus of alvarezsaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous. The type (and only known) species is Heptasteornis andrewsi, described as a presumed gigantic prehistoric owl in 1975. It was previously included in Elopteryx nopcsai and indeed the holotypes of both species were believed to be from the same individual as they were discovered, and initially were assigned the same specimen number. This appears to be in error however.

Herrerasaurus.etymology: Named for Victorino Herrera, the Argentine rancher who discovered the first specimen in 1958, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', meaning 'Herrera's lizard'.
Herrerasaurus.description: Herrerasaurus is likely a genus of saurischian dinosaur from the Late Triassic period. Measuring 6 m (20 ft) long and weighing around 350 kg (770 lb), this genus was one of the earliest dinosaurs from the fossil record. Its name means "Herrera's lizard", after the rancher who discovered the first specimen in 1958 in South America. All known fossils of this carnivore have been discovered in the Ischigualasto Formation of Carnian age (late Triassic according to the ICS, dated to 231.4 million years ago) in northwestern Argentina. The type species, Herrerasaurus ischigualastensis, was described by Osvaldo Reig in 1963 and is the only species assigned to the genus. Ischisaurus and Frenguellisaurus are synonyms.
diagnostic_features: Robust, high premaxilla with three teeth; tall maxilla with eight teeth
Dentary with twelve teeth; mandibular symphysis strong and taller than alveolar ramus
Sacrum with three vertebrae
Short, tall ilium with very robust anterior spine; pubis nearly perpendicular to vertebral axis with expanded distal 'foot' similar to Antrodemus
Gracile femur slightly curved in S-form with clear greater trochanter and distinct aliform fourth trochanter in upper 2/5 of bone
Robust tibia shorter than femur (tibia/femur index: 87); wide astragalus without ascending process; very small calcaneum
Central metatarsals more elongate than typical for size (3rd Mt./femur index: 45)

Hesperonychus.etymology: From Greek 'hesperos' meaning 'western' and 'onychos' meaning 'claw'. The type species, H. elizabethae, was named in honor of Dr. Elizabeth Nicholls of the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology.
Hesperonychus.description: Hesperonychus is a genus of small dromaeosaurid dinosaur. There is one described species, Hesperonychus elizabethae. The type species was named in honor of Dr. Elizabeth Nicholls of the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology who collected it as a student in 1982. It is known from fossils recovered from the Dinosaur Park Formation and possibly from the uppermost strata of the Oldman Formation of Alberta, dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous around 75 million years ago.

Heterodontosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'heteros' meaning 'different', 'odont' meaning 'tooth', and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', in reference to its unusual heterodont dentition. The species name honors George C. Tuck, who supported the expedition.
Heterodontosaurus.description: Heterodontosaurus is a genus of heterodontosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Early Jurassic, 200-190 million years ago. Its only known member species, Heterodontosaurus tucki, was named in 1962 based on a skull discovered in South Africa. The genus name means "different toothed lizard", in reference to its unusual, heterodont dentition; the specific name honors G. C. Tuck, who supported the discoverers. Further specimens have since been found, including an almost complete skeleton in 1966.

First mandibular tooth large and caniniform, projecting upward into diastema
Mandibular teeth closely-set with vertical ridges, enamel on inner surface only
Predentary present without teeth, separated from dentary by distinct suture

notable_specimens.significance: The most complete heterodontosaurid skeleton described to date. Found at the Voyizane locality, it preserves skull and skeleton in articulation with little displacement, and as an adult underpins the full description of the genus's anatomy.

A very complete specimen found near Grahamstown. Its rock was too hard to remove, so it was synchrotron-scanned in 2016; the data on its pelvis and gastralia underpinned a 2021 reinterpretation of ornithischian breathing, with Heterodontosaurus as an intermediate stage.

The front part of a juvenile skull, the key ontogenetic specimen for the genus, showing that the eye sockets became proportionally smaller and the snout longer with age. CT scans revealed unerupted replacement teeth even at this early stage, informing the tooth-replacement debate.

A left maxilla from the Voyizane locality. Its upper jaw was the first specimen in which unerupted replacement teeth were discovered in Heterodontosaurus, a find later corroborated by the juvenile skull AMNH 24000.

Heyuannia.etymology: From Heyuan; named after Heyuan city in Guangdong Province, China, where the type specimen was found
Heyuannia.description: Heyuannia is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous epoch, in what is now China and Mongolia. It was the first oviraptorid found in China; most others were found in neighboring Mongolia. Two species are known: H. huangi, named by Lü Junchang in 2002 from the Dalangshan Formation; and H. yanshini, originally named as a separate genus Ingenia from the Barun Goyot Formation by Rinchen Barsbold in 1981, and later renamed to Ajancingenia in 2013 due to the preoccupation of Ingenia. The latter name was eventually discarded due to various ethical issues surrounding the author.

Hierosaurus.description: Hierosaurus is an extinct genus of nodosaurid ankylosaur which lived during the Late Cretaceous 87 to 82 million years ago. Its fossils were found in the Smoky Hill Chalk Member of the Niobrara Formation, in western Kansas, which would have been near the middle of the Western Interior Sea during the Late Cretaceous. It was a nodosaurid, an ankylosaur without a clubbed tail.

Homalocephale.etymology: From Greek homalos (even, flat) and kephale (head); meaning 'even head' or 'flat-headed', referring to its flat skull roof unlike other pachycephalosaurs
Homalocephale.description: Homalocephale is a genus of pachycephalosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of what is now the Nemegt Formation, Mongolia. The genus was described in 1974 by Halszka Osmólska and Teresa Maryańska, and consists of a single species, H. calathocercos. Though Homalocephale has been regarded as a synonym (and juvenile form) of Prenocephale, juvenile specimens of the latter indicate that they were distinct. Homalocephale was 1.8 m (5.9 ft) long and possibly an omnivore.

dispute.summary: Homalocephale has been proposed to be a juvenile or female of Prenocephale (Longrich et al., 2010), but Evans et al. (2018) showed that juvenile Prenocephale retain a parietosquamosal ornamentation pattern distinct from Homalocephale, supporting its validity. Its exact position within Pachycephalosaurinae is unstable.

history.note: Placed at Pachycephalosaurinae, recovered closer to Pachycephalosaurus than to Stegoceras; ontogenetic synonymy with Prenocephale raised and rejected.

Huabeisaurus.etymology: Named for North China (Huabei, meaning 'north China' in Chinese) combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'North China lizard'.
Huabeisaurus.description: Huabeisaurus was a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian to Maastrichtian stages, around 99.7-70.6 million years ago) of what is present-day northern China. The type species, Huabeisaurus allocotus, was first described by Pang Qiqing and Cheng Zhengwu in 2000. It is known from numerous remains found in the 1990s, which include teeth, partial limbs and vertebrae. Due to its relative completeness, Huabeisaurus represents a significant taxon for understanding sauropod evolution in Asia. Huabeisaurus comes from Kangdailiang and Houyu, Zhaojiagou Town, Tianzhen County, Shanxi province, China. The holotype was found in the unnamed upper member of the Huiquanpu Formation, which is Late Cretaceous (?Cenomanian-?Campanian) in age based on ostracods, charophytes, and fission-track dating.

Dorsal vertebrae opisthocoelous with deep, regularly oval-shaped pleurocoels; neural spines high and unbifurcated
Caudal vertebrae clearly amphicoelous; neural arches situated on anterior part of centrum; spines unbifurcated; chevrons Y-shaped and unbifurcated distally
Ilium very large and long fan-shaped with pubic peduncle situated slightly anterior of middle of ilium lower edge and ischic peduncle undeveloped
Femur straight, long, narrow, and flat with oblate femur head; fourth trochanter dilated on posterior inner lateral edge slightly above shaft midpoint; humerus-to-femur length ratio 0.78 to 1

dispute.summary: Huadanosaurus was described by Qiu et al. (2025), who recovered it among the Jehol compsognathid-grade theropods that they grouped as Sinosauropterygidae, alongside Sinosauropteryx and Sinocalliopteryx. Its tyrannosauroid-like cranial features were interpreted as convergence rather than phylogenetic signal. It is placed in Compsognathidae in the family's traditional, broadly used sense; the Sinosauropterygidae hypothesis is reflected in the Compsognathidae clade dispute.

Huadanosaurus.etymology: From Chinese 'huadan' (the birthday of a great person or institution), commemorating several Chinese scientific anniversaries, and Greek 'sauros' (lizard).
Huadanosaurus.description: Huadanosaurus is an extinct genus of compsognathid-like coelurosaur from the Lower Cretaceous (Barremian) Dawangzhangzi bed of the Yixian Formation, Liaoning Province, China. The single species, Huadanosaurus sinensis, is known from an almost complete juvenile skeleton (IVPP V 14202) recovered from lacustrine deposits of the Jehol Biota; specimens of this species had previously been assigned to Sinosauropteryx prima before Qiu et al. (2025) erected the new genus. The holotype preserves stomach contents consisting of a eutriconodont mammal and a eutherian mammal, indicating active predation on small mammals.

(2019) recovered it just outside a reduced Compsognathidae. Cau and Paterna (2025) proposed that the proceratosaurid Sinotyrannus is a mature individual of Huaxiagnathus, which would make it a junior synonym and imply a tyrannosauroid-grade affinity; Jones et al. (2026) reject this, treating Sinotyrannus as a valid proceratosaurid. It is retained in Compsognathidae pending resolution of the synonymy.

Huayangosaurus.etymology: From Huayang (華陽), an alternate historical name for Sichuan Province, China, combined with Greek sauros (lizard); meaning 'Huayang lizard'
Huayangosaurus.description: Huayangosaurus is a genus of stegosaurian dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic of China. The name derives from "Huayang" (華陽), an alternate name for Sichuan (the province where it was discovered), and "saurus", meaning "lizard". It lived during the Bathonian to Callovian stages, around 165 million years ago, some 20 million years before its famous relative, Stegosaurus appeared in North America. At only approximately 4 meters (13 ft) long, it was also much smaller than its famous cousin. Found in the Lower Shaximiao Formation, Huayangosaurus shared the local Middle Jurassic landscape with the sauropods Shunosaurus, Datousaurus, Omeisaurus and Protognathosaurus, the ornithopod Xiaosaurus and the carnivorous Gasosaurus.

dispute.summary: Huayangosaurus is the basal-most well-known stegosaur and the type genus of the traditional family Huayangosauridae. That family is of disputed utility, as its only consistent additional member (Chungkingosaurus) is recovered variously within or outside it and recent works deprecate the node, so Huayangosaurus is retained at Stegosauria incertae sedis rather than placed in a near-monotypic family.

history.note: Placed at Stegosauria incertae sedis, Huayangosauridae not retained as a node (unstable membership, deprecated by recent works).

Hudiesaurus.etymology: Butterfly lizard; from Chinese hudie (butterfly) and Greek sauros (lizard)
Hudiesaurus.description: Hudiesaurus is an extinct genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day China during the Late Jurassic period. It was described by Chinese paleontologist Dong Zhiming in 1997. The genus contains a single species, Hudiesaurus sinojapanorum, named based on a single vertebra. However, he also assigned teeth and limb bones from a nearby locality to H. sinojapanorum. These fossils were unearthed by the Sino-Japanese Silk Road Expedition near Qiketai in Shanshan, Xinjiang province in rock layers coming from the Kalaza Formation. This formation dates to between the Late Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic, 154 to 143 million years ago. Dong believed that the vertebra was a dorsal (trunk) vertebra, but later analysis suggested that it is one of the last cervical (neck) vertebrae. In 2021, the limb bones were assigned to a distinct genus of sauropod, Rhomaleopakhus, and the teeth were classified as an indeterminate eusauropod.

Approximately transverse row of five to six small coels on the dorsal surface of the prezygapophyseal process, immediately posterior to the articular facet.

Spinoprezygapophyseal laminae (SPRLs) bifurcating near the base of the metapophysis — one branch ascending the anterior surface and fading before the summit, the other forming a thin sheet along the anterolateral margin to the summit.
Spinopostzygapophyseal lamina (SPOL) bifurcating into two distinct ridges immediately above the postzygapophysis.

Hypselosaurus.etymology: From Greek hypsilos (high, lofty) and sauros (lizard); meaning 'highest lizard'
Hypselosaurus.description: Hypselosaurus is a dubious genus of titanosaurian sauropod that lived in southern France during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 million years ago in the early Maastrichtian. Hypselosaurus was first described in 1846, but was not formally named until 1869, when Phillip Matheron named it under the binomial Hypselosaurus priscus. The holotype specimen includes a partial hindlimb and a pair of caudal vertebrae, and two eggshell fragments were found alongside these bones. Because of the proximity of these eggshells to the fossil remains, many later authors, including Matheron and Paul Gervais, have assigned several eggs from the same region of France all to Hypselosaurus, although the variation and differences between these eggs suggest that they do not all belong to the same taxon. Hypselosaurus has been found in the same formation as the dromaeosaurids Variraptor and Pyroraptor, the ornithopod Rhabdodon, and the ankylosaurian Rhodanosaurus, as well as indeterminate bones from other groups.

dispute.summary: Hypselosaurus priscus is based on non-diagnostic titanosaur material from the Late Cretaceous of Provence and is listed among sauropod nomina dubia (Weishampel and others, 2004); its holotype cannot be reliably distinguished from other sauropods, and eggs long referred to it likely pertain to more than one taxon.

Hypsibema.etymology: From Greek hypsi (high) and bema (step); meaning 'high step', because Edward Cope believed the animal walked particularly erect on its toes
Hypsibema.description: Hypsibema is a dubious genus of very large dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of eastern North America, of uncertain affinities. The type species, H. crassicauda, is known mainly from the Tar Heel Formation of North Carolina and the Marshalltown Formation of New Jersey, and its fragmentary material has been interpreted as sauropod as well as hadrosaurian. A second species, H. missouriensis from the Maastrichtian of Missouri, was originally named Neosaurus and then Parrosaurus before being referred to Hypsibema by Baird and Horner (1979); a proposed return of that species to Parrosaurus has not gained broad acceptance.

Iberospinus.etymology: Iberian spine; from Iberia (the Iberian Peninsula, where it was found in Portugal) and Latin spina (spine), referring to its spinosaurid neural spines
Iberospinus.description: Iberospinus is an extinct genus of spinosaurid dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) Papo Seco Formation of Portugal. The genus contains a single species, I. natarioi, known from several assorted bones belonging to one individual. Iberospinus represents one of five known spinosaurid taxa from the Iberian Peninsula, the others being Camarillasaurus, Protathlitis, Riojavenatrix, and Vallibonavenatrix. It is important for its implications of the geographical origin of Spinosauridae and the suggested presence of potentially semi-aquatic lifestyle earlier in the evolution of this clade.

Ichthyovenator.etymology: From Greek ichthys (fish) and Latin venator (hunter); meaning 'fish hunter', referring to its inferred piscivorous lifestyle
Ichthyovenator.description: Ichthyovenator is a genus of spinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now Laos, sometime between 120 and 113 million years ago, during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous period. It is known from fossils collected from the Grès supérieurs Formation of the Savannakhet Basin, the first of which were found in 2010, consisting of a partial skeleton without the skull or limbs. This specimen became the holotype of the new genus and species Ichthyovenator laosensis, and was described by paleontologist Ronan Allain and colleagues in 2012. The generic name, meaning "fish hunter", refers to its assumed piscivorous lifestyle, while the specific name alludes to the country of Laos. In 2014, it was announced that more remains from the dig site had been recovered; these fossils included teeth, more vertebrae (backbones) and a pubic bone from the same individual.

Iguanodon.etymology: From the modern lizard 'Iguana' and Greek 'odous/odontos' (tooth); meaning 'iguana tooth', referring to Mantell's original recognition that the fossil teeth resembled those of living iguanas at much larger scale.
Iguanodon.description: Iguanodon is one of the original three genera that Owen used to found Dinosauria in 1842 (alongside Megalosaurus and Hylaeosaurus) and is among the earliest dinosaurs ever scientifically described. Gideon Mantell erected the genus in 1825 on isolated teeth from the Tilgate Forest beds of Whiteman's Green, near Cuckfield in Sussex, recognizing their similarity to the teeth of living iguanas at vastly greater scale; he originally designated I. anglicus as the type species. The discovery in 1878 of more than thirty articulated skeletons in a coal mine at Bernissart in Belgium produced the first reliable picture of the animal's anatomy and underpinned Louis Dollo's classic restorations. Because Mantell's anglicus syntype teeth proved too fragmentary to anchor the genus, ICZN Opinion 1947 (2000) set aside all prior type-species fixations under plenary power, designating Iguanodon bernissartensis Boulenger in Beneden, 1881 as the new type species and skeleton Q (RBINS 1534) as its lectotype. Subsequent taxonomic revisions by Paul (2008) and Norman (2010) split many of the species historically referred to Iguanodon into separate genera — including Mantellisaurus (atherfieldensis), Barilium (dawsoni), Hypselospinus (fittoni, hollingtoniensis), and Dakotadon (lakotaensis) — leaving I. bernissartensis as essentially the only currently valid species and the genus as a Barremian-Aptian ankylopollexian of Western Europe.
diagnostic_features: Skull bearing 29 maxillary and 25 dentary tooth positions with an accessory palpebral bone above the orbit.

Manus massive with a large conical thumb (digit I) ungual modified into a defensive 'thumb spike'; phalanx 1 of digit I retained.
Sacrum of eight fused vertebrae with mediolaterally compressed dorsal centra.
Prepubic process shallow with a long posterior acetabular body of the pubis.
Adult body size on the order of 8-10 m and 3-4 metric tons, larger than most contemporaneous Wealden iguanodontians.

dispute.summary: Imperobator antarcticus is known from a fragmentary pes and cannot be confidently referred to any of the major paravian subclades. It is placed conservatively at Paraves incertae sedis.

Imperobator.etymology: From Latin 'imperobator' meaning 'powerful warrior'. The species name refers to Antarctica, the continent where it was found.
Imperobator.description: Imperobator is a genus of probable unenlagiid paravian theropod dinosaurs, that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in what is now James Ross Island in Antarctica. Imperobator is one of only two non-avian theropods known from Antarctica, crossing over to the landmass when it was part of Gondwana. The only described specimen was found in 2003 by an expedition launched by the University of California Museum of Paleontology and initially described as a dromaeosaur in 2007. The fossil was formally described as a new genus in 2019, and later searches reported more fossils from the site including teeth and skull bones.

Incisivosaurus.etymology: Named for its unusually large incisiform front teeth combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'incisor lizard'.
Incisivosaurus.description: Incisivosaurus is a genus of small, probably herbivorous theropod dinosaurs from the early Cretaceous Period of what is now the People's Republic of China. The first specimen to be described (by Xu et al. in 2002), IVPP V13326, is a skull that was collected from the lowermost levels (the fluvial Lujiatun beds) of the Yixian Formation (dating to the Barremian stage about 126 million years ago) in the Sihetun area, near Beipiao City, in western Liaoning Province. The most significant, and highly unusual, characteristic of this dinosaur is its apparent adaptation to an herbivorous or omnivorous lifestyle. It was named for its prominent, rodent-like front teeth, which show wear patterns commonly found in plant-eating dinosaurs. The specific name gauthieri honors Dr. Jacques Gauthier, a pioneer of the phylogenetic method of classification.

Ingentia.etymology: From Latin 'ingentia' meaning 'enormous' or 'gigantic', in reference to the animal's large size for its age in the fossil record.
Ingentia.description: Ingentia is a genus of early sauropodiform dinosaur, sometimes considered a basal sauropod, from the Late Triassic (late Norian-Rhaetian) of Argentina. The type specimen of Ingentia, PVSJ 1086, was discovered in the Quebrada del Barro Formation of northwestern Argentina. It was described in 2018 by Cecilia Apaldetti, Ricardo Nestor Martínez, Ignacio Alejandro Cerda, Diego Pol and Oscar Alcober who named the type and only species Ingentia prima, meaning "first huge one", as the taxon was one of the first very large sauropodomorphs to evolve, along with its close relative Lessemsaurus. A second specimen, PVSJ 1087, was referred, containing five tail vertebrae, both ulnae and radii, a left calfbone and a right foot.

Invictarx.description: Invictarx is a monospecific genus of nodosaurid dinosaur from New Mexico that lived during the Late Cretaceous (lower Campanian, 78.5 Ma) in what is now the upper Allison Member of the Menefee Formation. Irritator.etymology: From English/Latin irritation; named to reflect the frustration of paleontologists who discovered the skull had been heavily damaged and altered by fossil dealers
Irritator.description: Irritator is a genus of spinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now Brazil during the latest Aptian to early Albian of the Early Cretaceous Period, around 113 million years ago. It is known from a nearly complete skull found in the Romualdo Formation of the Araripe Basin. Fossil dealers had acquired this skull and sold it to the State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart. In 1996, the specimen became the holotype of the type species Irritator challengeri. The genus name comes from the word "irritation", reflecting the feelings of paleontologists who found the skull had been heavily damaged and altered by the collectors. The species name is a homage to the fictional character Professor Challenger from Arthur Conan Doyle's novels.

Dorsal surface of the parietals facing posterodorsally, with the vertical axis of the braincase inclined anteroventrally.
Posterior surface of the basisphenoid with a deep, dorsoventrally oval median recess.
Surangular with a broad lateral shelf.

Isaberrysaura.etymology: Named for Isabel Valdueza Berry, who reported the fossil site, combined with Greek 'saura' meaning 'lizard'.
Isaberrysaura.description: Isaberrysaura is an extinct genus of stegosaurian ornithischian dinosaurs from the Middle Jurassic Los Molles Formation of Patagonia, Argentina. The genus contains a single species, I. mollensis, described by Salgado in 2017 based on a single specimen. Although initially classified as a basal neornithischian, subsequent analyses have allied it with the Stegosauria as the morphology of its skull resembles those of other members of the group.

dispute.summary: The affinities of Isaberrysaura are contested. The describing authors (Salgado et al., 2017) recovered it as a basal neornithischian outside Thyreophora, whereas subsequent analyses (Han et al., 2018; Raven and Maidment, 2018; Sánchez-Fenollosa and Cobos, 2025) recover it as a basal stegosaur. Its membership in Stegosauria is not yet settled.

history.note: Placed at Stegosauria incertae sedis, recovered as a basal stegosaur by recent analyses but originally described as a basal neornithischian.

dispute.summary: Isanosaurus is placed as a basal, non-eusauropodan sauropod, but its position at the sauropod/sauropodiform boundary is unsettled. Pol and Gomez (2022) recover it within Sauropoda but outside Eusauropoda (grouped with Gongxianosaurus and vulcanodontids), and Jones (2026) likewise treats it as a basal sauropod, whereas Rauhut et al. (2020) recover it as a non-sauropodan sauropodiform lying immediately outside Sauropoda under the node-based definition (Vulcanodon plus Saltasaurus).

history.note: Placed at Sauropoda incertae sedis following the prevailing view (Pol and Gomez, 2022; Jones, 2026); the non-sauropod sauropodiform alternative (Rauhut et al., 2020) is unresolved.

Isanosaurus.etymology: Named for Isan, the northeastern region of Thailand, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'. The species name honors P. Attavipach, a supporter of paleontological research in Thailand.
Isanosaurus.description: Isanosaurus is an extinct genus of sauropod dinosaur from Thailand. It was originally dated to approximately 219-199 million years ago during the Late Triassic (late Norian to Rhaetian stages), which would make it one of the oldest known sauropods. Its age was later considered uncertain, and may be Early Jurassic or even as young as Late Jurassic. The only species is Isanosaurus attavipachi. Though important for the understanding of sauropod origin and early evolution, Isanosaurus is poorly known. Exact relationships to other early sauropods remain unresolved.

Opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae with parapophyses at mid-height
Strong ventral median ridge on cervical centra
Dorsal neural arch remarkably tall with spine longer rostrocaudally than transversely
Scapula with moderate dorsally rounded proximal expansion and slight distal expansion

Issi.etymology: From Kalaallisut (Greenlandic) meaning 'cold', in reference to it being the most northerly basal sauropodomorph ever discovered. The species name 'saaneq' means 'bone' in Kalaallisut.
Issi.description: Issi is a plateosaurid dinosaur from the Late Triassic Fleming Fjord Formation of Greenland. It contains one species, Issi saaneq; the full binomial name means "cold bone". Fossils of Issi were previously assigned to the species Plateosaurus trossingensis, but new finds allowed for a reassessment of that material that showed that it possessed features thought to be exclusive to Brazilian sauropodomorphs such as Unaysaurus and Macrocollum. This ultimately led to the designation of Issi as a distinct genus in 2021. This taxon is the first non-avian dinosaur described from Greenland.

Istiorachis.etymology: From Greek histion (sail) and rhachis (spine); meaning "sail spine", referring to the notably elongated vertebral neural spines
Istiorachis.description: Istiorachis is an extinct genus of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian age) Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, England. The genus contains a single species, Istiorachis macarthurae, known from a partial postcranial skeleton including several vertebrae, incomplete ribs, and part of the pelvis. Its vertebral neural spines are notably elongated, giving the animal a 'sail-backed' appearance.

More recent analyses instead recover it in a more stemward position, outside Khebbashia, in a clade with the South American rebbachisaurids Sidersaura and Astigmasaura (Lerzo et al., 2024; Bellardini et al., 2025).

Itapeuasaurus.etymology: Named for Itapeua, the beach locality in Maranhão, Brazil where the fossils were discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'Itapeua lizard'.
Itapeuasaurus.description: Itapeuasaurus is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Alcântara Formation (Itapecuru Group) of Maranhão in Brazil. The type and only species is Itapeuasaurus cajapioensis. It is the most complete Cenomanian-aged diplodocoid known from South America and it is also the first reported Cenomanian-aged rebbachisaurid discovered in South America.

Iuticosaurus.etymology: Named after the Jutes (Iuti in Latin), the Germanic people associated with the Isle of Wight; meaning "Jute lizard"
Iuticosaurus.description: Iuticosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of the Isle of Wight, England. The type and only valid species, Iuticosaurus valdensis, was erected by Le Loeuff (1993) for caudal vertebrae from the Wealden that Huene (1929) had originally named "Titanosaurus" valdensis. It was long regarded as the oldest titanosaur known from Europe.

Jakapil.etymology: From 'Ja-Kapïl', a Puelchean word meaning 'shield bearer', in reference to its thyreophoran armor. The species name 'kaniukura' means 'crest stone' in Mapudungun.

dispute.summary: Jakapil is a Late Cretaceous Patagonian thyreophoran. Its describers recovered it as a basal thyreophoran closely related to Scelidosaurus (Riguetti and others, 2022), and Jones (2026) follows this. Alternative matrices place it as a stem-eurypodan or basal ankylosaur, and Raven and others (2023) suggested marginocephalian affinities; the describers explicitly rejected a parankylosaur relationship.

Jeholornis.etymology: From the Jehol Group (the Lower Cretaceous geological unit of western Liaoning, named after the historical region of Jehol/Rehe) plus Greek 'ornis' (bird); meaning 'Jehol bird'.
Jeholornis.description: Jeholornis is a genus of avialan dinosaurs that lived between approximately 122 and 120 million years ago during the early Cretaceous Period in China. Fossil Jeholornis were first discovered in the Jiufotang Formation in Hebei Province, China (in what was previously Rehe Province, also known as Jehol — hence the name) and additional specimens have been found in the older Yixian Formation.

dispute.summary: The synonymy with Shenzhouraptor Ji et al., 2002 is actively contested. Most workers (Ji et al. 2003; Zhou and Zhang 2006, 2007; Li et al. 2010; Lefèvre et al. 2014) accept the synonymy: Shenzhouraptor sinensis and Jeholornis prima are treated as the same species, with Jeholornis having ICZN priority because Nature carries a specific publication date (25 July 2002) while the Geological Bulletin of China is a monthly journal without a specific issue date. Wang et al. (2020) dissented, identifying multiple distinguishing characters and recovering Shenzhouraptor sinensis phylogenetically outside Jeholornis sensu stricto. The intake follows the majority position (Jeholornis senior, Shenzhouraptor junior synonym) while flagging the dispute.

diagnostic_features: Lachrymal T-shaped with two vertical, elongated pneumatic fossae.
Mandibles robust with well-ossified (fused) symphysis.
First phalanx of third manual digit approximately twice the length of the second phalanx, forming a bow-shaped structure together.
Tail with at least twenty elongated caudal vertebrae behind the transition point, bearing distinctively elongated prezygapophyses and chevrons.
Lateral trabecula of the sternum bearing a rounded fenestra at its distal end.
Forelimb-to-hindlimb ratio (humerus + ulna + carpometacarpus over femur + tibiotarsus + tarsometatarsus) approximately 1.2.

synonyms.name: Shenzhouraptor
synonyms.reason: Ji et al. (2002) erected Shenzhouraptor sinensis for LPM 0193 in the same Jiufotang Formation, only days before (and in a less precisely dated journal than) Zhou and Zhang's Jeholornis prima Nature paper. Ji et al. 2003, Zhou and Zhang (2006, 2007), Li et al. (2010), and Lefèvre et al. (2014) treat Shenzhouraptor sinensis as a junior subjective synonym of Jeholornis prima with Jeholornis given priority on ICZN grounds (specific Nature publication date over monthly Geological Bulletin of China). Wang et al. (2020) dissent (see dispute field).

Jian.etymology: From Chinese 'jiān' (鹣), a mythical one-winged bird; alluding to the bird-like, probably volant nature of this microraptorine.
Jian.description: Jian changmaensis is an extinct species of microraptorine theropod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian age) Xiagou Formation of China. J. changmaensis is the only species in the genus Jian, known from a pectoral girdle and partial forelimb. After the discovery of more than 100 bird fossils in the formation, this specimen is the first non-avian dinosaur to be described from it.
diagnostic_features: Coracoid proportionally longer relative to humerus than in any other microraptorine (~36% of humerus length).
Humeral distal condyles developed primarily on the cranial surface of the bone rather than the craniodistal surface.
Well-developed foramen on the ventral (proximoventral) aspect of the proximal radius, not described in other dromaeosaurids.

Jianchangosaurus.etymology: Named after Jianchang County, Liaoning Province, China, where the type specimen was discovered; meaning "lizard from Jianchang County"
Jianchangosaurus.description: Jianchangosaurus is a genus of therizinosaurian dinosaur that lived approximately 126 million years ago during the early part of the Cretaceous Period from the Yixian Formation in what is now China. The type specimen, a juvenile, was discovered in Jianchang County, in the western part of Liaoning Province. It was described in 2013 by a team of paleontologists from the Henan Museum, who determined that it was among the most basal therizinosaurs.

dispute.summary: Jianchangosaurus is consistently recovered as one of the most basal therizinosaurs (Pu et al., 2013; Hartman et al., 2019), and that placement is not in question. Its validity, however, is contested: Cau (2024) argued that the genus is a junior synonym of Beipiaosaurus, treating its holotype as an immature individual, but this synonymy rests on a single analysis and has not been adopted by subsequent workers or reference works (e.g. Jones, 2026), which continue to treat Jianchangosaurus as a valid, distinct genus.

history.note: Retained as a valid basal therizinosaurian within Therizinosauria; the synonymy with Beipiaosaurus proposed by Cau (2024) is noted but not adopted pending broader corroboration.

Jiangshanosaurus.etymology: Named for Jiangshan County in Zhejiang Province, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Jiangshanosaurus.description: Jiangshanosaurus is a genus of herbivorous titanosauriform sauropod dinosaur that lived in China approximately 92-88 million years ago, during the Turonian and Coniacian stages of the Late Cretaceous.

Jianianhualong.etymology: Named after Jianianhua (the company that funded the research) combined with Chinese long (dragon); meaning "Jianianhua dragon"
Jianianhualong.description: Jianianhualong is a genus of troodontid theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of China. It contains a single species, Jianianhualong tengi, named in 2017 by Xu Xing and colleagues based on an articulated skeleton preserving feathers. The feathers at the middle of the tail of Jianianhualong are asymmetric, being the first record of asymmetrical feathers among the troodontids. Despite aerodynamic differences from the flight feathers of modern birds, the feathers in the tail vane of Jianianhualong could have functioned in drag reduction while the animal was moving. The discovery of Jianianhualong supports the notion that asymmetrical feathers appeared early in the evolutionary history of the Paraves.
diagnostic_features: Maxillary rostral ramus triangular in outline and relatively high dorsoventrally

Long manual phalanx II-1 with prominent proximoventral heel and large groove along medial surface
Highly elongated manual phalanx III-2 (slightly longer than metacarpal III)
Ilium with slightly concave dorsal margin in lateral view
Metatarsal IV without prominent ventral flange

Jinchuanloong.etymology: From 'Jinchuan' (the district of Jinchang City, Gansu Province, where the holotype was found) and Mandarin Chinese 'loong' (dragon).
Jinchuanloong.description: Jinchuanloong is an extinct genus of non-neosauropod eusauropod sauropod from the late Bathonian (Middle Jurassic) lower Xinhe Formation of Jinchuan District, Jinchang City, Gansu Province, north-western China. The single species, Jinchuanloong niedu, is known from a single subadult individual (estimated body length ~10 m) preserving a nearly complete skull with mandible articulated with the atlas-axis complex and the first five cervicals, plus 29 articulated middle and posterior caudal vertebrae. The phylogenetic analysis of Li et al. (2025) recovers Jinchuanloong outside Mamenchisauridae as the sister taxon to a Turiasauria + Neosauropoda clade.

Postorbital very robust in lateral view; ratio of anteroposterior length to dorsoventral height of the posterior process of the postorbital is 0.9.

Posteroventral process of the jugal contributes only 22% of the ventral margin of the infratemporal fenestra; dorsal process of the jugal contacts the lacrimal and makes a small contribution to the antorbital fenestra.

Jingiella.etymology: Named for the Jing region or Jingia locality in Guangxi, China (diminutive '-ella' suffix), originally named 'Jingia' before a nomenclatural amendment.
Jingiella.description: Jingiella is an extinct genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Dongxing Formation of Guangxi, China. The genus contains a single species, J. dongxingensis, known from vertebrae and limb bones. The original description of Jingiella referred to it using the name "Jingia" which was preoccupied by a moth genus named in 1983, and an amendment was published shortly thereafter, establishing Jingiella as the new replacement name.

Jintasaurus.description: Jintasaurus is a genus of hadrosauriform dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous of what is now Jiuquan, Gansu, northwestern China. dispute.summary: The affinities of Juravenator are uncertain because the holotype is an immature individual. It was described as a small basal coelurosaur close to Compsognathus, loosely within Compsognathidae (Chiappe and Göhlich, 2010), and Jones et al. (2026) place it there. However, Rauhut et al. (2012) and Foth et al. (2020) showed that its coelurosaurian characters may be juvenile artifacts, that it is drawn toward the base of Tetanurae as the sister taxon of the megalosauroid Sciurumimus when both juveniles are analyzed together, and that its supposed tail "scales" are better interpreted as adipocere. It is placed conservatively at Coelurosauria incertae sedis.

dispute.summary: The family-level placement of Kaatedocus is disputed. Tschopp and Mateus (2012) and Tschopp et al. (2015) recovered it as a diplodocine diplodocid, sister to Barosaurus, and the Princeton Encyclopedia (Jones, 2026) follows this view. Whitlock and Wilson Mantilla (2020) instead recovered it as the basalmost dicraeosaurid on cranial characters, a result reproduced when Kaatedocus was added to an independent matrix; under that hypothesis the diplodocid characters previously cited for it are reinterpreted as more general flagellicaudatan features.

history.note: Placed at Flagellicaudata, the least inclusive clade accepted by both hypotheses, pending resolution of its diplodocine (Tschopp et al., 2015) versus dicraeosaurid (Whitlock and Wilson Mantilla, 2020) placement.

The type and only species is Kaatedocus siberi, described in 2012 by Emanuel Tschopp and Octávio Mateus.

dispute.summary: The validity of Kaijiangosaurus lini is unresolved. It was described only in a 1984 book, on a holotype of seven cervical vertebrae (CCG 20020), and has never been the subject of a peer-reviewed redescription. Rauhut (2003) regarded it as a nomen dubium, whereas Carrano, Benson and Sampson (2012) treated it as a fragmentary taxon requiring restudy — noting that the referred material may not all belong to one taxon — and suggested a basal tetanuran or averostran placement without declaring it dubious. Paul (2024) suggested it may be a junior synonym of the contemporaneous Gasosaurus constructus. It is placed conservatively at Tetanurae incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Tetanurae incertae sedis; its validity relative to Gasosaurus is unresolved.

Kansaignathus.etymology: Named for the area near the town of Konsoy ('Kansai' in Russian) in Tajikistan where it was discovered, combined with Greek 'gnathos' meaning 'jaw'.
Kansaignathus.description: Kansaignathus is an extinct genus of dromaeosaurid theropod from the Late Cretaceous Yalovach Formation (or Ialovachsk Formation) of Tajikistan. The genus contains only one species, the type species, K. sogdianus. The generic name of Kansaignathus comes from near the town of Konsoy ("Kansai" in Russian) where it was discovered and the Greek word "gnathos" meaning "jaw". The specific epithet "sogdianus" is derived from the historical region of Sogdiana, which was an ancient name for the Fergana Valley region where the fossil was discovered. Kansaignathus is known from a single right dentary bone and a few post-cranial bone fragments. It was the first, and so far the only, dinosaur from Tajikistan to be described and named.

dispute.summary: Kayentavenator elysiae, based on an immature partial skeleton, was described as a basal tetanuran closer to Allosaurus than to coelophysoids (Gay, 2010), but subsequent work treats the holotype as a specimen of the coelophysoid "Syntarsus" (Megapnosaurus) kayentakatae, making Kayentavenator a possible junior synonym (Ezcurra, 2012, 2017). Because the tetanuran and coelophysoid hypotheses span Neotheropoda, it is placed conservatively at Neotheropoda incertae sedis.

Kentrosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'kentron' (prickle or spike) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'prickle lizard', referring to its prominent spikes
Kentrosaurus.description: Kentrosaurus is a genus of stegosaurid dinosaur from the Late Jurassic in Lindi Region of Tanzania. The type species is K. aethiopicus, named and described by German paleontologist Edwin Hennig in 1915. Often thought to be a "primitive" member of the Stegosauria, several recent cladistic analyses find it as more derived than many other stegosaurs, and a close relative of Stegosaurus from the North American Morrison Formation within the Stegosauridae.

dispute.summary: Kentrosaurus is securely a stegosaurid, but its subfamily placement is contested, having been recovered in Stegosaurinae (Maidment et al., 2008), as a stemward stegosaurid (Jones and Viola, 2026), and in Dacentrurinae (Sánchez-Fenollosa and Cobos, 2025). It is placed at Stegosauridae without a subfamily.

history.note: Placed at Stegosauridae, subfamily (Dacentrurinae vs Stegosaurinae) contested.

Khankhuuluu.etymology: From Mongolian 'khan' (prince or lord) and 'khuuluu' (dragon); meaning 'dragon prince'
Khankhuuluu.description: Khankhuuluu is an extinct genus of early tyrannosauroid theropod dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of what is now the Gobi Desert in Mongolia. The genus contains a single species, Khankhuuluu mongoliensis, known from several skull bones and two partial skeletons, including shoulder, pelvic, and hindlimb bones, and several vertebrae from the back and tail. The remains were discovered in 1972 and 1973 and first described in 1977 as belonging to the Chinese Alectrosaurus. Later researchers recognized the uniqueness of the bones, and they were eventually named as belonging to a new species in 2025. Khankhuuluu is a medium-sized tyrannosauroid with a shallow skull and long, slender legs. Its skeleton demonstrates a unique combination of anatomical traits seen in both earlier-diverging (basal) tyrannosauroids and the later-diverging (derived) tyrannosaurids.

Kholumolumo.etymology: From the Basuto (Sesotho) name for a type of dragon-like creature that the local Basuto people associated with dinosaur fossils.
Kholumolumo.description: Kholumolumo , formerly "Kholumolumosaurus" or "Thotobolosaurus", is an extinct genus of massopodan sauropodomorph dinosaur, which was closely related to Sarahsaurus, from the lower Elliot Formation of Maphutseng, Lesotho. The type species, Kholumolumo ellenbergerorum was formally described in 2020.

history.note: Placed at Massopoda incertae sedis following Peyre de Fabrègues and Allain (2019) and Jones (2026); the Lessemsauridae alternative is recorded.

Kileskus.etymology: From the Khakas language word 'kileskus' meaning 'lizard'. The species name 'aristotocus' refers to its many offspring.
Kileskus.description: Kileskus is a genus of tyrannosauroid dinosaur known from partial remains found in Middle Jurassic (Bathonian stage) Itat Formation of Sharypovsky District, Krasnoyarsk Krai (Russia). Fossils recovered include the holotype maxilla, a premaxilla, a surangular, and a few bones from the hand and foot. Additional remains referred to the species include cervical and caudal vertebrae, as well as a fibula. The skull bones are similar to those of Proceratosaurus. The type species is K. aristotocus, named in 2010 by Averianov and colleagues.

Klamelisaurus.etymology: Named after the Kelameili (Klamelisaurus) Mountains in the Xinjiang region of China; meaning "Kelameili Mountains lizard"
Klamelisaurus.description: Klamelisaurus is a genus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic Shishugou Formation of China. The type species is Klamelisaurus gobiensis, which was named by Zhao Xijin in 1993, based on a partial skeleton discovered in 1982 near the abandoned town of Jiangjunmiao. Zhao described Klamelisaurus as the only member of a new subfamily, Klamelisaurinae, among the now-defunct primitive sauropod order Bothrosauropodoidea. Since Zhao's description, Klamelisaurus received limited attention from researchers until Andrew Moore and colleagues redescribed it in 2020.

dispute.summary: Kol ghuva was described by Turner et al. (2009) as a derived alvarezsaurid, more derived than Alvarezsaurus and Patagonykus, on the basis of its extreme arctometatarsalian foot. Because the holotype is a single articulated foot, the placement is poorly constrained, and some subsequent authors have suggested it may instead be a basal oviraptorosaurian. It is placed in Alvarezsauridae following the describing analysis and Jones et al. (2026).

Kol.description: Kol is an extinct genus of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia. The type and only species is Kol ghuva. The type specimen was excavated from the Ukhaa Tolgod locality of the Djadochta Formation, dating to about 75 million years ago. It is believed to have been about twice the size of the contemporaneous Shuvuuia. However, unlike Shuvuuia, which is known from many well preserved specimens, and although Ukhaa Tolgod has been thoroughly explored, Kol is known only from one complete foot, suggesting that it must have been relatively rare in that ecosystem.

"Koshi" means an old Japanese regional name including Fukui prefecture where fossils of the genus were discovered.

Kosmoceratops.etymology: From Greek kosmos (ornate/decorated) combined with ceratops (horned face); meaning "ornate horned face", referring to the elaborate skull ornamentation
Kosmoceratops.description: Kosmoceratops is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur that lived in North America about 76-75.9 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period. Specimens were discovered in Utah in the Kaiparowits Formation of the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in 2006 and 2007, including an adult skull and postcranial skeleton and partial subadults. In 2010, the adult was made the holotype of the new genus and species Kosmoceratops richardsoni; the generic name means "ornate horned face", and the specific name honors Scott Richardson, who found the specimens. The find was part of a spate of ceratopsian discoveries in the early 21st century, and Kosmoceratops was considered significant due to its elaborate skull ornamentation.

Nasal horncore transversely constricted, long-based, blade-like with flattened distal portion
Supraorbital horncores dorsolaterally directed proximally with ventral curvature distally tapering to point
Parietosquamosal frill relatively short and broad (max width ~2x max length) with small caudally positioned parietal fenestrae
Ten well developed hook-like processes on caudal frill margin (three epiparietals, one epiparietosquamosal, one episquamosal per side)
Most ornate skull of any known dinosaur with 15 well developed horns or horn-like structures

A disarticulated subadult or adult whose femur was histologically sampled, showing sustained rapid growth and supporting an elevated, endothermic metabolism in Kosmoceratops. The analysis determined the specimen was subadult to adult, ruling out that it represented an immature Vagaceratops.

Kotasaurus.etymology: Named for the Kota Formation of Telangana, India, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'Kota Formation lizard'. The species name refers to Yamanpalli, the village near the discovery site.
Kotasaurus.description: Kotasaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic period (Sinemurian-Pliensbachian). The only known species is Kotasaurus yamanpalliensis. It was discovered in the Kota Formation of Telangana, India and shared its habitat with the related Barapasaurus. So far the remains of at least 12 individuals are known. The greater part of the skeleton is known, but the skull is missing, with the exception of two teeth. Like some sauropods, it had a tail club that would have been used for intraspecific combat or interspecific defense.

Kritosaurus.etymology: From Greek kritos (separated) and sauros (lizard); meaning "separated lizard", referring to the arrangement of the cheek bones in the type skull
Kritosaurus.description: Kritosaurus is an incompletely known genus of hadrosaurid (duck-billed) dinosaur. It lived about 74.5-66 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous of North America. The name means "separated lizard" (referring to the arrangement of the cheek bones in an incomplete type skull), but is often mistranslated as "noble lizard" in reference to the presumed "Roman nose" (in the original specimen, the nasal region was fragmented and disarticulated, and was originally restored flat).
diagnostic_features: Dorsolateral margin of the maxilla (rostral and adjacent to the jugal articular surface) 40% or more of the distance between the rostral end of the maxilla and the caudoventral corner of the jugal's orbital margin (autapomorphy).
Jugal with the orbital constriction deeper than the infratemporal constriction.

Infratemporal fenestra larger than the orbit, with its dorsal margin greatly elevated above the dorsal orbital margin in adults (postorbital squamosal ramus forming more than a 20° angle with the maxillary tooth row).
Frontal participating in the orbital margin via an intervening apex between the prefrontal and postorbital (convergent in Brachylophosaurini).
Paired caudal parasagittal processes of the nasals resting over the frontals, with the rostromedial margin of the frontals inserting between the nasal processes.

Kryptohadros.etymology: From Ancient Greek "kryptos" (hidden) and "hadros" (thick or bulky, commonly used in hadrosauroid names); meaning "hidden hadrosauroid".
Kryptohadros.description: Kryptohadros is an extinct genus of hadrosauroid ornithopod dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian age) Densuș-Ciula Formation of Romania. The genus contains a single species, Kryptohadros kallaiae, known from a partial skull and skeleton. Phylogenetic analyses revealed Kryptohadros is closely related to the coeval Transylvanian Telmatosaurus and the Italian Tethyshadros, together forming a group of southeastern European-endemic taxa, called the Telmatosauridae. Kryptohadros is the second named non-hadrosaurid hadrosauroid from the Hațeg Basin, following Telmatosaurus, which was named by Franz Nopcsa in 1903.

(2012) argued the associated postcranium is a chimera and referred it to a carcharodontosaurid, possibly Eocarcharia (though the postcranial elements do not overlap with the skull-only Eocarcharia holotype); later studies agree the postcrania are allosauroid. Its position within Abelisauridae is unstable across analyses.

Kryptops.etymology: From Greek kryptos (covered/hidden) and ops (face); meaning "covered face", referring to the heavily textured surface of the maxilla
Kryptops.description: Kryptops is an extinct genus of possibly chimeric abelisaurid theropod dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of Niger. It is known from a partial maxilla (upper jaw bone) found at the Gadoufaoua locality in the western Ténéré Desert, in rocks of the Aptian-Albian-age Elrhaz Formation. The fossils were collected in 2000 by a University of Chicago expedition to Niger led by American paleontologist Paul Sereno. They were then described in 2008 by Sereno and Steve Brusatte. The genus contains a single species, Kryptops palaios. Sereno and Brusatte referred several postcranial remains to Kryptops, but later studies have shown that these elements belong to an allosauroid theropod, leaving Kryptops to be only known from the incomplete maxilla.

Labocania.etymology: Named after the La Bocana Roja Formation in Baja California, Mexico, where the type specimen was likely recovered
Labocania.description: Labocania is an extinct genus of theropod dinosaur of disputed affinities, known from the Late Cretaceous of Mexico. Initially regarded as an indeterminate theropod, later studies have mentioned possible affinities with tyrannosaurids, abelisaurids, or carcharodontosaurids. More recent research based on additional fossil material found support for a position within the tyrannosaurine clade Teratophoneini. Two species have been proposed: L. anomala (the type species), likely from the La Bocana Roja Formation, and L. aguillonae from the Cerro del Pueblo Formation.

dispute.summary: Labocania anomala was described by Molnar (1974) as Theropoda incertae sedis — tyrannosaurid-like in some postcranial features but with cranial elements resembling other large theropods, so he declined a family assignment. Its affinities remain debated; more recent material has been argued to support a tyrannosaurine position.

history.note: Placed conservatively at Tyrannosauroidea incertae sedis; affinities range from Theropoda indet. (Molnar, 1974) to tyrannosaurine in recent work.

Lambeosaurus.etymology: Named for Canadian paleontologist Lawrence M. Lambe, with the Greek suffix '-saurus' meaning 'lizard'.
Lambeosaurus.description: Lambeosaurus is a genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of western North America. The first skull of Lambeosaurus found was used by paleontologist Lawrence M. Lambe to justify the creation of the new genus Stephanosaurus, although it was not part of the latter's original material. Its incomplete nature led William A. Parks to name Lambeosaurus lambei for this skull in 1923 to honor Lambe. Multiple species of Lambeosaurus have been named since, including L. clavinitialis and L. magnicristatus in 1935, and L. laticaudus in 1981 which was later moved to its own genus Magnapaulia. It has also been identified that some species earlier identified as belonging to Tetragonosaurus and Corythosaurus are now considered juveniles of Lambeosaurus. It is the eponymous member of the subfamily Lambeosaurinae and tribe Lambeosaurini. Lambeosaurins, which also includes Corythosaurus and Hypacrosaurus from western North America, are understood to be some of the most specialized ornithopods.

dispute.summary: Lametasaurus is a chimera based on associated but probably non-conspecific elements and is widely regarded as a nomen dubium. Its elements have been referred to sharply different clades: the osteoderms have been read as nodosaurid/ankylosaurian and, alternatively, as titanosaurian, while parts of the pelvis and hindlimb have been compared to abelisaurid theropods (raising the possibility that Lametasaurus is a senior synonym of Indosaurus or Rajasaurus). Recent work identifies ankylosaurian synapomorphies in some osteoderms, confirming the composite nature regardless of the other material. With hypotheses spanning Ornithischia, Sauropodomorpha, and Theropoda and the syntypes lost, the genus is placed conservatively at Dinosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Abelisauridae as a nomen dubium pending revision.

Reparented from Abelisauridae to Dinosauria incertae sedis: the chimeric syntypes yield competing ornithischian (nodosaurid/ankylosaurian), sauropodomorph (titanosaurian), and theropod (abelisaurid) referrals, so Dinosauria is the least-inclusive clade all hypotheses share. Removed diet, locomotion, and the abelisaur-tibia-based weight estimate, which presupposed the theropod reading.

The syntype material is lost, and the genus is generally treated as a nomen dubium.

It has been classified as either a basal sauropod or more basal sauropodomorph.

Lanzhousaurus.description: Lanzhousaurus is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur that lived in the Gansu region of what is now China during the Early Cretaceous (Barremian). Described by You, Ji, and Li in 2005, the type and only species is Lanzhousaurus magnidens, known from a partial skeleton recovered from the Hekou Group. It has been estimated to be about 10 meters (33 ft) in length and 6 metric tons (6.6 short tons) in weight.
diagnostic_features: Large individual teeth (~4 cm wide) with small tooth count per tooth row (14 in dentary)
Dentary teeth diamond-shaped with multiple weak ridges on lingual surface
Maxillary teeth narrow, lozenge-shaped with one prominent primary ridge flanked by weak secondary ridges
Marginal denticles present as mammillations on both mesial and distal edges of teeth
Enamel present on both lingual and labial sides of teeth (weak interlocking)
Hatchet-shaped sternal plates with relatively long blade (>50% of total length)

species.etymology: From Latin 'magnus' meaning 'great' and 'dens' meaning 'tooth', referring to the exceptionally large teeth that distinguish this genus.

Laosaurus.etymology: From Greek laas (stone or fossil) and sauros (lizard); meaning "stone or fossil lizard"
Laosaurus.description: Laosaurus is a genus of neornithischian dinosaur. The type species, Laosaurus celer, was first described by O.C. Marsh in 1878 from remains discovered in the Upper Jurassic (Kimmeridgian) Morrison Formation of Wyoming. The validity of this genus is doubtful because it is based on fragmentary fossils. A second species also from the Morrison Formation, L. gracilis, and a species from the Upper Cretaceous Allison Formation of Alberta, Canada, L. minimus, are also considered dubious.

dispute.summary: Laosaurus is a nomen dubium based on fragmentary Late Jurassic material from the Morrison Formation; its species have been variously reassigned or considered indeterminate (Galton, 1977).

history.note: Placed at Neornithischia incertae sedis; fragmentary nomen dubium not placeable more precisely.

diagnostic_features: Long bones not hollow with thick walls and small cavities
Vertebrae biconcave with neural arches loosely united to centra
Dorsal and anterior caudals more elongated than in most dinosaurs
Phalanges avian in character
Anterior limbs much smaller than posterior limbs

species.name: Laosaurus celer
species.etymology: From Latin 'celer' meaning 'swift' or 'fast', in reference to the inferred agility of this small ornithischian.

type_specimen.institution: Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History
type_specimen.material: Fragmentary caudal material, described by Marsh (1878) as a median caudal vertebral centrum, the proximal end of an ulna, and pedal phalanges.

Lapampasaurus.etymology: Named after La Pampa Province of Argentina, where it was found, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'La Pampa lizard'
Lapampasaurus.description: Lapampasaurus is an extinct genus of hadrosaurid known from the Late Cretaceous Allen Formation (late Campanian or early Maastrichtian stage) of La Pampa Province, Argentina. It contains a single species, Lapampasaurus cholinoi. The generic name refers to the Argentine province of La Pampa. The specific name honors the late collector José Cholino. The material includes cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae, the forelimb girdle, and the partial hindlimb.

dispute.summary: Lapampasaurus cholinoi is known from very fragmentary remains, coded for only 11 of 365 characters by Alarcón-Muñoz and others (2023), who excluded it from their results; when included it falls within Saurolophinae near Kamuysaurus, but Jones (2026) treats it as an indeterminate hadrosaurid.

history.note: Placed at Hadrosauridae incertae sedis; tentative saurolophine affinity (Alarcón-Muñoz and others, 2023) too weakly supported to adopt.

Scapula with deltoid crest of sharp lateral edge and convex dorsal surface
Pedal ungual phalanx longer than wide with grooves and superficial foramina
Shallow longitudinal ventral elevation on pedal ungual phalanx

Laplatasaurus.etymology: Named for La Plata, Argentina, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'La Plata lizard'. The species name refers to the Araucanos (Mapuche) people.
Laplatasaurus.description: Laplatasaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in South America, with the holotype and only known specimen found in the Anacleto Formation.
diagnostic_features: Caudal vertebrae with narrow flattening and shallow groove on lower face of body instead of prominent separated haemal facets as in Titanosaurus
Caudal vertebrae with high and pointed articular cones posteriorly, with very little wedge-shaped tapering of the vertebral body downward
Very long and slender prezygapophyses extending notably anteriorly past the preceding vertebra
Humerus markedly more slender than in Titanosaurus and Argyrosaurus, with a distinctly elevated bent lateral process forming a corner above it
Fibula with enormous double muscular insertion (peroneal muscle in two distinct tumescences) in upper third of external side, unlike Titanosaurus (one) or Antarctosaurus (two shallower ridges)
Scapula with anterior longitudinal edge forming a single homogeneous concave arc, not composed of two opposing curves as in Titanosaurus

Lapparentosaurus.etymology: Named in honor of French paleontologist Albert-Félix de Lapparent, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Lapparent's lizard'
Lapparentosaurus.description: Lapparentosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic. Its fossils were found in Madagascar (Isalo III Formation). It contains one species, Lapparentosaurus madagascariensis. The genus and species were named by José Bonaparte in 1986. The classification of Lapparentosaurus is controversial, as it exhibits a combination of characteristics of basal sauropods and titanosauriforms.

Laquintasaura.etymology: Named for the La Quinta Formation where it was discovered, combined with the feminine Greek suffix for lizard.
Laquintasaura.description: Laquintasaura is a genus of Venezuelan ornithischian dinosaur containing a single species, Laquintasaura venezuelae. It is known for being one of the most primitive ornithischians in the fossil record, as well as the first dinosaur to have been identified from Venezuela. The name is derived from the La Quinta Formation, where it was discovered, and the feminine Greek suffix for lizard, with the specific name referring to the country of Venezuela. It is known from hundreds of fossil elements, all derived from a single extensive bonebed locality. Initially discovered by French paleontologists, numerous expeditions have been conducted to excavate from the bonebed, largely led by Marcelo R Sánchez-Villagra. Once thought to represent remains of Lesothosaurus, it was formally named in a 2014 study; much of the abundant material was not yet prepared at the time and research remains ongoing.

dispute.summary: Laquintasaura is an unstable early ornithischian recovered either as an early-diverging thyreophoran (Baron and others, 2017; Yao and others, 2025) or as a basal ornithischian outside Genasauria (Barrett and others, 2014; Riguetti and others, 2022). Jones (2026) leaves it unresolved at the base of Ornithischia.

history.note: Placed at Ornithischia incertae sedis; analyses are divided between basal Thyreophora and basal Ornithischia outside Genasauria.

Sharply inflected dorsal margin of ischium dorsal to obturator process
Femoral fibula epicondyle medially inset in posterior or ventral view
Astragalus with deep U-shaped notch in anterior surface

Latirhinus.etymology: From Latin latus (broad) and Greek rhis (nose); meaning "broad nose"
Latirhinus.description: Latirhinus is an extinct genus of lambeosaurine hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Mexico. The type species, Latirhinus uitstlani, was named in 2012 on the basis of a partial skeleton from the Campanian-age Cerro del Pueblo Formation. The specific name uitstlani means "southern" in the Náhuatl language of Mexico, a reference to the species' southern occurrence in the Cretaceous landmass Laramidia.

dispute.summary: Latirhinus uitstlani is generally placed within Lambeosaurinae, but Prieto-Márquez and others (2019) recovered it at the base of Hadrosauridae in a clade with Aquilarhinus, and its holotype may combine lambeosaurine and saurolophine elements. Placed conservatively within Lambeosaurinae following the prevailing view.

history.note: Placed at Lambeosaurinae following Jones (2026); the original description (Prieto-Márquez et al., 2012) tentatively assigned it to Saurolophinae (no cladistic analysis) and Prieto-Márquez and others (2019) recovered it at the base of Hadrosauridae, neither adopted (P2, P5).

Broader narial foramen than any other known hadrosaurid taxon
Anterodorsally curved deltoid crest of the scapula (convergent with Lambeosaurinae)
Hook-shaped nasal with mediolaterally compressed form
Relatively gracile humeri with deltopectoral crest comprising 55% of total length

Leaellynasaura.etymology: Named after Leaellyn Rich, the daughter of paleontologists Tom Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich, combined with Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "Leaellyn's lizard"
Leaellynasaura.description: Leaellynasaura is a genus of small herbivorous ornithischian dinosaurs from the late Aptian to early Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, around 118-110 million years ago. It was first discovered in Dinosaur Cove, Australia. The only known species is Leaellynasaura amicagraphica. It was described in 1989, and named after Leaellyn Rich, the daughter of the Australian paleontologist couple Tom Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich who discovered it. The specific name, amicagraphica, translates to "friend writing" and honors both the Friends of the Museum of Victoria and the National Geographic Society for their support of Australian paleontology.

Ridges cover the entire internal and external (lingual and buccal) surfaces of the crown rather than being restricted to marginal denticles

Ledumahadi.description: Ledumahadi is a genus of lessemsaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Early Jurassic Elliot Formation in Free State Province, South Africa. The type and only species is L. mafube, known from a singular incomplete postcranial specimen. A quadruped, it was one of the first giant sauropodomorphs, reaching a weight of around 12 tonnes (13 short tons), despite not having evolved columnar limbs like its later huge relatives.

Leonerasaurus.etymology: Named after the Las Leoneras Formation in Argentina, where the fossil was found; meaning "Las Leoneras lizard"
Leonerasaurus.description: Leonerasaurus is a basal genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur. Currently, there is only one species known, named L. taquetrensis by Diego Pol, Alberto Garrido and Ignacio A. Cerda in 2011. The fossil, an incomplete subadult individual, was found in the Las Leoneras Formation in Argentina. This formation is probably Early Jurassic in age. Leonerasaurus was a small non-sauropod sauropodomorph, showing an unusual combination of basal and derived characters. This indicates that the evolution of early sauropodomorphs witnessed a great degree of convergent evolution.

dispute.summary: Leonerasaurus taquetrensis shows a mosaic of basal and sauropod-like characters and its position is inconsistent between studies, falling among basal sauropodiforms or basal massopodans.

history.note: Placed at Sauropodiformes incertae sedis; position inconsistent between analyses.

Leptoceratops.etymology: From Greek 'leptos' (small or slender), 'keras' (horn), and 'ops' (face); meaning 'small horn face'
Leptoceratops.description: Leptoceratops is a genus of ceratopsian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of North America. First found in Alberta in 1910, the type species Leptoceratops gracilis was named in 1914 by Barnum Brown for a partial skull and skeleton of two individuals found in the Scollard Formation of Alberta. Additional specimens found in the Scollard include one complete and two mostly complete skeletons together, uncovered in 1947 by Charles M. Sternberg. Specimens from Montana that were among the earliest referred to Leptoceratops have since been moved to their own genera Montanoceratops and Cerasinops, while new specimens of L. gracilis include bonebed remains from the Hell Creek Formation of Montana and a partial skeleton from the Lance Formation of Wyoming. Together with related taxa, Leptoceratops is the eponymous genus of the family Leptoceratopsidae. Leptoceratops is known from more than ten individuals, all from Maastrichtian deposits of Alberta, Montana and Wyoming, representing the entire skeleton.

Femur shaft practically straight and round in cross-section; fourth trochanter comparatively larger than in any described Ceratopsian

The rear part of a skull marking the first record of Leptoceratops from the Hell Creek Formation of Montana. Prepared in 1998, it preserves the first complete braincase yet described for the genus.
