Muttaburrasaurus.etymology: Named for Muttaburra, a town in Queensland, Australia near where the fossil was discovered, combined with Greek '-saurus' meaning 'lizard'.
Muttaburrasaurus.description: Muttaburrasaurus was a genus of herbivorous iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur that lived in what is now north-eastern Australia during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, about 96 million years ago. It has been recovered in some analyses as a member of the iguanodontian clade Rhabdodontomorpha, or alternately as a member of Elasmaria. After Kunbarrasaurus, it is Australia's most completely known dinosaur from skeletal remains. It was named after Muttaburra, the site in Queensland, Australia, where it was found. The dinosaur was selected from twelve candidates to become the official fossil emblem of the State of Queensland.

dispute.summary: Muttaburrasaurus langdoni was long recovered within Rhabdodontomorpha (Dieudonné and others, 2016; Madzia and others, 2021), but Fonseca and others (2024) recovered it within Elasmaria, interpreting its rhabdodontomorph resemblances as convergence, and Czepiński and Madzia (2025) likewise placed it outside Rhabdodontomorpha. Its redescription by Herne and others (2026) found it craniodentally distant from rhabdodontomorphs but undertook no phylogenetic analysis, leaving its relationships unresolved.

history.note: Placed at Rhabdodontomorpha following the then-prevailing view; the outside-Rhabdodontomorpha result of Czepiński and Madzia (2025) reflected, not adopted.

Re-evaluated and moved to Elasmaria, following Fonseca and others (2024), which recovers it within Elasmaria and treats its rhabdodontomorph similarities as convergent; Czepiński and Madzia (2025) likewise place it outside Rhabdodontomorpha. The older within-Rhabdodontomorpha result is superseded.

diagnostic_features: Posterodorsal and posteroventral processes of the premaxilla abutting along a tight lateral suture to form the anterolateral part of the enlarged cavum nasi proprium within the dorsally inflated muzzle.
Novel paired ossifications (prenasals) — either premaxillary processes or neomorphic bones — forming the dorsal roof and internal septa of the enlarged cavum nasi proprium.
Horizontal septum of the prenasal dividing the cavum nasi proprium into inferior and superior airways, with a sagittal septum further dividing the superior airway into left and right meatuses.
Thickened pendulous support ridge of the prenasal projecting ventrally into the superior airway meatus.
Toroidal fossa at the anterior end of the nasal body forming the posterior end of the superior airway meatus.
T-shaped lacrimal with a descending process projecting ventrally toward the dorsal opening of the maxillary neurovascular tract.
Pterygoid lacking palatine and vomeral contacts on the anterior face of the boss for the basipterygoid process.
Two protuberances at the dorsal tip of the ascending process of the supraoccipital, accommodated ventrally on the parietals.
Nasal excluded from the naris by the premaxilla (convergent with Lambeosaurinae).
Dentulous premaxilla bearing five alveoli, as in early-diverging neornithischians.
Caniniform premaxillary teeth lacking a substantial root-crown constriction, as in some heterodontosaurids.

Muyelensaurus.etymology: Named after 'Muyelen', an indigenous name for the Colorado River in Argentina, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Muyelen lizard'.
Muyelensaurus.description: Muyelensaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Argentina. It was more slender than other titanosaurs. Fossils have been recovered in the Neuquén province of Patagonia and were originally assigned to the Portezuelo Formation but further research showed that these layers belong to the Plottier Formation. The type species is M. pecheni. The name Muyelensaurus first appeared in a 2007 paper by Argentine paleontologists Jorge Calvo of the Universidad Nacional del Comahue and Bernardo González Riga of the Laboratorio de Paleovertebrados, and Brazilian paleontologist Juan Porfiri of the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro.

Mymoorapelta.description: Mymoorapelta is a nodosaurid ankylosaur from the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian-Tithonian, around 155 to 150 million years ago) Morrison Formation (Brushy Basin Member) of western Colorado and central Utah, USA. The animal is known from a single species, Mymoorapelta maysi, and few specimens are known. The most complete specimen is the holotype individual from the Mygatt-Moore Quarry, which includes osteoderms, a partial skull, vertebrae, and other bones. It was initially described by James Kirkland and Kenneth Carpenter in 1994. Along with Gargoyleosaurus, it is one of the earliest known nodosaurids.

Nagatitan.etymology: From Nāga, the mythological serpent-like creature of various Asian cultures (especially northeastern Thailand), and Greek 'titan' meaning 'giant'.
Nagatitan.description: Nagatitan is an extinct genus of euhelopodid sauropod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian–Albian) Khok Kruat Formation of Thailand. The genus contains a single species, Nagatitan chaiyaphumensis, known from a partial postcranial skeleton. With an estimated body length of about 27 meters and a mass of 25–28 tonnes, it is the largest dinosaur currently known from Southeast Asia.

Nankangia.etymology: Named after Nankang County (now Nankang District), Ganzhou City, Jiangxi Province, China, where the specimen was found
Nankangia.description: Nankangia is an extinct genus of caenagnathoid oviraptorosaurian dinosaur known from the Upper Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation of Nankang County, Ganzhou City of Jiangxi Province, southeastern China. It contains a single species, Nankangia jiangxiensis. N. jiangxiensis coexisted with at least four other caenagnathoids, including but not limited to Corythoraptor, Banji, Ganzhousaurus and Jiangxisaurus. The relatively short dentary and non-downturned mandibular symphysis of Nankangia suggest that it may have been more herbivorous than carnivorous. Its diet consisted of leaves and seeds.

Nanosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'nanos' (small or dwarf) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'small or dwarf lizard'.
Nanosaurus.description: Nanosaurus is an extinct genus of neornithischian dinosaur that lived about 155 to 148 million years ago, during the Late Jurassic in North America. Its fossils are known from the Morrison Formation of the south-western United States. The type and only species, Nanosaurus agilis, was described and named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877. The taxon has a complicated taxonomic history, largely the work of Marsh and Peter M. Galton, involving the genera Laosaurus, Hallopus, Drinker, Othnielia, and Othnielosaurus, the latter three now being considered to be synonyms of Nanosaurus. It had historically been classified as a hypsilophodont or fabrosaur, types of generalized small bipedal herbivore, but more recent research has abandoned these groupings as paraphyletic and Nanosaurus is today considered a basal member of Neornithischia.

dispute.summary: Nanosaurus is treated as a valid basal neornithischian by Carpenter and Galton (2018), who synonymized Drinker, Othnielia, and Othnielosaurus with it, and by Fonseca and others (2024) and Jones (2026). Boyd (2015) and Barrett and Maidment (2025) instead regard Nanosaurus agilis as a nomen dubium lacking diagnostic features.

history.note: Retained at Neornithischia incertae sedis following Fonseca and others (2024) and Jones (2026); the nomen dubium assessment of Boyd (2015) and Barrett and Maidment (2025) is recorded.

Nanotyrannus.etymology: Originally proposed by Bakker, Williams and Currie (1988) as Latin nano ("small") plus tyrannus ("tyrant"); the derivation is now usually corrected to Greek nanos ("dwarf" or "pygmy") and tyrannos ("king"), in reference to the small body size relative to other tyrannosauroids.
Nanotyrannus.description: Nanotyrannus is a genus of tyrannosauroid dinosaur that lived in what is now western North America during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous, 67 to 66 million years ago. Its fossils are known from the Hell Creek Formation. It was one of the last-known non-avian dinosaurs and lived until the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event. The first named species, N. lancensis, was described as a new species of Gorgosaurus in 1946 by Charles W. Gilmore based on a single skull. Re-examination of the specimen in 1988 by Robert T. Bakker, Michael Williams and Philip J. Currie moved the species to a new genus of tyrannosaurid, named Nanotyrannus in reference to its small body size compared to other tyrannosaurids.

dispute.summary: The validity of Nanotyrannus is actively contested. After the 1988 erection of the genus, Carr (1999) and Woodward et al. (2020) argued that the holotype CMNH 7541 is an immature Tyrannosaurus rex, citing tooth-grain immaturity and femoral osteohistology. Longrich and Saitta (2024), Zanno and Napoli (2025) — who erected a second species, N. lethaeus — and Griffin et al. (2025, ceratobranchial histology) reaffirmed Nanotyrannus as a distinct, skeletally mature taxon. No broad consensus yet.

history.note: Placed at Eutyrannosauria — the least-inclusive clade spanning both hypotheses: within Tyrannosaurinae if a juvenile Tyrannosaurus, or an early-diverging non-tyrannosaurid eutyrannosaurian (Nanotyrannidae, Zanno and Napoli 2025) if a distinct taxon; validity unresolved.

diagnostic_features: Muzzle width greatly constricted, only one fourth the width of the temporal region.
Extraordinarily wide basicranium between basitubera and basipterygoid processes.
Two large pneumatic foramina placed one behind the other near the midline of the basisphenoid.
Dorsal surface of the nasal lacks strong ridges and striae.
Parietal wing of the occiput with a sharp angle between dorsal and lateral edges.
Basicranial boxwork with flat ventral floor.

Nanshiungosaurus.etymology: Named after Nanxiong (formerly romanized as Nanshiung), a city in Guangdong Province, China, where it was discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Nanxiong's lizard'.
Nanshiungosaurus.description: Nanshiungosaurus is a genus of therizinosaurid that lived in what is now Asia during the Late Cretaceous of South China. The type species, Nanshiungosaurus brevispinus, was first discovered in 1974 and described in 1979 by Dong Zhiming. It is represented by a single specimen preserving most of the cervical and dorsal vertebrae with the pelvis. A supposed and unlikely second species, "Nanshiungosaurus" bohlini, was found in 1992 and described in 1997. It is also represented by vertebrae but this species however, differs in geological age and lacks authentic characteristics compared to the type, making its affinity to the genus unsupported.

Napaisaurus.etymology: From 'Napai' (the Napai Basin in Fusui County, Guangxi, where the holotype was discovered) and Greek 'sauros' (lizard).
Napaisaurus.description: Napaisaurus is an extinct genus of basal iguanodontian ornithopod from the Aptian (Early Cretaceous) second member of the Xinlong Formation, Napai Basin, Fusui County, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China. The single species, Napaisaurus guangxiensis, is known from a partial right pelvis (right ilium and ischium of a single individual). Ji and Zhang (2022) identify it as the first formally named basal iguanodontian dinosaur from southern China.
diagnostic_features: Preacetabular process of the ilium strongly curved ventrally and slightly inclined laterally, with a very long pubic peduncle extending anteroventrally, forming a narrow and deep U-shaped preacetabular notch with nearly parallel lateral margins.

Posterior portion of the postacetabular process expands significantly medially in the transverse direction, forming a short, wide brevis shelf on the ventral surface.
Articular surface of the ischial peduncle of the ilium is broad and concave.
Iliac peduncle of the ischium shows significant lateral thickening toward the distal end, with a strongly convex distal articular surface.

The specific name honors the discoverer, Salvador Palomo.

Nasutoceratops.etymology: From Latin 'nasutus' meaning 'large-nosed' and Latinized Greek 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face'; translates as 'large-nosed horned face', referring to its distinctive enlarged nasal region.
Nasutoceratops.description: Nasutoceratops is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur that lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period, about 76.0-75.5 million years ago. In 2013, the subadult was made the holotype of the new genus and species Nasutoceratops titusi; the generic name means "large-nosed horned face", and the specific name honors the paleontologist Alan L. Titus for his work at the GSENM. The dinosaur was noted for its large nose in news reports, and later featured in Jurassic World films.

Nedoceratops.etymology: From Russian 'nedo' (insufficient) and Greek 'keratops' (horned face); meaning 'insufficient horned face', in reference to the absence of a prominent nasal horn on the holotype skull.
Nedoceratops.description: Nedoceratops is a controversial genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period Lance Formation of North America. It is known only from a single skull discovered in Wyoming. Its status is the subject of ongoing debate among paleontologists: some authors consider Nedoceratops a valid, distinct taxon, while others consider it to be an unusual specimen of Triceratops.

dispute.summary: The validity of Nedoceratops is actively contested. Scannella and Horner (2010, 2011) treated USNM 2412 as a transitional or ontogenetic morph within Triceratops, arguing that Triceratops, Torosaurus, and Nedoceratops together represent different growth stages of a single anagenetic lineage. Farke (2011) rebutted this, treating Nedoceratops as a distinct chasmosaurine genus diagnosed by an undifferentiated nasal horncore, near-vertical postorbital horncores, and small parietal fenestrae; Maiorino et al. (2013) found its morphometric affinities equivocal, with the squamosal and frill within Triceratops morphospace though overall skull shape is ambiguous. No broad consensus has been reached.

history.note: Placed at Chasmosaurinae, the least-inclusive clade accepted whether Nedoceratops is a valid chasmosaurine or a growth stage of Triceratops; tribes dropped. Validity unresolved.

Neimongosaurus.etymology: Named after Nei Mongol (Inner Mongolia), the Chinese autonomous region where it was found, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Nei Mongol lizard'.
Neimongosaurus.description: Neimongosaurus is a genus of herbivorous therizinosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in China during the Late Cretaceous period. Its fossils are known from the strata of the Iren Dabasu Formation. It is known from two specimens, discovered in 1999 by researchers from the Ministry of Land and Resources and described two years later. One species, N. yangi, is known, named after Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian.

dispute.summary: Neimongosaurus is an intermediate-grade therizinosaur whose family-level assignment depends on how Therizinosauridae is defined. Under the narrow node-based definition of Zanno (2010) it lies outside Therizinosauridae as an intermediate therizinosauroid, a result followed by Hartman et al. (2019) and the Princeton Encyclopedia (Jones, 2026). Under the broader Therizinosaurus-anchored definition of Kobayashi et al. (2022, 2025) it is drawn into Therizinosauridae, recovered with Erliansaurus as the family's most basal clade. It is placed conservatively in Therizinosauroidea.

Nemegtomaia.etymology: Named for the Nemegt Basin of Mongolia where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'maia' meaning 'good mother', in reference to the brooding behavior of oviraptorids.
Nemegtomaia.description: Nemegtomaia is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur from what is now Mongolia that lived in the Late Cretaceous Period, about 72 to 70 million years ago. The first specimen was found in 1996, and became the basis of the new genus and species N. barsboldi in 2004. The original genus name was Nemegtia, but this was changed to Nemegtomaia in 2005, as the former name was preoccupied. The first part of the generic name refers to the Nemegt Basin, where the animal was found, and the second part means "good mother", in reference to the fact that oviraptorids are known to have brooded their eggs. The specific name honors the paleontologist Rinchen Barsbold. Two more specimens were found in 2007, one of which was found on top of a nest with eggs, but the dinosaur had received its genus name before it was found associated with eggs.

Nemegtosaurus.etymology: Named for the Nemegt Basin in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia where the skull was discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Nemegtosaurus.description: Nemegtosaurus was a sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Period of what is now Mongolia. Measuring an estimated 12-13 m (39-43 ft) long and weighing 20 t (44,000 lb), it was named after the Nemegt Basin in the Gobi Desert, where the remains - a single skull - were found. The skull resembles diplodocoids in being long and low, with pencil-shaped teeth. However, recent work has shown that Nemegtosaurus is in fact a titanosaur, closely related to animals such as Saltasaurus, Alamosaurus, and Rapetosaurus.

Neosodon.description: Neosodon was a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the late Tithonian-aged (Upper Jurassic) Sables et Gres a Trigonia gibbosa of Pas-de-Calais department, France. It has never been formally given a species name, but is often seen as N. praecursor, which actually comes from a different animal. Often in the past, it had been assigned to the wastebasket taxon Pelorosaurus, but restudy has suggested that it could be related to Turiasaurus, a roughly contemporaneous giant Spanish sauropod. It is only known from six teeth.

Neovenator.etymology: From Latin neo- ('new') and venator ('hunter'), meaning 'new hunter'
Neovenator.description: Neovenator is an extinct genus of carcharodontosaurian theropod dinosaur. It is known primarily from several skeletons found in the Early Cretaceous (Hauterivian-Barremian) Wessex Formation on the south coast of the Isle of Wight, southern England. The first remains of Neovenator were discovered in 1978 alongside those of the ornithopod Brighstoneus, after the collapse of part of Grange Chine. In 1996, Steve Hutt, David Martill and Michael Barker named the genus Neovenator. One species is known: the type species, N. salerii, after the Salero family who owned the site on which its remains were discovered.

Femoral head oriented anteromedially and inclined proximally

Newtonsaurus.etymology: From 'Newton' (honoring British paleontologist Edwin Tully Newton, 1840-1930, of the Geological Survey, who first described the holotype) and Greek 'sauros' (lizard).
Newtonsaurus.description: Newtonsaurus is an extinct genus of large neotheropod dinosaur from the Rhaetian (Late Triassic) Cotham Member of the Lilstock Formation, Penarth Group, recovered at Stormy Down near Bridgend in South Wales. The single species, Newtonsaurus cambrensis, is known from a natural mold of a left dentary preserved as two blocks of sandstone (basionym 'Zanclodon' cambrensis Newton 1899); Evans, Howells, Wintle and Benton (2025) re-evaluated the holotype and erected the new genus, recovering the taxon tentatively as a coelophysoid with morphological affinity to Dilophosaurus, although a stem-averostran position cannot be excluded. The estimated body length of 5-7 m, derived from a ~28 cm preserved dentary representing roughly half the mandible, makes Newtonsaurus a candidate for the largest known Late Triassic theropod. The genus name had been used as a nomen nudum in private compilations since 1999 and is formally established by this paper.
diagnostic_features: Anterior tip of dentary modestly expanded but not bulbous, forming a low dorsal convexity with its apex at the third tooth position.
16-17 dentary alveoli present, with the third (second as preserved) alveolus distinctly enlarged and subcircular in outline.
Lateral foramina along the labial groove anteroposteriorly elongated (elliptical, ~1.5 cm long) rather than circular.
Single Meckelian foramen at the anterior terminus of the Meckelian groove, level with the third alveolus.
Unfused, sub-pentagonal interdental plates separated from the medial dentary wall by a narrow paradental groove open for its entire length.
Relative mandible depth (depth/length ratio ~17.8%) intermediate between that of shallow coelophysoid forms and deeper-jawed forms.

Nigersaurus.description: Nigersaurus is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived during the middle Cretaceous period, about 115 to 105 million years ago. Fossils of this dinosaur were first described in 1976, but it was only named Nigersaurus taqueti in 1999 after further and more complete remains were found and described. The genus name means "Niger reptile", and the specific name honors the paleontologist Philippe Taquet, who discovered the first remains.

Ningyuansaurus.etymology: Derived from Ningyuan, an ancient name for Xingcheng City in western Liaoning Province, China, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'
Ningyuansaurus.description: Ningyuansaurus is a pennaraptoran dinosaur genus. It contains the single species Ningyuansaurus wangi, known from a fossil specimen from the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation (Aptian stage, 124.6 Ma ago) of Jianchang, western Liaoning Province, People's Republic of China. It was originally thought to be the basalmost species of oviraptorosaur, based on its long skull and a greater number of teeth in comparison to any other known oviraptorosaur. However, later analyses have variously recovered it outside Oviraptorosauria, as a halszkaraptorine or a basal troodontid, and its affinities remain unresolved. The generic name Ningyuansaurus is derived from Ningyuan, an ancient name for Xingcheng City. The specific name honors Wang Qiuwu, the private owner of the specimen who donated it for scientific study. The specimen is now in the Confuciusornis Museum in Xingcheng.

dispute.summary: The affinities of Ningyuansaurus are unresolved and it may lie outside Oviraptorosauria. The original description (Ji et al., 2012) recovered it as the basalmost oviraptorosaur, but Hartman et al. (2019) instead recovered it as a halszkaraptorine dromaeosaurid (sister to Mahakala), and Cau and Madzia (2021) recovered it under equal weighting as a basal troodontid within Sinovenatorinae, shifting to a basal oviraptorosaur only under implied weighting. It is therefore placed conservatively at Maniraptora.

history.note: Evicted from Oviraptorosauria and placed at Maniraptora; the oviraptorosaur, troodontid, and halszkaraptorine hypotheses are all supported by different analyses and none prevails.
Retained at Maniraptora incertae sedis; placement remains unresolved.

Ninjatitan.etymology: Named for 'Ninja', a nickname of Argentine paleontologist Sebastian Apesteguia, combined with Latin 'titan' meaning 'giant'; translates as 'Ninja giant'.
Ninjatitan.description: Ninjatitan is an exinct genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Berriasian-Valanginian age) Bajada Colorada Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, Ninjatitan zapatai, which was named and described in 2021 based on a partial postcranial skeleton discovered in 2014. Its generic name comes from a nickname of Argentine paleontologist Sebastian Apesteguia, and the specific name comes from technician Rogelio Zapata.

dispute.summary: Placed within Titanosauria as incertae sedis. Potentially the oldest known titanosaur, Ninjatitan is known from fragmentary remains and its precise position is poorly resolved: the describing authors (Gallina et al., 2021) recovered two hypotheses, a very basal titanosaur or a lognkosaurian, and a later analysis (Pérez Moreno et al., 2023) recovered it within Rinconsauria. Mannion and Carvalho (2026) instead recovered Ninjatitan outside Titanosauria altogether and raised the possibility that its holotype is a chimera. A basal position within Titanosauria is currently favored, as a derived (Late Cretaceous) subfamily placement would be hard to reconcile with its Early Cretaceous age.

history.note: Placed at Titanosauria incertae sedis; basal-titanosaur, lognkosaurian, and rinconsaurian positions have all been recovered, and Mannion and Carvalho (2026) recover it outside Titanosauria.

Nipponosaurus.etymology: Named for Nippon (Japan), the country that controlled Sakhalin Island where the fossils were found at the time of description, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Nipponosaurus.description: Nipponosaurus is a lambeosaurine hadrosaur from sediments of the Yezo Group, in Sinegorsk on the island of Sakhalin, which was part of Japan at the time of the species' classification. The type and only species is N. sachalinensis, known only from a single juvenile specimen discovered in 1934 and named in 1936, by Takumi Nagao, with further material of the same individual found in 1937. Since then, the taxon has been largely ignored, and its validity has been doubted, with synonymy with other Asian hadrosaurs or status as a nomen dubium being suggested. Redescriptions from 2004 and 2017, however, have supported recognition as a distinct species. Dating the only specimen has been difficult, but based on associated mollusc taxa, the species likely lived sometime in the upper Santonian or lower Campanian, around 80 million years ago.

Relatively short ulna compared with the femur (ulna/femur ratio ~0.49, well below the lambeosaurine average).

Noasaurus.etymology: Named after the Noroeste Argentino (northwestern Argentina) region, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Northwestern Argentina lizard'.
Noasaurus.description: Noasaurus is a genus of ceratosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Maastrichtian (Late Cretaceous) of Argentina. The type and only species is N. leali. The fragmentary holotype specimen of Noasaurus, PVL 4061, consisting of a few cranial and postcranial bones, was discovered from strata from the Lecho Formation of Southern Salta in 1975 by a team led by José Fernando Bonaparte. When described by Bonaparte and in PhD student Jaime Powell in 1980, it was believed to be a coelurosaur theropod and assigned to a family of its own; this family, Noasauridae, still exists, though has been reassigned to Ceratosauria.

Nodocephalosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'nodus' (knob), Greek 'kephale' (head), and Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'knob headed lizard', referring to the nodular ornamentation on its skull.
Nodocephalosaurus.description: Nodocephalosaurus is a monospecific genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur from New Mexico that lived during the Late Cretaceous (late Campanian to early Maastrichtian stage, 73.49 to 72 Ma) in what is now the De-na-zin member of the Kirtland Formation. The type and only species, Nodocephalosaurus kirtlandensis, is known only from a partial skull. It was named in 1999 by Robert M. Sullivan. Nodocephalosaurus has an estimated length of 4.5 meters (15 feet) and weight of 1.5 tonnes (3,306 lbs). It is closely related and shares similar cranial anatomy to Akainacephalus.

Nopcsaspondylus.etymology: Named for Baron Franz Nopcsa, the paleontologist who first described the fossil material, combined with Greek 'spondylos' meaning 'vertebra'; translates as 'Nopcsa's vertebra'.
Nopcsaspondylus.description: Nopcsaspondylus is a dubious genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Cenomanian-aged (Upper Cretaceous) Candeleros Formation of Neuquén, Argentina. It is based on a now-lost back vertebra described by Nopcsa in 1902 but not named at the time. The specimen had a small vertebral body and large hollows, now known to be typical of rebbachisaurids.

Notatesseraeraptor.etymology: From Latin 'nota' (feature), 'tesserae' (mosaic tiles), and 'raptor' (thief); meaning 'feature mosaic tile thief', referencing the mixture of features from dilophosaurids and coelophysoids.
Notatesseraeraptor.description: Notatesseraeraptor is a genus of carnivorous theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Triassic of what is now Switzerland. It was found in the Gruhalde Member of the Klettgau Formation. It was an early member of Neotheropoda with affinities to Dilophosaurus and Averostra. The new genus and species Notatesseraeraptor frickensis was named by Marion Zahner and colleagues in 2019.

Flattened ventral surfaces of sacral centra

Nothronychus.etymology: From Greek 'nothros' meaning 'slothful' and 'onyx' meaning 'claw'; translates as 'slothful claw', a reference to its therizinosaur-like elongated claws and presumed slow-moving herbivorous habits.
Nothronychus.description: Nothronychus is a genus of therizinosaurid theropod dinosaurs that lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous period. The type species, Nothronychus mckinleyi, was described by James Kirkland and Douglas G. Wolfe in 2001. It was recovered near New Mexico's border with Arizona, in an area known as the Zuni Basin, from rocks assigned to the Moreno Hill Formation, dating to the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous. A second specimen, described in 2009 as a second species, Nothronychus graffami, was found in the Tropic Shale of Utah, dating to between one million and 500,000 years older than N. mckinleyi.
diagnostic_features: Distinctly subcircular obturator process of the ischium.
Ovoid, dorsoventrally elongate obturator foramen, its maximum length more than 200% of its maximum width.
Contact between the pubis and ischium restricted to the proximal half of the obturator process.
Deep notch between the ventral aspect of the obturator process and the cranial ischial shaft.

In the type species N. mckinleyi, the ventral notch between the obturator process and the iliac shaft is craniocaudally narrow (wide in N. graffami), the cranial caudal centra are platycoelous, and the caudal centra bear a hypertrophied caudoventral heel about one-third the centrum length.
In N. mckinleyi, the glenoid lacks a caudal buttress and the caudal process of the ischium is poorly defined and elongate, extending to the shaft opposite the obturator process.

species.etymology: Named for rancher Bobby McKinley, on whose land the fossil findings were made.

Notoceratops.etymology: From Greek 'notos' (southern), 'keras' (horn), and 'ops' (face); meaning 'southern horned face', referring to its discovery in the southern part of South America.
Notoceratops.description: Notoceratops is a dubious genus of extinct ornithischian dinosaur. The genus was described based on an incomplete, toothless left dentary (now lost) from the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia (in Argentina), probably dating to the Campanian or Maastrichtian. Initially classified as a putative ceratopsian found in the Lago Colhué Huapi Formation, the lost fragmentary holotype precludes confident referral of this taxon within ornithischians, with some researchers suggesting that it belongs to a hadrosaur instead.

dispute.summary: Notoceratops bonarellii is based on a now-lost dentary; its ceratopsian identity has been both supported and questioned (some regard it as possibly hadrosaurian), and it is treated as a nomen dubium.

history.note: Placed at Ceratopsia incertae sedis; nomen dubium.

Notohypsilophodon.etymology: From Greek 'notos' meaning 'south wind' (indicating its southern provenance in South America) combined with the genus name Hypsilophodon, indicating its similarity to that ornithopod.
Notohypsilophodon.description: Notohypsilophodon is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Argentina. It was described as the only "hypsilophodont" known from South America, although this assessment is not universally supported, and Gasparinisaura is now believed to have been a basal euornithopod as well.

history.note: Placed at Elasmaria following Rozadilla and others (2016) and Jones (2026) (P3, recency and dedicated sampling); the Thescelosaurinae alternative is recorded.

dispute.summary: The placement of Nqwebasaurus is contested. Most recent analyses recover it as the basalmost ornithomimosaur (Choiniere et al., 2012; Serrano-Brañas et al., 2020), but it has also been recovered outside Ornithomimosauria, near the base of Alvarezsauroidea (Hartman et al., 2019), and it was originally described as a coelurosaur of uncertain affinities (de Klerk et al., 2000). It is placed conservatively as the basalmost ornithomimosaur.

Nqwebasaurus.description: Nqwebasaurus is a probable ornithomimosaurian theropod from the Early Cretaceous of South Africa. The genus contains a single species, Nqwebasaurus thwazi, representing the oldest known coelurosaur in Africa and the evidence for basal coelurosaurian dinosaurs inhabiting Gondwana since the earliest Cretaceous period.

Nullotitan.etymology: Named in honor of geologist Francisco Nullo, combined with Greek 'titan' (giant); meaning 'Nullo's giant'.
Nullotitan.description: Nullotitan is an extinct genus of lithostrotian titanosaur dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous Chorrillo Formation of Santa Cruz Province, Argentina. The genus contains a single species, Nullotitan glaciaris. It was a contemporary of the ornithopod Isasicursor, which was described in the same paper.

dispute.summary: Placed within Saltasauroidea as incertae sedis. The describing authors (Novas et al., 2019) did not run a phylogenetic analysis and suspected a colossosaurian affinity on the basis of individual characters, whereas the only cladistic analysis to include it (Cerda et al., 2021) recovered Nullotitan as the sister taxon of Saltasauridae, within Saltasauroidea. It is placed following that analysis, with the describers' colossosaurian suspicion noted.

history.note: Placed at Saltasauroidea incertae sedis per the analysis of Cerda et al. (2021); the describers (Novas et al., 2019) instead suspected a colossosaurian position.

It was originally described as a monitor-like lizard (Owen, 1854), later referred to Dromaeosauridae/Velociraptorinae on tooth and jaw characters (Milner, 2002), and subsequently noted to resemble proceratosaurid tyrannosauroids (Rauhut et al., 2010). It is retained provisionally at Dromaeosauridae incertae sedis.

Nuthetes.etymology: From Koine Greek 'nouthetes' meaning 'one who admonishes' or 'a monitor', referring to the similarity of its teeth to those of a modern monitor lizard.
Nuthetes.description: Nuthetes is a genus of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaur, either a dromaeosaurid or tyrannosauroid, known only from fossil teeth and jaw fragments found in rocks of the middle Berriasian age (Early Cretaceous) in the Cherty Freshwater Member of the Lulworth Formation in England and also the Angeac-Charente bonebed in France. If it was a dromaeosaurid, Nuthetes would have been a small predator.

species.etymology: From Latin 'destructor' meaning 'destroyer', a reference to the adaptations of the teeth for piercing, cutting, and lacerating prey.

Obelignathus.etymology: Named for Obelix, the fictional character from the Asterix and Obelix cartoon, combined with Greek 'gnathos' meaning 'jaw'; refers to the robust morphology of the holotype dentary likened to the strength of that character.
Obelignathus.description: Obelignathus is an extinct genus of rhabdodontomorph ornithopod dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous 'Grès à Reptiles' Formation of France. The genus contains a single species, O. septimanicus, known from a right dentary. The species was initially classified as a species of the coeval Rhabdodon.

dispute.summary: Obelignathus septimanicus (formerly Rhabdodon septimanicus) is recovered as an early-diverging rhabdodontomorph under equal weighting and most implied-weighting analyses, but as an elasmarian under one implied-weighting setting, by Czepiński and Madzia (2025); its position is unstable.

history.note: Placed at Rhabdodontomorpha following the majority result of Czepiński and Madzia (2025); the elasmarian alternative (recovered under one implied-weighting setting) reflected, not adopted.

diagnostic_features: Dentary robust, anteroposteriorly shorter (~3x longer than high) compared to other rhabdodontomorphs (~4x)
Absence of buccal platform lateral to alveolar row
Absence of horizontal buccal crest due to poorly developed anterolateral ridge of coronoid process
Coronoid process placed directly posterior to alveolar row, not laterally separated
Coronoid process rotated lateroposteriorly; lateral and coronoid surfaces face more posteriorly and anteriorly respectively
Meckelian canal mediolaterally and dorsoventrally deep, reaching 50% of dentary height (vs. 22-38% in other rhabdodontomorphs)

species.etymology: Named for Septimania, a historic region of France corresponding to Languedoc, where the type locality in Montouliers is located, with the Latin suffix '-icus' meaning 'of' or 'pertaining to'.

Oblitosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'oblitus' (forgotten or obsolete) and Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'forgotten lizard', referring to how its fossils were long overlooked.
Oblitosaurus.description: Oblitosaurus is a genus of ankylopollexian ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Spain. The type species is Oblitosaurus bunnueli.

Femur with sub-circular distal medial condyle
Femur with pronounced, narrow lateromedial ridge on ventral surface
Tibia with internal condyle projected dorsally above dorsal margin of cnemial crest
Metatarsal IV with sub-triangular or ellipsoid proximal articulation facet

history.note: Placed at Somphospondyli following Mocho et al. (2019) and Jones (2026); the basal macronarian alternative is noted.

Oceanotitan.etymology: From Latin 'oceanus' meaning 'ocean', because the fossil was found at the base of a coastal cliff overlooking the Atlantic Ocean, combined with 'Titan' from Greek mythology meaning 'giant'.
Oceanotitan.description: Oceanotitan is a genus of sauropod dinosaur known from the Upper Jurassic (latest Kimmeridgian stage, about 149 million years ago) Lourinhã Formation of Portugal. It is represented by a single specimen consisting of several tail vertebrae and appendicular bones. It contains one species, Oceanotitan dantasi. Oceanotitan is classified as possibly one of the earliest members of the Somphospondyli, a group of sauropods that includes the titanosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Sagittal groove on dorsal surface of anterior-most caudal vertebral neural spines
Lateral depressions on distal tips of anterior to middle caudal neural spines, dorsally connected posteriorly
Anterior caudal vertebrae with medial accessory articulation on prezygapophysis
Transverse furrow on chevron articulations
Circular, rough tuberosity on medial surface of scapula
Elliptical concavity on ventral face of scapular blade near acromion
Ischium shorter than pubis
Robust fourth trochanter on midline of femoral posterior face
Distal condyles of femur expanded onto anterior portion of shaft
Rectangular morphology of fibular proximal end

Ohmdenosaurus.etymology: Named after the village of Ohmden in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, near where the specimen was found, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Ohmden lizard'
Ohmdenosaurus.description: Ohmdenosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Jurassic epoch in what is now Germany. The only specimen - a tibia (shinbone) and ankle - was discovered in rocks of the Posidonia Shale near the village of Ohmden. The specimen, which was originally identified as a plesiosaur, is exhibited in a local museum, the Urweltmuseum Hauff. In the 1970s, it caught the attention of German paleontologist Rupert Wild, who recognized it as the remains of a sauropod. Wild named Ohmdenosaurus in a 1978 publication; the only known species is Ohmdenosaurus liasicus.
diagnostic_features: Stocky, massive tibia strongly expanded at both joint ends
Cnemial crest sloping, bowed inward laterally, and bounded laterally by a sulcus
Lateral crest on the tibial shaft extending distally to about the shaft midpoint
Proximal tibial joint end perpendicular to the shaft's long axis
Flat, sandal-shaped astragalus lacking an ascending process
Small, disk-shaped calcaneus, with the ankle joint bearing bony sesamoids

species.name: Ohmdenosaurus liasicus
species.etymology: From Latin 'liasicus' meaning 'of the Lias', referring to the Lias, an old name for the Lower Jurassic of Europe, in which the holotype was found.

Ojoceratops.description: Ojoceratops is a genus of ceratopsian dinosaur which lived in what is now New Mexico, United States. Ojoceratops fossils have been recovered from strata of the Ojo Alamo Formation (Naashoibito Member), dating to the late Cretaceous period (late Maastrichtian age, 66 million years ago). The type species is Ojoceratops fowleri.
diagnostic_features: Squamosal enlarged base lacking embayment of otic notch
Squamosal forms 115° angle at epijugal 1 position
Squamosal distal end truncated and squared off
Squamosal medial border concave, lateral border convex forming 80° arc
Parietal median bar expands laterally to ~90 mm with ovoid depressions on lateral wings

species.etymology: Honors Denver Fowler, who discovered the holotype and collected a number of the specimens described in Sullivan and Lucas (2010).

Ojoraptorsaurus.etymology: Combines a reference to the Ojo Alamo Formation (where it was found) with Latin raptor ('plunderer') and Latinised Greek sauros ('lizard'); meaning 'Ojo Alamo plunderer lizard'
Ojoraptorsaurus.description: Ojoraptorsaurus is a dubious genus of oviraptorosaurian dinosaur from the late Cretaceous. Ojoraptorsaurus is only known from pubic bones found at the Naashoibito Member of the Ojo Alamo Formation dating to the late Maastrichtian, about 66 million years ago. It was first named by Robert M. Sullivan, Steven E. Jasinski and Mark P.A. van Tomme in 2011 and the type species is Ojoraptorsaurus boerei. The generic name combines a reference to the formation with a Latin raptor, "plunderer", and a Latinised Greek saurus, "lizard". The specific name honors oceanographer Arjan Boeré who found the specimen.

dispute.summary: Ojoraptorsaurus is a caenagnathid but its validity is contested. It was named from a pair of fused pubes, and Funston and Williamson (2024) reassessed its proposed diagnostic features as non-autapomorphic in light of newer pelvic material, concluding that it should be regarded as a nomen dubium. The Princeton Encyclopedia (Jones, 2026) still treats it as valid.

history.note: Placed at Caenagnathidae; its validity is disputed, having been argued to be a nomen dubium by Funston and Williamson (2024).

diagnostic_features: Spoon-shaped depression on anterior dorsal surface of pubic boot
Enclosed pubic fossa recessed ≥1 cm from acetabular rim on medial shaft surface
Distal pubic shaft above boot slightly convex anteriorly

Oksoko.etymology: From Öksökö, a mythical two-headed bird in Yakut (Sakha) folklore of Siberia
Oksoko.description: Oksoko is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation of Omnogov Province, Mongolia. The type and only species is Oksoko avarsan. It is notable for having only two functional fingers, having lost the third manual digit, suggesting a trend toward digit reduction within oviraptorosaurs.

Olorotitan.etymology: From Latin olor ('swan'), referencing the swan-like elongated neck and crest of this hadrosaur, combined with Greek Titan (a giant); meaning 'giant swan'
Olorotitan.description: Olorotitan is a monotypic genus of lambeosaurine duck-billed dinosaur, containing a single species, O. arharensis. It was among the last non-avian dinosaurs to go extinct during the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event, having lived from the middle to late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period. The remains were found in the Udurchukan Formation beds of Kundur, Arkharinsky District, Amur Oblast, Eastern Russia, in the vicinity of the Amur River.

Sacrum very elongated with 15-16 vertebrae (vs. typical 10-12 in adult hadrosaurids)
Scapula more elongated than other hadrosaurids with length/width ratio of 6.2
Additional articulation between adjacent neural spines on proximal third of tail (knob-cup articulation)

Omeisaurus.etymology: Named after Mount Emei (Omei) in Sichuan Province, China, where it was discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Omei lizard'.
Omeisaurus.description: Omeisaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Middle to Late Jurassic Period (Bathonian-Oxfordian stage) of what is now China. Its name comes from Mount Emei, where it was discovered in the lower Shaximiao Formation of Sichuan Province.
diagnostic_features: Processus pseudospinosus remarkably developed with straight upper border; 255 mm long wing on neck vertebrae
Only 3 primary sacral vertebrae with strongly built sacral ribs and plate-like lamellae
First caudal vertebra with broad transversal fan-like expansion of caudal rib
Coracoid very short and distally rounded with straight scapula border, breadth exceeds length
Femur head well differentiated with prominent fourth trochanter visible from anterior view
Fibula with round shaft lacking ridge from proximal to distal end characteristic of other sauropods

diagnostic_features: Lateral (pleurocoel) depressions of the cervical and dorsal vertebrae more strongly developed than in O. junghsiensis
First caudal rib narrower and less ventrally extended than the broader, more downward-extending first caudal rib of O. junghsiensis

species.name: Omeisaurus jiaoi
species.etymology: Honors Jiao Zheng of the Zigong Dinosaur Museum development group.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete postcranial skeleton lacking skull and cervical vertebrae: 12 dorsal vertebrae, 5 sacral vertebrae, 29 caudal vertebrae, partial dorsal ribs and chevrons, essentially complete pectoral girdle, pelvic girdle, and fore and hind limbs.

diagnostic_features: First caudal vertebra lacks the fan-shaped caudal ribs seen in the Omeisaurus type species and O. tianfuensis; the rib is laterally directed with only slight anteroposterior expansion of the tip.
Tail markedly shorter than in O. tianfuensis: length of the first 25 caudal vertebrae is only 121% of total dorsal length, versus 148% in O. tianfuensis.
First chevron is very slender and articulates with the first caudal vertebra, unlike O. tianfuensis, in which the largest chevron articulates with the second caudal vertebra.
Scapula is more slender with a more expanded distal end (maximum distal width about 2x minimum shaft width) than in O. tianfuensis (about 1.6x).
Dorsal neural spine apices are not greatly expanded and anterior caudal vertebrae lack ventral keels, unlike O. luoquanensis, which also has lower, plate-like anterior caudal neural spines.

Ondogurvel.etymology: From Mongolian 'ondo' meaning 'egg' and 'gurvel' meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'egg lizard'.
Ondogurvel.description: Ondogurvel is a genus of alvarezsaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) Barun Goyot Formation in southern Mongolia. The type and only species is O. alifanovi, known from a partial skeleton consisting of fragments of two last dorsal vertebrae, three anterior sacral vertebrae, right ilium, left and right pubis and ischium, articulated right tibia, fibula, metatarsals II and IV, and phalanges IV-1 and IV-2, right carpometacarpus, left and right manual phalanx II-1, right femur, left pedal phalanx II-1, and fragments of unidentified phalanges.

Supraacetabular crest of ilium arcuate and convex dorsally, with anterior end placed more ventral than posterior end
Vertical ridge on medial side of ischium distal to obturator foramen
Lack of fourth trochanter on femur
Tibia distal end much less expanded transversely relative to shaft
Prominent flat platform ('step') on lateral side of distal lateral tibial condyle

Oohkotokia.etymology: From Blackfoot 'ooh'kotoka' meaning 'large stone' and Latin suffix '-ia' meaning 'derived from', giving the meaning 'child of stone', referring to its extensive body armor; the name also honors the Blackfoot people on whose land the specimen was found.
Oohkotokia.description: Oohkotokia is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur within the subfamily Ankylosaurinae. It is known from the upper levels of the Two Medicine Formation (late Campanian stage, about 74 Ma ago) of Montana, United States. The discovery of Oohkotokia supports that Ankylosaurine dinosaurs existed and flourished continuously in Montana and/or Alberta throughout the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian stages in the Late Cretaceous period. It was a large, heavily built, quadrupedal, herbivore, that could grow up to 5 meters (16 ft) long and weigh up to 2 metric tons (2.2 short tons).

dispute.summary: The validity of Oohkotokia is contested. Arbour and Currie (2015) treated it as a junior synonym of Scolosaurus cutleri, whereas Penkalski (2018) and Wiersma and Irmis (2018) found it distinct. Retained as a valid ankylosaurine pending consensus.

Opisthocoelicaudia.etymology: From Greek 'opisthen' (behind/posterior), 'koilos' (hollow), Latin 'cauda' (tail), and Latin '-ia' (suffix); meaning 'hollow-backed tail', referring to the opisthocoelouos (posteriorly hollowed) tail vertebrae.
Opisthocoelicaudia.description: Opisthocoelicaudia is a genus of sauropod dinosaur of the Late Cretaceous Period discovered in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia. The type species is Opisthocoelicaudia skarzynskii. A well-preserved skeleton lacking only the head and neck was unearthed in 1965 by Polish and Mongolian scientists, making Opisthocoelicaudia one of the best known sauropods from the Late Cretaceous. Tooth marks on this skeleton indicate that large carnivorous dinosaurs had fed on the carcass and possibly had carried away the now-missing parts. To date, only two additional, much less complete specimens are known, including part of a shoulder and a fragmentary tail. A relatively small sauropod, Opisthocoelicaudia measured about 11.4-13 m (37-43 ft) in length. Like other sauropods, it would have been characterized by a small head sitting on a very long neck and a barrel shaped trunk carried by four column-like legs. The name Opisthocoelicaudia means "posterior cavity tail", alluding to the unusual, opisthocoel condition of the anterior tail vertebrae that were concave on their posterior sides. This and other skeletal features lead researchers to propose that Opisthocoelicaudia was able to rear on its hindlegs.

Orkoraptor.etymology: From Aoniken 'Orr-Korr', the local name for the La Leona River near the fossil site, combined with Latin 'raptor' meaning 'thief'; translates as 'Toothed River thief'.
Orkoraptor.description: Orkoraptor is a genus of medium-sized megaraptoran theropod dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Period of Argentina. It is known from incomplete fossil remains including parts of the skull, teeth, tail vertebrae, and a partial tibia. The specialized teeth resemble those of some maniraptoriform theropods, namely the deinonychosaurs and compsognathids. This and other anatomical features led the authors who described it (Novas, Ezcurra, and Lecuona) to suggest that it was a maniraptoran coelurosaur. However, subsequent studies found it to be a megaraptoran. Found in the Cerro Fortaleza Formation of Southern Patagonia, it is one of the southernmost carnivorous dinosaurs known from South America.

dispute.summary: Ornithodesmus cluniculus is based on a single sacrum long misidentified as a bird (Seeley, 1887) and then a pterosaur before Howse and Milner (1993) reidentified it as a small theropod and regarded the genus as a nomen vanum given the limited material. It was later referred to Dromaeosauridae (Naish and Martill, 2007) and recovered as a very basal dromaeosaurid, possibly a member of Unenlagiidae (Hartman et al., 2019). Given the fragmentary type its validity and precise placement remain debated; it is retained at Dromaeosauridae incertae sedis.

Ornithodesmus.etymology: From Greek 'ornis' (bird) and 'desmos' (link or bond); meaning 'bird link'.
Ornithodesmus.description: Ornithodesmus is a genus of small, dromaeosaurid dinosaur from the Isle of Wight in England, dating to about 125 million years ago. The name, along with that of the type and only species, O. cluniculus, was originally assigned to a bird-like sacrum (a series of vertebrae fused to the hip bones), initially believed to come from a bird and subsequently identified as a pterosaur. More complete pterosaur remains were later assigned to Ornithodesmus. More recently, a detailed analysis determined that the original specimen in fact came from a small theropod, specifically a dromaeosaur, making it one of the first dromaeosaurs known to science. All pterosaurian material previously assigned to this genus has been renamed Istiodactylus.

Ornithomimoides.etymology: From Greek 'ornis' (bird), 'mimos' (mimic), and '-oides' (resembling); meaning 'bird mimic-like', indicating resemblance to ornithomimosaurs.
Ornithomimoides.description: Ornithomimoides is a dubious genus of theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) Lameta Formation of India. The type species, O. mobilis, and the doubtfully referred O.? barasimlensis were named and described by Huene and Matley in 1933, and are known only from isolated vertebrae of the Lameta "Carnosaur bed"; O. mobilis is based on five large vertebrae and O.? barasimlensis on a smaller set. Novas et al. (2004) reinterpreted the type vertebrae as proximal caudals of an indeterminate abelisauroid and, finding no diagnostic features, considered the genus a nomen dubium.

It is usually classified into two species: the type species, Ornithomimus velox, and a referred species, Ornithomimus edmontonicus.

Oryctodromeus.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'oruktēs' meaning 'digger' and 'dromaios' meaning 'runner'; translates as 'digging runner', reflecting its unique status as the first non-avian dinosaur with evidence of burrowing behavior.
Oryctodromeus.description: Oryctodromeus is an extinct genus of small orodromine thescelosaurid dinosaur. Fossils are known from the Late Cretaceous Blackleaf Formation of southwestern Montana and the Wayan Formation of southeastern Idaho, USA, both of the Cenomanian stage, roughly 105-96 million years ago. A member of the small, presumably fast-running herbivorous family Thescelosauridae, Oryctodromeus is the first non-avian dinosaur published that shows evidence of burrowing behavior.

Ouranosaurus.etymology: From Tuareg 'ouranou' meaning 'brave' or 'valiant' (the local name for the monitor lizard) and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', giving the meaning 'brave lizard' or 'valiant lizard'.
Ouranosaurus.description: Ouranosaurus is a genus of herbivorous basal hadrosauriform dinosaur that lived during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous of modern-day Niger and Cameroon. Ouranosaurus measured about 7-8.3 meters (23-27 ft) long and weighed 2.2 metric tons (2.4 short tons). Two rather complete fossils were found in the Elrhaz Formation, Gadoufaoua deposits, Agadez, Niger, in 1965 and 1970, with a third indeterminate specimen known from the Koum Formation of Cameroon. The animal was named in 1976 by French paleontologist Philippe Taquet, the type species being Ouranosaurus nigeriensis. The generic name is a combination of ourane, a word with multiple meanings, and sauros, the Greek word for lizard. The specific epithet nigeriensis alludes to Niger, its country of discovery (in Latin, the adjectival suffix -iensis means "originating from"). As such, Ouranosaurus nigeriensis could be interpreted as "brave lizard originating from Niger".

Overosaurus.etymology: Named after the Cerro Overo locality in Patagonia, Argentina, combined with Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "Overo lizard".
Overosaurus.description: Overosaurus is an extinct genus of sauropod dinosaurs, containing only a single species, Overosaurus paradasorum. This species lived approximately 86 to 84 million years ago during the latter part of the Cretaceous Period in what is now Patagonia (in southern Argentina). Overosaurus paradasorum was relatively small compared to other sauropods from Patagonia, like the saltasaurids and other aeolosaurines, estimated as approximately 10 m (33 ft). It was a ground-dwelling herbivore.

Oviraptor.etymology: From Latin ovum ('egg') and raptor ('thief'), meaning 'egg thief', based on the initial (later revised) interpretation that it was stealing eggs
Oviraptor.description: Oviraptor is a genus of oviraptorid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period. The first remains were collected from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia in 1923 during a paleontological expedition led by Roy Chapman Andrews, and in the following year the genus and type species Oviraptor philoceratops were named by Henry Fairfield Osborn. The genus name refers to the initial thought of egg-stealing habits, and the specific name was intended to reinforce this view indicating a preference over ceratopsian eggs. Despite the fact that numerous specimens have been referred to the genus, Oviraptor is only known from a single partial skeleton regarded as the holotype, as well as a nest of about fifteen eggs and several small fragments from a juvenile.

Dentary anterior to the coronoid process proportionately longer than in Citipati, its dorsal edge descending less steeply anterior to the mandibular fenestra.
Maxilla relatively longer than in other oviraptorids (though shorter than in caenagnathid outgroups).
Anterior end of the jugal not extending forward beneath the antorbital fenestra (as it does in Citipati), resembling Khaan.

Owenodon.etymology: Named for Richard Owen, the British paleontologist who first described the specimen, combined with Greek 'odon' meaning 'tooth'.
Owenodon.description: Owenodon is a genus of iguanodontian dinosaur known from a partial lower jaw discovered in Early Cretaceous-aged rocks of Dorset, United Kingdom, and possibly also Romania and Spain. The first and only definitive specimen was found in the Durlston Formation of the Purbeck Limestone Group, dating to the middle Berriasian stage.

Fifteen alveoli, the most posterior curving laterally into the base of the coronoid process; coronoid process elevated but obliquely inclined posterodorsally and not anteroposteriorly expanded near its apex.

Pachycephalosaurus.etymology: From Greek pachys (παχύς, 'thick'), kephalon (κεφαλή, 'head'), and sauros (σαῦρος, 'lizard'), meaning 'thick-headed lizard'
Pachycephalosaurus.description: Pachycephalosaurus is a genus of pachycephalosaurid ornithischian dinosaur. The type species, P. wyomingensis, is the only known definitive species. The possibly synonymous taxon, Stygimoloch, might represent a distinct genus or a second species, P. spinifer. It lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now western North America. Remains have been excavated in Montana, South Dakota, Wyoming, and Alberta. Mainly known from a single skull and a few extremely thick skull roofs (at 22 cm (8.7 in) thick), Pachycephalosaurus is estimated to have reached 4.5 m (15 ft) long and weighed 370-450 kg (820-990 lb). More complete fossils would come to be found in the following years.

Padillasaurus.etymology: Named for Carlos Bernardo Padilla, founder of the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Padillasaurus.description: Padillasaurus is an extinct genus of titanosauriform sauropod known from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian stage) Paja Formation in Colombia. It contains a single species, Padillasaurus leivaensis, known only from a single partial axial skeleton. Initially described as a brachiosaurid, it was considered to be the first South American brachiosaurid ever discovered and named. Before its discovery, the only known brachiosaurid material on the continent was very fragmentary and from the Jurassic period. However, a more recent study finds it to be a basal somphospondylan.

Palaeoscincus.etymology: From Greek 'palaios' meaning 'ancient' and 'skinkos' meaning 'lizard' (related to skink); translates as 'ancient lizard'.
Palaeoscincus.description: Palaeoscincus is a dubious genus of ankylosaurian dinosaur based on teeth from the mid-late Campanian-age Upper Cretaceous Judith River Formation of Montana. Like several other dinosaur genera named by Joseph Leidy (Deinodon, Thespesius, and Trachodon), it is an historically important genus with a convoluted taxonomy that has been all but abandoned by modern dinosaur paleontologists. Because of its wide use in the early 20th century, it was somewhat well known to the general public, often through illustrations of an animal with the armor of Edmontonia and the tail club of an ankylosaurid.

The genus contains a single species, P. micros (from the Greek word for "small"), which is known from a single specimen consisting of a mostly complete and fully-articulated left foot, which preserves the iconic dromaeosaur-like "killing claw".

Panguraptor.etymology: Named after Pangu, the Chinese creator deity (also evoking the supercontinent Pangaea), combined with Latin raptor (seizer, robber); meaning "Pangu plunderer".
Panguraptor.description: Panguraptor is a genus of coelophysoid theropod dinosaur known from fossils discovered in Lower Jurassic rocks of southern China. The type and only known species is Panguraptor lufengensis. The generic name refers to the deity Pangu but also to the supercontinent Pangaea for which in a geological context the same characters are used: 盘古. Raptor means "seizer", "robber" in Latin. The specific name is a reference to the Lufeng Formation. It was described in 2014 by You Hai-Lu and colleagues.
diagnostic_features: Diagonal rostrodorsal-caudoventral ridge on the lateral surface of the maxilla, extending beyond the antorbital fossa with a shallow groove dorsal to it (autapomorphy).
Group of four elliptical, laterally facing foramina on the lateral surface of the maxilla anterior to the antorbital fenestra, one behind the diagonal ridge and three in front (autapomorphy).
Distinct bony ridge along the dorsal margin of the lateral surface of the scapula (autapomorphy).
Hooked structure at the ventrolateral corner of the proximal head of distal tarsal IV (autapomorphy).
Large, deep, circular anterior pleurocoel on cervical vertebrae III-X, versus the shallow elliptical pleurocoel of other coelophysoids.
Cervical rib length subequal to the centrum length from cervicals III to VIII, rather than markedly exceeding it as in other coelophysoids.

Panoplosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'panoplos' meaning 'fully armored' or 'well-armored' and '-saurus' meaning 'lizard', referring to its extensive armor plating.
Panoplosaurus.description: Panoplosaurus is a genus of armored dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada. Few specimens of the genus are known, all from the middle Campanian of the Dinosaur Park Formation, roughly 76 to 75 million years ago. It was first discovered in 1917, and named in 1919 by Lawrence Lambe, named for its extensive armor, meaning "well-armored lizard". Panoplosaurus has at times been considered the proper name for material otherwise referred to as Edmontonia, complicating its phylogenetic and ecological interpretations, at one point being considered to have existed across Alberta, New Mexico and Texas, with specimens in institutions from Canada and the United States. The skull and skeleton of Panoplosaurus are similar to its relatives, but have a few significant differences, such as the lumpy form of the skull osteoderms, a completely fused shoulder blade, and regularly shaped plates on its neck and body lacking prominent spines. It was a quadrupedal animal, roughly 5 m (16 ft) long and 1,600 kg (3,500 lb) in weight. The skull has a short snout, with a very domed surface, and bony plates directly covering the cheek. The neck had circular groups of plates arranged around the top surface, both the forelimb and hindlimb were about the same length, and the hand may have only included three fingers. Almost the entire surface of the body was covered in plates, osteoderms and scutes of varying sizes, ranging from large elements along the skull and neck, to smaller, round bones underneath the chin and body, to small ossicles that filled in the spaces between other, larger osteoderms.

Lacrimal caputegulae small, contacting the nasal caputegulae medially and not extending over the dorsal skull surface
Postorbital boss covered by numerous small, randomly arranged caputegulae

Panphagia.etymology: From Greek 'pan' meaning 'all' and 'phagein' meaning 'to eat', referring to its interpreted omnivorous diet as a basal sauropodomorph.
Panphagia.description: Panphagia is a genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur described in 2009. It lived around 231 million years ago, during the Carnian age of the Late Triassic period in what is now northwestern Argentina. Fossils of the genus were found in the La Peña Member of the Ischigualasto Formation in the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión Basin. The name Panphagia comes from the Greek words pan, meaning "all", and phagein, meaning "to eat", in reference to its inferred omnivorous diet. Panphagia is one of the earliest known dinosaurs, and is an important find which may mark the transition of diet in early sauropodomorph dinosaurs.

dispute.summary: Panphagia protos is an early sauropodomorph from the Late Triassic of Argentina whose membership in Saturnaliidae is not firmly established. Langer et al. (2019) recovered it within the clade in most of their most-parsimonious trees but described its position as floating, nesting outside a less inclusive Saturnaliidae in others. Ezcurra (2010) recovered it outside Saturnaliinae as a more basal guaibasaurid, and Martinez and Alcober (2009), describing the genus, placed it as the most basal sauropodomorph, sister to Saturnalia and all more derived members of the group.

history.note: Placed at Saturnaliidae following its common recovery there; the basal-Sauropodomorpha-incertae-sedis alternative is recorded.

Paralititan.etymology: From Greek parali (tidal, of the sea) and titan (giant); meaning "tidal giant".
Paralititan.description: Paralititan is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day Egypt during the Late Cretaceous period. It was described by American paleontologist Joshua B. Smith and colleagues in 2001. The genus contains a single species, Paralititan stromeri, named based on a fragmentary skeleton including vertebrae and limb bones. These fossils were unearthed by an American expedition to the Bahariya Oasis in western Egypt in rock layers of the Bahariya Formation. This formation dates to the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, which lasted 101 to 94 million years ago. An incomplete dorsal (back) vertebra that had been described by German paleontologist Ernst Stromer in 1932 was also assigned to Paralititan. However, this vertebra had been destroyed during the Bombing of Munich in World War II.

dispute.summary: Placed within Lithostrotia as incertae sedis. The fragmentary holotype and brief original description leave the position very uncertain. The describing analysis (Smith et al., 2001) nested Paralititan within Titanosauridae using a small matrix, whereas a recent analysis recovers it within Saltasauridae, close to Maxakalisaurus (Vila et al., 2022). It is placed at Lithostrotia pending resolution.

history.note: Placed at Lithostrotia incertae sedis; a saltasaurid position is reported in recent work.

Pararhabdodon.etymology: From Greek 'para' meaning 'near' or 'beside' combined with the genus name Rhabdodon (meaning 'fluted tooth'); translates as 'near fluted tooth', indicating its close relationship to Rhabdodon.
Pararhabdodon.description: Pararhabdodon is a genus of tsintaosaurin hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Maastrichtian-aged (Late Cretaceous) Tremp Group of Spain. The first remains were discovered from the Sant Romà d'Abella fossil locality and assigned to the genus Rhabdodon, and later named as the distinct species Pararhabdodon isonensis in 1993. Known material includes assorted postcranial remains, mostly vertebrae, as well as maxillae from the skull. Specimens from other sites, including remains from France, a maxilla previously considered the distinct taxon Koutalisaurus kohlerorum, an additional maxilla from another locality, the material assigned to the genera Blasisaurus and Arenysaurus, and the extensive Basturs Poble bonebed have been considered at different times to belong to the species, but all of these assignments have more recently been questioned. It was one of the last non-avian dinosaurs known from the fossil record that went extinct during the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event.

Parasaurolophus.etymology: From Greek para (beside, near) and the genus name Saurolophus (crested lizard); meaning "beside crested lizard", reflecting Parks's view that the new genus's affinities lay with Saurolophus from the Edmonton Formation.
Parasaurolophus.description: Parasaurolophus is one of the most recognizable lambeosaurine hadrosaurs, distinguished by an elongate hollow cranial crest formed largely of the premaxillae (with the nasals) that projects well posterior to the occiput. Parks erected the genus in 1922 on a skull and partial articulated skeleton (ROM 768) collected by a University of Toronto expedition in 1920 from the Belly River beds of the Red Deer River, Alberta — strata now assigned to the lower Dinosaur Park Formation. Parks himself raised the question of whether the hollow tubes carried air, anticipating the long-running interpretation that the crest housed elongated nasal passages and may have functioned as a resonating chamber for vocal display. Three further species are recognized today — P. tubicen and P. cyrtocristatus from the San Juan Basin and Kaiparowits regions of the southwestern United States, and the disputed Asian P. jiayinensis (often referred to its own genus, Charonosaurus). Material remains rare across the entire range, and Evans, Bavington and Campione (2009) documented that even the Alberta type material likely represents a subadult, with the crest not yet at its fully developed adult expression.
diagnostic_features: Tubular narial crest, short to long and slightly curved, composed largely of the premaxillae — unique among hadrosaurs.
Prefrontals lapping onto the ventral lateral surface of the premaxilla where the skull roof meets the narial crest.
Frontals arising from the posterior base of the crest and extending posteriorly to meet the nasals anterior to the rear extent of the squamosals.
Narial crest divided externally into dorsal and ventral tracts by a longitudinal lateral groove running nearly its full length on each side.
Crest interior comprises parallel thin-walled bony tubes continuous with the external nares.
Anteriorly extended pubic peduncle of the ilium strongly decurved distally and forming an externally overlapping joint with the pubis.
Cervical postzygapophyses on vertebrae 8-13 strongly elongate and curved ventrally, reaching ~110 mm in length.

species.name: Parasaurolophus walkeri
species.etymology: Honoring Sir Edmund Walker, Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the Royal Ontario Museum, which sponsored the 1920 University of Toronto expedition that recovered the holotype.

type_specimen.material: Articulated skull with complete crest, 13 cervical and 17 dorsal vertebrae, sacrum, six caudal vertebrae, both scapulocoracoids, both fore limbs, partial pelvis (left side only), and left femur, with associated skin impressions; tail and most of the hindlimbs not preserved.

species.name: Parasaurolophus cyrtocristatus
species.etymology: From Greek 'kyrtos' ('curved') and Latin 'cristatus' ('crested'), referring to the short, strongly downcurved crest.

location.locality: Coal Creek, near Tsaya, McKinley County

type_specimen.material: Cranial crest, dorso-caudal cranium, left dentary fragment, cervical-caudal vertebrae, scapulae, humeri, forelimb bones, ischia, ilia, pubes, femora, tibiae, ribs, chevrons, phalanges.

diagnostic_features: Cranial crest short, about one-third the length of P. walkeri's (~260 mm behind the occiput versus ~860 mm), curving strongly posteroventrally rather than arcing dorsocaudally.
Total skull length exceeding ~1425 mm (versus ~1733 mm in P. walkeri).
Narial passages separated by a median bony septum (as in P. walkeri; absent in P. tubicen).
Internal narial tubes simple and paired, running from the external nares to the crest apex and U-bending forward into the choana.
Lateral diverticula positioned medially between the dorsal and ventral ascending tracts, divided dorsally by a sagittal septum.
Radius (585 mm) longer than the humerus (565 mm), unlike P. walkeri (humerus 520 mm exceeding radius 496 mm).

species.name: Parasaurolophus tubicen
species.etymology: From Latin 'tubicen' ('trumpeter'), alluding to the elongate, trumpet-like narial crest.

type_specimen.material: Incomplete skull and narial crest, including posterior skull roof (parietal, postorbital, squamosal), basicranium (basioccipital, basisphenoid), right maxilla, jugal, and partial palatine.

diagnostic_features: Narial crest internally more complex than in P. walkeri, with a pair of dorsal tubes plus two further tube pairs that U-bend and coalesce into a single ventral tube pair.
Lateral diverticula paired, forming a tight U-bend and fusing anteriorly with the ventral ascending tubes before entering the choana.
Dorsal and dorsolateral surfaces of the narial crest bearing anastomosing furrows, absent in P. walkeri.
Narial crest long, in contrast to the short, sharply curved crest of P. cyrtocristatus.

Paraxenisaurus.etymology: From Greek para (near, beside) and xenos (strange) and sauros (lizard); meaning "strange lizard".
Paraxenisaurus.description: Paraxenisaurus is an extinct genus of ornithomimosaurian theropod from the Late Cretaceous Cerro del Pueblo Formation of Coahuila in Mexico. The genus contains a single species, P. normalensis, which is known from a few bones of tail, hips, hands, and feet. The specific epithet was given in honor of the Benemérita Normal School of Coahuila, a teacher training institution, where the fossils were reposited. It is a member of the family Deinocheiridae and is the only member of that clade known from Laramidia.

Pareisactus.description: Pareisactus is a genus of rhabdodontid ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (lower Maastrichtian) Conquès Member of the Tremp Formation in the Southern Pyrenees of Spain. The type and only species is P. evrostos, known only from a single scapula.

Parksosaurus.etymology: Named after Canadian paleontologist William A. Parks, who discovered the specimen, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Parks's lizard'
Parksosaurus.description: Parksosaurus is a genus of neornithischian dinosaur from the early Maastrichtian-aged (Upper Cretaceous) Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, Canada. It is based on most of a partially articulated skeleton and partial skull, showing it to have been a small, bipedal, herbivorous dinosaur. It is one of the few described non-hadrosaurid ornithopods from the end of the Cretaceous in North America, existing around 70 million years ago.

dispute.summary: Parksosaurus is most often recovered within Thescelosaurinae, close to Thescelosaurus (Boyd, 2015; Manitkoon and others, 2023), the position followed by Jones (2026). Herne and others (2019) instead recovered it as the basalmost ornithopod, and Rozadilla and others (2016) near basal Iguanodontia.

history.note: Placed at Thescelosaurinae following the prevailing view; the basal-ornithopod alternative of Herne and others (2019) is recorded.

It is a tooth taxon, often considered dubious because of the fragmentary nature of the fossils, which include "buckets" of teeth from many disparate times and places but no other remains, and should be considered a form taxon.

Parvicursor.description: Parvicursor is a genus of very small alvarezsaurid maniraptoran dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of Mongolia. It had long, slender legs adapted for fast running.

Patagonykus.etymology: Named for Patagonia, the region of Argentina where it was found, combined with Greek 'onyx' meaning 'claw'; translates as 'Patagonian claw'.
Patagonykus.description: Patagonykus is a genus of alvarezsauroid theropod dinosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of Argentina. It was discovered in exposures of the Portezuelo Formation (Turonian-Coniacian) of the Rio Neuquén Subgroup in the Neuquén Basin, Neuquén Province. The holotype consists of an incomplete but well-preserved skeleton, lacking a skull, but including many vertebrae, the coracoids, a partial forelimb, pelvic girdle, and hindlimbs. Patagonykus has been classed with the Alvarezsauridae, a family which includes such taxa as the Mongolian Mononykus and the also Argentinian Alvarezsaurus. In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 1 meter (3.3 ft) and its weight at 3.5 kilograms (7.7 lb).

Patagopelta.etymology: Named after Patagonia, the region in Argentina where it was found, combined with Latin pelta (shield); meaning "Patagonian shield".
Patagopelta.description: Patagopelta is an extinct genus of ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (upper Campanian-lower Maastrichtian) Allen Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, P. cristata, known from several partial skeletons, isolated bones, and osteoderms. While originally described as a member of the family Nodosauridae, later discoveries provided support for parankylosaurian affinities. Patagopelta is a small armored dinosaur, comparable in size to the 'dwarf' nodosaurid Struthiosaurus, at about 2 m (6.6 ft) long. It is larger, more robust, and more heavily armored than other paranklyosaurs such as Stegouros.

dispute.summary: The placement of Patagopelta is contested. Its describers (Riguetti et al., 2022) and Jones and Viola (2026) place it as a nodosaurine nodosaurid, whereas Soto-Acuña et al. (2024) recovered it within Parankylosauria. It is placed at Nodosauridae following the prevailing view.

history.note: Placed at Nodosauridae, with a recovered-as-parankylosaurian alternative noted.

Patagosaurus.etymology: Named for Patagonia, the region of Argentina where it was found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Patagonia lizard'.
Patagosaurus.description: Patagosaurus is an extinct genus of eusauropod dinosaur from the middle Toarcian of Patagonia, Argentina. It was first found in deposits of the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, which date to around 178 million years ago. Although originally twelve specimens were assigned to the taxon, at least one of them may belong to a different genus. Patagosaurus probably lived alongside genera such as Piatnitzkysaurus, Condorraptor, and Volkheimeria.
