Sarcolestes.etymology: From Ancient Greek sarx (flesh) and lestes (robber); meaning "flesh robber".
Sarcolestes.description: Sarcolestes is an extinct genus of ankylosaurian ornithischian dinosaur from the Oxford Clay of England. The current type and only species is S. leedsi, and the holotype is a single partial left mandible. The genus and species were named in 1893 by Richard Lydekker, who thought they belonged to a theropod.

dispute.summary: Sarcolestes is one of the earliest ankylosaurs (Callovian) but is known from a single fragmentary mandible, too incomplete to assign to a family. It is retained at Ankylosauria incertae sedis.

Dental succession with replacing teeth perforating jaw internally, subsequently breaking into main alveoli (unlike crocodilians)
Theropod characters: quadratic cavity narrower than crocodilians, articular production behind cavity less pronounced, surangular upper margin rises above quadratic cavity plane

Sarcosaurus.description: Sarcosaurus is a genus of basal neotheropod dinosaur, roughly 3.5 meters (11 ft) long. It lived in what is now England and maybe Ireland and Scotland during the Hettangian-Sinemurian stages of the Early Jurassic, about 199-196 million years ago. Sarcosaurus is one of the earliest known Jurassic theropods, and one of only a handful of theropod genera from this time period. Along with Dracoraptor hanigani it is one of the two described neotheropods from the lowermost Jurassic of the United Kingdom.
diagnostic_features: Ilium with the main axis of the preacetabular process strongly anteroventrally oriented in lateral view (also in Eoabelisaurus).
Ilium with an only slightly posteriorly projecting ischiadic peduncle (autapomorphy).
Ilium without a laterally exposed ventromedial margin of the brevis fossa, only a short portion of its base exposed (also in Cryolophosaurus).
Ilium with a poorly transversely expanded brevis fossa (also in non-coelophysid neotheropods).
Femur with a dorsolateral trochanter on the proximal end (also in the referred WARMS G667-690 and other non-averostran neotheropods).
Femoral fourth trochanter poorly posteriorly expanded, raised as a low ridge (also in WARMS G667-690, coelophysids, and early ceratosaurians).

Saurolophus.etymology: From Greek sauros (lizard) and lophos (crest); meaning "lizard crest".
Saurolophus.description: Saurolophus is a genus of large hadrosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of North America and Asia, in what is now the Horseshoe Canyon and Nemegt formations respectively (about 70 to 66 million years ago). It is one of the few dinosaur genera known from multiple continents. The type species, S. osborni, was described by Barnum Brown in 1912 from Canadian fossils. A second valid species, S. angustirostris, is represented by numerous specimens from Mongolia, and was described by Anatoly Konstantinovich Rozhdestvensky. Saurolophus is distinguished by a spike-like crest which projects up and back from the skull. It was a herbivorous dinosaur which could move either bipedally or quadrupedally.

Sauroniops.etymology: From Sauron, the fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien, and Greek 'ops' (eye); meaning 'eye of Sauron'.
Sauroniops.description: Sauroniops is a controversial genus of carnivorous carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian stage) of Morocco. It is known from the Gara Sbaa Formation of the Kem Kem beds and contains a single species, S. pachytholus.

dispute.summary: The validity of Sauroniops is actively contested. Ibrahim et al. (2020) argued that S. pachytholus is a junior synonym of Carcharodontosaurus saharicus, interpreting the holotype as an immature C. saharicus frontal and finding the diagnostic characters unconvincing. Paterna and Cau (2022) rebutted this, reaffirming the diagnosis and reporting additional Kem Kem carcharodontosaurid material distinct from C. saharicus. Kellermann, Cuesta and Rauhut (2025) declined the synonymy but treated Sauroniops as a nomen dubium, holding that erecting a taxon on a single frontal is inappropriate pending more material.

history.note: Retained at Carcharodontosauridae incertae sedis; validity (nomen dubium per Kellermann et al., 2025) and the proposed synonymy with Carcharodontosaurus remain unresolved.

diagnostic_features: Dorsoventrally thickened frontal with body depth ranging 28% (medial suture) to 38% (anteromedial margin of supratemporal fossa) of bone length.
Thick dome-like eminence in the anterolateral corner of the dorsal surface of the frontal at the level of the prefrontal-lacrimal articulations.
Prefrontal facet of the frontal trapezoidal, mostly restricted to the anterodorsal margin of the lateral surface, not participating in the orbital fossa.
Frontal with interdigitate suture for prefrontal restricted to the anteroventral corner of the facet, formed by a low shelf and a small finger-like projection.
Hypertrophied 'D-shaped' lacrimal facet with maximum depth four times the depth of the anterior half of the postorbital facet.

Dorsal surface of frontal anterior to supratemporal fossa raised and facing anterodorsally, forming a saddle-shaped concavity with the anterolateral dome, confluent with anteromedial rugosities posterior to the nasal facet.

Sauropelta.etymology: From Greek 'sauros' (lizard) + 'pelte' (small shield), meaning 'lizard shield', referring to the bony armor covering the body.
Sauropelta.description: Sauropelta is a genus of nodosaurid dinosaur that existed in the Early Cretaceous Period of North America. One species (S. edwardsorum) has been named. Anatomically, Sauropelta is one of the most well-understood nodosaurids, with fossilized remains recovered in the U.S. states of Wyoming, Montana, and possibly Utah. It is also the earliest known genus of nodosaurine; most of its remains are found in a section of the Cloverly Formation dated to 108.5 million years ago.
diagnostic_features: Long mandibular tooth row with 25-27 alveoli extending close to symphysis, distinct from nodosaurs with fewer alveoli
Unfused atlas-axis with odontoid only fused to axis centrum, a primitive acanthopholid condition not seen in nodosaurs
Dermal armor consisting of hollow-based plates with concave to deeply hollowed inferior surfaces, more delicate than nodosaurs
Unfused ribs to dorsal vertebrae and unfused chevrons to caudal centra, distinct from nodosaur condition
Long slender femur relative to humerus with well-rounded internal condyles projecting far backward
Long narrow anterior iliac blade extending forward with long preacetabular process, characteristic of acanthopholids

notable_specimens.significance: Called one of the best-preserved nodosaurid skeletons known, preserving a large amount of body armor in situ. On display at the American Museum of Natural History, it let Carpenter accurately describe and reconstruct Sauropelta's armor arrangement.
Preserves the cervical armor and most of a skull, missing only the end of the snout, supplying cranial anatomy absent from the skull-less holotype skeleton.

dispute.summary: Saurophaganax maximus has historically been treated as a giant allosaurid, either a distinct genus or a species of Allosaurus (A. maximus; Smith, 1998). Danison et al. (2024) argued that the referred material is a chimera of a large Allosaurus and a diplodocid sauropod and that the holotype neural arch is undiagnostic, rendering Saurophaganax a nomen dubium; they erected Allosaurus anax for the theropod material. Pending broad acceptance of that reassessment — and following its retention as a valid taxon in the Tetanurae analysis of Carrano et al. (2012) — the genus is kept conservatively at Allosauridae.

history.note: Retained at Allosauridae; the chimera and nomen dubium argument of Danison et al. (2024), and the proposed transfer of the valid theropod material to Allosaurus anax, are noted but not yet adopted.

Saurophaganax.etymology: From Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', 'phagein' meaning 'to eat', and 'anax' meaning 'ruler' or 'lord'; meaning 'lord of lizard-eaters.'
Saurophaganax.description: Saurophaganax is a dubious, chimeric genus of large saurischian dinosaur, possibly a sauropod, from the Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian) Morrison Formation of Oklahoma, United States. This taxon was historically considered to represent a species of Allosaurus or very large allosaurid. However, re-examinations of the attributed specimens suggested that it is a chimera of multiple dinosaur genera, since some specimens most likely belong to a diplodocid sauropod, while the other referred specimens could be reassigned to a novel species of Allosaurus.
diagnostic_features: Horizontal lamina along base of each side of neural spine, arising from spine base cranially but free caudally
Atlas lacks prezygapophyses for proatlas and does not roof over neural canal
Chevrons craniocaudally expanded distally

Sauroplites.etymology: From Greek sauros (lizard) and hoplites (armed foot soldier, hoplite); meaning "saurian hoplite".
Sauroplites.description: Sauroplites is a genus of herbivorous ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of China.
diagnostic_features: Transverse rows of large dermal plates with at least six plates per side in at least one row (vs. three in Palaeoscincus), circular to rhombic in outline with marginal pit-and-ridge zones for connective-tissue attachment
Large plate M with a deep V-shaped cross-section (upper and lower lamellae separated by a deep pocket) and a serrated keel bearing at least six small marginal spines posteriorly
Composite plate F with a central near-circular main portion fused with peripheral smaller ossicles and a deep central concavity on the internal surface
Ribs bearing a pronounced rugose dorsal surface from ~6 cm above the tuberculum, functioning as integument-attachment surface, with strongly broadened cross-section in that zone
Fused pelvic armor of co-ossified polygonal plates (~10 cm diameter) interspersed with rows of much smaller, variably sized plates; no external elevations on individual pelvic plates

Sauroposeidon.description: Sauroposeidon is a genus of sauropod dinosaur known from several incomplete specimens including a bone bed and fossilized trackways that have been found in the U.S. states of Oklahoma, Wyoming, and Texas.

Saurornithoides.etymology: From Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', 'ornis' (stem 'ornith') meaning 'bird', and 'eidos' meaning 'form' or 'resemblance', referring to its bird-like skull.
Saurornithoides.description: Saurornithoides is a genus of troodontid maniraptoran dinosaur, which lived during the Late Cretaceous period. These creatures were predators, which could run fast on their hind legs and had excellent sight and hearing. The name is derived from the Greek stems saur~ (lizard), ornith~ (bird) and eides (form), referring to its bird-like skull.
diagnostic_features: Diapsid skull with five craniofacial fenestrations and one mandibular fenestration
Long pointed rostrum suggesting avian affinities but reptilian/megalosaurian in form
Teeth subhomodont, flattened, serrate on posterior borders only (unlike Velociraptor)
Four premaxillary and fifteen maxillary teeth with uniform replacement and closely compacted crowns
Hind limb with four digits of typical megalosaurian type; terminal claw 30 mm recurved

Saurornitholestes.etymology: From Greek sauros (lizard), ornithos (bird), and lestes (thief); meaning "lizard-bird thief".
Saurornitholestes.description: Saurornitholestes is a genus of carnivorous dromaeosaurid theropod dinosaur from the late Cretaceous of Canada (Alberta and Saskatchewan) and the United States (Montana, New Mexico, Alabama, and South Carolina). Two species have been named that are regarded as valid: Saurornitholestes langstoni in 1978 and Saurornitholestes sullivani in 2015. Saurornitholestes was a small, bipedal, meat-eating dinosaur, equipped with a sickle-like claw on each foot.

Savannasaurus.etymology: From English 'savanna', referring to the open grassland/savanna landscape of Queensland, Australia where its fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Savannasaurus.description: Savannasaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Winton Formation of Queensland, Australia. It contains one species, Savannasaurus elliottorum, named in 2016 by Stephen Poropat and colleagues. The holotype and only known specimen, originally nicknamed "Wade", is the most complete specimen of an Australian sauropod, and is held at the Australian Age of Dinosaurs museum. Dinosaurs known from contemporary rocks include its close relative Diamantinasaurus and the theropod Australovenator; associated teeth suggest that Australovenator may have fed on the holotype specimen.
diagnostic_features: Undulating anterior articular surface of the anterior caudal centra (concave dorsally, convex ventrally)
Anteriormost caudal centra with shallow lateral pneumatic fossae (local autapomorphy within Somphospondyli)
Sternal plate with a straight lateral margin (reversal) and lacking an anteroposteriorly elongate ridge along the anterior part of the ventral surface
Metacarpal IV with an hourglass-shaped distal end; pubis with a ridge extending anteroventrally from the ventral margin of the obturator foramen on the lateral surface
Ischium with the proximal plate's anteroposterior length greater than 40% of the element's overall proximodistal length
Astragalus taller proximodistally than wide mediolaterally or long anteroposteriorly, with mediolateral width and anteroposterior length essentially equal

dispute.summary: Scansoriopteryx heilmanni and Epidendrosaurus ningchengensis were described within months of one another from separate juvenile specimens and are widely regarded as the same taxon. Which name has priority turns on publication medium rather than on the anatomy: Epidendrosaurus appeared online first, Scansoriopteryx in print first, and Article 21 of the ICZN does not recognize online-only publication. Scansoriopteryx is treated as the senior synonym here and by Jones et al. (2026), though the two names remain in competing use in the literature.

history.note: Placed at Scansoriopterygidae (type genus); the Epidendrosaurus synonymy and priority question remains unresolved.

Scansoriopteryx.etymology: From Latin 'scansorius' meaning 'climbing' and Greek 'pteryx' meaning 'wing'; meaning 'climbing wing', in reference to its arboreal adaptations.
Scansoriopteryx.description: Scansoriopteryx is a genus of maniraptoran dinosaur. Described from only a single juvenile fossil specimen found in Liaoning, China, Scansoriopteryx is a sparrow-sized animal that shows adaptations in the foot indicating an arboreal (tree-dwelling) lifestyle. It possessed an unusual, elongated third finger which may have supported a membranous wing, much like the related Yi qi. The type specimen of Scansoriopteryx also contains the fossilized impression of feathers.
diagnostic_features: Third digit of manus elongated to nearly twice that of second digit with robust, hypertrophied metacarpal
Elongate ventral process of postorbital in definite contact with ascending process of jugal
Large fenestra in lower jaw
Expanded/flared posterior end of scapula
Separate clavicles instead of furcula
Small, unexpanded pubic peduncle with short, non-retroverted pubis
Longer ischia and nearly closed acetabulum unlike archaeopterygids
Anisodactyl pes with longer hallux and reduced middle phalanges in digits III and IV
Semilunate distal carpal block with bird-like wrist articulation

synonyms.reason: Founded on a different juvenile specimen (IVPP V12653) but widely regarded as the same taxon. Epidendrosaurus appeared online first while Scansoriopteryx appeared in print first, so under Article 21 of the ICZN, which does not recognize online-only publication, Scansoriopteryx holds priority; some workers nonetheless treat it as the junior name.

Scelidosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'skelis'/'skelidos' (rib of beef, hind leg) + 'sauros' (lizard), intended to mean 'limb lizard'; the name references the animal's robust limbs.
Scelidosaurus.description: Scelidosaurus is a genus of herbivorous armored ornithischian dinosaur from the Jurassic of England.

dispute.summary: Scelidosaurus is a well-known basal thyreophoran. Most analyses recover it as the sister taxon of Eurypoda (Stegosauria plus Ankylosauria), basal to both (Sereno, 1986; Maidment and others, 2008; Jones, 2026). Norman (2020) instead placed it on the line leading to Ankylosauria, after the divergence of Stegosauria.

history.note: Placed at Thyreophora (basal grade) following the prevailing sister-to-Eurypoda topology; the sister-to-Ankylosauria placement of Norman (2020) is recorded.

Scolosaurus.description: Scolosaurus is an extinct genus of ankylosaurid dinosaurs within the subfamily Ankylosaurinae. It is known from the lower levels of the Dinosaur Park Formation and upper levels of the Oldman Formation in the Late Cretaceous (latest middle Campanian stage, about 76.5 Ma ago) of Alberta, Canada. The genus contains two species, S. cutleri and S. thronus. The type species, S. cutleri, measured up to 5.6 meters (18 ft) in length and 2.2 metric tons (2.4 short tons) in body mass.

Scutellosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'scutellum' (diminutive of 'scutum', shield; small shield) + Greek 'sauros' (lizard), meaning 'little shield lizard', referring to the small scutes covering its body.
Scutellosaurus.description: Scutellosaurus is a genus of basal thyreophoran dinosaur that lived approximately 196 million years ago during the early part of the Jurassic Period in what is now Arizona, USA. It is classified in Thyreophora, the armored dinosaurs; its closest relatives may have been Emausaurus and Scelidosaurus, another armored dinosaur which was mainly a quadrupedal dinosaur, unlike bipedal Scutellosaurus. It is one of the earliest representatives of the armored dinosaurs and the basalmost form discovered to date. Scutellosaurus was a small, lightly-built, ground-dwelling herbivore, that could grow up to an estimated 1.3 meters (4.3 ft) long.

Secernosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'secerno' meaning 'to separate' or 'sever' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'severed lizard', referring to its geographic separation from other hadrosaurs in South America.
Secernosaurus.description: Secernosaurus is a genus of herbivorous hadrosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous of what is now Argentina. This genus and its close relatives lived in South America, unlike most hadrosaurids, which lived in the Laurasian continents of Eurasia and North America. It has been suggested that the ancestors of Secernosaurus crossed into South America when a land bridge temporarily formed between North and South America during the Late Cretaceous and allowed biotic interchange between the two continents.

Sefapanosaurus.etymology: From Sesotho 'sefapano' (cross) + Greek 'sauros' (lizard), meaning 'cross lizard', referring to the distinctive cross-shaped astragalus (ankle bone).
Sefapanosaurus.description: Sefapanosaurus was an early, herbivorous sauropodomorph dinosaur occurring in the southern regions of Gondwana some 200 million years ago in the Late Triassic or Early Jurassic. The sauropodomorphs were the dominant terrestrial herbivores throughout much of the Mesozoic Era, from their origins in the mid-Triassic (approximately 230 Ma) until their decline and fall at the end of the Cretaceous (approximately 66 Ma). A distinctive feature of this dinosaur is the cross-shaped astragalus or talus bone in its ankle. The generic name is derived from the Sesotho word sefapano, meaning 'cross' and the Greek word saurus, meaning 'lizard'. The specific name refers to Zastron, the type locality, where the specimen was discovered.

Segnosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'segnis' meaning 'slow' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'slow lizard.' The specific name galbinensis refers to the Galbin region of the Gobi Desert.
Segnosaurus.description: Segnosaurus is a genus of therizinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous, about 102-86 million years ago. Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens were discovered in the Gobi Desert in the 1970s, and in 1979 the genus and species Segnosaurus galbinensis were named. The generic name Segnosaurus means "slow lizard" and the specific name galbinensis refers to the Galbin region. The known material of this dinosaur includes the lower jaw, neck and tail vertebrae, the pelvis, shoulder girdle, and limb bones. Parts of the specimens have gone missing or become damaged since they were collected. Remains from Japan originally assigned to Allosaurus were reassigned to Segnosaurus sp. (of unspecified species) in 2025.

Sektensaurus.description: Sektensaurus is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur, possibly an elasmarian, from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) of Patagonia, Argentina. Its remains were uncovered in the fluvial tuffs of the Lago Colhué Huapí Formation in the Golfo San Jorge Basin. The type and only species is S. sanjuanboscoi. Sektensaurus is the first non-hadrosauroid ornithopod of central Patagonia. The discovery of the genus increases the anatomical knowledge of ornithopods and adds new data on the compositions of dinosaur faunas that lived in Patagonia close to Antarctica at the end of the Cretaceous.

Serendipaceratops.description: Serendipaceratops is a genus of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaur, possibly an ankylosaur, from the early Cretaceous Period of Australia. The type species, S. arthurcclarkei, was named in 2003.

dispute.summary: Serikornis sungei was erected as a distinct basal paravian, the sister taxon of Eosinopteryx (Lefèvre et al., 2017), but its status as a separate genus has been challenged. Agnolín et al. (2019) rejected each of its proposed autapomorphies — arguing that the enlarged anterior maxillary teeth are loose and of variable size, that the distinctive ischial process is taphonomically distorted, and that the coracoid character rests on a surface not exposed in the holotype — and concluded that it is a junior synonym of Anchiornis huxleyi. That synonymy has not been adopted by subsequent workers, who continue to score Serikornis as a distinct taxon in phylogenetic analyses (e.g. Foth et al., 2025); it is retained here as a valid anchiornithid.

history.note: Placed at Anchiornithidae with the other Anchiornis-like taxa; validity relative to Anchiornis remains unresolved, and the clade-level position debate is recorded on Anchiornithidae.

Dispute reframed as valid-versus-synonym and sourced — the sole synonymy proposal (Agnolín et al., 2019) has not been adopted, with later analyses (Foth et al., 2025) continuing to score Serikornis as a distinct taxon; status kept valid.

Serikornis.etymology: From Greek 'serikos' (silken, of silk) + 'ornis' (bird), meaning 'silk bird', likely referring to the soft, silky appearance of the preserved feathers.
Serikornis.description: Serikornis is a genus of small, feathered anchiornithid dinosaur from the Upper Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation of Liaoning, China. It is represented by the type species Serikornis sungei. Some researchers believe it is a junior synonym of Anchiornis.

Coracoid tuber well-developed and laterally projected, forming subglenoid shelf along caudoventral margin
Distal end of lateral process of coracoid thickened, forming ventral rounded bump
Smooth ventral side of coracoid devoid of small pits

dispute.summary: Shanag is a small basal dromaeosaurid whose finer placement is unsettled. It is most often recovered among the basal dromaeosaurids, between Microraptorinae and Eudromaeosauria (Turner et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2026), but is sometimes recovered within Microraptorinae, and Agnolín and Novas (2013) suggested it may be a basal averaptoran closer to birds. It is placed at Dromaeosauridae incertae sedis pending resolution.

Shanag.description: Shanag is a genus of paravian theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Period of Mongolia. It may be a dromaeosaurid, but some researchers are skeptical of this classification. The type species is S. ashile.

Shantungosaurus.etymology: Named after Shandong (historically romanised as Shantung) Province in China, where fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard), meaning 'Shandong lizard'.
Shantungosaurus.description: Shantungosaurus is an extinct genus of very large herbivorous saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaur found in the Late Cretaceous Wangshi Group of the Shandong Peninsula in China, containing a single species, Shantungosaurus giganteus. The stratigraphic interval of Shantungosaurus ranges from the top of the Xingezhuang Formation to the middle of the Hongtuya Formation, middle to late Campanian in age. Shantungosaurus is so far the largest hadrosauroid taxon in the world, with size estimates around 15-17 meters (49-56 ft) in length and 13-16 metric tons (14-18 short tons) in body mass.

Dorsal surface of skull relatively flat with ventral concavity from posterior supratemporal fenestra forward to middle of frontal bone
Long dental battery with a single dental groove and a long toothless region anterior to the dentary
Ischium straight and long with extremely weak, small apical expansion at terminal end
Exceptionally large body size with total assembled length exceeding the known Hadrosaurinae

dispute.summary: Shanyangosaurus niupanggouensis is known from a partial postcranium and is poorly constrained. It has been assigned to Avetheropoda (Holtz et al., 2004) and, in a more recent analysis, recovered as a basal oviraptorosaur close to Caudipteryx (Hartman et al., 2019), though that result is regarded as far from definitive. It is placed conservatively at Avetheropoda incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Avetheropoda incertae sedis; a more precise coelurosaurian (possibly oviraptorosaurian) affinity is unresolved.

Shanyangosaurus.etymology: Named after the Shanyang Formation (Shanyang County, Shaanxi, China) where it was found, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Shanyang lizard"
Shanyangosaurus.description: Shanyangosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur found in Shaanxi, China, and known only from a partial sacrum, partial scapula, humeri, femur, tibia, metatarsals, and phalanges found in the Maastrichtian aged Shanyang Formation. The bones are reportedly hollow; this, along with other features of the femur and known foot bones, suggest it is a member of the coelurosauria, but a specific family cannot be determined without more material. Holtz et al. assigned Shanyangosaurus to Avetheropoda.
diagnostic_features: Femur lacking a fourth trochanter
Femur distinctly curved anteriorly, relatively short, with a deep, wide intercondylar groove at the distal end
Tibia slender and twisted, with an elongated, flattened cnemial crest and a flattened distal end lacking deep grooves
Lesser trochanter of the femur in the form of a narrow ridge, with a small, shallow caudofemoral attachment scar lacking distinct margins
Tibia longer than the femur (ratio about 126%) and the metatarsus greatly elongated (about 53% of femur length)

dispute.summary: Shaochilong maortuensis is recovered as a derived carcharodontosaurid, the first from Asia (Brusatte et al., 2009; Carrano et al., 2012; Jones, 2026), but the two most recent analyses instead place it within Coelurosauria: Kellermann et al. (2025) recover it as a tyrannosauroid in all their analyses (rebutting the proposed carcharodontosaurid characters), and Rauhut et al. (2024) recover it as a coelurosaur. Carcharodontosauridae (Allosauroidea) and Tyrannosauroidea (Coelurosauria) are the two branches of Avetheropoda, the least-inclusive clade all these hypotheses accept.

history.note: Retained at Carcharodontosauridae incertae sedis (prevailing view; P5), with the recent tyrannosauroid hypothesis (Kellermann et al., 2025) reflected but not adopted.

Broadened to Avetheropoda incertae sedis. The carcharodontosaurid versus tyrannosauroid/coelurosaur dispute is live — the two most recent analyses (Rauhut et al. 2024; Kellermann et al. 2025) recover it within Coelurosauria — so the conservative shared node is adopted.

Shaochilong.etymology: From Chinese '鲨齿' (shāchǐ) meaning 'shark tooth' and '龙' (lóng) meaning 'dragon'; meaning 'shark-toothed dragon', referring to its shark-like serrated teeth.
Shaochilong.description: Shaochilong is an extinct genus of tetanuran theropod dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian to Albian stages) Miaogou Formation of China, though a more restrictive suggestion from the Aptian to the Albian has been suggested based on faunal composition. It was usually described as a carcharodontosaurid, but other phylogenies have suggested a different position as a tyrannosauroid or as a member of polytomic allosauroid. The genus contains a single species, Shaochilong maortuensis, which was originally placed in the genus Chilantaisaurus as C. maortuensis, but was re-described and reclassified in 2009.

Large pneumatic foramen at anterodorsal corner of dorsal tympanic recess of prootic
Frontal sagittal crest rises from broad dorsal surface unlike in coelurosaurs and abelisaurids

Shenzhousaurus.etymology: Named after Shenzhou, a poetic name for China, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Shenzhou lizard"
Shenzhousaurus.description: Shenzhousaurus is a genus of basal ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of China.The holotype (NGMC 97-4-002, National Geological Museum of China) was collected from near the bottom (fluvial beds) of the Yixian Formation (Aptian) at the Sihetun fossil site, Beipiao, western Liaoning Province. This specimen consists of a partial skeleton preserved on a sandstone slab in a "death pose," its head above the torso. The distal parts of the hindlimbs, distal portion of the tail, and the forelimbs (except for part of the right hand) and the pectoral girdle are missing. The head is crushed, exposing the left side obliquely.

Straight ischium, postacetabular process gently curved rather than truncated
Digit I shorter than digits II and III in hand (primitive condition for Tetanurae)
Primitive manual proportions with metacarpal I much shorter than II or III

Carrano, Benson and Sampson (2012) allowed for the possibility that it belongs to Metriacanthosaurinae, and Jones and Viola (2026) place it there, but dedicated analyses more often recover it in an unresolved basal position within Metriacanthosauridae (Zou et al., 2025). It is placed conservatively at Metriacanthosauridae incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Metriacanthosauridae incertae sedis; its possible assignment to Metriacanthosaurinae is unresolved.

Shidaisaurus.etymology: Named for the Jin-Shidai ('Golden Age') Company, which oversaw excavation and inspection of the Jurassic World Park near the discovery site, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Shidaisaurus.description: Shidaisaurus is a genus of metriacanthosaurid dinosaur. Its fossil was found in early Middle Jurassic-age rocks of the Chuanjie Formation in Yunnan, China. It is known from a partial skeleton, holotype DML-LCA 9701-IV, found at the bottom of an assemblage of nine dinosaur individuals, lacking most of the tail vertebrae, ribs, pectoral girdle, and limb bones. Shidaisaurus was described in 2009 by Wu and colleagues. The type species is Shidaisaurus jinae. Generic name and specific name in combination refer to the Jin-Shidai ("Golden Age") Company that oversaw excavation and inspection of the Jurassic World Park near the site.

Ischium relatively long (more than 96% the length of pubis)
Absence of pleurocoels in axis and anterior dorsal vertebrae

Shingopana.etymology: From Swahili 'shingo' meaning 'neck' and 'pana' meaning 'wide'; meaning 'wide neck', in reference to the animal's broad neck.
Shingopana.description: Shingopana is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod from the Upper Cretaceous (late Campanian-early Maastrichtian age) Galula Formation of Tanzania. It is known from only the type species, S. songwensis. Gorscak & O'Connor's phylogenetic testing suggest Shingopana is more closely related to the South American titanosaur family of Aeolosaurini than any of the titanosaurs found so far in North and South Africa.

The specific name refers to the unexpected discovery of another species of alvarezsaur from the Shishugou Formation (other alvarezsaurs from this formation include Haplocheirus and possibly Aorun). Shixinggia.etymology: Named for Shixing County, Guangdong, China, where the fossil was discovered.
Shixinggia.description: Shixinggia is a genus of oviraptorosaurian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period of Shixing County, Guangdong, China, for which it was named. While no skull was recovered, the specimen (BVP-112) is known from a fair amount of post-cranial material that shows it was a fairly derived oviraptorosaur of superfamily Caenagnathoidea.

dispute.summary: Shixinggia is known only from postcranial material, and whether it is an oviraptorid or a caenagnathid is unresolved. Its describers (Lü and Zhang, 2005) and a later analysis (Funston et al., 2020) place it within Oviraptoridae, the latter as the basalmost member of Heyuanninae, but the incompleteness of the specimen leaves open the possibility that it is instead a caenagnathid.

history.note: Placed at Heyuanninae following Funston et al. (2020); its oviraptorid versus caenagnathid identity is not firmly established.

Shuangbaisaurus.etymology: From "Shuangbai" (Shuangbai County in Yunnan, China, where the holotype was found) and Greek "sauros" (lizard); meaning "Shuangbai lizard".
Shuangbaisaurus.description: Shuangbaisaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur, possibly a junior synonym of Sinosaurus. It lived in the Early Jurassic of Yunnan Province, China, and is represented by a single species, S. anlongbaoensis, known from a partial skull. Like the theropods Dilophosaurus and Sinosaurus, Shuangbaisaurus bore a pair of thin, midline crests on its skull. Unusually, these crests extended backwards over the level of the eyes, which, along with the unusual orientation of the jugal bone, led the describers to name it as a new genus. However, Shuangbaisaurus also possesses a groove between its premaxilla and maxilla, a characteristic which has been used to characterize Sinosaurus as a genus. Among the two morphotypes present within the genus Sinosaurus, Shuangbaisaurus more closely resembles the morphotype that is variably treated as a distinct species, S. sinensis, in its relatively tall skull.

Ventral edge of the premaxilla notably elevated, higher than the ventral edge of the maxilla, placing the last two premaxillary teeth above the maxillary ventral edge
Small, round upper temporal fenestra with diameter shorter than the transverse width of the parietals in between and about half the length of the skull table posterior to the orbit
Quadratojugal and posterior process of jugal directed posteroventrally

dispute.summary: Siamosaurus suteethorni is based solely on isolated teeth, and both its affinities and its validity have been contested. Buffetaut and Ingavat (1986) tentatively referred it to Spinosauridae, but Sues et al. (2002) considered the material insufficient to establish even dinosaurian affinities, and Weishampel et al. (2004) placed it no more precisely than Theropoda indeterminate. Its spinosaurid identity has since gained support: Buffetaut et al. (2008) cited converging lines of evidence — including a spinosaurid skeleton from the tooth-bearing Khok Kruat Formation — and Carrano et al. (2012) referred the teeth to ?Spinosauridae. Nonetheless the genus is widely treated as a nomen dubium, because its teeth cannot be distinguished from those of other spinosaurids (Holtz et al., 2004; Sales and Schultz, 2017; Smyth et al., 2020); associated skeletal material may eventually permit a more secure identification.

history.note: Placed at Spinosauridae following Carrano et al. (2012); retained as a nomen-dubium-grade, teeth-based taxon that cannot be resolved to a subfamily.

Dispute expanded across the literature — its affinity has ranged from non-dinosaurian (Sues et al., 2002) to spinosaurid (Buffetaut et al., 2008; Carrano et al., 2012), while its tooth-based validity remains widely regarded as a nomen dubium.

Siamosaurus.etymology: Named for Siam, the ancient name of Thailand, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Siam lizard.'
Siamosaurus.description: Siamosaurus is a potentially dubious genus of spinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now Thailand and possibly China during the Early Cretaceous period (Barremian to Aptian) and is the first reported spinosaurid from Asia. It is confidently known only from tooth fossils; the first were found in the Sao Khua Formation, with more teeth later recovered from the younger Khok Kruat Formation. The only species Siamosaurus suteethorni, whose name honors Thai paleontologist Varavudh Suteethorn, was formally described in 1986. In 2009, four teeth from China previously attributed to a pliosaur-under the species "Sinopliosaurus" fusuiensis-were identified as those of a spinosaurid, possibly Siamosaurus. It is yet to be determined if two partial spinosaurid skeletons from Thailand and an isolated tooth from Japan also belong to Siamosaurus.

dispute.summary: Siats was originally described as a megaraptoran within Neovenatoridae (Allosauroidea). Siluosaurus.description: Siluosaurus is a genus of ornithischian dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian-Albian) Xinminbao Group of Gansu, China, founded on two small teeth. The type species is S. zhanggiani.

dispute.summary: Siluosaurus is a nomen dubium based on two isolated teeth from the Early Cretaceous of China. Dong (1997) named it as a hypsilophodontid — a now-abandoned grouping — and described the teeth as the smallest ornithopod teeth then known. It has since been treated as a dubious, tooth-based taxon (Butler et al., 2008; Makovicky et al., 2011), and Fonseca et al. (2024) found its teeth resemble those of both an ornithopod (Convolosaurus) and a ceratopsian (Archaeoceratops), placing it no more precisely than Cerapoda indeterminate.

Sinocephale.description: Sinocephale is a genus of pachycephalosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now Inner Mongolia, China, during the Cretaceous period. The genus contains a single species, Sinocephale bexelli, which was originally named as a species of the genus Troodon in 1953, and later transferred to the genus Stegoceras in 1964. After decades of being considered dubious, it was re-evaluated in 2021 and recognized as a valid taxon, being given its own genus, Sinocephale. The original holotype was lost, with modern research conducted using rediscovered plaster casts.

Sinoceratops.description: Sinoceratops is an extinct genus of ceratopsian dinosaur that lived from 77.3 to 73.5 million years ago during the latter part of the Cretaceous Period in what is now Shandong province in China. It was named in 2010 by Xu Xing et al. for three skulls from Zhucheng, China. The name of the type species Sinoceratops zhuchengensis means "Chinese horned face from Zhucheng", after the location of its discovery. Sinoceratops was a medium-sized, averagely-built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore. It could grow up to an estimated 5 meters (16 ft) in length and weigh up to 2 tonnes (2.0 long tons; 2.2 short tons).

Sinopeltosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'sino-' (Chinese, after the Sinae) and 'peltē' (small shield) plus 'sauros' (lizard); meaning approximately 'Chinese small-shielded lizard', a replacement name for the preoccupied Sinopelta Ulansky, 2014a.
Sinopeltosaurus.description: Sinopeltosaurus is a dubious genus of extinct thyreophoran ornithischian dinosaur described by Roman Ulansky for the articulated ankle specimen FMNH CUP 2338 from the Lower Jurassic Lufeng Formation of Yunnan, China. The type and only species is S. minimus. The specimen was originally described by Irmis and Knoll (2008) as an indeterminate basal ornithischian and was later identified as a nomen dubium by Galton and Carpenter (2016), who listed it as Ornithischia indet., possibly Thyreophora indet. Ulansky's companion paper used the variant name 'Sinopelta minima' for the same animal; Galton and Carpenter (2016) acted as first revisers under the ICZN and selected Sinopeltosaurus minimus as the official combination.

dispute.summary: Sinopeltosaurus, based on an articulated tarsus from the Early Jurassic of China, is a nomen dubium; the material was originally described as an indeterminate ornithischian (Irmis and Knoll, 2008) and is most plausibly an early-diverging thyreophoran (Galton and Carpenter, 2016; Jones, 2026), though the original naming did not meet ICZN requirements.

Sinornithosaurus.description: Sinornithosaurus is a genus of feathered dromaeosaurid dinosaur from the early Cretaceous Period (late Barremian) of the Yixian Formation in what is now China. It was the fifth non-avian feathered dinosaur genus discovered by 1999. The original specimen was collected from the Sihetun locality of western Liaoning. Additional specimens have been found in the younger Dawangzhangzi bed, dating to around 122 million years ago.

Sinosauropteryx.etymology: From Latin/Greek 'Sino-' meaning 'Chinese', Greek 'sauros' meaning 'reptile' or 'lizard', and 'pteryx' meaning 'wing'; meaning 'Chinese reptilian wing.'
Sinosauropteryx.description: Sinosauropteryx is an extinct genus of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs. Described in 1996, it was the first dinosaur taxon outside of Avialae (birds and their immediate relatives) to be found with evidence of feathers. It was covered with a coat of very simple filament-like feathers. Structures that indicate the color pattern have also been preserved in some of its feathers, which show that Sinosauropteryx had a countershading pattern in its body with a banded tail. The reddish brown coloration previously inferred for Sinosauropteryx is based on the melanosomes preserved in the specimen of a separate genus, Huadanosaurus. Some contention has arisen with an alternative interpretation of the filamentous impression as remains of collagen fibers, but this has not been widely accepted.
diagnostic_features: Extremely short, primitive, uniform feathers unlike later avian forms

dispute.summary: Sinosaurus triassicus is a basal neotheropod of uncertain position. With corrected character coding it is recovered as a stem-averostran ("pre-tetanuran") near Dilophosaurus and Cryolophosaurus, outside Averostra (Rauhut, 2003; Wang and others, 2017; Jones and Viola, 2026), though earlier work placed it as a basal tetanuran inside Averostra (Carrano and others, 2012). It is placed conservatively at Neotheropoda incertae sedis. The species "Dilophosaurus" sinensis is referred to Sinosaurus.

Sinosaurus.etymology: From Latin Sinae, "Chinese", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Chinese lizard"
Sinosaurus.description: Sinosaurus is an extinct genus of basal theropod dinosaur which lived during the Early Jurassic (Hettangian-Sinemurian). Fossils of the animal have been found in the Lufeng Formation, in the Yunnan Province of China. The type species, S. triassicus, was named by Chung Chieng Young in 1940. A second species, S. sinensis, was originally assigned to Dilophosaurus, but was later reassigned to Sinosaurus. Sinosaurus is morphologically similar to Dilophosaurus including the presence of a similarly shaped cranial crest, though its precise taxonomic position is uncertain, and the two genera may not be closely related.

Sinotyrannus.etymology: From Latin 'Sinae' (a classical name for the Chinese) and Greek 'tyrannos' (tyrant); meaning 'Chinese tyrant'.
Sinotyrannus.description: Sinotyrannus is an extinct genus of large proceratosaurid tyrannosauroid theropod from the Aptian (Early Cretaceous) lower Jiufotang Formation of Kazuo County, western Liaoning Province, China — part of the Jehol Biota. The single species, Sinotyrannus kazuoensis, is known from a disarticulated skeleton (KZV-001) including the anterior skull and mandibles, three articulated dorsal vertebrae, ribs, partial ilia, and manual phalanges. Originally placed within Tyrannosauroidea (and tentatively Tyrannosauridae) by Ji et al. (2009), subsequent phylogenetic analyses (Loewen et al. 2013, and others) recovered Sinotyrannus as a basal proceratosaurid. With an estimated body length of ~9-10 m, it is one of the largest known Early Cretaceous tyrannosauroids. Cau and Paterna (2025) proposed Sinotyrannus as the adult morphotype of the coeval compsognathid Huaxiagnathus, but that hypothesis is single-paper-recent and not yet a community consensus; the genus is treated as valid here.

Skorpiovenator.etymology: From Greek skorpios, "scorpion", combined with Latin venator, "hunter" - means "scorpion hunter", named because the excavation site was infested with scorpions
Skorpiovenator.description: Skorpiovenator is a genus of abelisaurid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian to Turonian) Huincul Formation of Argentina. The sole species of Skorpiovenator, S. bustingorryi, was named in honor of Manuel Bustingorry, the late owner of the farm on which the type specimen was discovered. Formally described in 2009, the type specimen is one of the most complete and informative abelisaurids yet known, described from a nearly complete and articulated skeleton. A tibia fragment was assigned to Skorpiovenator in 2022.

Sonidosaurus.description: Sonidosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous. It was a titanosaur which lived in what is now Inner Mongolia. The type species, Sonidosaurus saihangaobiensis, was described by Xu, Zhang, Tan, Zhao, and Tan in 2006. It was a small titanosaur, about 9 meters (30 ft) long. It was first discovered in the Saihangaobi, Iren Dabasu (Erlian) Formation, in 2001 in a quarry which would later yield the remains of Gigantoraptor.

Sonorasaurus.etymology: Named for the Sonora River in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona, USA, where its fossils were first found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', thus meaning 'Sonora lizard'.
Sonorasaurus.description: Sonorasaurus is a genus of brachiosaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Early to Late Cretaceous (Albian to Cenomanian stages, around 112 to 93 million years ago). Its fossils have been found in southern Arizona, United States. Its name, which means "Sonora lizard", comes from the Sonora River that flows in the Sonoran Desert where its fossils were first found. The type species is S. thompsoni, described by Ratkevich in 1998.

Sphaerotholus.etymology: From Greek 'sphaira' (sphere, ball) + Greek 'tholos' (dome, domed building), meaning 'spherical dome' or 'ball dome', referring to the characteristic rounded domed skull of this pachycephalosaurid.
Sphaerotholus.description: Sphaerotholus is a genus of pachycephalosaurid dinosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of the western United States and Canada. To date, five species have been described: the type species, S. goodwini, from the Den-na-zin Member of the Kirtland Formation and possibly the Fossil Forest Member of the Fruitland Formation (Late Campanian) of San Juan County, New Mexico, USA; S. buchholtzae, from the Hell Creek Formation (Late Maastrichtian) of western Carter County, Montana, USA and the Frenchman Formation of Saskatchewan, Canada; S. edmontonensis, from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, Canada; S. lyonsi, from the Dinosaur Park Formation (Campanian) of Alberta, Canada; and S. triregnum from the Hell Creek Formation of Garfield County, Montana, USA.

Parietosquamosal shelf small, inflated, and does not include the parietals

Spicomellus.etymology: From Latin 'spica' meaning 'spike' and Latin 'mellum' meaning 'collar', referring to the spiked osteoderms fused to the rib of the holotype specimen
Spicomellus.description: Spicomellus is an extinct genus of unusual early ankylosaurian dinosaur from the El Mers III Formation (Bathonian age) of Morocco. The genus contains a single species, Spicomellus afer, representing the oldest named definitive ankylosaur. The species was initially described in 2021 based on a single rib with fused osteoderms, rendering its life appearance and relationships uncertain. In 2025, several additional bones, including osteoderms and cranial and postcranial remains, were described, revealing that it bears a unique array of spines over the body, including extremely elongated spikes around the neck and pelvis. It likely had a tail weapon, making it the oldest known ankylosaur with this structure.

dispute.summary: Spicomellus is the earliest known definitive ankylosaur, but its position is unresolved; Maidment et al. (2025) recover it as an early-diverging ankylosaurid while reference works leave it unplaced to family. It is retained at Ankylosauria incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Ankylosauria incertae sedis, family placement of this earliest ankylosaur not firmly resolved.

Spinophorosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'spina' meaning 'spine' or 'thorn', Greek 'phoros' meaning 'bearing' or 'carrying', and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to its spine-bearing tail clubs.
Spinophorosaurus.description: Spinophorosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Niger during the Middle Jurassic period. The first two specimens were excavated in the 2000s by German and Spanish teams under difficult conditions. The skeletons were brought to Europe and digitally replicated, making Spinophorosaurus the first sauropod to have its skeleton 3D printed, and were to be returned to Niger in the future. Together, the two specimens represented most of the skeleton of the genus, and one of the most completely known basal sauropods of its time and place. The first skeleton was made the holotype specimen of the new genus and species Spinophorosaurus nigerensis in 2009; the generic name ("spine-bearing lizard") refers to what was initially thought to be spiked osteoderms, and the specific name (Niger and -ensis) refers to where it was found. A juvenile sauropod from the same area was later assigned to the genus.

Spinosaurus.etymology: From Latin spina (spine, thorn) and Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "spine lizard", named for the conspicuously tall neural spines of the trunk vertebrae that supported a dorsal sail.
Spinosaurus.description: Spinosaurus is the type genus of Spinosauridae and one of the most distinctive Cretaceous theropods, recognized for the enormously tall neural spines of its dorsal vertebrae that supported a dorsal sail or hump. The genus was erected by Ernst Stromer in 1915 on a partial skeleton recovered in 1912 by his collector Richard Markgraf from the Bahariya beds of the Western Desert of Egypt (specimen BSP 1912 VIII 19 in the Bayerische Staatssammlung in Munich). The original type material — including the iconic mandibles and elongate-spined dorsals — was destroyed in the British bombing of Munich in April 1944, leaving only Stromer's plates and descriptions. Stromer (1934) added more material, including a smaller specimen he treated informally as "Spinosaurus B" (later partly the basis of Russell's 1996 S. maroccanus). Ibrahim et al. (2014) designated FSAC-KK 11888, a partial skeleton from the Kem Kem beds of southeastern Morocco, as the neotype of S. aegyptiacus, and proposed on the basis of pachyostotic limb bones, retracted nostrils, and reduced hindlimbs that Spinosaurus was a semi-aquatic predator capable of obligate quadrupedal locomotion on land. Subsequent work (notably Ibrahim et al. 2020 on the paddle-tail and Sereno et al. 2022 in response) has continued to debate the degree of aquatic adaptation, but the broad picture of a piscivorous, river-dwelling spinosaurid with reduced hindlimbs and dense limb bones is now widely accepted.
diagnostic_features: Dentary rami long and low-set in the middle, bearing about 15 awl-shaped teeth per ramus, with strongly heterodont positions (large 2nd-4th, small 5th-10th, larger 11th-14th).
Teeth straight to gently curved, sub-circular in cross-section, with smooth (non-serrated) anterior and posterior keels.
Fleshy nostril retracted to a posteriorly placed narial fossa on the skull, far from the snout tip.
Free dorsal vertebral centra elongate, hourglass-shaped in dorsal view, and strongly opisthocoelous, lacking a ventral keel.
Neural spines of dorsal vertebrae extraordinarily tall (up to ~8x centrum height), laterally compressed, broadened ventrally and dorsally, supporting a dorsal sail.
Anterior dorsal centra exceptionally broad and concavoconvex, creating a horizontal cervicodorsal hinge.
Long bones (femur, tibia, manual phalanges) with solid shafts lacking an open medullary cavity; bone density 30-40% greater than in other large theropods (pachyostosis).
Femur substantially shorter than tibia and hindlimb length only ~19% of body length; iliac blade reduced to roughly half the surface area of other comparably sized theropods.

Stegoceras.etymology: From Greek 'stege' (στέγη) meaning 'roof' and 'keras' (κέρας) meaning 'horn'; meaning 'horn roof', referring to the domed skull.
Stegoceras.description: Stegoceras is a genus of pachycephalosaurid (dome-headed) dinosaur that lived in what is now North America during the Late Cretaceous period, about 77.5 to 74 million years ago (mya). The first specimens from Alberta, Canada, were described in 1902, and the type species Stegoceras validum was based on these remains. The generic name means "horn roof", and the specific name means "strong". Several other species have been placed in the genus over the years, but these have since been moved to other genera or deemed junior synonyms. Currently only S. validum and S. novomexicanum, named in 2011 from fossils found in New Mexico, remain. The validity of the latter species has also been debated, and it may not even belong to the genus Stegoceras.

Stegosaurus.etymology: From Greek stegos (roof) and sauros (lizard); meaning "roof lizard", in reference to the parasagittal rows of large dermal plates that Marsh initially interpreted as forming a roof-like carapace over the back of the animal.
Stegosaurus.description: Stegosaurus is the type genus of Stegosauridae and one of the most readily recognized dinosaurs, characterized by two parasagittal rows of large, erect dermal plates running from the cervicodorsal junction to near the tail tip and by four long tail spines (the "thagomizer") at the distal end of the tail. Marsh erected the genus and the order Stegosauria in 1877 on a partial skeleton from the Morrison Formation of Colorado, originally naming S. armatus as the type species. C. W. Gilmore's 1914 monograph on USNM 4934 (Felch Quarry No. 1, Garden Park, Colorado) supplied the first detailed osteology of the genus and resolved decades of argument over the plate arrangement, demonstrating from articulated evidence that the plates of the two rows alternate rather than pair. Because Marsh's S. armatus material is too fragmentary to anchor the genus, ICZN Opinion 2320 (2013) set aside all prior type-species fixations under plenary power and designated S. stenops Marsh, 1887, with USNM 4934 as its holotype, as the new type species — the form on which most of our modern picture of the genus rests. Besides the type species, S. ungulatus (Marsh, 1879) is also widely recognized as valid; other named forms are subsumed in Stegosaurus (S. duplex as a junior synonym of S. ungulatus, and Diracodon laticeps), while the synonymies of Hesperosaurus and Wuerhosaurus proposed by Maidment et al. (2008) remain contested in subsequent literature and are not accepted here.
diagnostic_features: Skull comparatively very small with a brain cavity proportionally among the smallest of any large terrestrial vertebrate.
Sacrum with an enormously enlarged neural canal forming a chamber many times the cranial capacity, fully roofed over by bone.
Two parasagittal rows of erect, flattened, kite-shaped dermal plates extending from the cervicodorsal junction to near the tail tip; plates of opposite rows alternating rather than paired.
Tail bearing four large dermal spines arranged in two pairs near the distal end (thagomizer); roughly 20-22 dermal plates total.
Pes tetradactyl with digit IV reduced to a vestigial metatarsal; digit V absent.
Tibia distinctive in having the greatest diameter of both ends lying approximately in the same plane.
Postzygapophyses on the posterior cervical vertebrae elongate posteriorly, overhanging the back of the centrum.
Supra-acetabular process of the ilium diverging at approximately 90 degrees from the anterior process.

Stegouros.etymology: From Greek 'stegos' meaning 'roof' and 'oura' meaning 'tail'; meaning 'roofed tail', referring to the roof-like covering of osteoderms over the tail.
Stegouros.description: Stegouros is an extinct genus of ankylosaurian dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous Dorotea Formation of southern Chile. The genus contains a single species, Stegouros elengassen, known from a semi-articulated, near-complete skeleton. Stegouros is a member of the Parankylosauria, a clade of small Gondwanan armored dinosaurs. It is characterized by its small body size and distinct arrangement of fused osteoderms forming a macuahuitl-like tail weapon.

Its remains have been found in the late Campanian-aged Two Medicine Formation, the same geological unit which its relatives Rubeosaurus (now seen as a synonym of Styracosaurus), Einiosaurus, and Achelousaurus were discovered in.

Stenonychosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'stenos' meaning 'narrow', 'onyx/onychos' meaning 'claw', and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'narrow claw lizard', referring to the narrow enlarged claw on the second toe.
Stenonychosaurus.description: Stenonychosaurus is a disputed genus of troodontid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, as well as possibly the Two Medicine Formation. The type and only species, S. inequalis, was named by Charles Mortram Sternberg in 1932, based on a foot, fragments of a hand, and some caudal vertebrae from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta. S. inequalis was reassigned in 1987 by Phil Currie to the genus Troodon, which was reverted by the recognition of Stenonychosaurus as a separate genus from the possibly dubious Troodon in 2017 by Evans et al. and also later in the same year by Van der Reest and Currie.
diagnostic_features: Inequality in length of the three functional digits of the hind foot

Specialized digit II with moderately sized, slightly curved, laterally compressed ungual
Metatarsal II much shorter than metatarsals III and IV
Caudal vertebrae amphiplatyan with well-developed longitudinal groove on inferior surface

Bone histology lacked the resorption patterns of an egg-laying female, leading to the inference that the male brooded the eggs, a trait possibly shared by maniraptorans and basal birds.

Stenopelix.description: Stenopelix is a genus of basal ceratopsian from the Early Cretaceous (late Berriasian stage, approximately 140 million years ago) of Germany. The genus is based on a partial skeleton lacking the skull, and its classification is based on characteristics of the hips.

Struthiomimus.etymology: From Greek 'stroutheios' (στρούθειος) meaning 'of the ostrich' and 'mimos' (μῖμος) meaning 'mimic' or 'imitator'; meaning 'ostrich mimic', referring to its long-legged, ostrich-like build.
Struthiomimus.description: Struthiomimus is a genus of ornithomimid dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of what is now western North America. They were long-legged, bipedal, ostrich-like dinosaurs with toothless beaks. The type species, Struthiomimus altus, is one of the more common, smaller dinosaurs found in Dinosaur Provincial Park. Their overall abundance, in addition to their toothless beak, suggests that these animals were mainly herbivorous or (more likely) omnivorous, rather than purely carnivorous. Similar to the modern ostriches, emus, and rheas (among other birds), these dinosaurs likely lived as opportunistic omnivores, supplementing a largely plant-based diet with a variety of small mammals, reptiles, amphibians, insects, invertebrates, and anything else they could fit into their mouth, as they foraged.

Styracosaurus.etymology: From Ancient Greek styrax, "spike at the butt-end of a spear-shaft", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "spiked lizard"
Styracosaurus.description: Styracosaurus is an extinct genus of herbivorous dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian stage) of North America. It had four to six long parietal spikes extending from its neck frill, a smaller jugal horn on each of its cheeks, and a single horn protruding from its nose, which may have been up to 60 centimeters (2 feet) long and 15 centimeters (6 inches) wide. The function or functions of the horns and frills have been debated for many years.

Suchomimus.etymology: From Greek souchos ('crocodile') and Latin mimus ('mimic'), meaning 'crocodile mimic', alluding to its elongated skull and piscivorous adaptations
Suchomimus.description: Suchomimus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Niger during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous period, 112 million years ago. The only known species is S. tenerensis, originally described in 1998 by paleontologist Paul Sereno and colleagues from several fossils discovered one year earlier in the Elrhaz Formation. Although these fossils come from multiple specimens, they represent one of the most anatomically well-documented spinosaurids. The animal's generic name, which means "crocodile mimic", alludes to its elongated skull and piscivorous adaptations, while the specific name refers to the Ténéré Desert, where the fossils were discovered.

Broadened and heightened posterior dorsal, sacral, and anterior caudal neural spines
Robust humeral tuberosities

Suchosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'souchos' (crocodile, after the Egyptian crocodile-god Sobek) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'crocodile lizard'.
Suchosaurus.description: Suchosaurus is a dubious genus of large theropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now Europe. The type species, S. cultridens, was first mentioned by Richard Owen at the British Association meeting in 1841 and formally described in his 1842 Report on British Fossil Reptiles, based on a chimeric assemblage of fossil teeth and vertebrae discovered in the Tilgate Forest of Sussex, England, in sediments of the Wealden Supergroup.

Supersaurus.etymology: From Latin super, "above" or "super", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "super lizard", reflecting its enormous size
Supersaurus.description: Supersaurus is a genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Late Jurassic period. The type species, S. vivianae, was first discovered by Vivian Jones of Delta, Colorado, in the middle Morrison Formation of Colorado in 1972. The fossil remains came from the Brushy Basin Member of the formation, dating between 153 and 145 million years ago. It is among the longest dinosaurs ever discovered, with the three known specimens reaching 33-40 meters (108-131 ft) in length, with the largest individual possibly exceeding 40 meters (130 ft) in size. Mass estimates for the WDC and BYU specimens tend to be around 35-44 metric tons (39-49 short tons) in body mass. A potential second species, S. lourinhanensis (Dinheirosaurus), is known from Portugal and has been dated to a similar time.
diagnostic_features: Elongate cervical vertebrae (elongation index 4-7) with extreme narrowing of the ventral body at midlength and well-developed parallel ventral keels
Cervicals with a small ventral pleurocoel between the parapophyses bearing dual pneumatopores divided by a septum; lateral pleurocoels simple, shallow, with small pneumatopores
Posterior dorsal vertebrae opisthocoelous, with tall neural spines (more than half the vertebral height) and a reduced neural arch
Anterior dorsal centra with a moderate midline keel and shallow lateral sulci
Anterior caudal vertebrae with a prominent ventral keel and shallow pleurocoels
Ribs pneumatized, with anteroposteriorly expanded shafts
Scapular blade expanded dorsally; deltoid ridge perpendicular to the acromial ridge

The number from the erecting paper is followed here.

Suuwassea.etymology: From the Crow language, derived from 'suuwassa' meaning 'the first thunder heard in spring'; the root 'suu' means 'thunder' and 'wassa' means 'ancient', evoking the 'thunder lizard' epithet often applied to sauropods.
Suuwassea.description: Suuwassea is a genus of dicraeosaurid sauropod dinosaur found in Upper Jurassic strata of the Morrison Formation, located in southern Carbon County, Montana, United States. The fossil remains were recovered in a series of expeditions during a period spanning the years 1999 and 2000 and were described by J.D. Harris and Peter Dodson in 2004. They consist of a disarticulated but associated partial skeleton, including partial vertebral series and limb bones.

Suzhousaurus.etymology: Named after Suzhou (a region in Gansu Province, China) where the fossils were found, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Suzhou lizard"
Suzhousaurus.description: Suzhousaurus is an extinct genus of large therizinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of China. The genus is known from two specimens discovered in the Xiagou and Zhonggou Formations, both part of the Xinminbao Group. These findings were made during fieldwork in 1999 and 2004.

dispute.summary: Suzhousaurus is a large, latest-diverging intermediate therizinosaur whose family-level assignment depends on how Therizinosauridae is defined. Zanno (2010) recovers it just outside Therizinosauridae as the most derived therizinosauroid, a result followed by the Princeton Encyclopedia (Jones, 2026); under the broader Therizinosaurus-anchored definition of Kobayashi et al. (2022, 2025) it is drawn into Therizinosauridae, within a derived subclade alongside Therizinosaurus and Paralitherizinosaurus. It is placed conservatively in Therizinosauroidea.

history.note: Placed at Therizinosauroidea (outside Therizinosauridae) following Zanno (2010) and Jones (2026), who treat it as the most derived therizinosauroid; Kobayashi et al. (2022, 2025) include it in a more broadly defined Therizinosauridae.

Syngonosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'syngonos' meaning 'congenital' or 'related by birth', combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', likely referring to the fused or closely associated bones in the specimen.
Syngonosaurus.description: Syngonosaurus is an extinct genus of ornithopod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous. It was an iguanodontian discovered in the Cambridge Greensand of England and was first described in 1879. The type species, S. macrocercus, was described by British paleontologist Harry Seeley in 1879 and it was later synonymised with Acanthopholis, but the genus was reinstated in a 2020 study, when Syngonosaurus and Eucercosaurus were reinterpreted as basal iguanodontians.

It includes one species, Tachiraptor admirabilis, described from a fossilized tibia and ischium. They were small bipedal dinosaurs, with a deduced total body length of just over 1.5 m (4.9 ft).

Talarurus.etymology: From Greek talaros, "wicker basket", combined with Greek oura, "tail" - means "basket tail" or "wicker tail", referring to the club-like tail
Talarurus.description: Talarurus is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period, about 96 million to 89 million years ago. The first remains of Talarurus were discovered in 1948 and later described by the Russian paleontologist Evgeny Maleev with the type species T. plicatospineus. It is known from multiple yet sparse specimens, making it one of the most well known ankylosaurines, along with Pinacosaurus. Elements from the specimens consists of various bones from the body; five skulls have been discovered and assigned to the genus, although the first two were very fragmented.

Taleta.etymology: From Arabic 'taleta' (three), in reference to this being the third duck-billed dinosaur recovered from Couche III of the Moroccan phosphates, after Ajnabia odysseus and Minqaria bata.
Taleta.description: Taleta is an extinct genus of arenysaurin lambeosaurine hadrosaurid dinosaur from the late Maastrichtian Couche III of the Oulad Abdoun Basin (Sidi Chennane mines, Central Morocco), a shallow-marine phosphorite depositional setting. The single species, Taleta taleta, is known from associated left and right maxillae of a single individual (MHNM.KH.1557) preserving in-situ dentition; phylogenetic analysis recovers it within Arenysaurini, forming an African clade with Ajnabia odysseus and Minqaria bata. Longrich et al. (2025) interpret the three Moroccan arenysaurins as a dispersal-driven adaptive radiation seeded from southern Europe.

Primary ridge of maxillary teeth extremely tall and prominent, roughly doubling the mediolateral width of the crown, and interlocking with the alveolar margin.

Tameryraptor.etymology: From Egyptian Tamery, meaning "the beloved land" (an ancient Egyptian name for Egypt), combined with Latin raptor, "thief" - means "thief from the beloved land"
Tameryraptor.description: Tameryraptor is an extinct genus of large carcharodontosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian age) in what is now Egypt. It is known from a partial skeleton collected in rock layers from the Bahariya Formation by crews of German paleontologist Ernst Stromer in 1914, comprising an incomplete skull, vertebrae, and several other postcranial elements. Stromer described the specimen in 1931, referring it to the previously named Megalosaurus saharicus on the basis of its tooth anatomy, and placing it in a new genus, Carcharodontosaurus. In 1944, it was destroyed in the Bombing of Munich during the Second World War. The specimen remained assigned to Carcharodontosaurus saharicus until a review of photographs of the fossil material in 2025 allowed researchers around German paleontologist Maximilian Kellermann to recognize the material as belonging to a distinct taxon known from a single species, Tameryraptor markgrafi.

Taohelong.etymology: From Chinese Tao (the Tao River), he ("river"), and long ("dragon") - means "dragon of the Tao River"
Taohelong.description: Taohelong is a genus of nodosaurid dinosaur known from Early Cretaceous rocks in north-central China. It is based on Gansu Dinosaur Museum (GSDM) 00021, fossils including a tail vertebra, ribs, a left ilium (the main bone of the hip), and bony armor recovered from the Hekou Group in the Lanzhou-Minhe Basin. The animal's armor includes part of a "sacral shield", a carpet of osteoderms over the hips found in some other ankylosaurians. Taohelong was named and described in 2013 by Yang Jing-Tao, You Hai-Lu, Li Da-Qing, and Kong De-Lai. The type species is Taohelong jinchengensis. The generic name means "dragon (long) of the river (he) Tao". The specific name refers to the provenance at Jincheng.

Tarbosaurus.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'tarbos' meaning 'terror' or 'alarm' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tarbosaurus.description: Tarbosaurus is a genus of large tyrannosaurid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous epoch. It contains the type and single species Tarbosaurus bataar, which is known from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia, with more fragmentary remains found further afield in the Subashi Formation of China. Tarbosaurus is represented by dozens of fossil specimens, including several complete skulls and skeletons. These remains have allowed studies focusing on its phylogeny, skull mechanics, and brain structure. Further fossil remains have been reported from other geologic formations of Asia, however, these remains are fragmentary and cannot be confidently assigned to Tarbosaurus or the type species.

dispute.summary: The generic placement of the single Mongolian species is long debated. Maleev (1955) named the type material Tyrannosaurus bataar (holotype PIN 551-1) and, in a companion paper, erected Tarbosaurus for the related Tarbosaurus efremovi. Rozhdestvensky (1965) interpreted Maleev's several Mongolian species as growth stages of one animal and, keeping the genus Tarbosaurus, coined the combination Tarbosaurus bataar. Carpenter (1992) judged the differences from Tyrannosaurus to fall within normal individual and ontogenetic variation and sank Tarbosaurus into Tyrannosaurus (Tyrannosaurus bataar), whereas Olshevsky, Ford and Yamamoto (1995) instead split the material among Tarbosaurus, Jenghizkhan and Maleevosaurus. Most work since 1999 recognizes a single species; the majority retains Tarbosaurus bataar, with a minority (e.g. Carr and others) treating it as Tyrannosaurus bataar.

history.note: Retained as Tarbosaurus bataar, the majority usage since 1999; the Tyrannosaurus bataar assignment (Carpenter 1992; Carr and others) is recorded as a minority view.

Tastavinsaurus.etymology: Named in honor of the Rio Tastavins in Spain, where the fossils were found.
Tastavinsaurus.description: Tastavinsaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur belonging to the Titanosauriformes. It is based on a partial skeleton from the Early Cretaceous Xert Formation of Spain. The type species is Tastavinsaurus sanzi, named in honor of the Rio Tastavins in Spain and Spanish paleontologist José Luis Sanz. The genus is known from two specimens, one from the Xert Formation and one from the Forcall Formation. Tastavinsaurus was originally described as a somphospondylan, but it may be a brachiosaurid. The clade Laurasiformes was coined for Tastavinsaurus and its close relatives, which may include Cedarosaurus, Soriatitan, and Venenosaurus.

Taurovenator.etymology: From Latin 'taurus' meaning 'bull' and 'venator' meaning 'hunter', hence 'bull hunter'.
Taurovenator.description: Taurovenator, from Latin taurus, meaning "bull", and venator, meaning "hunter", is an extinct genus of large, probable carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now Argentina during the Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous, around 95 to 93.9 million years ago. Initially only known from a single postorbital skull bone described from the Huincul Formation, Taurovenator violantei was named in 2016 by Argentine paleontologist Matias Motta and colleagues. Debate came about over the validity of the species, with some paleontologists arguing that Taurovenator was synonymous with the earlier-named carcharodontosaurid Mapusaurus. However, the 2024 description of a well-preserved partial skull and skeleton referrable to Taurovenator aided in distinguishing the two taxa.

Tawa.description: Tawa is a genus of possible basal theropod dinosaurs from the Late Triassic period. The fossil remains of Tawa hallae, the type and only species were found in the Hayden Quarry of Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, US. Its discovery alongside the relatives of Coelophysis and Herrerasaurus supports the hypothesis that the earliest dinosaurs arose in Gondwana during the early Late Triassic period in what is now South America, and radiated from there around the globe. The specific name honors Ruth Hall, founder of the Ghost Ranch Museum of Paleontology.

Tazoudasaurus.etymology: Named after Tazouda, one of the fossil localities near Toundoute in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'
Tazoudasaurus.description: Tazoudasaurus is a genus of gravisaurian (probably vulcanodontid) sauropod dinosaurs from the late Early Jurassic (Toarcian). It was recovered in the "Toundoute Continental Series" (Azilal Formation), located in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco in North Africa. Along with Patagosaurus, Volkheimeria, Bagualia, and Perijasaurus (perhaps Barapasaurus and Kotasaurus as well), it represents one of the few sauropods named from this stage on Gondwana, as well as the only one from Africa.

D-shaped tooth crowns with denticulate margins
20 dentary teeth with non-overlapping crowns
V-shaped mandibular symphysis
Elliptical femur cross-section in midshaft

Tehuelchesaurus.description: Tehuelchesaurus is a genus of eusauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic (Oxfordian to Tithonian) of Argentina. It is named in honor of the Tehuelche people, native to the Argentinian province of Chubut, where it was first found.

Absence of the prezygoparapophyseal lamina in the middle and posterior dorsal vertebrae
Accessory posterior centrodiapophyseal lamina giving a ventrally bifurcated appearance
A single intrapostzygapophyseal lamina in the mid-dorsal vertebrae supporting a weakly developed hyposphene
Dorsal neural spines longer anteroposteriorly than wide transversely
Absence of lateral expansion at the dorsal end of the dorsal neural spines
Absence of a postspinal lamina in the dorsal neural spines
Acromion process of the scapula almost four times the minimum width of the scapular shaft

Teinurosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'teinein' meaning 'to stretch' and 'oura' meaning 'tail', combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', likely referring to an elongated tail vertebra.
Teinurosaurus.description: Teinurosaurus is a genus of carnivorous theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic in what is now France. The type species is Teinurosaurus sauvagei. It has been estimated to be 11.4 m (37 ft) in length and 3.6 t (4.0 short tons) in weight.

Telmatosaurus.etymology: From Greek telma/telmat-, "swamp" or "marsh", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "marsh lizard"
Telmatosaurus.description: Telmatosaurus is a genus of basal hadrosauromorph dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Romania. It was relatively small for its group, measuring approximately 5 m (16 ft) in length and 600 kg (1,300 lb) in body mass, which has been explained as an instance of insular dwarfism.

dispute.summary: Telmatosaurus transsylvanicus was historically treated as the most basal hadrosaurid (Weishampel and others, 1993), but recent analyses place it among the derived non-hadrosaurid hadrosauromorphs, outside Hadrosauridae (Tsogtbaatar and others, 2019; Jones, 2026). Magyar and others (2026) group it with Tethyshadros and Kryptohadros in a proposed family Telmatosauridae.

history.note: Placed at Hadrosauromorpha following the prevailing view; the basalmost-hadrosaurid interpretation and the proposed Telmatosauridae both reflected, not adopted.

Tengrisaurus.etymology: Named after Tengri, the sky deity of Mongolian/Siberian mythology, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Tengri lizard"
Tengrisaurus.description: Tengrisaurus is an extinct genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous (Valanginian) Murtoi Formation of Russia. The genus was described in 2017 by Averianov and Skutschas, containing a single species, Tengrisaurus starkovi, known from several isolated vertebrae. Despite being among the oldest named definitive titanosaurs, it is an anatomically derived member of the clade Colossosauria.
