Tenontosaurus.etymology: From Greek tenon ('sinew') and sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'sinew lizard', referring to the bony tendons stiffening its back and tail
Tenontosaurus.description: Tenontosaurus is a genus of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur. It had an unusually long, broad tail, which like its back was stiffened with a network of bony tendons. The genus is known from the late Aptian to Albian ages of the Early Cretaceous period sediments of western North America, dating between 115 and 108 million years ago. It contains two species, Tenontosaurus tilletti (described by John Ostrom in 1970) and Tenontosaurus dossi (described by Winkler, Murry, and Jacobs in 1997). Many specimens of T. tilletti have been collected from several geological formations throughout western North America. T. dossi is known from only a handful of specimens collected from the Twin Mountains Formation of Parker County, Texas.

dispute.summary: Tenontosaurus is recovered as an early-diverging rhabdodontomorph (with Iani and Convolosaurus) by the recent comprehensive analyses (Fonseca and others, 2024; Czepiński and Madzia, 2025), but earlier work and Jones (2026) place it as a basal iguanodontian outside Rhabdodontomorpha.

history.note: Placed at Rhabdodontomorpha following the most recent comprehensive analyses; the basal-Iguanodontia alternative reflected, not adopted.

Teratophoneus.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'teras' meaning 'monster' and 'phoneus' meaning 'murderer', translating as 'monstrous murderer'.
Teratophoneus.description: Teratophoneus is a genus of tyrannosaurine theropod dinosaur that lived during the late Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous period, (about 76.5 to 75.5 million years ago) in what is now Utah. It contains a single known species, T. curriei, named in honor of paleontologist Philip J. Currie. It is known from an incomplete skull and postcranial skeleton recovered from the Kaiparowits Formation.

Terminocavus.etymology: From Latin 'terminus' meaning 'end' and 'cavus' meaning 'cavity', meaning 'coming to the end of the cavity', referring to the nearly closed parietal embayment before its complete loss in more derived taxa
Terminocavus.description: Terminocavus is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Period of what is now North America. The genus contains a single species, the type species Terminocavus sealeyi, known from a parietal and some other associated fragments. The holotype specimen was discovered in the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico in 1997, and was later described and named in a 2020 study. It was similar in anatomy to Pentaceratops and Anchiceratops, which it was closely related to, but had a distinctive heart-shaped upper frill with very narrow notch. It has been hypothesized to form an anagenetic series with several other chasmosaur species.

Epiparietals remain large and triangular through to adulthood

That finer Telmatosauridae placement rests on a single analysis and is not adopted.

Texacephale.etymology: From 'Texas', the U.S. state where the fossil was found, and Greek 'kephale' meaning 'head', in reference to its place of discovery.
Texacephale.description: Texacephale is a possibly dubious genus of pachycephalosaurid dinosaur from the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous. Its fossils come from the Aguja Formation of Big Bend National Park, in Texas, and were described in 2010 by Longrich, Sankey and Tanke. The generic name means Texas + "head" (kephale in Greek) in reference to its place of discovery, and the specific name langstoni honors Wann Langston. It may be a synonym of Stegoceras.

dispute.summary: The validity of Texacephale is contested. It was described as a valid pachycephalosaurid with three autapomorphies (Longrich et al., 2010), but Jasinski and Sullivan (2011) and Woodruff et al. (2025) regard its diagnostic traits as artifacts of taphonomic distortion and treat it as dubious. It is retained at Pachycephalosauridae pending revision.

history.note: Placed at Pachycephalosauridae (basal, no subfamily), valid per Longrich et al. (2010) but regarded as dubious by later authors.

Tharosaurus.etymology: Named for the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, India, where the holotype was found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tharosaurus.description: Tharosaurus is an extinct genus of potentially dubious eusauropod sauropod dinosaurs from the Middle Jurassic Jaisalmer Formation of India. The genus contains a single species, Tharosaurus indicus, known from a fragmentary skeleton including several vertebrae and a rib. When it was named in 2023, Tharosaurus was interpreted as the earliest known diplodocoid and the first member of this clade described from India. However, a later revision of the fossil material argued for a position outside of this clade, as an indeterminate eusauropod. This revision could not find unique features in the Tharosaurus specimen, so it was classified as a nomen dubium.

It has been referred to Ornithomimosauria (Allain et al., 2014), but the holotype was earlier reidentified as an oviraptorosaur and it is widely treated as a nomen dubium (Naish and others, 2001). It is placed conservatively at Ornithomimosauria following the most recent assessment.

Thecocoelurus.etymology: A contraction of the genus names Thecospondylus and Coelurus, translating to 'sheathed hollow form', reflecting the specimen's dual taxonomic history under those two genera
Thecocoelurus.description: Thecocoelurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur from the early Cretaceous period of England. Its type specimen was discovered in strata from the Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight by the Reverend William Fox, and after his death, it, alongside the rest of his collection, became the property of the British Museum of Natural History. The specimen was named in 1888 by Harry Govier Seeley, who assigned it to the genus Thecospondylus . In 1901, it was reassigned by Baron Franz Nopcsa to Coelurus. In 1923, the specimen was removed from either genus by Friedrich von Huene, who assigned it to a genus of its own. Thecocoelurus currently consists of one species, T. daviesi. The validity of the genus has been questioned, with a 2001 publication finding it to be a nomen dubium, although this treatment has not been maintained.

Thecodontosaurus.etymology: From Greek theke (case, socket), odous (tooth) and sauros (lizard); meaning "socket-tooth lizard", reflecting Riley and Stutchbury's observation that the teeth are set in distinct deep alveoli — a configuration unusual among the reptiles known to them at the time.
Thecodontosaurus.description: Thecodontosaurus is a genus of herbivorous basal sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived during the late Triassic period (Carnian age). Its remains are known mostly from Triassic "fissure fillings" in southern England. Thecodontosaurus was a small bipedal animal, about 2 m (6.6 ft) long. It is one of the first dinosaurs to be discovered and is one of the oldest that ever existed. Many species have been named within the genus, but only the type species Thecodontosaurus antiquus is seen as valid today.
diagnostic_features: Teeth set in deep, distinct alveoli to nearly half their length — the feature for which Riley and Stutchbury named the genus.
Hollow-rooted teeth in which a replacement crown forms within the same alveolar cavity as the functional tooth.
Tooth crowns lancet-shaped, with serrated anterior and posterior edges and serrations directed toward the apex.
Dentary short and deep, with maximum dorsoventral depth greater than 20% of dentary length.
All teeth retain a recurved lateral profile; the middle and posterior teeth do not become lanceolate as in other basal sauropodomorphs.
Posterior dorsal and anterior sacral centra with a keyhole-shaped neural canal in transverse section and an extensively ventrally excavated centrum.
Mid-caudal vertebrae with the anterior edge of the transverse process continuing as a sharp ridge across the neural arch.
Proximal caudal centra with the ventral furrowing reduced or lost; ventral surface transversely convex with a median ridge in at least one specimen.

Therizinosaurus.etymology: From Greek therizein ('to reap' or 'to cut') and sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'scythe lizard', named for its enormous scythe-like claws
Therizinosaurus.description: Therizinosaurus is a genus of very large therizinosaurid dinosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Asia. It contains a single species, Therizinosaurus cheloniformis, known from the fossiliferous Nemegt Formation. The first remains of Therizinosaurus were found in 1948 by a Mongolian field expedition in the Gobi Desert and later described by Evgeny Maleev in 1954. The genus is only known from a few bones, including gigantic manual unguals (claw bones), from which it gets its name, and additional findings comprising fore and hindlimb elements that were discovered from the 1960s through the 1980s.
diagnostic_features: Enormous sickle-like ungual phalanges on forelimbs, 60-65cm in length with grooved surfaces
Massive metacarpal bones with great mobility at distal articulation

Ribs with T-shaped dorsal section and well-developed intercostal muscle attachment sites
Reduced or nearly absent bony armor unlike typical sea turtles

Thescelosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'theskelos' meaning 'marvelous' or 'wondrous' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'marvelous lizard'.
Thescelosaurus.description: Thescelosaurus is a genus of ornithischian dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in western North America. It was named and described in 1913 by the paleontologist Charles W. Gilmore; the type species is T. neglectus. Two other species, T. garbanii and T. assiniboiensis, were named in 1976 and 2011, respectively. Additional species have been suggested but are currently not accepted. Thescelosaurus is the eponymous member of its family, the Thescelosauridae. Thescelosaurids are either considered to be basal ("primitive") ornithopods, or are placed outside of this group within the broader group Neornithischia.
diagnostic_features: Ventral surfaces of cervical vertebrae flattened and rugosely roughened, unlike rounded or keeled surfaces in other dinosaurs
Posterior thoracic ribs single-headed, fusion to transverse process differs from double-headed ribs anterior
Four phalanges on third digit of fore foot, an unusual number found only in Hypsilophodon among dinosaurs
Projecting lip-like process on outer posterior side of proximal femur, not before observed in orthopodous dinosaurs
Fifth metatarsal vestigial and attached to posterior side of metatarsal IV, partly functional
Pelvic arch sufficiently diagnostic to separate genus at once from all other known dinosaurs

Thyreosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'thyreos' meaning 'shield' (a large oblong shield) and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to the distinctive shield-like dermal armor of the animal.
Thyreosaurus.description: Thyreosaurus is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic El Mers III Formation of Morocco. The genus contains a single species, Thyreosaurus atlasicus, known from a partial disarticulated skeleton consisting of several dorsal vertebrae, ribs, a limb bone, and dermal bones. Thyreosaurus is characterized by a unique dermal armor with an asymmetrical texture, indicating that it may have been recumbent. Alongside Adratiklit, Thyreosaurus increases the diversity of unique stegosaurs occurring in the Middle Jurassic of Africa.

Prezygapophyses with horizontal orientation in lateral view and continuous prezygodiapophyseal lamina lacking deep notch
Prominent ventral notch between postzygapophyses and ventral keel on all dorsal centra

Tianchisaurus.etymology: From Chinese meaning 'heavenly pool lizard', referring to Tianchi (Heavenly Lake) near the discovery locality in Xinjiang, China.
Tianchisaurus.description: Tianchisaurus, also invalidly called Tianchiasaurus and "Jurassosaurus", is a genus of ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic (Oxfordian-Kimmeridgian) Toutunhe Formation of China. While many later-diverging ankylosaurids had bony clubs at the tips of their tails, Tianchisaurus likely lacked such a structure.

Tianyulong.etymology: From 'Tianyu' (the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature in Pingyi, where the holotype is housed) and Mandarin Chinese 'long' (dragon).
Tianyulong.description: Tianyulong is an extinct genus of heterodontosaurid ornithischian dinosaur from Jianchang County, western Liaoning Province, China. The single species, Tianyulong confuciusi, is known from a small (~70 cm) subadult skeleton (STMN 26-3) preserving partial cranium, postcranial skeleton, and three patches of filamentous integumentary structures along the neck, back, and tail. Zheng, You, Xu and Dong (2009) originally assigned the holotype to the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation of the Jehol Group, but subsequent reassignment of the source horizon places it in the Middle-Late Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation. The filaments are unbranched, hollow, apparently rigid singular structures up to ~60 mm long; the authors did not claim homology with theropod protofeathers, noting closer morphological similarity to Psittacosaurus bristles and treating convergent acquisition as the default interpretation. Tianyulong is recovered as the basalmost well-known heterodontosaurid in the original phylogenetic analysis.
diagnostic_features: Semi-circular diastema demarcated on the lateral surface at the premaxilla-maxilla junction.
Barely developed buccal emargination.
Dorsally placed mandibular jaw joint positioned well above the level of the dentary tooth row.
Only one premaxillary tooth, which is caniniform.
Distinct gap between the dentary teeth and coronoid process.
Adjacent maxillary and dentary tooth crowns distinctly separate, lacking mesial and distal marginal denticles and ridges on the buccal surfaces.

dispute.summary: The finer placement of Tianyuraptor is unsettled. It has been recovered as a basal microraptorine (Turner et al., 2012; Agnolín and Novas, 2013) and, more often in recent work, as a short-armed basal dromaeosaurid just outside Microraptorinae and stemward of Eudromaeosauria, sometimes in a clade with Zhenyuanlong and Daurlong (Lü and Brusatte, 2015; Wang et al., 2022; Jones et al., 2026). It is placed at Dromaeosauridae incertae sedis pending resolution.

history.note: Placed at Dromaeosauridae incertae sedis (least-inclusive uncontested clade); microraptorine and basal short-armed-dromaeosaurid hypotheses proposed.

Tianyuraptor.etymology: Named after the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature where the holotype specimen is housed, combined with Latin 'raptor' meaning 'robber', referring to the action of grabbing prey
Tianyuraptor.description: Tianyuraptor is a genus of short-armed dromaeosaurid dinosaur ('running lizard'; a type of small dinosaur considered to be closely related to birds) that lived during the Early Cretaceous, about 122 million years ago. Its remains have been found in western Liaoning, China. It was similar to other dromaeosaurids found in Liaoning, with the exception of being somewhat more primitive. The type specimen, formally named in 2009, shows features not seen in previously known Northern Hemisphere (Laurasian) dromaeosaurids, but present in Southern Hemisphere (Gondwanan) species and early birds. Because of this, the scientists who first studied Tianyuraptor described it as a "transitional species", bridging the gap between northern and southern types of dromaeosaurid. Tianyuraptor also differs from previously known dromaeosaurids in that it possesses a relatively small furcula ("wishbone"), and unusually short forelimbs.

Tianzhenosaurus.etymology: From Tianzhen County (Shanxi Province, China, where the holotype was found) and Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Tianzhen lizard'.
Tianzhenosaurus.description: Tianzhenosaurus is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous Huiquanpu Formation of Shanxi Province, China. The genus contains two species, T. youngi (the type species) and T. chengi.

dispute.summary: The validity of Tianzhenosaurus is contested. Sullivan (1999) and Arbour and Currie (2015) treated T. youngi as a junior subjective synonym of the Mongolian ankylosaurid Saichania chulsanensis, finding no taxonomically significant differences between the holotype skulls. In 2024, Pang, Li and Guo described a second species, T. chengi, treating Tianzhenosaurus as a valid genus. No broad consensus has been reached.

history.note: Placed at Ankylosaurinae, kept valid although Arbour and Currie (2015) synonymize it with Saichania.

diagnostic_features: Skull low, flat, medium-sized, isosceles triangle shape; skull roof covered with irregular bony tubercles.
Orbit small, surrounded by bony ring; narial opening horizontally elongate; septomaxilla does not separate narial openings.
Occipital condyle narrow, high; not visible in dorsal view; opisthotic extends lateroventrally as curved process.
Mandible deep with convex ventral border; no mandibular ornamentation; tooth crowns with cingula on labial sides, swollen bases, and middle ridge on lingual sides.
Eight fused vertebrae in sacrum (three dorsosacrals, four sacrals, one caudosacral); cervical centrum short amphicoelous; dorsal centrum long amphiplatyan.
Tail club present; scapula rectangular plate-like; femur thick lacking fourth trochanter.

Titanoceratops.etymology: From Greek 'titanos' meaning 'titan' (giant) and 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face', in reference to its exceptionally large size among horned dinosaurs.
Titanoceratops.description: Titanoceratops is a controversial genus of chasmosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur that lived in the Late Cretaceous period (Campanian stage, about 75 million years ago) in what is now New Mexico. Titanoceratops was named for its large size, being one of the largest known horned dinosaurs and the type species was named T. ouranos, after Uranus (Ouranos), the father of the Greek titans. It was named in 2011 by Nicholas R. Longrich for a specimen previously referred to Pentaceratops. Longrich believed that unique features found in the skull reveal it to have been a close relative of Triceratops, classified within the subgroup Triceratopsini. However, other researchers have expressed skepticism, and believe Titanoceratops to simply be an unusually large, old specimen of Pentaceratops.

dispute.summary: Titanoceratops is contested between a valid genus and an exceptionally large individual of Pentaceratops. Longrich (2011) erected it for OMNH 10165 and recovered it as the earliest triceratopsin, and Dalman et al. (2022) likewise recovered it within Triceratopsini. Lehman (1998) had interpreted the same specimen as an aberrant large Pentaceratops sternbergii, and Fowler and Freedman Fowler (2020) treat it as aff. Pentaceratops and exclude it from their matrix. Its resolution below subfamily level is therefore unsettled.

history.note: Placed at Chasmosaurinae, accepted whether Titanoceratops is a valid basal triceratopsin or a large Pentaceratops; tribes dropped.

Tonganosaurus.etymology: Named for the town of Tong'an in Sichuan Province, China, near where it was found, plus Greek sauros ('lizard')
Tonganosaurus.description: Tonganosaurus is a genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur, similar to Omeisaurus. It is known from one specimen consisting of twenty vertebrae, a front limb and pectoral girdle, and a complete hind limb with partial hip. It was discovered in the Yimen Formation, China. The horizon of the specimen and the age of the Yimen Formation is controversial. The formation has been divided into three levels, and Tonganosaurus appears to be of late Early Jurassic (Pliensbachian) in age. Tonganosaurus is the oldest known member of the mamenchisaurids, being almost 15 million years older than the next-oldest members of the group. It was first named by Li Kui, Yang Chun-Yan, Liu Jian, and Wang Zheng-Xin in 2010, and the type species is Tonganosaurus hei.

Torosaurus.etymology: From Greek toros, "perforated" or "full of holes", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "perforated lizard", in reference to the large openings in its frill
Torosaurus.description: Torosaurus is a genus of herbivorous chasmosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur that lived during the late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, between 68 and 66 million years ago, though it is possible that the species range might extend to as far back as 69 million years ago. Fossils have been discovered across the Western Interior of North America, from as far north as Saskatchewan to as far south as Texas.

dispute.summary: Whether Torosaurus is a valid genus or the fully mature growth stage of Triceratops is contested. Scannella and Horner (2010) argued from frill ontogeny and bone histology that all known Torosaurus skulls are senescent Triceratops, formally synonymizing the two. Longrich (2011), Maiorino et al. (2013, proportional mismatches), and Mallon et al. (2022, putative subadult Torosaurus specimens) rejected the synonymy on the absence of transitional forms, and most recent phylogenetic analyses (Dalman et al., 2022) continue to recover the two as distinct. No broad consensus has been reached.

history.note: Placed at Chasmosaurinae, the least-inclusive clade accepted whether Torosaurus is a distinct triceratopsin or mature Triceratops; tribes dropped. Validity unresolved.

Torvosaurus.etymology: From Latin torvus ('savage' or 'fierce') and Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'savage lizard'
Torvosaurus.description: Torvosaurus is a genus of large megalosaurine theropod dinosaur that lived approximately 165 to 146.5 million years ago during the Callovian to Tithonian ages of the late Middle and Late Jurassic period in what is now Colorado, Portugal, Germany, and possibly England, Spain, Tanzania, and Uruguay. It contains two currently recognized species, Torvosaurus tanneri and Torvosaurus gurneyi, plus a third unnamed species from Germany.

Obturator foramen fully enclosed in the pubis, terminating distally in a small anteroposteriorly expanded pubic foot
Ilium with a very low dorsal blade tapering to a rounded posterior point and a wide brevis shelf; acetabulum wide but shallow

Trachodon.etymology: From Greek trachys (rough) and odon (tooth); meaning "rough tooth", referring to the granulated inner surface of the hadrosaurid tooth Leidy described.
Trachodon.description: Trachodon is a dubious genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of what is now Montana in the western United States. The only species is T. mirabilis, though many others have been assigned to the genus. T. mirabilis was described by Joseph Leidy in 1856 based on a set of teeth; however, this was later shown to be a mixture of hadrosaurid and ceratopsian teeth. These fossils were unearthed in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden during an expedition to the Missouri River in Montana, USA, in rock from the Judith River Formation. This formation dates to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, which lasted from 79 to 75.3 million years ago. One of the teeth, an incomplete hadrosaurid tooth, was later chosen as the holotype.

dispute.summary: Trachodon is a nomen dubium founded on isolated teeth and long used as a wastebasket taxon for hadrosaurid remains.

Tralkasaurus.etymology: From Mapudungun 'tralka' meaning 'thunder' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', giving 'thunder lizard'.
Tralkasaurus.description: Tralkasaurus is a genus of abelisaurid dinosaur from the Huincul Formation from Río Negro Province in Argentina. The type and only species is Tralkasaurus cuyi, named in 2020 by Mauricio Cerroni and colleagues based on an incomplete skeleton. A medium-sized abelisaurid, Tralkasaurus exhibits a conflicting blend of characteristics found among the early-diverging abelisauroids with others that characterize the highly specialized clade Brachyrostra, and thus its position within the clade is poorly-resolved.

Transylvanosaurus.etymology: Named after Transylvania, Romania (from Latin trans, "across", and silva, "forest"), combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "lizard from across the forest"

Triceratops.etymology: From Greek tri (three), keras (horn) and ops (face); meaning "three-horned face", referring to the paired supraorbital horn-cores and the median nasal horn-core that ornament the skull.
Triceratops.description: Triceratops is the best-known ceratopsid dinosaur and among the most recognizable of all non-avian dinosaurs, defined by its three large facial horns, prominent toothless beak and solid, unfenestrated parietal-squamosal frill. Marsh erected the genus in 1889 by transferring his earlier Ceratops horridus (Marsh, 1888) to the new combination Triceratops horridus, on a partial skull (later cataloged YPM 1820) recovered from the "Laramie" — now Lance — Formation of Wyoming. Through the 1890s and early 1900s Marsh and others named more than a dozen further species, of which only two are currently accepted today (T. horridus, the type, and T. prorsus), both restricted to the latest Maastrichtian of the Western Interior of North America. Forster (1996) sank most nominal species into one of these two through a cladistic and morphometric revision; Scannella et al. (2014) subsequently documented a stratigraphic pattern in the Hell Creek Formation suggesting a primarily anagenetic transition from T. horridus low in the section to T. prorsus near the K-Pg boundary. Several other names (T. galeus, T. sulcatus, T. maximus, T. eurycephalus, T. albertensis) rest on inadequate material and are now treated as nomina dubia. The proposed synonymy of Torosaurus with mature Triceratops (Scannella and Horner, 2010) has not been broadly accepted in subsequent literature (Longrich and Field 2012; Maiorino et al. 2013) and is not adopted here.
diagnostic_features: Three large facial horns: paired supraorbital horn-cores plus a median nasal horn formed by the epinasal, seated on coossified nasals.
Edentulous premaxillae fronting an unpaired rostral bone (os rostrale) anterior to the premaxillae, forming a projecting toothless beak.
Parietal-squamosal frill solid and unfenestrated, extremely thick and heavily vascularised on its dorsal surface.
Squamosal short and broad with convex, rounded lateral margins; never thinned or fenestrated.
Frill saddle-shaped in dorsal aspect, with an upturned caudal margin and a strong parietal midline ridge.
Epoccipital ossifications fused along the parietal-squamosal margin, with one epoccipital spanning the midline of the parietal.
Frontal fontanelle small and circular, or absent in mature individuals, due to closure of the frontoparietal sutures.
Huge occipital portion of the frill extending posteriorly and laterally, bent ventrally at the sides to overhang the neck.

Trigonosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'trigōnon' (triangle), in reference to the Triângulo Mineiro region of Minas Gerais, Brazil where the holotype was found, and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'triangle lizard'.
Trigonosaurus.description: Trigonosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian dinosaurs from the Maastrichtian Serra da Galga Formation of Brazil. The type species, Trigonosaurus pricei, was first described by Campos, Kellner, Bertini, and Santucci in 2005. It was based on two specimens, both consisting mainly of vertebrae. The two specimens were originally believed to have come from the same individual. However, one specimen was described as the holotype of Caieiria in 2022, while the holotype may have instead come from Baurutitan. Before its description, it was known as the "Peirópolis titanosaur", after the place it was found.

dispute.summary: The validity of Trigonosaurus is contested. Silva Junior et al. (2022) proposed that T. pricei is a junior subjective synonym of Baurutitan britoi (which has page priority within the same 2005 journal volume) and erected the postcranial paratype (MCT 1719-R) as a separate new genus, Caieiria allocaudata. Fronimos (2023) explicitly rejected the synonymy, citing morphological differences in the first caudal vertebra of the two taxa.

history.note: Placed in Aeolosaurini following the phylogenetic analysis of Silva Junior et al. (2022); the proposed synonymy with Baurutitan is contested by Fronimos (2023).

Anterior caudal vertebrae (2-5) with two pronounced dorsal depressions on the transverse process; middle caudals with one such depression.
Prezygapophyses on caudal vertebrae extended forward with wide articular faces.

Articular surfaces for haemal arches strongly developed from caudal 3 through the last preserved element (caudal 20); transverse processes well developed throughout the anterior and medial caudal sequence.

Trimucrodon.etymology: From Latin tri- ('three') and mucro ('dagger point' or 'sharp tip'), and Greek odous ('tooth'), meaning 'three-pointed tooth', referring to the tricuspid teeth
Trimucrodon.description: Trimucrodon is a genus of ornithischian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Lourinhã Formation of Portugal. The type, and currently only, species is T. cuneatus.

dispute.summary: Trimucrodon cuneatus is based on three isolated tricuspid teeth — one designated as the holotype — from the Late Jurassic of Portugal, and its validity is contested. Thulborn (1973) diagnosed it on tooth-crown characters, notably the strongly divergent, prominent foremost and hindmost marginal denticles, and referred it to the now-abandoned Fabrosauridae. Weishampel and Witmer (1990) treated it as a nomen dubium, an indeterminate ornithischian outside Ornithopoda. Sereno (1991) declined that assessment — made, he noted, without comparison — and considered the taxon poorly established but distinct on its denticle pattern, placing it at Ornithischia incertae sedis. Weishampel et al. (2004) again regarded it as dubious while allowing that further study could support its validity, and Jones (2026) treats it as an indeterminate ornithischian. It is placed conservatively at Ornithischia incertae sedis.

history.note: Placed at Ornithischia incertae sedis; tooth-based nomen dubium.

Dispute rebalanced against primary sources — Sereno (1991) considered it possibly valid and distinct, against the nomen-dubium treatments of Weishampel and Witmer (1990), Weishampel et al. (2004), and Jones (2026).

Trinisaura.etymology: Named to commemorate Argentine geologist Trinidad 'Trini' Diaz, combined with Greek sauros ('lizard')
Trinisaura.description: Trinisaura is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur that lived during the late Campanian stage of the Upper Cretaceous, around 73 to 72 million years ago in what is now James Ross Island off the coast of northern Antarctica near Patagonia. It is known from a single, incomplete postcranial skeleton that includes several vertebrae, a partial pelvis, and nearly complete right hindlimb. The fossils were collected in 2008 by paleontologists Juan Moly and Rodolfo Coria from the sandstone of the Snow Hill Island Formation. It remained undescribed in the collections of the Museo de La Plata until its description by Coria and colleagues in 2013, being the basis of the novel genus and species Trinisaura santamartaensis. The genus name is to commemorate the efforts of Argentine geologist Trinidad "Trini" Diaz and the Latin root -sauros, meaning "lizard". The species name is after Santa Marta Cove, where the fossils were collected.

dispute.summary: Triunfosaurus was described as a basal titanosaur (Carvalho et al., 2017), but Poropat et al. (2017) reassessed it as an indeterminate somphospondylan. A redescription by Mannion and Carvalho (2026) provides a revised diagnosis and recovers it as a somphospondylan lying either just outside Titanosauria (equal weighting) or as an early-diverging titanosaur (extended implied weighting); its titanosaurian affinities cannot be excluded.

Triunfosaurus.etymology: Named for the Triunfo Basin in Paraíba, Brazil, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Triunfosaurus.description: Triunfosaurus is a genus of somphospondylan sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of Brazil. It contains a single species, T. leonardii, described by Carvalho et al. in 2017. It was initially described as a basal titanosaur, potentially the earliest known; however, subsequent research questioned its identification as a titanosaur and reassigned it to the Somphospondyli.

Anteriormost haemal arch with ridges along the lateral margins of the proximal rami, forming flange-like processes that continue onto the distal blade.

dispute.summary: Troodon formosus, the type genus of Troodontidae, is widely regarded as a nomen dubium because its holotype is an isolated, undiagnostic tooth (Zanno et al., 2011; Evans et al., 2017; van der Reest and Currie, 2017), leading some authors to transfer its referred material to Stenonychosaurus. Varricchio et al. (2025) instead propose a neotype and an ICZN petition to retain Troodon. Where its referred material is scored it is recovered as a derived troodontine (with Saurornithoides and Zanabazar), the placement adopted here.

Troodon.etymology: From Greek 'troo' (wounding) and 'odon' meaning 'tooth', hence 'wounding tooth', referring to the distinctive serrated teeth.
Troodon.description: Troodon is a controversial genus of relatively small, bird-like theropod dinosaurs definitively known from the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous period (about 77 million years ago). It includes at least one species, Troodon formosus, known from Montana. Discovered in October 1855, T. formosus was among the first dinosaurs found in North America, although it was thought to be a lizard until 1877.

Tsagantegia.description: Tsagantegia is a genus of medium-sized ankylosaurid thyreophoran dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period. The genus is monotypic, including only the type species, T. longicranialis. The specimen consists of a very partial individual, comprising the skull and lacking postcranial remains. Since it only preserves the skull, Tsagantegia is mainly characterized by its elongated snout and the flattened facial osteoderms, greatly differing from other ankylosaurs.

Tsintaosaurus.etymology: Named for the city of Qingdao (formerly romanized as Tsintao), China, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tsintaosaurus.description: Tsintaosaurus is a genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of China. It was about 8.3 meters (27 ft) long and weighed 2.5 tonnes (2.8 short tons). The type species is Tsintaosaurus spinorhinus, first described by Chinese paleontologist C. C. Young in 1958. As a hadrosaur, Tsintaosaurus had the characteristic 'duck bill' snout and a battery of powerful teeth which it used to chew vegetation. It usually walked on all fours, but could rear up on its hind legs to scout for predators and flee when it spotted one. Like other hadrosaurs, Tsintaosaurus probably lived and traveled in herds.

Turanoceratops.etymology: Combines 'Turan', an old Persian name for Turkestan (the region of discovery in Uzbekistan), with Greek 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face'.
Turanoceratops.description: Turanoceratops is a genus of herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Bissekty Formation of Uzbekistan. The fossils dated from the mid-late Turonian stage, roughly 90 million years ago. The skull bore a pair of long brow horns like those seen in the Ceratopsidae, although Turanoceratops appears to have been transitional between earlier ceratopsians and ceratopsids, and not a ceratopsid itself.

dispute.summary: Turanoceratops tardabilis is the basis of a long dispute over the first Asian ceratopsid. Sues and Averianov (2009) recovered it within Ceratopsidae as the sister to Centrosaurinae, but Farke and others (2009) reanalyzed it as the sister taxon to Ceratopsidae lying outside it — a position independently recovered by the describers of Sinoceratops (Xu and others, 2010) and followed by Jones (2026).

history.note: Placed at Ceratopsoidea, the least-inclusive clade both hypotheses accept; the within-Ceratopsidae position of Sues and Averianov (2009) reflected, not adopted.

Re-evaluated; Ceratopsoidea retained. The outside-Ceratopsidae position now rests on three independent analyses (Farke and others 2009; Xu and others 2010; Jones 2026) against the single within-Ceratopsidae result of Sues and Averianov (2009), but that minority view is unretracted, so the mutually-accepted node holds.

diagnostic_features: Tooth crowns with variably developed secondary ridges, unlike the condition in more derived ceratopsids
Only two or three teeth in each vertical dental file, fewer than in more derived ceratopsids
Teeth double-rooted, unlike Zuniceratops and more basal neoceratopsians
Frontal excluded from the orbital margin, unlike more basal neoceratopsians
Shallow supracranial cavity complex present, unlike more basal neoceratopsians

It is known from a partial skull and associated mandible that were unearthed in 1971 by a Polish-Mongolian Expedition to the Barun Goyot Formation of the Gobi Desert. The specimen was described in 1974 by Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska as a new genus and species.

Tyrannosaurus.etymology: From Greek tyrannos (tyrant) and sauros (lizard); meaning "tyrant lizard", a name Osborn coined to convey the genus's exceptional size relative to all then-known carnivorous land vertebrates.
Tyrannosaurus.description: Tyrannosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur. The type species Tyrannosaurus rex (rex meaning 'king' in Latin), often shortened to T. rex, is one of the best represented theropods. It lived throughout what is now western North America, on what was then an island continent known as Laramidia, and had a much wider range than other tyrannosaurids. Fossils are found in a variety of geological formations dated to the late Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, 69 to 66 million years ago, with isolated specimens possibly indicating an earlier origin in the middle Campanian age. It was one of the last known members of the tyrannosaurids and among the last non-avian dinosaurs to exist before the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event.
diagnostic_features: Megalocephalic skull with deep, massively built proportions, brought close to the sacrum by a shortened presacral column of approximately 23 vertebrae.
Fused nasals forming an arched midline ridge on the snout that reinforces the skull against bite-induced stress.
Teeth heterodont and broadly oval to D-shaped in cross-section, with transverse diameter exceeding anteroposterior; alveolar reinforcing plates on the inner surface of the maxilla and dentary.
Squamosal bearing a distinctive horizontal anterior bar projecting into the laterotemporal fenestra.
Forelimb extremely reduced; functionally didactyl manus with powerful recurved unguals; humerus little more than half the length of the femur.
Five sacral vertebrae coossified into a single neural plate with three small fenestrations between S2 and S5.
Pubis, ilium and ischium firmly coalesced; pubis terminating distally in a hugely expanded pedicle ("pubic boot").
Caudal series of approximately 53 vertebrae forming a long, flexible balancing tail without the rod-like rigidity of ornithomimids.

synonyms.name: Dynamosaurus imperiosus

The name is technically senior to Tyrannosaurus rex but, having been used in fewer than 25 publications since 1899, is suppressed under ICZN Article 23.9 in favor of Tyrannosaurus rex (nomen protectum).

species.name: Tyrannosaurus rex
species.etymology: From Latin rex, "king", chosen by Osborn to evoke the animal's standing as the largest carnivorous land vertebrate then known.

type_specimen.material: Partial skeleton with both jaws and portions of the skull, vertebrae, ribs, scapula, humerus, ilium, pubis, ischium, and metapodials.

notable_specimens.significance: The most complete (about 85 percent) and largest Tyrannosaurus skeleton, from the Hell Creek Formation. Histology shows it reached full size at age 19 and died at about 28, the longest estimated life of any tyrannosaur known.

The second most complete Tyrannosaurus skeleton, 199 bones representing 70 percent of the total, from the Hell Creek Formation. Its pathologies include broken and healed ribs, a broken and healed neck, and a hole in the back of the head about the size of a Tyrannosaurus tooth.

Reported to measure 13 meters in length. Using a mass estimation technique extrapolating from femur circumference, Scotty was estimated as the largest known Tyrannosaurus specimen at 8.87 t in body mass.

From the Hell Creek Formation. Yielded medullary tissue in its femur, found only in female birds during ovulation, confirming it as a female that died during ovulation; the only Tyrannosaurus conclusively sexed. Also a source of reported soft-tissue blood vessels and collagen.

notable_specimens.institution: Houston Museum of Nature and Science
notable_specimens.significance: Preserves patches of mosaic scales on the tail, hip, and neck, used in a 2017 review concluding that feather covering of large tyrannosaurids, if present, was limited to the upper side of the trunk. Also shows pathologies: a hole penetrating its jugal and severe tail trauma with bone remodeling.

The first complete Tyrannosaurus forelimbs were identified in 1989 belonging to MOR 555, confirming that the genus had short two-fingered arms about 1 meter long, as had been suggested from the related Gorgosaurus.

Tyrannotitan.etymology: From Greek tyrannos ('tyrant') and titan ('giant'), meaning 'tyrant titan'
Tyrannotitan.description: Tyrannotitan is a genus of large theropod dinosaur belonging to the carcharodontosaurid family. It is known from a single species, T. chubutensis, which lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina. Tyrannotitan is considered to share a close relationship with other prominent South American carcharodontosaurids such as Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus. Unlike its relatives, it was bulkier and more robust. This taxon is known from two specimens, both of which are highly incomplete.

Uberabatitan.etymology: Named after Uberaba, the city in Minas Gerais, Brazil where it was found, combined with Greek titan meaning 'giant'; translates as 'Uberaba titan'
Uberabatitan.description: Uberabatitan is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Brazil. It is known from bones including neck, back, and tail vertebrae, pelvic bones, and limb bones. These fossils were found in the uppermost portion of the Maastrichtian-age Serra da Galga Formation of the Bauru Group, in Uberaba, Minas Gerais. The type species, described by Salgado and Carvalho in 2008, is U. ribeiroi. To date, it is the most recent titanosaur from Bauru Group rocks; other titanosaurs from the Bauru Group, including Baurutitan and Trigonosaurus, come from lower (thus older) levels.

Udanoceratops.description: Udanoceratops is a genus of large leptoceratopsid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of Mongolia. The holotype specimen, the partial skeleton of an adult with its bones encapsulated in calcium carbonate, was discovered in the 1980s as part of the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition, and was subsequently transported to the Paleontological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences. In 1992, it was described by paleontologist Sergei Kurzanov. The sole species of Udanoceratops, also the type species, is Udanoceratops tschizhovi, named after a colleague of Kurzanov, D. O. Tschizhov. Additional remains have been assigned to Udanoceratops, though these may be misattributions.

Ultrasaurus.etymology: From Latin ultra (beyond, exceeding) and Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "ultra lizard", reflecting Kim's inference that the animal exceeded Supersaurus in size.
Ultrasaurus.description: Ultrasaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur discovered by Haang Mook Kim in South Korea. However, the name was first used unofficially (as a nomen nudum) in 1979 by Jim Jensen to describe a set of giant dinosaur bones he discovered in the United States. Because Kim published the name for his specimen before Jensen could do so officially, George Olshevsky renamed the specimen as Ultrasauros. Jensen's giant sauropod was later found to be a chimera, and the type remains are now assigned to Supersaurus.

Neural spine of caudal vertebra (DGBU-1978A) 17.0 cm long, 11.5 cm wide, 4.5 cm wider than equivalent element in Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis

The genus contains a single species, Ulughbegsaurus uzbekistanensis, known from multiple maxilla fragments.

Rugose lateral surface texture characteristic of Carcharodontosauria

Unaysaurus.etymology: From 'unay', a word meaning 'black water' in the Tupi language indigenous to Brazil, referring to the black-water stream near the discovery site, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Unaysaurus.description: Unaysaurus is a genus of herbivorous unaysaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur. Discovered in southern Brazil, in the geopark of Paleorrota, in 1998, and announced in a press conference on Thursday, December 3, 2004, it is one of the oldest dinosaurs known. It is closely related to plateosaurid dinosaurs found in Germany, which indicates that it was relatively easy for species to spread across the giant landmass of the time, the supercontinent of Pangaea. The fossils of Unaysaurus are well-preserved. They consist of an almost complete skull, including a lower jaw, and partial skeleton with many of the bones still connected to each other in their natural positions. It is one of the most complete dinosaur skeletons (including complete skull) ever recovered in Brazil.
diagnostic_features: Well developed laterodorsally oriented process formed by frontal and parietal (more developed than in Plateosaurus)
Medial depression on mediodorsal surface of the parietals
Two fossae on the maxillary medial lamina
Deep ventral depression on the basisphenoid
Conspicuous blunt ridge running on lateral surface of deltopectoral crest

Unenlagia.etymology: From Mapuche 'unum' meaning 'bird' and 'llag' meaning 'half', meaning 'half-bird', reflecting its interpreted transitional position between birds and basal theropods.
Unenlagia.description: Unenlagia is a genus of unenlagiine theropod dinosaur that lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period. The genus Unenlagia has been assigned two species: U. comahuensis, the type species described by Novas and Puerta in 1997, and U. paynemili, described by Calvo et al. in 2004.

Twisted scapular shaft with dorsal-facing external surface

Laterally oriented humeral articulation of scapula (previously unreported in non-avian dinosaurs)
Laterally oriented glenoid cavity enabling avian-style forelimb folding and elevation

The genus contains a single species, U. ceibalii, known only from a single fossilized pubis (a pelvic bone).

Utahraptor.etymology: Named for the state of Utah, USA, where the fossils were found, combined with Latin 'raptor' meaning 'robber' or 'plunderer'.
Utahraptor.description: Utahraptor is a genus of large dromaeosaurid (a group of feathered carnivorous theropods) dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period from around 139 to 135 million years ago in what is now the United States. The genus was described in 1993 by American paleontologist James Kirkland and colleagues with the type species Utahraptor ostrommaysi, based on fossils that had been unearthed earlier from the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah. Later, many additional specimens were described including those from the skull and postcranium in addition to those of younger individuals.

Utetitan.etymology: From 'Ute', honoring the original Ute peoples of central Utah on whose ancestral lands the holotype was recovered, and Greek 'titan' (giant).
Utetitan.description: Utetitan is an extinct genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the late Maastrichtian (Late Cretaceous) of southwestern North America. The single species, Utetitan zellaguymondeweyae, is based on USNM 15560 — a partial postcranial skeleton from the lower North Horn Formation at Joe's Valley on the Wasatch Plateau, Emery County, Utah — formerly the primary referred specimen of Alamosaurus sanjuanensis. Paul (2025) split this material away from Alamosaurus on the basis of scapular and ischial autapomorphies, restricted A. sanjuanensis to its New Mexican type horizon, and erected the new subfamily Utetitaninae for the new genus; that clade-name is single-paper-recent and not adopted as a parent here per the project's taxonomy policy.
diagnostic_features: Acromion process of the scapula strongly prominent.
Posterior profile of the scapula strongly sinuous, producing a prominent triangular glenoid process.
Paired tubercles dorsal to the scapular glenoid fairly prominent and widely separated.
Postero-dorsal edge of the scapular blade flares prominently posteriorly.
Lateral process of the ischium modest in size.

dispute.summary: Valdoraptor is a nomen dubium based on a partial metatarsus from the Early Cretaceous of England, and its affinity is contested. It is most often referred to Ornithomimosauria (Allain et al., 2014), where it would rank among the oldest known members of the clade, but some workers favor a noasaurid ceratosaur affinity, and its diagnostic characters are regarded as homoplastic. It is placed conservatively at Ornithomimosauria.

history.note: Retained at Ornithomimosauria following Allain et al. (2014); its status as a nomen dubium and the alternative noasaurid affinity are recorded as unresolved.

Valdoraptor.etymology: From Latin 'Valdus' (Wealden, referring to the Wealden Group) and 'raptor' (plunderer); meaning 'Wealden plunderer'.
Valdoraptor.description: Valdoraptor is a genus of ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of England. It is known only from bones of the feet. The holotype, BMNH R2559 (incorrectly given by Owen as BMNH R2556), was found near Cuckfield in layers of the Tunbridge Wells Sand Formation dating from the late Valanginian. The specimen is damaged, lacking parts of the upper and lower ends. It has a conserved length of 21.5 centimeters (8.5 in) and an estimated total length of 24 centimeters (9.4 in). This genus is paleontologically significant for being the first ornithomimosaur specimen known from England and represents the earliest record of ornithomimosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Metatarsal II mediolaterally compressed.
Prominent dorsolateral ridge on metatarsal II.

Valdosaurus.etymology: From 'valdo', a modification of Old English 'weald' meaning 'a wood' (referring to the Weald region of England), combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Valdosaurus.description: Valdosaurus is a genus of bipedal herbivorous dryosaurid dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous of the Isle of Wight and elsewhere in England. Originally its remains were believed to belong to Hypsilophodon. In 1889, Richard Lydekker assigned them to Camptosaurus, alongside a partial lower jaw, and applied the name Camptosaurus valdensis. In the 1970s, Peter Galton reassigned these remains to a new species of Dryosaurus, then to an entirely new genus and species, that being Valdosaurus proper. The type and only species of Valdosaurus, named by Galton, is V. canaliculatus.

A complete hind limb with a femur about 50 cm long, attributed to a skeletally mature adult and used to establish the taxon's maximum size at roughly 4 meters body length, in contrast to the juvenile-sized 14 cm type femora.

dispute.summary: Vallibonavenatrix cani was described as a spinosaurine (Malafaia et al., 2020) and again recovered as a spinosaurine by Rauhut et al. (2025), but its position is unstable across other analyses, which recover it as a baryonychine or a basal spinosaurid outside both subfamilies (Barker et al., 2021; Mateus and Estraviz-López, 2022) or, as an unstable-wildcard result, a megalosaurid (Isasmendi et al., 2024). Spinosauridae is the least-inclusive clade the credible hypotheses accept.

history.note: Placed at Spinosaurinae following the describing paper and Rauhut et al. (2025); its position is unstable across analyses.

Broadened to Spinosauridae incertae sedis. The subfamily placement flip-flops across analyses (spinosaurine, baryonychine, or basal spinosaurid outside both subfamilies), so the conservative shared node is adopted.

It is placed accordingly.

Vectaerovenator.etymology: Named after Vectis (the Latin name for the Isle of Wight), combined with Latin aero meaning 'air' (referring to the pneumaticity of the vertebrae) and venator meaning 'hunter'; translates as 'Isle of Wight air-filled hunter'
Vectaerovenator.description: Vectaerovenator is a genus of tetanuran theropod from the Early Cretaceous period of what is now England (Lower Greensand Group; Ferruginous Sands). It contains one species, Vectaerovenator inopinatus; its holotype, consisting of the specimens IWCMS 2020.400, 2020.407, and 2019.84, comprises two anterior dorsal vertebrae, a cervical vertebra and a mid‐caudal vertebra from the late Aptian Ferruginous Sands of the Isle of Wight in southern England, discovered in 2019. Comparative anatomical analysis shows that this taxon shares homoplastic features with megalosauroids, carcharodontosaurs, and some coelurosaurs, and cannot be reliably placed beyond Tetanurae incertae sedis, but has enough autapomorphies that it can be considered a valid genus.

dispute.summary: Velocipes guerichi is a nomen dubium based on the proximal part of a fibula. Rauhut and Hungerbühler (2000) judged the specimen too poorly preserved to establish even what bone it is, and treated it as an indeterminate vertebrate; Welles (1984) had earlier found the holotype undiagnostic. Skawiński and others (2017) re-examined the specimen, reaffirmed its identification as a theropod fibula against that view, and argued it preserves phylogenetically informative characters, but concluded that it cannot be identified more precisely than an indeterminate theropod and offered no diagnosis. Earlier referrals to Ceratosauria (Tykoski and Rowe, 2004; Weishampel and others, 2004) are not supported by that re-examination.

Velociraptor.etymology: From Latin velox (swift) and raptor (thief, plunderer); meaning "swift thief", chosen by Osborn to evoke the rapid, predatory habits inferred from the holotype's slender skull and recurved unguals.
Velociraptor.description: Velociraptor is a small dromaeosaurid theropod from the late Campanian of central Asia, defined by a long, low skull, recurved serrated teeth, and a hyperextensible sickle-clawed second pedal digit. Osborn erected the genus and the type species V. mongoliensis in 1924 on a partial skull and front-limb claw collected by Peter Kaisen in August 1923 at the Flaming Cliffs (Shabarakh Usu / Bayn Dzak) of the Djadokhta Formation in central Mongolia, during the Central Asiatic Expedition of the American Museum of Natural History. Soviet-Mongolian expeditions during the 1960s-70s recovered substantially more material, culminating in the famous "Fighting Dinosaurs" specimen (MPC-D 100/25), a near-complete skeleton of V. mongoliensis preserved in a death struggle with a Protoceratops andrewsi from Tugrugeen Shire. Barsbold (1983) reviewed the new material and erected Velociraptorinae for the genus. Turner et al. (2007) reported quill knobs on the ulna of a V. mongoliensis specimen, providing direct anatomical evidence for pennaceous wing feathering — making Velociraptor one of the better-attested feathered non-avian dinosaurs. Velociraptor's cultural prominence outside paleontology stems primarily from its oversized depiction in the Jurassic Park franchise, which conflates V. mongoliensis with the much larger Deinonychus antirrhopus.

Pronounced lacrimal boss at the dorsal margin of the preorbital bar; lacrimal broadly exposed on the skull roof.
Cervical centra with strongly developed epipophyses overhanging the postzygapophyseal facets; axis centrum pneumatic.
Anterior caudal vertebrae bearing elongate ossified tendons of the prezygapophyses and chevrons that form a stiffening sheath over 8-10 caudals.
Pelvis opisthopubic and dolichoiliac, with the pubis directed posteroventrally and a shortened ischium bearing a distally placed obturator process.
Pedal digit II hyperextensible and bearing an enlarged, sickle-shaped predatory ungual; metatarsal III mediolaterally pinched proximally and slightly shorter than II and IV.

It is the oldest known titanosaur from the northern hemisphere, and is considered important for being related to the Lognkosauria, a group known only from South America later in the Late Cretaceous. Vulcanodon.etymology: Named after the volcano near which it was found in Zimbabwe, combined with Greek odon meaning 'tooth'; translates as 'volcano tooth'
Vulcanodon.description: Vulcanodon is an extinct genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Jurassic uppermost Forest Sandstone of southern Africa. The only known species is V. karibaensis. Discovered in 1969 in Zimbabwe, it was regarded as the earliest known sauropod for decades, and is still one of the most primitive genera that has been discovered.

Forelimb about 78% the length of the hindlimb
Femur straight and columnar, lacking sigmoidal curvature

Wannanosaurus.etymology: Named for Wannan (southern Anhui), the region of China where the fossils were discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.

It is retained at Pachycephalosauria incertae sedis.

Weewarrasaurus.description: Weewarrasaurus is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of the Griman Creek Formation near Lightning Ridge, in New South Wales, Australia. The type and only species is W. pobeni, known from the holotype, an isolated dentary preserved in opal, as well as a secondary referred dentary. It is thought to have co-existed with multiple other ornithopods of different sizes and lineages.

Wellnhoferia.etymology: Named after German paleontologist Peter Wellnhofer, who described the Solnhofen specimen of Archaeopteryx in 1988
Wellnhoferia.description: Wellnhoferia is a genus of early prehistoric bird-like theropod dinosaur closely related to Archaeopteryx. It is known from a single species, W. grandis, that lived in what is now Germany, during the Late Jurassic. While Wellnhoferia was similar to Archaeopteryx, it had a shorter tail and its fourth toe was shorter than that of Archaeopteryx. Andrzej Elżanowski (2001) of the Institute of Zoology of the University of Wrocław, Poland, determined the differences resulted from a "phylogenetic reduction rather than individual variation."

Pedal digit IV composed of only four phalanges with long ungual lacking pronounced ventral curvature and widely separated flexor tubercle
Nearly symmetric pattern of pedal rays II-IV with metatarsals II and IV of equal length
Manual digit I ungual approximately one-third length of basal phalanx
Pedal digit II relatively longer and pedal digit IV relatively shorter than in Archaeopteryx, conferring greater symmetry to foot

Willinakaqe.etymology: From Mapuche willi ('south'), iná ('mimic'), and kaqe ('duck'), meaning 'Southern duck-mimic'
Willinakaqe.description: Willinakaqe is a dubious genus of saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaur described based on fossils from the late Cretaceous (late Campanian-early Maastrichtian stage) of the Río Negro Province of southern Argentina.

dispute.summary: Cruzado-Caballero and Coria (2016) revised Willinakaqe salitralensis and found that the referred material may represent more than one hadrosaurid taxon, that all characters of the original diagnosis are invalid, and that the holotype right premaxilla (MPCA-PV SM 8) is itself too weathered and incomplete to support a diagnosis. They termed the species a nomen vanum; because the holotype is simply undiagnostic rather than a chimera, it is treated here as a nomen dubium.

history.note: Placed at Hadrosauridae incertae sedis; nomen vanum/dubium.

Corrected the dispute prose (the holotype is not itself a chimera) and removed the original diagnostic_features, which that revision invalidated. Also dropped the size estimate (paul2024a), which was scaled from the referred, possibly-multi-taxon material. Sourced the revision as cruzado-caballero2016a.

Wudingloong.etymology: From 'Wuding' (Wuding County, Yunnan Province, China, where the type locality lies) and Mandarin Chinese 'loong' (dragon).
Wudingloong.description: Wudingloong is an extinct genus of early-diverging massopodan sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Hettangian-early Sinemurian (Early Jurassic) Yubacun Formation at Wande Town in Wuding County, Yunnan Province, southern China. The single species, Wudingloong wui, is known from a partial articulated skeleton (LFGT-YW002) preserving most of the skull, the anterior axial column, and a complete right forelimb. Wang et al. (2025) recover Wudingloong as sister to Plateosauravus + Ruehleia, outside Massospondylidae and Sauropodiformes, and argue it is both the earliest-diverging and stratigraphically oldest sauropodomorph known from East Asia.

Humerus with a slender shaft (minimum width 0.12x total length) and a flat, low, only slightly convex humeral head.
Ungual of manual digit I large and robust, with length ~2.9x and proximal height and width ~3.2x those of the ungual of manual digit III.
Metacarpal V gracile with an hourglass-shaped outline; proximal end approximately as wide transversely as the distal end.

Originally described as a bird of uncertain affinity (Harrison and Walker, 1973), it was reassessed by Naish and Martill (2007) as an indeterminate maniraptoran and a nomen dubium. It is placed conservatively at Maniraptora incertae sedis.

Wyleyia.etymology: Named in honor of J. F. Wyley, who discovered the specimen in Weald Clay deposits of Henfield, Sussex, England.
Wyleyia.description: Wyleyia is an extinct genus of indeterminate maniraptoran dinosaurs containing a single species, Wyleyia valdensis, known from the early Cretaceous period of Sussex, England. The genus is known from a single specimen, a damaged right humerus. It was named to honor J. F. Wyley, who found the specimen in Weald Clay deposits of Henfield in Sussex (England). The specific name valdensis means "from the Weald".

species.etymology: From Latin 'valdensis' meaning 'from the Weald', referring to the Weald Clay deposits of Sussex, England, where the holotype humerus was found.

Xenoceratops.etymology: From Greek 'xenos' meaning 'foreign' or 'alien' and 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face', referring to the scarcity of ceratopsian species known from the Foremost Formation.
Xenoceratops.description: Xenoceratops is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous (middle Campanian stage), and is known to have lived in what is currently Alberta, Canada. The genus has one known species, Xenoceratops foremostensis, after its place of discovery, the Foremost Formation.
diagnostic_features: Two epiparietals (P2-P3) on posterior parietal ramus
Wide-based, short, thick P2 processes adjacent to midline with dorsolateral curl
Elongate, dorsoventrally depressed spike at P3 locus, posterolaterally oriented and straight not curled
Additional epiparietals fuse into ovoid depressions on lateral parietal margin
Lacks P1 processes; lacks imbricated epiparietals on lateral ramus
Lacks midline parietal bumps when viewed laterally; arched cross-section of anteriormost midline ramus

species.name: Xenoceratops foremostensis
species.etymology: Named for the town of Foremost, Alberta, Canada, near which the holotype skull fragments were excavated from the Foremost Formation.

dispute.summary: Originally described as a neosauropod of uncertain affinity (Taylor and Naish, 2007) and later treated as a nomen dubium by some, Xenoposeidon was reinterpreted as the earliest known rebbachisaurid on the basis of a shared neural-arch lamina arrangement (Taylor, 2018), a placement resting on morphological argument rather than a numerical analysis. A competing titanosaur interpretation has also been raised.

history.note: Placed at Rebbachisauridae following Taylor (2018) and the Princeton Encyclopedia (Jones, 2026); the assignment rests on a single shared character and has not yet been tested in a quantitative analysis.

Xenoposeidon.etymology: From Greek xenos meaning 'strange' or 'alien' and Poseidon (the Greek god of the sea), in allusion to the sauropod genus Sauroposeidon; translates as 'strange Poseidon'
Xenoposeidon.description: Xenoposeidon is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of England, living about 140 million years ago. It is known from a single partial vertebra with unusual features, unlike those of other sauropods. This bone was first discovered in the early 1890s but received little attention until it was found by University of Portsmouth student Mike Taylor, who formally described and named it in 2007 with Darren Naish.
diagnostic_features: Neural arch covers dorsal surface of centrum, with posterior margin continuous with cotyle
Neural arch slopes anteriorly 35 degrees relative to the vertical
Broad, flat area of featureless bone on lateral face of neural arch
Accessory infraparapophyseal and postzygapophyseal laminae meeting ventrally to form a V
Neural canal is asymmetric: small and circular posteriorly but tall and teardrop-shaped anteriorly
Supporting laminae form vaulted arch over anterior neural canal

species.name: Xenoposeidon proneneukos
species.etymology: From Ancient Greek meaning 'forward sloping', describing the distinctive anterior lean of the neural arch, the most conspicuous anatomical feature of the holotype vertebra.

type_specimen.material: A mid posterior dorsal vertebra consisting of partial centrum and neural arch.

species.authors: Taylor, M. P.; Naish, D.

Xenotarsosaurus.etymology: From Greek xenos ('strange'), tarsos ('tarsus' or 'ankle'), and sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'strange ankle lizard', referring to the exceptional build of the ankle
Xenotarsosaurus.description: Xenotarsosaurus is a genus of abelisaurid theropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous of Argentina.

Astragalus and calcaneus fused, undifferentiated, with no visible boundary with tibia in posterior view

Femur gracile with head projected antero-medially at ~45°, greater trochanter continuing with femoral head, fourth trochanter projecting postero-medially
Tibia with relatively delicate proximal end and cavities at base of cnemial crest

dispute.summary: Xenovenator espinosai, a thick-skulled Mexican troodontid, was recovered within Troodontinae by its describers (Rivera-Sylva et al., 2026), who placed it in a new tribe Troodontini (with Albertavenator and the North American Troodon complex). The tribe is not adopted here as a node (single analysis); the genus is placed in Troodontinae.

history.note: Moved from Troodontini (tribe dropped) to Troodontinae following Rivera-Sylva et al. (2026).

Xenovenator.etymology: From Greek xenos ('strange') and Latin venator ('hunter'), meaning 'strange hunter'
Xenovenator.description: Xenovenator is an extinct genus of troodontid theropod dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian age) of North America. The type species of the genus, Xenovenator espinosai, is known from fragmentary skull bones found in the Cerro del Pueblo Formation of Mexico. It is characterized by an unusually expanded and rugose skull roof, somewhat comparable to that seen in pachycephalosaurs. This may imply Xenovenator individuals engaged in combat with other members of their species, a behavior for which adaptations had not been previously observed in non-avian paravians.
diagnostic_features: Frontals extensively fused with strongly interdigitating sutures
Strong doming of frontals projecting above orbital margins
Frontals and parietals massively thickened (up to 12 mm posteriorly) with variable thickness
Dorsal surface of frontals and parietals rugose and striated with transverse ridge texture
Nasal processes broad and transversely arched between lacrimals forming broad midline ridge
Orbital fossae widely separated ventrally with orbital margins expanded laterally
Triangular parietal table just behind frontoparietal suture, not seen in other troodontids
Laterosphenoids and orbitosphenoids strongly expanded anteriorly to enclose braincase ventrally
Supratemporal fossae extend strongly anterolaterally with frontoparietal suture projecting posteriorly
L-shaped frontal-lacrimal contact with complex posterior and medial facets

Xiangyunloong.etymology: From Chinese 'Xiangyun' (auspicious clouds), the name of the county where the specimen was found, and 'loong', the Pinyin for the traditional Chinese dragon symbolizing power and auspiciousness.
Xiangyunloong.description: Xiangyunloong is a genus of non-sauropodan massopodan sauropodomorph dinosaur known from the Early Jurassic Fengjiahe Formation at Daaonai, Xiangyun County, Yunnan Province, China. The genus contains a single species, Xiangyunloong fengming, known from a partial postcranial skeleton of a skeletally mature individual estimated at about 9–10 m in length.
diagnostic_features: Lateral expansion developed at the middle region of the dorsal end of cervical neural spines.
Hyposphene of dorsal vertebrae equal to or greater than the height of the neural canal.
Highly developed posterodorsal corner present at the neural spine of the last dorsal vertebra.
Presence of a prezygapophyseal centrodiapophyseal fossa (PRCDF) in the first caudal vertebra, framed by ACDL, CPRL, and PRDL laminae.
Ilium with anteroposteriorly reduced but laterally and ventrally flaring supracetabular crest.

type_specimen.material: Partial skeleton: three cervical, five dorsal, and fifteen caudal vertebrae; several dorsal rib fragments; nearly a dozen chevrons; an incomplete left ilium; and a right ischium.

history.note: Placed conservatively at Somphospondyli given the unresolved euhelopodid versus titanosaurian debate; finer placement remains unresolved.

Xianshanosaurus.etymology: Named after Xianshan Hill near the fossil locality in the Ruyang Basin, Henan Province, China, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Xianshanosaurus.description: Xianshanosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian-Albian) of the Ruyang Basin in Henan Province, China. Its type and only species is Xianshanosaurus shijiagouensis. It was described in 2009 by a team of paleontologists led by Lü Junchang. Xianshanosaurus may be a titanosaur, and Daxiatitan may be its closest relative, but its evolutionary relationships remain controversial.
diagnostic_features: Elongated tooth with a distinct ridge on the lingual surface of the tooth crown.
Neural spines of anterior caudal vertebrae plate-like with coarse areas on the middle portions of the anterior and posterior surfaces.
Distinct fossae present on the anterolateral surface of the base of the prezygapophysis and the anterior surface of the base of the transverse process.
Coracoid foramen located closely to the scapula-coracoid suture.
Shallow concavity present on the proximal end of the dorsal ribs.

dispute.summary: Xiaotingia has been recovered in many positions: as an archaeopterygid at the base of Deinonychosauria (Xu et al., 2011), as an anchiornithid on the avialan stem (Foth and Rauhut, 2017; Pei et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2026), as a more stemward avialan outside the anchiornithids (Foth et al., 2025), as a sinovenatorine troodontid (Hartman et al., 2019), and as a basal scansoriopterygid (Lefèvre et al., 2017). The competing avialan and deinonychosaur hypotheses agree only on Eumaniraptora, where it is placed.

Xingtianosaurus.description: Xingtianosaurus is an extinct genus of oviraptorosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now China during the Early Cretaceous. The type and only species, X. ganqi, was named and described in 2019. It was placed in the Caudipteridae, alongside Caudipteryx and Similicaudipteryx.

Xingxiulong.etymology: Named for the Xingxiu Bridge (Xingxiu meaning 'constellation' in Chinese) in Yunnan, China, combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'.
Xingxiulong.description: Xingxiulong is a genus of bipedal massopodan sauropodomorph from the Early Jurassic of China. It contains two species; the type species is X. chengi, described by Wang et al. in 2017 from three specimens, two adults and an immature individual, that collectively constitute a mostly complete skeleton. Adults of this species measured 4-5 meters (13-16 ft) long and 1-1.5 meters (3.3-4.9 ft) tall. A second species, X. yueorum, was described by Chen et al. in 2025 based on a partial articulated postcranial skeleton of an adult individual larger than X. chengi.

dispute.summary: Xingxiulong chengi was described as a basal sauropodiform, sister to Jingshanosaurus (Wang and others, 2017), but a basal massopodan position is only slightly less parsimonious and is recovered by some analyses (Wang and others, 2025).

history.note: Placed at Sauropodiformes incertae sedis following its describers; the basal-Massopoda alternative is recorded.

Xinjiangtitan.etymology: From Xinjiang, the autonomous region of northwestern China where it was found, and titan ('giant'), meaning 'Xinjiang titan'
Xinjiangtitan.description: Xinjiangtitan is an extinct genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod that lived during the Middle Jurassic of what is now Xinjiang, northwestern China. Its type and only species is Xinjiangtitan shanshanesis (Chinese: 鄯善新疆巨龙; pinyin: Shànshàn Xīnjiāngjùlóng), known from a single incomplete skeleton recovered from the Qiketai Formation. The holotype preserves one of the most complete vertebral columns of any sauropod found in Asia, and has the longest complete neck known for any animal.

First and second sacral ribs simultaneously connected to second sacral rib, with first sacral rib not participating in sacrocostal yoke
Pubis very flat with well-developed ambiens process extending distally
Fourth trochanter located on posteromedial edge of femur

Xiongguanlong.description: Xiongguanlong is an extinct genus of tyrannosauroid theropod from the Early Cretaceous period of what is now China. The type and only species is X. baimoensis. The generic name comes from Jiayuguan City (formerly called "Xiong Guan" or "grand pass") and the Mandarin word "long" which means dragon. The specific epithet, "baimoensis" is a latinization of the Mandarin word for "white ghost" in reference to one of the geological features of the type locality (nicknamed the "White Ghost Castle").

Mediolaterally constricted anterior dorsal centra

Xixiasaurus.etymology: Named for Xixia County, Henan Province, China, where the holotype was discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', translatable as 'Henan Xixia lizard'.
Xixiasaurus.description: Xixiasaurus is a genus of troodontid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period in what is now China. The only known specimen was discovered in Xixia County, Henan Province, in central China, and became the holotype of the new genus and species Xixiasaurus henanensis in 2010. The names refer to the areas of discovery, and can be translated as "Henan Xixia lizard". The specimen consists of an almost complete skull (except for the hindmost portion), part of the lower jaw, and teeth, as well as a partial right forelimb.
diagnostic_features: Fewer maxillary teeth (22) than Byronosaurus (>30) and Mei (24)
Distinct opening on the lateral surface of the base of the nasal process of the premaxilla
Rostral end of the upper jaw forming a tapered U-shape in ventral view
Mandibular symphyseal region slightly inflected medially
Unserrated teeth on anterior and posterior carinae, unlike most other troodontids

dispute.summary: Xuanhanosaurus qilixiaensis is weakly constrained — its holotype is a fragmentary postcranium with much missing data. Benson (2010) recovered it as a basal megalosauroid, in the clade that became Piatnitzkysauridae, whereas Carrano et al. (2012) recovered it within Metriacanthosauridae among the allosauroids, a result followed by Zou et al. (2025) and Jones (2026). Because Piatnitzkysauridae (Megalosauroidea) and Metriacanthosauridae (Allosauroidea) lie in different major tetanuran lineages, Tetanurae is the least-inclusive clade both hypotheses accept.

history.note: Placed at Piatnitzkysauridae following the prevailing analyses; the metriacanthosaurid (allosauroid) alternative remains unresolved.

Broadened to Tetanurae incertae sedis. The basal-megalosauroid (Piatnitzkysauridae; Benson 2010) and metriacanthosaurid (Allosauroidea; Carrano et al. 2012) hypotheses straddle Megalosauroidea and Allosauroidea, so the conservative shared node is adopted.

Xuanhanosaurus.etymology: Named for Xuanhan County in Sichuan, China, where the fossils were recovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Xuanhanosaurus.description: Xuanhanosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) of the Sichuan Basin, China, around 166 million years ago. This taxon represents one of the various non-coelurosaurian tetanuran taxa found on the Middle Jurassic of the region, uncovered in the Lower Shaximiao Formation. Although it has been known for more than 40 years, this taxon has been the subject of very few studies, although most seem to agree that it is a tetanuran, possibly a basal allosauroid, highlighting the fact that it has a vestigial fourth metacarpal.

Forelimbs possess ambulatory function, contrasting with later-stage tyrannosaurids

Cervical vertebrae with posterior concavity and undeveloped anterior projection

dispute.summary: Xunmenglong was described as a small compsognathid in a polytomy with Compsognathus, Huaxiagnathus, and Juravenator, a placement Jones et al. (2026) follow. Cau (2024) instead recovered it among the earliest-diverging branches of Tetanurae, outside Coelurosauria. It is retained in Compsognathidae; the basal-tetanuran hypothesis is reflected in the Compsognathidae clade dispute.

history.note: Retained at Compsognathidae; basal-Tetanurae hypothesis (Cau, 2024) reflected at the clade level.

Xunmenglong.etymology: From Chinese xun ('swift'), meng ('fierce'), and long ('dragon'), meaning 'swift fierce dragon'
Xunmenglong.description: Xunmenglong is a genus of compsognathid theropod dinosaur from the Huajiying Formation of Hebei Province, China. The type and only species is Xunmenglong yinliangis. The holotype material consists of a pelvis, tail base and hindlimbs that had previously been part of a chimera containing three different animals. The animal is described as being the smallest known member of Compsognathidae, being about the size of the sub-adult Scipionyx holotype specimen, or approximately 50 centimeters (1.6 ft) in length.

The type and only species is Yamanasaurus lojaensis, representing the first non-avian dinosaur described from Ecuador. The holotype, consisting of fragments of a humerus, ulna, tibia, two sacral vertebrae and a single caudal, was discovered in 2017.

Yanbeilong.description: Yanbeilong is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous (Albian age) Zuoyun Formation of Shanxi, China. The genus contains a single species, Yanbeilong ultimus, known from a single partial skeleton including several vertebrae and the pelvic girdle.
