Yangchuanosaurus.etymology: Named for Yongchuan (historically romanized as Yangchuan), the district in Sichuan Province, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Yangchuanosaurus.description: Yangchuanosaurus is an extinct genus of metriacanthosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in China from the Middle Jurassic to Late Jurassic periods (Bathonian to Tithonian stages), and was similar (although slightly larger) in size and appearance to its North American and European relative, Allosaurus. Yangchuanosaurus hails from the Upper Shaximiao Formation and was the largest predator in a landscape that included the sauropods Mamenchisaurus and Omeisaurus and the stegosaurs Chialingosaurus, Tuojiangosaurus and Chungkingosaurus. This theropod was named after the area in which was discovered, Yongchuan, in China.

Yantaloong.etymology: From Chinese 'Yanta' (wild goose tower, a noted historical site in the Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture where the holotype was collected) and Mandarin 'loong' (dragon).
Yantaloong.description: Yantaloong is an extinct genus of basal eusauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic middle Zhanghe Formation at Zhongbanjing Village, Yuanmou County, Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province, China. The single species, Yantaloong lini, is known from six nearly complete presacral vertebrae of an adult individual. Phylogenetic analyses by Zhang et al. (2026) recover Yantaloong as an early-branching member of an expanded Turiasauria, in a clade with Lapparentosaurus, Atlasaurus, and Jobaria, sister to the 'traditional' Iberian / North American turiasaurians. The authors claim Yantaloong is the first turiasaurian sauropod known from East Asia and argue its presence undermines the hypothesized East Asian sauropodomorph isolation. The expanded Turiasauria definition is single-paper-recent; the conservative parent Eusauropoda is used here pending broader adoption.
diagnostic_features: Posterior-most cervical vertebra bears a bifurcated posterior centrodiapophyseal lamina (bif.PCDL) and a bifurcated centropostzygapophyseal lamina (bif.CPOL).
Anterior-most dorsal vertebra has both an upper and a lower anterior centroparapophyseal lamina (u.ACPL and l.ACPL), with a small fossa at the anteroventral corner of the parapophysis.

Middle dorsal vertebrae bear a lamina-like anteromedial centropostzygapophyseal lamina (am.CPOL) and a prezygoparapophyseal lamina (PRPL) bifurcated both dorsally and ventrally with a ventral PRPL fossa.
Middle dorsal vertebrae possess a rhombus-shaped hyposphene supported by a vertical ventral infrahyposphenal lamina and paired ventrolateral infrahyposphenal laminae.
Posterior dorsal neural arches bear a dorsoventrally elongated oval-shaped hyposphene.

Yehuecauhceratops.etymology: From Nahuatl yehuecauh meaning 'ancient' combined with Greek keras meaning 'horn' and ops meaning 'face'; translates as 'ancient horned face'
Yehuecauhceratops.description: Yehuecauhceratops is a genus of horned centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Coahuila, Mexico. It contains a single species, Y. mudei, described from two partial specimens by Rivera-Sylva et al. in 2016 and formally named by Rivera-Sylva et al. in 2017. It was a small centrosaurine with a body length of 3 meters (9.8 ft), making it smaller than Agujaceratops and Coahuilaceratops, the other two ceratopsids in its environment; the three may have been ecologically segregated. A ridge bearing a single roughened projection near the bottom of the squamosal bone, which probably supported a small horn, allows Yehuecauhceratops to be distinguished from other centrosaurines. Its affinities to nasutoceratopsin centrosaurines, such as Avaceratops and Nasutoceratops, are supported by various morphological similarities to the former.

The genus contains a single species, Yeneen houssayi, known from at least one partial skeleton. Its discovery highlights the diversity of titanosaurs in this formation, which also includes Bonitasaura, Inawentu, Overosaurus, Rinconsaurus, and Traukutitan.

Yimenosaurus.etymology: Named after Yimen County (also written as Yiman) in Yunnan Province, China where it was found, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Yiman reptile'
Yimenosaurus.description: Yimenosaurus is an extinct genus of plateosaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived in China in the Early Jurassic. The genus was first named in 1990 by Ziqi Bai, Jie Yang and Guohui Wang, along with its type and only species, Yimenosaurus youngi. The species name honors renowned Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian, the father of Chinese paleontology, known as C.C. Young in English. Known material includes the holotype, an almost complete skull and mandible, as well as incomplete cervical and dorsal vertebrae, a mostly complete sacrum, an ilium, ischia, partial ribs and complete femur, and a paratype, a well-preserved postcrania with a fragmentary skull. In 2010 Paul estimated its length at 9 meters (30 ft) and its weight at 2 tonnes (2.2 short tons).

dispute.summary: Yimenosaurus youngi was assigned to Plateosauridae by Bai et al. (1990) in its original description, and has not since been scored in a numerical phylogenetic analysis, so the placement remains provisional.

history.note: Reparented from the deprecated Prosauropoda to Plateosauridae following the historical assignment; not tested in a modern analysis.

Yingshanosaurus.etymology: Named after Yingshan (a locality in Sichuan Province, China), combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Yingshan lizard'
Yingshanosaurus.description: Yingshanosaurus is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaurs from the Middle Jurassic of what is now Southwestern China. It is known from a partial skeleton discovered in 1983, including back, sacrum, and tail vertebrae, forelimb and hindlimb bones, shoulder and hip bones, and several osteoderms, including plates and a shoulder spine. The genus contains a single species, Yingshanosaurus jichuanensis, named and described in 1994. For some time after its discovery and scientific description, many paleontologists were unaware of the Chinese research published on it and questioned its validity.

Yizhousaurus.etymology: Named for the Yizhou region (Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Region) of Yunnan, China, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Yizhousaurus.description: Yizhousaurus is a genus of basal sauropodiform dinosaurs which existed in what is now Lufeng Formation, Yunnan Province of southern China during the lower Jurassic period. Identified from a nearly complete and exquisitely preserved skeleton, it is the most complete basal sauropod currently known with intact skull. Although its name was revealed in a 2010 Geological Society of America abstract by Sankar Chatterjee, T. Wang, S.G. Pan, Z. Dong, X.C. Wu, and Paul Upchurch, it wasn't validly named and described until 2018. The type species is Yizhousaurus sunae.

dispute.summary: Yizhousaurus sunae is a sauropodiform with a convergently sauropod-like skull. Zhang et al. (2018), describing the genus, recovered it within Sauropodiformes as a non-sauropodan sauropodomorph close to Anchisaurus and Mussaurus, nearer the base of Sauropoda than other Lufeng sauropodomorphs but not within Sauropoda itself.

history.note: Placed at Sauropodiformes incertae sedis following Jones (2026); the basal-Sauropoda alternative is recorded.

Yuanmouraptor.etymology: From 'Yuanmou' (Yuanmou County, Yunnan Province, China, the type locality) and Latin 'raptor' (robber).
Yuanmouraptor.description: Yuanmouraptor is an extinct genus of basal metriacanthosaurid theropod from the early Middle Jurassic (Aalenian-Bajocian) Zhanghe Formation at Xiabanjing Village, Yuanmou County, Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province, China. The single species, Yuanmouraptor jinshajiangensis, is known from a near-complete skull with mandible (reconstructed length ~60 cm) articulated with 10 cervical vertebrae and the first dorsal (LFGT-ZLJ0115). Zou et al. (2025) recover Yuanmouraptor as the most basal-branching member of Metriacanthosauridae in their equal-weights phylogenetic analysis.

Yuanmousaurus.description: Yuanmousaurus was a sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic period of China. It is known from incomplete remains, recovered in 2000 from the Zhanghe Formation in Yuanmou County in Yunnan Province. Yuanmousaurus was a relatively large sauropod and may have reached about 17 meters (56 ft) in length. It was a basal member of the Sauropoda, but its exact systematic position is unclear. A recent study placed Yuanmousaurus within the family Mamenchisauridae. It may be a dubious genus. The only and type species was Yuanmousaurus jiangyiensis.

Yueosaurus.description: Yueosaurus is an extinct genus of basal neornithischian dinosaur known from Zhejiang Province, China.

dispute.summary: Yueosaurus tiantaiensis, formerly treated as a basal ornithopod, is agreed to be a basal neornithischian and not an iguanodontian. Several analyses recover it as a jeholosaurid alongside Jeholosaurus (Boyd 2015; Madzia and others 2017; Manitkoon and others 2023), but Fonseca and others (2024) place Jeholosaurus within Thescelosaurinae and do not recognize Jeholosauridae, leaving its finer position unresolved.

history.note: Reparented from Iguanodontia to Neornithischia incertae sedis following Boyd (2015) and the basal-neornithischian consensus; not an iguanodontian.

Re-evaluated; retained at Neornithischia incertae sedis. A jeholosaurid placement (Boyd 2015; Madzia and others 2017; Manitkoon and others 2023) is not adopted because Fonseca and others (2024), the most recent comprehensive analysis, recovers Jeholosaurus and Changchunsaurus within Thescelosaurinae and does not recognize Jeholosauridae; Neornithischia is the least-inclusive clade all hypotheses accept.

Yunmenglong.description: Yunmenglong is an extinct genus of somphospondylan sauropod known from the late Early Cretaceous of Henan Province, central China. Its remains were discovered in the Haoling Formation of the Ruyang Basin. Yunmenglong shares some characters with Euhelopus, Qiaowanlong, and Erketu; a phylogenetic analysis places it as a sister taxon of Qiaowanlong, both grouped with Erketu in a position more derived than Euhelopus but basal to Titanosauria.

Yunnanosaurus.etymology: Named for Yunnan Province, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Yunnanosaurus.description: Yunnanosaurus is an extinct genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived approximately 199 to 183 million years ago in what is now the Yunnan Province, in China, for which it was named. Yunnanosaurus was a large sized, moderately-built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore, that could also walk bipedally, and ranged in size from 7 meters (23 feet) long and 2 m (6.5 ft) high to 4 m (13 ft) high in the largest species.

dispute.summary: Yunnanosaurus huangi is most commonly recovered among non-sauropodan sauropodiforms: Sekiya et al. Rauhut et al. (2020) instead recovered it within Massospondylidae, in a subclade with Jingshanosaurus and Seitaad.

history.note: Placed at Sauropodiformes incertae sedis following the prevailing view and Jones (2026); the Massospondylidae alternative is recorded.

Zalmoxes.etymology: Named after Zalmoxis (also spelled Zamolxis), a deity or legendary king worshipped by the Getae people of ancient Thrace and Dacia (modern Romania), where the fossil was found.
Zalmoxes.description: Zalmoxes is a genus of probable rhabdodontid ornithopod dinosaur from the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Romania. The genus is known from specimens first named as the species Mochlodon robustum in 1899 by Franz Nopcsa before being reclassified as Rhabdodon robustum by him in 1915. In 1990, this name was corrected to Rhabdodon robustus by George Olshevsky and, in 2003, the species was once more reclassified as the type species Zalmoxes robustus. Zalmoxes represents one of the most common vertebrates of Transylvania during the latest Cretaceous period. The generic name refers to the Dacian deity Zalmoxis and the specific name robustus refers to the robustness of the remains. Another species, Zalmoxes shqiperorum, was named in 2003, but this species has since been reassigned to a separate genus of ceratopsian, Ferenceratops.

Zavacephale.description: Zavacephale is an extinct genus of pachycephalosaurian dinosaurs known from the Early Cretaceous Khuren Dukh Formation of Mongolia. The genus contains a single species, Zavacephale rinpoche, known from a partial articulated skeleton including a nearly complete skull. It is both the oldest definitive pachycephalosaur known, as well as the most complete. Its skull bears a well-developed dome structure, as seen in most members of the clade.

Medial shelf of ilium extends the length of the postacetabular process (autapomorphy)

Zhejiangosaurus.description: Zhejiangosaurus is an extinct genus of ankylosaurian dinosaur from the Upper Cretaceous (Cenomanian stage) of Zhejiang, eastern China. It was first named by a group of Chinese authors Lü Junchang, Jin Xingsheng, Sheng Yiming and Li Yihong in 2007 and the type species is Zhejiangosaurus lishuiensis ("from Lishui", where the fossil was found). It has no diagnostic features, and thus is a nomen dubium.

Zhenyuanlong.etymology: Named after Sun Zhenyuan, who discovered the specimen, combined with Chinese Pinyin lóng (龙/龍) meaning 'dragon'; thus 'Zhenyuan's dragon'
Zhenyuanlong.description: Zhenyuanlong is a genus of dromaeosaurid dinosaur from the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China. It lived during the Aptian age of the early Cretaceous period, approximately 125 million years ago. It is known from a single specimen belonging to the species Zhenyuanlong suni (Chinese: 孫氏振元龍). This type specimen preserved a nearly complete skeleton that contains traces of feathers, including long tail feathers and large wings. In addition to further complicating diversity of Liaoning dromaeosaurids, this specimen provides the first direct evidence of well-developed pennaceous feathers in a large, non-flying dromaeosaur, raising the question of what function such wings would serve.

Zhongyuansaurus.description: Zhongyuansaurus is an extinct genus of ankylosaurid dinosaurs known from the Early Cretaceous Haoling Formation of what is now Henan Province, China. The genus contains two species, Z. luoyangensis, named in 2007, and Z. junchangi, named in 2025, both known from a single partial skeleton. Zhongyuansaurus is similar to Gobisaurus, prompting some researchers to regard the genera as synonymous.

Zhuchengceratops.etymology: Named for Zhucheng, the city in Shandong Province, China where the fossil was found, combined with Latinized Greek 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face'.
Zhuchengceratops.description: Zhuchengceratops is a genus of extinct leptoceratopsid ceratopsian that lived during the Upper Cretaceous of modern-day China. It was first described in 2010, by Xu et al., who created the binomial Zhuchengceratops inexpectus. The name is derived from the location of Zhucheng, the Latinized-Greek ceratops, or "horned face", and the unexpected articulated nature of the holotype. The skeleton was found in the Wangshi Group, which is of Late Cretaceous age, and most fossils are only disarticulated bones of Shantungosaurus.

Zhuchengtitan.etymology: Named after Zhucheng, Shandong Province, China where it was found, combined with Greek titan meaning 'giant'; translates as 'Zhucheng titan'
Zhuchengtitan.description: Zhuchengtitan is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Shandong, China. It contains a single species, Z. zangjiazhuangensis, named by Mo Jinyou and colleagues in 2017 from a single humerus. Zhuchengtitan can be identified by the extreme width of the top end of its humerus, as well as the expansion of the deltopectoral crest on its humerus; both of these characteristics indicate that it was likely closely related to Opisthocoelicaudia. However, it differs from the latter by the flatter bottom articulating surface of its humerus. Zhuchengtitan lived in a floodplain environment alongside Shantungosaurus, Zhuchengtyrannus, and Sinoceratops.

Ziapelta.etymology: Named after the Zia sun symbol, the stylized sun emblem of the Zia Pueblo people of New Mexico, where the fossil was found, combined with Greek 'pelta' meaning 'small shield', referring to its ankylosaur armor.
Ziapelta.description: Ziapelta is an extinct genus of ankylosaurid. Its fossils have been found in the Hunter Wash and De-na-zin members of the Kirtland Formation of Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) New Mexico. It was named in 2014, in a research paper led by ankylosaur researcher Victoria Arbour. There is a single species in the genus, Ziapelta sanjuanensis. The genus is named after the Zia sun symbol, a stylized sun with four groups of rays, having religious significance to the Zia people of New Mexico, and the iconic symbol on the state flag of New Mexico, and pelta (Latin), a small shield, in reference to the osteoderms found on all ankylosaurids. The specific name is in reference to San Juan County and the San Juan basin, where the fossils were found. Multiple specimens have been described to date, though the fossils are mostly from the front part of the animal. Its closest relative appears to be either Scolosaurus or Nodocephalosaurus, depending on what cladistic model is used.

Zigongosaurus.etymology: Named for Zigong City in Sichuan, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Zigongosaurus.description: Zigongosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Middle-Late Jurassic-aged Shaximiao Formation of Zigong, Sichuan, China. Because of incomplete knowledge of Jurassic Chinese sauropods, it has been hard to interpret, with some sources assigning it to Omeisaurus, some to Mamenchisaurus, and some to its own genus.
diagnostic_features: Anterior edge of the maxilla above the tooth row bears a forward-and-downward projecting process contacting the premaxillary suture; maxillary foramen not prominent
Maxilla bearing 12-14 teeth and mandible 15-17 teeth
Prefrontal forming the main component of the dorsal orbital border; posterior part of the temporal bone exceptionally thick (up to 18 mm); upper temporal fenestra oval and narrow anteroposteriorly

Premaxillary teeth largest, with long pointed crowns bearing small apical tubercles but no serrations; cheek-tooth crowns convex externally and concave internally with a prominent internal median ridge
Anterior end of the dentary symphysis projecting downward with a rough external surface; lower margin of the dentary bearing a longitudinal groove extending to the symphysis

species.name: Zigongosaurus fuxiensis
species.etymology: Named for Fuxi, a locality in Sichuan Province, China, near the fossil site.

Zizhongosaurus.etymology: Named after Zizhong County in Sichuan Province, China where it was found, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Zizhong lizard'
Zizhongosaurus.description: Zizhongosaurus is a genus of basal herbivorous sauropod dinosaur which lived in the Early Jurassic (Toarcian) Period of China. It was a large-bodied herbivore characterized by a long neck.
diagnostic_features: Small primitive sauropod with relatively long anterior limbs
Humerus with straight and rounded shaft
Dorsal vertebrae with high neural spine with apex as expanded plate descending slightly anteriorly and concave posteriorly
Lateral spine surface ornamented with dorsally radiating vertical striations
Well-developed diapophyses forming right angle with neural spine at neural arch
Hyposphene present

Zuniceratops.etymology: From Zuni, referring to the Zuni people of New Mexico near where the specimen was found, and Greek keratops meaning 'horned face'; thus 'Zuni horned face'
Zuniceratops.description: Zuniceratops is a genus of ceratopsian dinosaurs that lived during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now New Mexico, United States. Only a single species is known, Zuniceratops christopheri.
diagnostic_features: Well-defined elongate post-orbital brow horns with flattened lateral margins
Vertical-shear wear pattern on dentary teeth
Single-rooted replacement teeth with one per file, lacking double-rooted dental batteries
Elongate frill with squamosal forming lateral and part of distal margin of parietal fenestra
Decurved ischium more curved than Centrosaurus but less than Triceratops
Gracile appendicular skeleton resembling protoceratopsids
Caudal extension of tooth row on maxilla beyond ascending process

species.name: Zuniceratops christopheri
species.etymology: Named for Christopher James Wolfe, the eight-year-old who discovered the first specimens in 1996.

type_specimen.institution: Arizona Museum of Natural History (formerly Mesa Southwest Museum)
type_specimen.material: Disarticulated but associated cranial and postcranial remains including basioccipital, postorbital horn cores, maxillae, dentary fragments, caudal vertebrae, coracoid, humeri, and other skeletal elements.

species.authors: Wolfe, D. G.; Kirkland, J. I.

notable_specimens.significance: The best-preserved Zuniceratops specimen, a fully adult individual represented by a right postorbital horn and associated elements; documents the mature growth stage of the taxon, in contrast to the juvenile holotype MSM P2101.

dispute.summary: Zuolong is usually recovered as a basal coelurosaur (Choiniere et al., 2010; Sayão et al., 2020, as sister to Aratasaurus), and Jones et al. (2026) follow this, but Cau (2018) placed it further stemward as a basal tetanuran outside Coelurosauria. It is placed at Coelurosauria incertae sedis following the prevailing view.

history.note: Placed at Coelurosauria incertae sedis; basal coelurosaur per most analyses, basal tetanuran per Cau (2018).

Zuolong.etymology: Named in honor of General Zuo Zongtang (also known as General Tso), a 19th-century Chinese military leader, combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'.
Zuolong.description: Zuolong is an extinct genus of tetanuran theropod from the Late Jurassic period of China. The type and only species is Z. salleei. The generic name of Zuolong is in honor of General Zuo Zōngtáng (also known as "General Tso") with the Chinese word "long" which means dragon. The specific epithet "salleei" is in honor of Hilmar Sallee, who funded the expedition which led to the specimen's discovery.
diagnostic_features: Large slit-like quadrate foramen inclined medially at ~45° with associated deep fossa on the quadrate
Sacral centrum 5 with obliquely oriented posterior articular surface angled anterodorsally
Fovea capitis very large, occupying almost entire posterodorsal surface of femoral head
Distal condyle of metatarsal III large with anteromedially projecting flange

species.name: Zuolong salleei
species.etymology: Named for Hilmar Sallee, who funded the expedition that led to the discovery of the holotype specimen.

Zuoyunlong.etymology: Named for Zuoyun County in Shanxi, China, where the fossils were discovered, combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'.
Zuoyunlong.description: Zuoyunlong is an extinct genus of herbivorous ornithopod dinosaur belonging to the Hadrosauroidea that lived during the Late Cretaceous in the area of present China.
diagnostic_features: Very short postacetabular process about 50% as long as iliac central plate (unique autapomorphy)
Relatively long, stick-shaped pubic peduncle of ilium
Ischial peduncle of ilium formed by single large knob
Modest lateral swelling along dorsal edge of ilium, approximately 90% length of central plate
Apex of lateral swelling located dorsal and slightly caudal to caudal end of ischial peduncle
Elongate, subtriangular distal boot of ischium that is ventrally directed with pointed extremity

species.name: Zuoyunlong huangi
species.etymology: Named for Chinese paleontologist Huang Weilong.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete right ilium and distal end of right ischium. Ilium 62cm long, missing most preacetabular process. Ischium distal boot elongate, subtriangular, ventrally directed.

dispute.summary: Zupaysaurus rougieri has been recovered as a coelophysid or a close relative of Liliensternus and Dilophosaurus, and as the earliest- branching member of the stem lineage to Averostra; recent analyses place it outside Coelophysoidea (Ezcurra, 2017; Ezcurra and others, 2020).

history.note: Placed at Neotheropoda, the least-inclusive uncontested clade.

Zupaysaurus.etymology: From Quechua supay meaning 'devil' and Greek sauros (σαυρος) meaning 'lizard'; thus 'devil lizard'
Zupaysaurus.description: Zupaysaurus is an extinct genus of early theropod dinosaur living during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. Fossils of the dinosaur were found in the Los Colorados Formation of the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión Basin in northwestern Argentina. Although a full skeleton has not yet been discovered, Zupaysaurus can be considered a bipedal predator, up to 4 meters (13 ft) long. It may have had two parallel crests running the length of its snout.
diagnostic_features: Oval, anteroventrally oriented antorbital fenestra
Two parasagittal crests on snout formed by nasals
Maxilla with parallel dorsal and ventral borders (unlike most other theropods)
Tibial-astragalar articulation locked medioposteriorly by astragalar process in posteriorly open tibial notch
Transversely expanded distal end of tibia with wide postfibular wing
Tooth row ending anterior to orbit (tetanuran trait)

species.name: Zupaysaurus rougieri

Zuul.etymology: Named after Zuul, the fictional monster from the 1984 film Ghostbusters, due to the resemblance of its skull to the creature's face
Zuul.description: Zuul is a genus of herbivorous ankylosaurine dinosaur from the Campanian Judith River Formation of Montana. The type species is Zuul crurivastator. It is known from a complete skull and tail, which represents the first ankylosaurin known from a complete skull and tail club, as well as the most complete ankylosaurid specimen thus far recovered from North America. The specimen also preserved in situ osteoderms, keratin, and skin remains.
diagnostic_features: Frontonasal and frontoparietal caputegulae imbricated with distinct posteriorly located peaked apices.
Prefrontal, frontoparietal, and middle supraorbital caputegulae strongly pyramidal with small bases and tall peaks.
Squamosal horns with prominent longitudinal furrows on the lateral surface converging toward the apex.
Lateral caudal osteoderms along the tail club handle with strongly concave leading edges and posteriorly offset apices.
Tail club knob dorsoventrally flat with height-to-length ratio less than 0.20.

species.name: Zuul crurivastator
species.etymology: From Latin 'crus' meaning 'shank' and 'vastator' meaning 'destroyer', reading as 'Destroyer of Shins' in reference to the presumed defensive tactic of smashing the lower legs of predatory theropods with its tail club.

type_specimen.material: Nearly complete cranium, both lower jaws, disarticulated cervical vertebrae, articulated dorsal and sacral vertebrae, dorsal ribs, pelvic elements, complete articulated tail with tail club, in situ osteoderms, ossicles, and skin impressions.

species.authors: Arbour, V. M.; Evans, D. C.
